papers.title: Attraction from repulsion in an interacting Chern band: chiral superconductivity, generalized Hall crystals, and competing fractional Chern insulators
papers.abstract: Experiments realizing strong interactions in partially filled Chern bands have observed fractional Chern insulators (FCIs), superconductors, and topological crystals in close proximity. Yet the microscopic relation between them remains poorly understood. Here, we use tensor network simulations to study repulsively interacting spinless fermions in a tunable topological band of the checkerboard lattice. We characterize the competing phases and identify key features of the experimental phenomenology. FCIs from the Jain sequence transition into chiral p-wave superconductivity both below and above half filling as the band dispersion is enhanced. By contrast, at half filling, a generalized Hall crystal with quantized Hall conductance and a doubled unit cell forms for sufficiently strong coupling. Surprisingly, a weak-coupling approach starting from a metallic parent state captures the nature of both ordered phases at intermediate coupling. We find that fluctuations in the metal generate longer-range attraction, which we analyze within the random-phase approximation. This approach captures the pairing symmetry as well as the radial form factors of the Cooper pairs, and incorporating this attraction into Hartree-Fock selects the observed Hall crystal. Together, these results identify fluctuation-induced attraction from repulsion as a common microscopic ingredient of ordering, while our tensor network computations establish the direct competition of both phases with FCIs.

papers.intro:
Recent experiments in moiré materials have observed superconductivity of correlated electrons in topological bands, often near repulsively stabilized states such as fractional Chern insulators (FCIs) or electronic crystals [15, 68, 22], suggesting a favorable setting for pairing from repulsion. In this context, it has been proposed that chiral superconductivity could emerge as a weak-coupling Kohn-Luttinger instability of a metal [23, 34], further enhanced by quantum geometric effects [49, 50, 21, 36, 33, 67, 6, 75]. Alternatively, strong-coupling ‘anyonic’ descriptions of chiral superconductors [26, 25, 9, 27, 5] connected to nearby fractionalized phases have been put forward [28, 35, 54, 7, 57, 42, 53, 71, 41, 55, 24, 3, 40, 1, 12, 16, 20, 38, 2, 48, 60, 63, 61, 69, 73, 74, 31, 70, 8, 56, 64, 47, 17, 37, 19]. While strong-coupling approaches often struggle to identify which phases are energetically favored by a given microscopic Hamiltonian, weak-coupling approaches are uncontrolled in the strongly correlated limit relevant to experiments. Identifying how repulsive interactions produce superconductivity and, within the same microscopic framework, how the superconducting state competes with nearby quantum Hall and crystalline phases remains an open problem.

III, we analyze the metallic regime within the random phase approximation and show that higher-order many-body processes generate longer-range attractive components of the effective interaction that favor chiral pp-wave pairing. Section IV presents our tensor-network results across a broad range of fillings and characterizes the resulting superconducting phase through its correlation lengths and Cooper-pair wave function. papers.title: Bulk-Defect Correspondence in Algebraic Classical Spin Liquids
papers.abstract: Local constraints in algebraic classical spin liquids give rise to singular momentum-space correlations. This so called pinch-point singularity carries a momentum-space winding number that determines the low-energy structure of the algebraic spin liquid. We show that nonmagnetic vacancies in two dimensions reveal this topological invariant in the real-space winding of the surrounding spin textures. Under explicit conditions, we prove this bulk-defect correspondence for rank-$n$ $\mathrm{U}(1)$ spin liquids and verify it numerically for the Coulomb spin liquids of the kagome and checkerboard lattices and the rank-2 $\mathrm{U}(1)$ spin liquid of the honeycomb-snowflake model. In this way we show that vacancies can be used as general probes for distinguishing the emergent gauge theories of strongly correlated classical disordered magnets.

papers.title: Gaussian Identification in MIMO Channels
papers.abstract: We study the identification capacity of discrete-time Gaussian multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) channels under per-antenna, per-symbol peak-amplitude constraints. We establish upper and lower bounds on the identification capacity that scale linearly with the channel rank $r.$ The number of reliably identifiable messages can grow super-exponentially with blocklength $n,$ following $M_n(R)=2^{(n\log n)R},$ where $R$ is an achievable rate. The channel rank provides a spatial-multiplexing advantage, enabling higher achievable rates and, consequently, stronger super-exponential codebook growth. These results characterize the rank-dependent gain in achievable identification performance.

papers.intro:
The fundamental limits of communication depend not only on the statistical properties of the underlying channel but also on the objective imposed on the communication system. While classical channel coding concerns the reliable reconstruction of transmitted messages [1, 2], identification coding addresses the different task of determining whether a particular message was transmitted [3, 4, 5]. This distinction leads to markedly different codebook-growth laws. In particular, with randomized encoders (RI) [3], the number of reliably identifiable messages can grow doubly exponentially with the blocklength nn, according to Mn​(R)=22n​RM_{n}(R)=2^{2^{nR}}. Deterministic identification (DI) [6, 7] exhibits a fundamentally different codebook-growth regime from its randomized counterpart. In particular, continuous-alphabet channels [7, 8] follow super-exponential growth. Specifically, for a broad class of channel models, including Gaussian channels with fading [7, 9, 10], Poisson channels with and without memory and their affine extensions [11, 12, 13], the number of identifiable messages scales as Mn​(R)=2(n​log⁡n)​RM_{n}(R)=2^{(n\log n)R}. These results demonstrate that the fundamental limits of identification, particularly the growth of the codebook with blocklength, depend on the underlying channel model and the associated channel characteristics. This observation motivates the study of identification over multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) channels and raises the question of how their spatial structure, channel gains, and fading characteristics influence the fundamental limits of identification and the design of identification codes. This remarkable scaling has motivated renewed interest in identification within post-Shannon theory, goal-oriented communication paradigms and semantic communication frameworks [14, 15], as well as in the development of explicit identification code constructions [16, 17, 18, 9, 19].

The development of MIMO communication was driven by the growing demand for data under limited spectrum and transmit-power resources. Unlike conventional approaches such as increasing bandwidth, using higher-order modulation, densifying networks, or raising transmit power, MIMO improves capacity by exploiting the spatial dimension of the wireless channel [20, 21]. For an NT×NRN_{T}\times N_{R} MIMO link, the number of independent spatial data streams is limited by the channel rank: r=rank⁡(𝐇)≤min⁡(NT,NR).r=\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{H})\leq\min(N_{T},N_{R}). Thus, a full-rank channel can provide up to min⁡(NT,NR)\min(N_{T},N_{R}) spatial degrees of freedom, although antenna correlation, limited angular spread, line-of-sight propagation, and other channel conditions may reduce this number [20]. MIMO communication employs multiple antennas at the transmitter, receiver, or both to exploit the spatial structure of a wireless propagation channel [22, 23, 24]. Unlike a single-input single-output (SISO) system, which is described by a single complex channel coefficient, a MIMO system is characterized by a channel matrix representing the propagation paths between transmit–receive antenna pairs. This spatial structure enables two complementary techniques. Spatial diversity transmits redundant signal representations across multiple antennas or paths, improving robustness against fading. Spatial multiplexing, in contrast, transmits independent data streams simultaneously over the same time–frequency resource. When the channel matrix has sufficient rank and the receiver has adequate channel-state information and processing capability, these streams can be separated to increase spectral efficiency [25, 20, 26]. Massive MIMO systems consider wireless links equipped with a very large number of transmit and/or receive antennas [27, 28, 29] and therefore provides a natural framework for identification, particularly in rich-scattering scenarios such as i.i.d. Rayleigh fading [30], where the channel matrix is full rank with probability one and the resulting spatial degrees of freedom can dramatically increase the identification codebook size.

The Gaussian MIMO channel constitutes a canonical model for modern wireless communication systems [31, 32]. In particular, the Gaussian model isolates the role of the channel matrix and its spatial degrees of freedom, making channel rank a natural parameter for studying the impact of spatial dimensions on communication. For the classical Shannon transmission problem, consider a point-to-point Gaussian MIMO channel with channel matrix 𝐇\mathbf{H}. At high SNR, its capacity satisfies [20] ℂ=r​log⁡(SNR)+O⁡(1).\mathbb{C}=r\log(\mathrm{SNR})+O(1). Thus, the rank determines the number of independent spatial dimensions and the corresponding spatial multiplexing gain. At the first-order scale, the logarithm of the Shannon codebook size satisfies log⁡Mn=n​ℂ+o⁡(n).\log M_{n}=n\mathbb{C}+o(n). Thereby, using Telatar’s high-SNR characterization, log⁡Mn=n​r​log⁡(SNR)+O⁡(n).\log M_{n}=nr\log(\mathrm{SNR})+O(n). Thus, the channel rank appears directly as the coefficient of the leading-order growth of the logarithm of the achievable codebook size. This raises the question of whether channel rank plays an analogous role in identification. Despite the fundamentally different operational objectives of identification and message transmission, our results show that the achievable identification rates scale also linearly with the channel rank. Thus, although spatial multiplexing has different operational interpretations in the two settings, the channel rank rr plays an analogous structural role: it determines the multiplicative factor in the leading-order growth of the logarithm of the achievable message-set size. Relative to a rank-one channel, this yields an asymptotic rr-fold spatial gain, with the growth scaling as n​log⁡(SNR)n\log(\mathrm{SNR}) for Shannon transmission and n​log⁡nn\log n for Ahlswede identification problem.

papers.title: FuzzInsight: Navigating the Efficiency-Effectiveness Trade-off in Coverage-Guided DNN Fuzzing
papers.abstract: Collecting and labeling diverse test datasets for evaluating Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) is costly and time-consuming. This has motivated coverage-guided fuzzing techniques that generate defect-revealing corner cases from limited test data. However, their effectiveness depends heavily on configuration choices, particularly coverage criteria and seed-selection strategies. We present a configuration-oriented analysis and decision guidelines for scalable DNN fuzzing targeting two bottlenecks: inefficient seed utilization and the cost of coverage guidance. Our analysis shows that existing seed-selection strategies repeatedly prioritize a small subset of inputs, leaving many collected seeds unexplored. To address this issue, we propose Equalized Sampling, a constraint-based strategy that increases mean seed queue utilization to 77%, improving on prior approaches by 13 percentage points. We further evaluate 84 fuzzing configurations on four benchmark datasets: MNIST, SVHN, GTSRB, and CIFAR-100. Results show that the non-structural criteria LSCD, LSC, and MDSC achieve coverage outcomes comparable to structural and alternative non-structural criteria while requiring substantially less computation. These criteria also promote broad behavioral exploration of the DNN under test, reducing the need to monitor multiple coverage metrics. Among them, LSCD provides a modest but consistent runtime advantage. Finally, we show that retraining with generated corner cases improves generalization robustness by up to 77 percentage points on average without degrading performance on the original test distribution. Together, these findings provide a practical blueprint for selecting fuzzing configurations that balance efficiency, behavioral exploration, and model hardening.

papers.intro:
To assess the quality of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), test engineers evaluate their ability to generalize to unseen scenarios using metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, etc., on a test dataset. Trusting the performance of DNNs solely based on these metrics can be misleading, primarily due to concerns about the quality of the test dataset (Li† et al., 2022; Kaminwar et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022; Riccio et al., 2020). A high-quality test dataset should closely capture and reflect real-world in-field properties for the trustworthy assessment of DNNs. However, collecting and labeling test data requires significant time and resources (Li† et al., 2022; Kaminwar et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022; Hu et al., 2024; Riccio et al., 2020).

Like traditional software systems, DNNs can exhibit undesired or erroneous behavior due to hidden, unidentified defects that often manifest in corner cases: rare inputs residing in low-probability regions of the input space. In this work, we focus on corner cases discovered via fuzzing. We start with correctly classified inputs from the test set and apply realistic perturbations from the operational domain (e.g., subtle changes in lighting, rotation, or sensor-related noise). A generated input is considered a corner case if it successfully triggers a misclassification, thereby exposing a region of the input space where the DNN lacks robustness. An important factor influencing test dataset quality is the extent to which it includes corner cases, which are essential for exposing such defects and limitations in DNNs’ ability to generalize. Including such corner case data can enhance test data quality and give test engineers an opportunity to address and improve DNN robustness.

Including such corner case data can enhance test data quality and give test engineers an opportunity to address and improve DNN robustness.

Prior surveys and industrial reports suggest growing interest in automated corner case generation for DNNs using Coverage-Guided Fuzzing (CGF) (Kaminwar et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022; Li† et al., 2022; Riccio et al., 2020). Inspired by traditional software fuzzing, CGF has effectively alleviated the challenges of test data generation and corner-case identification for DNNs (Ma et al., 2018; Odena et al., 2019; Xie et al., 2019; Tian et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2025). However, the data-centric nature of DNNs and the broad spectrum of available coverage criteria make it difficult to determine an efficient and effective fuzzing configuration in practice. Most existing DNN fuzzing frameworks, such as DeepHunter (Xie et al., 2019) or TensorFuzz (Odena et al., 2019), primarily rely on structural coverage criteria. These white-box approaches calculate coverage based on internal neuron activations, requiring full access to the DNN’s architecture. In contrast, emerging non-structural criteria such as Surprise Coverage (SC) (Kim et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2023; Weiss et al., 2021; Yan et al., 2024) and Latent Space Class Dispersion (LSCD) (Vekariya et al., 2025) work in a gray-box manner and do not require complete access to the DNN architecture. Specifically, gray-box criteria rely on high-level representations (e.g., logits or latent vectors) to summarize DNN behavior without monitoring individual neuron activations. This can make them more scalable and easier to apply in practice. Despite their demonstrated effectiveness in evaluating dataset quality under various fault conditions (Humbatova et al., 2020; Vekariya et al., 2025), these non-structural metrics remain largely unexplored for guiding test data generation in fuzzing.

However, the data-centric nature of DNNs and the broad spectrum of available coverage criteria make it difficult to determine an efficient and effective fuzzing configuration in practice. Most existing DNN fuzzing frameworks, such as DeepHunter (Xie et al., 2019) or TensorFuzz (Odena et al., 2019), primarily rely on structural coverage criteria. These white-box approaches calculate coverage based on internal neuron activations, requiring full access to the DNN’s architecture. In contrast, emerging non-structural criteria such as Surprise Coverage (SC) (Kim et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2023; Weiss et al., 2021; Yan et al., 2024) and Latent Space Class Dispersion (LSCD) (Vekariya et al., 2025) work in a gray-box manner and do not require complete access to the DNN architecture. Specifically, gray-box criteria rely on high-level representations (e.g., logits or latent vectors) to summarize DNN behavior without monitoring individual neuron activations. This can make them more scalable and easier to apply in practice. Despite their demonstrated effectiveness in evaluating dataset quality under various fault conditions (Humbatova et al., 2020; Vekariya et al., 2025), these non-structural metrics remain largely unexplored for guiding test data generation in fuzzing.

papers.title: Exploring Cosmic Rays from Gravity-Limited Acceleration at Supermassive Black Holes
papers.abstract: We show that horizon-scale magnetic fields around supermassive black holes (SMBHs), only limited by gravity, yield a universal, model-independent ceiling on electromagnetic energy density. For rotating SMBHs, this field enables particle acceleration up to $\sim\!10^{27}$\,eV set solely by fundamental constants. We identify a parameter space in accretion rate and magnetic field strength in which quiescent nuclei simultaneously satisfy the transparency conditions for Ultra-High-Energy Cosmic Rays (UHECR) escape and the field requirements for reaching Ultra-High Energies (UHE), naturally complementing photon-rich Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN), which favor neutrino production but suppress UHECR escape. We observe that, when including curvature energy losses, the energy of the primaries scales weakly as $E_{\rm curv}\!\propto\!M^{1/4}$ and allows to achieve UHE across different compositions and SMBHs masses ($10^6$--$10^{10}\,M_\odot$), without requiring extreme spins or super-Eddington accretion. A cross-correlation of the Pierre Auger Observatory (PAO) public data with galaxies hosting reliably measured SMBH masses, separating AGN from quiescent hosts, reveals marginal local excesses ($\lesssim\!2.8σ$) consistent with isotropy after correcting for the look-elsewhere effect. The framework provides a direct link between black-hole physics and the maximum energies of cosmic particles, and defines concrete observational tests for next-generation UHECR datasets.

papers.title: Generative Policy Improvement from Observational Data
papers.abstract: We study how to improve decision policies from observational data to generate better actions when actions are complex, structured objects, such as text messages or images. This task is subject to two major challenges: (i) action-level overlap is often too weak for reliable off-policy evaluation and improvement, and (ii) generating new structured actions often requires expensive training or fine-tuning (e.g., of an LLM) and can be ill-defined due to information loss in action representations. To address both, we propose PolicyLift, a three-stage framework for generative policy improvement with structured actions from observational data. In Stage 1, PolicyLift learns a small set of discrete action codes that capture high-level strategies in the observed action space and are tailored to support policy improvement under limited overlap. In Stage 2, it learns a context-dependent policy over these action codes. At deployment time, Stage 3 "lifts" the learned code-level policy back to the original action space by generating actions from the historical behavior system in a code-conditioned way. We show theoretically that improving the policy over action codes guarantees improvement of the induced policy in the original action space. We demonstrate PolicyLift across experiments in synthetic and real-world text generation tasks with consistent policy improvements over the behavior policy.

papers.intro:
Learning decision policies from observational data, i.e., off-policy learning (OPL), asks how to improve a behavior policy using logged interactions rather than new online experiments (Athey and Wager, 2021; Dudík et al., 2014; Kallus et al., 2022; Swaminathan and Joachims, 2015). Existing work studies off-policy evaluation (OPE) and OPL primarily under relatively simple action spaces, such as binary, categorical, or low-dimensional interventions, where actions correspond to choices like whether to treat a patient, which product to recommend, or which price to offer (Kitagawa and Tetenov, 2018; Athey and Wager, 2021; Kallus et al., 2022). In many modern systems, actions are complex and high-dimensional; for example, an online platform can generate a personalized headline or advertisement (Matias et al., 2021; Meguellati et al., 2024) or a mental health support system may suggest an empathic reply in an online peer-support conversation (Sharma et al., 2023).

1 Limited overlap. OPE and OPL require overlap (Dudík et al., 2014; Kallus et al., 2022), which means that the behavior policy covers the actions a new target policy would select. For complex actions, this is often implausible: the behavior system concentrates on a vanishingly small subset of the action space for each context. Even when the behavior system is stochastic, the randomness is often local and thus does not induce meaningful coverage across qualitatively different actions. Existing approaches to limited overlap either constrain the policy class (Kallus, 2021; Schweisthal et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024) or optimize conservative objectives (Jin et al., 2025), but these operate in the original action space and cannot resolve the fundamental coverage gap in high-dimensional structured spaces.2 Information loss. It is unclear a priori how to learn action representations that both make overlap plausible and still allow mapping coarse latent actions back to raw actions. A representation-level decision (e.g., a text style) is not yet a deployable action: deployment still requires a specific response in the original action space (e.g., natural language). Prior work learns improved policies in a subspace of the actions (Saito and Joachims, 2022; Peng et al., 2023), but if the representation does not fully mediate the effect of the action on the outcome (Saito et al., 2023), instantiating raw actions (e.g., via a decoder) can induce a systematic mismatch between the value optimized in representation space and the value delivered in the original action space. Finally, it lifts the learned code-level policy back to the original action space by using the behavior system itself as a generator. We call this behavior-consistent lifting (BCL) and show that, when the behavior system is sampled until an action with the target code is found, BCL eliminates the deployment gap, so improvements in true code-level value transfer exactly to the deployed policy over structured actions.

papers.title: Results from the GIF++ Long-Term Study of Eco-Friendly Gas Mixtures for RPCs
papers.abstract: Gaseous detectors play a crucial role in high-energy physics experiments, yet their operation often relies on fluorinated gases with a very high Global Warming Potential (GWP). Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs) operated in avalanche mode typically use high-performance gas mixtures based on high-GWP F-gases such as C$_2$H$_2$F$_4$ and SF$_6$. As environmental concerns grow and regulations become increasingly stringent, the development of sustainable gas mixtures has become a global priority. Within the RPC ECOGas@GIF++ Collaboration, a long-term R&D program has investigated eco-friendly gas mixtures for RPCs and assessed their performance under irradiation. RPCs operated with an HFO-1234ze/CO$_2$ mixture were exposed to high particle fluxes at CERN GIF++, accumulating $\mathcal{O}(10^2~\mathrm{mC/cm^2})$ over three years. This ageing campaign is now complete, and the detector performances have been systematically evaluated across a broad range of particle rates. This paper presents preliminary final results from the campaign, along with future perspectives.

papers.title: The bar-driven central complex of NGC 6946: A panchromatic and spatially resolved view of its star formation history and interstellar medium
papers.abstract: We present a multi-wavelength analysis of the nearby spiral galaxy NGC 6946, combining optical IFS, infrared, and radio observations. We aim to characterise both the integrated and spatially resolved properties of the stellar populations and ISM, and to interpret them in the context of bar-driven galaxy evolution. We used the SED fitting code SINOPSIS to derive stellar population properties, and different prescriptions to derive ISM properties including atomic and molecular gas masses and the dust mass,temperature, and emissivity index. We find that the central 2.6 kpc hosts $40\%$ of the stellar mass, as well as the bulk of the molecular gas and dust, and has sustained enhanced star formation over cosmic time. A major star formation episode occurred 0.6 Gyr ago. The spatially resolved KS relation shows that molecular gas alone explains only part of the current SFR variance, while alternative prescriptions incorporating stellar mass and dynamical equilibrium pressure yield only modest improvements. We also find radial enhancements in the effective oxygen yield and gas mass fraction relative to surrounding regions, consistent with sustained gas accumulation. Together with the molecular gas streaming motions previously detected kinematic studies, our results are consistent with, and provide independent support for, the inward transport of gas driven by a system of nested bars and with a scenario in which a recent episode of bar-driven gas inflow enhanced the central molecular gas reservoir and sustained elevated star formation. These findings point to efficient HI-to-H$_2$ conversion, likely promoted by the combined effect of the secondary bar and the large dust content, ultimately regulating star formation. We also find indications consistent with a young stellar bar. The current decline in star formation despite large gas reservoirs suggests recent bar-driven quenching.

papers.intro:
Galaxies, the building blocks of the Universe’s large-scale structure, exhibit a wide range of physical properties reflecting their formation and evolution history. Since galactic emission spans the entire electromagnetic spectrum, panchromatic studies are required to capture the full range of physical phenomena and facilitate a comprehensive analysis. In the optical, the spectral energy distribution (SED) is mainly determined by the star formation history (SFH) of the galaxy: this shapes the UV emission via young, massive stars, and the optical and near-infrared (NIR) via intermediate and low-mass stars. Metallicity also plays a role, affecting both absorption and emission lines strengths as well as colours. On the other hand, interstellar dust is responsible for reddening by efficiently absorbing UV and optical light, and re-emitting it in the infrared (Draine 2003). As such, dust plays a crucial role at both short and long wavelengths. Gas also shapes the optical spectra through emission lines from ionised elements and contributes at longer wavelengths through free-free radiation. This allows us to use SEDs to infer the physical processes and properties that drive the evolution of galaxies. To extract the optical SED, integral field spectroscopy (IFS) is an observational technique that is based on the construction of 3D spectral maps (two spatial dimensions, one spectral) using an integral field unit (IFU) that takes multiple simultaneous spectra across the field of view. Major IFS galaxy surveys include: the Calar Alto Legacy Integral Field Area survey CALIFA (Sánchez et al. 2012), with ∼\sim600 local galaxies (0.005<z<0.030.005<z<0.03) covering a significant luminosity range; the Mapping Nearby Galaxies at APO MaNGA (Bundy et al. 2015), surveying ∼\sim10000 nearby galaxies, sampling galaxies across ∼\sim3 orders of magnitude in stellar mass (M∗>109​M⊙M_{*}>10^{9}M_{\odot}) without morphological or environmental restrictions, achieving 1−21-2 kpc spatial resolution to study internal structures. Other surveys include the Sydney-AAO Multi-object Integral field spectrograph (SAMI) survey (Bryant et al. 2015), the ATLAS3D survey (Cappellari et al. 2011), the PPAK IFS Nearby Galaxies Survey (PINGS) (Rosales-Ortega et al. 2010), and the Physics at High Angular resolution in Nearby GalaxieS with MUSE (PHANGS–MUSE) survey (Emsellem et al. 2022) and Metal-THINGS (Lara-López et al. 2021). To complement the optical data and trace the interstellar medium (ISM) components, the dust properties are also analysed. While dust constitutes only ∼1%\sim 1\% of the total ISM mass (with gas making up the remaining ∼99%\sim 99\%, Draine 2011), it is a critical component. Dust influences the energetic balance that regulates ISM heating and cooling (Galliano et al. 2018) and drives several key processes. By attenuating and reddening starlight and nebular emission, dust grains introduce important uncertainties into measurements of galactic stellar masses, SFRs, metallicities, and the total energy budget of galaxies. Most relevant to this work, the formation of molecules (notably H2) occurs on the surfaces of dust grains (Hollenbach et al. 1971), which subsequently shield these molecules from dissociating radiation (Wakelam et al. 2017). Thus, dust facilitates the formation of molecules and the eventual formation of stars (Scoville et al. 2013, e.g.). The Herschel Space Observatory, operating across the far-infrared (70–500 μ\mum), samples the peak of the dust SED. This makes it sensitive to both the diffuse, cold dust (T<25T<25 K) that dominates the total dust mass in galaxies (Draine et al. 2007), and the warmer dust (T>30T>30 K) radiating at shorter wavelengths that often dominates the total infrared luminosity.

On the other hand, as the bulk of the ISM mass is in the form of gas – both atomic and molecular – observations of the 21 cm line of atomic neutral hydrogen (HI) are fundamental for understanding the processes governing star formation, the dynamics and structure of the ISM, and the distribution of (dark) matter (Walter et al. 2008; de Blok et al 2008; Dib et al. 2021). Atomic gas, primarily HI, dominates the mass budget of gas of most star-forming galaxies and is typically their most extended component, often stretching far beyond the stellar and molecular discs. The 21 cm emission line provides a powerful tool for mapping the distribution and kinematics of this phase of the ISM (Thomas et al. 2004; Bigiel and Blitz 2012). HI plays an important role as the indirect fuel for star formation (Schaye 2004; Bigiel et al. 2008). Although stars form directly from molecular clouds, atomic hydrogen is the essential reservoir from which molecular gas forms. Consequently, the HI content directly influences a galaxy’s evolutionary timeline and all properties linked to its star formation activity. Given that all galactic components are intrinsically linked, multi-wavelength studies are essential to uncover the relationships between them and establish the causal chains driving galactic evolution.

papers.title: Scaling Online Exploration for Robot Agents
papers.abstract: Robot learning has advanced by scaling demonstration datasets and model capacity; however, deploying a new robot embodiment or task typically necessitates a dedicated teleoperation corpus. The resulting policies remain bounded by their imitation distributions, limiting generalization and continual self-improvement. We introduce RAX (Robot Agent eXploration), an open-source framework for robot agents centered on scaling exploration: enabling agents to improve by acquiring online experience and synthesizing executable programs. In RAX, a general-purpose coding agent generates robot control code, operating without action demonstration data, hand-engineered action primitives, or value-function guidance. Through online exploration, the agent identifies decision sequences that achieve task goals and compiles them into modular programs encapsulating the full perception-planning-control loop. Using RAX, we present a systematic multi-embodiment study on scaling online exploration across precision and long-horizon manipulation tasks using single-arm, bimanual, dexterous, mobile, and humanoid systems in simulation and on real robots. Generalization performance on unseen environments improves consistently as exploration scales. In simulation, RAX outperforms top baseline models by +37.4% on average. On real robots, RAX autonomously learns memory-dependent, articulated, high-precision, deformable, and long-horizon mobile manipulation tasks without human demonstrations, continually improving performance by composing verified skills from prior exploration sessions. As exploration scales, we observe emergent capabilities including active perception, error recovery, safety guardrails, and human-robot collaboration. We open-source RAX as a generalist robot-agent platform in which new robot embodiments are integrated through their APIs alone, without teleoperated data collection or policy training.

Robot learning has made substantial progress by scaling demonstration data and model capacity with imitation learning, aiming to replicate the training recipe that transformed language modeling (Kaplan et al., 2020). Vision-language-action (VLA) models and World-Action models (WAMs) fine-tune pretrained VLMs and video generation models, respectively, using large teleoperation corpora (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024). However, deploying a new robot or task still requires a dedicated teleoperation corpus of its own (O’Neill et al., 2024; Team et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Intelligence et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026e; Yuan et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026; Bi et al., 2026). Furthermore, the knowledge of such policy models is inherently bounded by the demonstrations they imitate. Consider a mobile robot tasked with loading a car in an unfamiliar house: while opening doors, grasping bags, and placing objects may each be familiar skills, the robot must adapt to novel scenes, visual appearances, and task compositions while discovering new approaches. This adaptation and discovery process is absent during imitation learning on static teleoperation data. Consequently, these policies struggle to generalize and self-improve, even when provided with environment interactions and test-time compute. This limitation motivates a central question: can robots self-improve and learn to discover new skills through autonomous online experience and active exploration?

Humans learn physical skills by attempting a task, observing the outcome, diagnosing failures, and practicing until their behavior becomes reliable. LLM agents exhibit a similar pattern in software domains: they explore unfamiliar systems by executing programs, inspecting outputs, and revising their work (Yang et al., 2024). Instead of training policies exclusively on teleoperated demonstration data, we let agents program robots directly (Lozano-Perez, 1983) without hand-designed action primitives. The agent explores online to discover decisions that drive task success, then automates these decision-making principles into modular robot programs that integrate perception, planning, and control. It continuously debugs and tests these programs through online execution. These programs encode the agent’s underlying principles for how to generate successful actions based on environment perception, rather than merely mimicking the actions themselves, thereby enabling more robust generalization. Furthermore, the agent can compose, modify, and update these programs when confronting increasingly complex scenes and tasks, continually improving through online experience.

We introduce RAX (Robot Agent eXploration), a cognitive architecture for robot agents. Its core organizing principle is scaling exploration: robot agents should improve by gathering their own online experience and optimizing their programs. In RAX, a general-purpose coding agent receives a natural-language instruction, at most a few goal images or visual demonstrations, and a budget of exploration episodes. It interacts directly through the robot’s perception and control interfaces without requiring human teleoperation or value function guidance. The underlying language model parameters remain fixed and no policies are trained; instead, learning updates a persistent workspace of programs, notes, and verified skills. The agent converts successful interactions into autonomous code programs and stores reusable knowledge for subsequent episodes and tasks.

As exploration scales, we observe several emergent system capabilities: the agent constructs task-relevant 3D perception models, plans actions via pose search in 3D joint space, generates fully automated programs with closed-loop visual and force feedback, and adapts its programs when encountering novel task conditions. Furthermore, we observe agentic behaviors on real robots, including active perception, error recovery, safety guardrails, and active human-robot interaction. For example, the robot executes end-effector contact probing for precise localization when depth measurements are inaccurate. In mobile manipulation experiments, following an initial collision with a cabinet, the agent automatically instantiates a safety check to verify workspace clearance before every base rotation. To test code robustness, the agent actively requests the human operator to vary object layouts, systematically testing the spatial generalization of the autonomous program.

In RAX, we equip the agent with rich multimodal sensing by exposing metric depth and force signals through the robot interface. A unified architecture supports tabletop bimanual arms, dexterous hands, mobile household robots, and humanoids through interfaces to each robot’s sensors, controllers, and kinematic models (Section 4). Unlike standard VLAs or WAMs operating on RGB images alone, the agent autonomously leverages these rich sensing signals to construct 3D point clouds and fit object models directly from perception. It then searches for actions to manipulate these 3D models while accounting for their unique shapes and affordances. Force feedback further enables the agent to resolve spatial uncertainty through contact and enable close-loop control on force signals in insertion tasks. Such multimodal world modeling have been largely absent from generalist policy models, yet naturally align with human cognitive processes.

papers.title: Deterministic Bounds on Accuracy and Stability of Metric-Space Regression and Classification
papers.abstract: Data-driven approaches often face ambiguity in datasets due to sensor or target noise, insufficient information, and noise in the input data. While best-fit machine learning methods can accommodate such noise through uncertainty estimates, they are prone to overfitting and it is challenging to quantify ambiguity of the relation between inputs and targets. We introduce a geometric framework that quantifies this ambiguity through the average kernel size, computed with data-dependent, i.e. model-independent, feasible sets derived from worst-case input and target noise. The framework provides computable, deterministic, non-asymptotic bounds on the best achievable empirical error and accuracy for a finite, constructed dataset, independent of the predictive model class, and applies to regression and classification with pseudo-metric input spaces and metric target spaces. The ambiguity of the input-target relation implies three consequences: an empirical error floor, an accuracy-stability trade-off, and, under standard probabilistic assumptions, a strictly positive distribution-training error gap when training below the accuracy bounds. Under standard Borel assumptions for Euclidean norms, the distributional analogue of the average kernel size is related to Bayes risk as it reduces to the optimal distribution root-mean-squared error times the square root of two. Experiments spanning tabular regression, image regression and classification datasets yield nontrivial bounds on the best achievable empirical error and accuracy on a constructed dataset, alongside descriptive comparisons with model performance on the original datasets. The bounds provide a computable, model-independent reference scale on the constructed dataset and comparisons with model performance on the original dataset are descriptive.

papers.title: The Magnetized Universe: From planet-forming disks to the high-redshift universe
papers.abstract: The interstellar medium (ISM) is magnetized at all scales and phases in our Galaxy and other galaxies across the Universe. Spectro-polarimetric millimetre observations are essential to probe the role of the interstellar magnetic fields in the dynamics of the cold universe, and how this affects the star formation process, and planet formation in nearby star forming regions. Such observations are also essential for understanding magnetic fields in active stars and the shaping and evolution of the circumstellar environments of evolved stars. While ALMA has been revolutionary in advancing our knowledge about magnetic fields in the ISM, the limitations in calibration, especially for circular polarization, and sensitivity for large samples, have hindered robust measurements of field strengths, which are essential for fully assessing their role in ISM dynamics. An ALMA2040 that broadens spectro-polarimetric capabilities to include robust circular calibration and increases sensitivity with more collecting area will enable crucial observations of magnetic fields across the Universe and over a wide range of spatial scales to fully ascertain the influences of magnetic fields from galaxy assembly to forming planets.

papers.title: Sparking Dynamic, Relativistic Magnetic Reconnection in a Twisted Flux Tube
papers.abstract: Magnetic reconnection around neutron stars (NSs) forms small-scale currents while transferring energy to electron-positron pairs. These dissipating currents cover a wide range of scales, potentially leaving an imprint on time-variable X-ray bursts and pulsed radio emission. We present a reduced, planar model of internal reconnection in a magnetic flux tube with relativistic magnetization, finite resistivity, and strong guide field. Comparing with realistic NS parameters, this model represents the dynamics of a slender magnetic flux tube that is much thinner than the stellar radius. The seed current profile is smooth and does not spontaneously reconnect; instead, a discrete and localized current perturbation is introduced, representing e.g. localized energy release from a NS crust or magnetosphere. Three high-resolution relativistic magnetohydrodynamics simulations are described: one has uniform resistivity and Lundquist number such that reconnection proceeds in the plasmoid-mediated regime; the other two account for the feedback of charge starvation on the resistivity in current layers, where density is depleted; we provide a more general explanation for this depletion. All simulations produce a few dominant magnetic X-points and a secondary Kelvin-Helmholtz instability that excites high-wavenumber currents. We quantify the reconnection rate, the intermittency of dissipation, and the time profile of current spikes. We further present three-dimensional simulations confirming a limited growth of the ideal kink mode in the strong guide field regime. Applications are discussed, including to radio pulse microstructure and current damping below the magnetar surface during an X-ray flare, leading to mass loss and X-ray afterglow.

papers.intro:
A longstanding problem in plasma astrophysics centers on the stability of a twisted magnetic field that is coupled to dilute plasma and tied to the surface of a star. Heating of plasma outside the star is facilitated by small-scale current structure and magnetic reconnection [74, 82]. The study of small-scale reconnection presented here is motivated by the peculiar behavior of magnetars [32], compact stars supporting ∼1020\sim 10^{20} Ampere currents that show dramatic variability ranging from sub-millisecond to year-long timescales [55].

Magnetars are especially sensitive probes of current driven instabilities because the magnetic field is the dominant energy source for their radiative emissions, which range across the full electromagnetic spectrum, from the radio to gamma ray bands. Some magnetars produce peculiar radio pulsations with extreme intermittency and variability (e.g. Dai et al. 29, Lower et al. 61, Huang et al. 52), while others produce repeating, sub-second X-ray bursts that can show strong intraburst variability [36, 53].

The observations of rapid variability in magnetars combine with the problem of plasma heating at extreme magnetization to motivate the present study of magnetic reconnection on small scales. We are interested in the dynamics of currents around the kinetic scale de=c/ωpd_{e}=c/\omega_{p}, where ωp\omega_{p} is the plasma frequency and cc is the speed of light. Outside a neutron star, the transfer of magnetic energy to particles and radiation is concentrated in zones where the current becomes charge-starved (e.g. in strongly sheared Alfvén waves or small scale current sheets: Thompson and Blaes 99, Nättilä and Beloborodov 70). Except in the most luminous outbursts, charged particles must rapidly relax to the lowest Landau state and form a nearly one-dimensional gas.

An understudied aspect of the problem is the effect of a compact and localized perturbation on a smooth current structure. The magnetic configuration studied in this paper has initial axial symmetry and carries vanishing net current. Spontaneous tearing is too slow to be observed; instead the perturbation plays a key role in triggering rapid reconnection of the non-potential magnetic field. The evolution is studied in two dimensions (2D) at large magnetization (σ∼102\sigma\sim 10^{2}) by solving the equations of resistive, relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (MHD). The presence of a local perturbation is motivated in a magnetar by the possibility of a localized yielding in the crust, driven e.g. by fault-like response to large-scale magnetic stresses [104] or plastic flow driven by Hall waves [101, 60, 58].

We adopt both a small, uniform resistivity and a recently developed non-uniform resistivity law that accounts for the effects of charge starvation [69, 86]. The physical scale at which charge starvation sets in depends strongly on the radiative state of the magnetar. During a bright X-ray burst with super-Eddington luminosity, the plasma may approach local kinetic equilibrium at a temperature ∼me​c2\sim m_{e}c^{2} [33]; in a quiescent state, the persistent output of hard X-rays can be accommodated by a flow of e±e^{\pm} pairs with density ∼102\sim 10^{2} times the charge starvation value [4, 103]. In the outburst regime, the kinetic scale may then be as small as de∼10−11d_{e}\sim 10^{-11} cm; whereas in quiescence, the plasma frequency is inferred to be ∼1014\sim 10^{14} Hz in the inner magnetosphere, corresponding to de∼10−3d_{e}\sim 10^{-3} cm. This motivates our dual approach to modeling the resistivity, where we focus on representing as wide a range of hydromagnetic scales as possible, or, alternatively, on directly resolving dissipation at kinetic scales.

The paper is organized as follows. Small-scale twisting of a stellar magnetic field is described qualitatively in Section II. The model, numerical methods, and the description of the employed plasma resistivity model are summarized in Section III. Results are presented in Section IV. The role played by charge starvation of small-scale currents is investigated in Section V. Our results are summarized in Section VI along with implications for magnetars and pulsars. The Appendices present a complementary three-dimensional (3D) model, describe the approach to mesh refinement and tests of numerical convergence, and review our approach to handling charge-starvation effects using a non-uniform adaptive resistivity law.

papers.title: Amplifying gene expression sensitivity by surface condensation on DNA
papers.abstract: Condensation of proteins on DNA is a central aspect of genome organisation, and has been proposed as a mechanism of gene regulation in eukaryotes, notably by mediating the action of distal enhancers on promoter activity. However, the physics of this interaction and its impact on the precision of gene regulation remain to be fully elucidated. Here, we study a simplified system of two regulatory regions of the DNA, a distal enhancer and a promoter, with affinity to a self-attracting ligand that effectively binds them together. Using 3-dimensional lattice simulations and a mean-field theory of the ligand-water mixture coupled to a Rouse polymer, we show that small differences in ligand concentrations can be greatly amplified at the level of transcriptional activity compared to a free ligand receptor. We quantify this sensitivity using the Fisher information rate, which can be decomposed into two contributions. First, the formation of a pre-wet layer of ligands around regulatory regions increases ligand concentrations at the promoter site, enhancing concentration differences. Second, the DNA polymer itself switches between a closed state, where enhancer and promoter are in contact through an attractive capillary bridge formed by ligands, and an open state where they are apart. That attractive force determines the typical dwell time of the closed configuration where the gene is most active, and strongly depends on the ligand bulk concentration, contributing to the sensitivity of gene expression. These results suggest a general mechanism and theoretical framework for the precise regulation of genes through tunable genome organization.

papers.intro:
Cellular differentiation, during development [1, 2] and in response to stress [3, 4, 5] often requires rapid and accurate readout of transcription factor concentrations. In eukaryotes, in addition to proximal enhancers, transcription is often controlled by regulatory elements located far away on the genome, called ‘distal enhancers’ [6, 7, 8, 9]. Recent experiments suggest a new type of transcriptional control involving distal enhancers that relies on physical effects similar to condensation effects in fluid mixtures [10]. These ideas are inspired by the discovery of such membraneless compartments in a variety of cellular contexts [11, 12, 13], and their potential role in driving expression [14, 15] and in sensing concentration changes [5, 16]. Yet the quantitative effects of enhancer dynamics and protein condensation on the accuracy of concentration sensing are not well understood. Can dynamic promoter-enhancer contact, coupled with local condensation of regulatory molecules on DNA, result in a highly sensitive readout of transcription factor concentrations?

Fundamental limits and features of the general problem of concentration sensing have been studied for individual receptors at [17] and far from equilibrium [18, 19], under time [20] and physical constraints [21, 22], in changing environments [23, 24], and in the context of information transmission [25, 26], maximum likelihood estimation [27, 28] and sequential decision-making [29, 21, 22]. However, most theoretical models inspired by gene regulation attempt to decouple receptors from the complexity of their crowded local environment in the nucleus. Often, they assume receptors are limited by the random binding of transcription factors (TF) diffusing across homogeneous concentration gradients.

Often, they assume receptors are limited by the random binding of transcription factors (TF) diffusing across homogeneous concentration gradients.

Observations of TF clusters located around regulatory regions of DNA [30] further challenge the view of a homogeneous TF gradient in the nucleus, suggesting that concentration heterogeneities potentially obtained by liquid-liquid phase separation influence the concentration readout [10, 31]. This picture aligns with an emerging view of droplet formation as a sensing mechanism actively used by cells [5, 32]. In eukaryotes, the expression of many genes relies on distal enhancers to interact with the promoter and drive gene expression [33, 7, 8]. The large measured distances (150-350 nm) separating promoters and enhancers during episodes of transcription [7, 34, 35, 36, 30] have suggested the existence of an ‘action at a distance’ mediated by droplets. This model explains the long-range interaction, either by the presence of a droplet whose concentration fluctuates near a critical point [37], or an enhancer site diffusing and occasionally interacting with the droplet without ever reaching the gene [36, 38].

However, contrary to the action-at-a-distance scenario, enhancer control of transcription, known to exhibit high sensitivity to changes in concentration [39, 40], is traditionally thought to be mediated by close contact events. This leads to alternative models that suggest localized condensation, or prewetting, as opposed to large scale droplet formation, occurs only on regulatory surfaces [41, 15]. One recent compilation of high resolution imaging, theory and simulation argues that current live imaging techniques cannot resolve spatial scales under ∼50\sim 50 nm [34], and cannot precisely resolve action at a distance from close contact. Theory and experiments on surface condensation on DNA [42, 43] have shown that capillary forces due to condensed proteins can collapse sections of chromatin into small globules of significantly smaller size than phase-separated droplets, whose typical diameter is in the hundreds of nanometers [44]. This provides evidence that prewetting, a known phase transition whose control parameter is protein concentration, could help bring together distant locations on a polymer.

We start by exploring the effects of a complex local environment on the precision of TF concentration readout using lattice simulations of a DNA polymer coupled to self-attractive regulatory molecules. From these simulations emerges a picture in which TF concentration is locally increased at the regulatory sites, enhancing sensitivity. In addition, regulatory regions attract each other through these TF clouds [45], further improving sensitivity. Informed by those results, we then build an effective continuous theory based on the Flory-Huggins free energy for binary mixtures coupled to a Rouse polymer for the DNA. The theory allows us to both interpret the simulations and to overcome their computational limitations. It explains the contributions of enhancer-promoter attraction, DNA dynamics, and local condensation of ligands, to the sensitivity of gene expression.

papers.title: The Reliance Hypothesis: Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness Rises as Language Resource Level Falls
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) faithfulness matters for monitoring, explaining and safely deploying large language models, yet it has been studied mostly in English. Languages differ in level, the amount of text available to learn from, so models know less in lower-resource languages, which may change how much they rely on their reasoning. To our knowledge, we are the first to relate CoT faithfulness to both resource level and task type (knowledge- or reasoning-intensive). On parallel multiple-choice questions from Multilingual Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMMLU) in eight languages, faithfulness rises as resource level falls on knowledge-intensive tasks but not on reasoning-intensive ones, a gap that points the same way across four models and several faithfulness measures. We propose, and find support for, the Reliance Hypothesis: models rely more on their reasoning when they cannot recall the answer, as in lower-resource languages on knowledge-intensive tasks. Model confidence partly explains the effect of resource level, but not the knowledge-reasoning gap. Languages in which models are less confident rely more on reasoning, yet less confident answers within a language do not, a Simpson's paradox. In lower-resource languages, models rely on their reasoning for more answers, not more strongly for each. CoT monitoring may therefore be most informative in lower-resource languages, where it is least often validated.

In English, the model can recall the answer and ignores the mistake; in Yoruba, where its knowledge is thinner, it follows the mistake to a different answer. We formalise this intuition as the Reliance Hypothesis: models rely more on their reasoning when they cannot simply recall the answer, as in lower-resource languages on knowledge-intensive tasks.

We test the hypothesis on parallel multiple-choice questions from Multilingual Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMMLU; OpenAI, 2024), which covers both knowledge- and reasoning-intensive subjects, in eight languages whose resource levels span nearly eight orders of magnitude, with four open-weight models and four interventions on the reasoning chain Lanham et al. (2023). We measure faithfulness as reliance on the CoT: how far each intervention shifts the model’s confidence in its original answer, and compare knowledge- and reasoning-intensive subtasks, so that the same languages and models serve as their own control. Our contributions are as follows: (i) To our knowledge, we are the first to relate CoT faithfulness to both resource level and task type. (ii) We show that faithfulness rises as resource level falls on knowledge-intensive tasks, but not on reasoning-intensive ones, a gap that points the same way across models and metrics and largely survives robustness checks. (iii) We propose and test the Reliance Hypothesis, finding that model confidence partly mediates the effect of resource level, but that confidence alone cannot explain why the effect is stronger on knowledge-intensive tasks. (iv) We characterise reliance further: models rely more on reasoning in languages where they are less confident, yet within a language, their less confident answers rely on it no more than others (a Simpson’s paradox: a trend across groups that vanishes within them); and lower-resource languages rely on their reasoning more often, not more heavily (4% of answers in English vs. 35% in Yoruba). Faithfulness is thus highest where models know least, suggesting CoT monitoring may be most informative where it is least often validated.

papers.title: Many Biases, One Circuit: Post-Training Tunes a Pretrained Cue-Routing Mechanism
papers.abstract: Language models often abandon a correct answer when the prompt contains a cue, a hint toward a wrong option such as "I think the answer is B." Sycophancy and related biases show this failure. They are often studied separately and blamed on alignment. We test this view causally, tracing the attention heads behind these biases through the stages of two post-training pipelines. In multiple-choice tests on most models, four cue types rely largely on the same few heads, a shared circuit already present in pretrained models. Most base models follow cues in plain text. Fine-tuning a base model on about 200 generic assistant examples without cues activates these heads in chat format, so cue-following can be a side effect of assistant tuning. The final reinforcement learning (RL) stage strengthens the effect of cues in almost every comparison. In Tulu-3-8B and OLMo-2-7B, we swap the attention patterns of six middle layers between the RL checkpoint and its predecessor. For suggested-answer cues, this shifts each checkpoint's cue effect most of the way to the other's level. Post-training thus seems to change when and how strongly models use this circuit. Mitigation for these multiple-choice biases could target this circuit.

papers.intro:
Language models often give up a correct answer when the prompt contains a cue. A cue is text added to the prompt that points to one answer option without giving real evidence for it. For example, a model that answers a question correctly may switch to option B after the user adds the sentence “I think the answer is B.” We call such a switch to the cued wrong option caving. Caving is a simple and measurable form of sycophancy (Sharma et al., 2023; Perez et al., 2023), and it also affects the reasoning given for the answer (Turpin et al., 2023). Other cues also cause caving, such as a fake earlier answer attributed to the model, an irrelevant fact about a wrong option, or a few-shot example in which the same question has a wrong label (Chua et al., 2025). These are usually treated as separate biases. In multiple-choice tests, we find that they rely mostly on the same few attention heads.

Where does this shared mechanism come from? A common explanation is that alignment teaches models to follow cues. Human raters can prefer agreement (Sharma et al., 2023). Reward models can learn this preference, and policy optimization can strengthen it (Shapira et al., 2026). Mechanistic work mostly studies the final released models. Studies that also test base models find many of the relevant heads already present (Pandey, 2026; Chen et al., 2026b). Chen et al. (2026b) also find that post-training strengthens the heads that carry a stated opinion. No study we know of follows a cue-following circuit through a post-training pipeline stage by stage. It is therefore untested which stage changes such a circuit, and whether this change in the circuit explains the shift in behavior. We study two training pipelines with public intermediate checkpoints (Tulu-3 on Llama-3.1 and OLMo-2 at three sizes) and four more model families. We ask three questions. Does post-training build the heads behind cue-following? What makes an aligned model follow cues in its chat format? How does the final RL stage change the effect of cues on the answer?

For the first question, we give an aligned model the base model’s query and output weights for these heads. If alignment had built cue-following into these heads, this copy should change the aligned model’s caving. For the second, we fine-tune a base model on a small set of generic assistant examples without cues and test whether it starts to follow cues in chat format. The third question compares a checkpoint after direct preference optimization (DPO) with the reinforcement learning (RL) checkpoint trained from it. In a chosen set of layers, we give each checkpoint the attention patterns that the other checkpoint produces on the same prompt. If the RL stage strengthens the cue’s effect by changing attention in those layers, the swap should make each checkpoint behave more like the other. To our knowledge, no earlier study has swapped attention between successive post-training checkpoints to explain a change in behavior. We set pass or fail rules for the swap tests in advance, and Appendix I reports them, including several that were not met. Figure 1 summarizes our answers, and Appendix A lists every main test.

2. Generic assistant tuning activates the heads in chat format. Most base models we test already follow cues in plain text, without a chat template. With their chat template, they rarely answer correctly and therefore rarely cave. Fine-tuning a base model on about 200 generic assistant examples without cues is enough to produce caving in chat format. Eight generic dialogue turns in the prompt have part of the same effect when written as chat turns. Written without chat roles, the same texts do not raise the cue’s effect (§4). Assistant tuning can thus produce cue-following in chat format as a side effect, with no training data that target it.

papers.title: Role of Device Size on Island Divertor Performance of W7-X-like Configurations
papers.abstract: To examine how the island divertor performs in future low-shear stellarator reactors, we simulate (using EMC3-Eirene [1]) 3 different scales of W7-X: its current size, increased by a factor 2, and increased by a factor 4, where 4 times W7-X corresponds roughly to a reactor-scale device. For a single magnetic configuration, the standard magnetic configuration in W7-X, we examine how increasing the size of W7-X alters the divertor performance of the island divertor. We analyze how device scale shifts the location of the ionization source and the downstream density and temperature trends in the island divertor for achieving detachment. Local field line analysis shows that factor 2 and factor 4 size scalings achieve target densities $>10^{21} \ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ via plasma ``self-baffling" within the open island divertor geometry. Finally, the heat and particle flux deposition on the scaled-up island divertor configurations are calculated. We observe a separation in the target heat and particle flux distribution with increased machine size in agreement with [2]. The target heat fluxes are $<5 \ \mathrm{MW}/\mathrm{m}^2$ at high separatrix densities. This shows that the separation of the heat and particle flux channels remains to be largely unproblematic. This analysis helps guide how to improve the open island divertor geometries for future stellarator reactors.

papers.intro:
The so-called “island divertor” concept in Wendelstein 7-X (W7-X) is the leading divertor candidate for future stellarator reactors. However, to date the study of this concept has been primarily focused on the experimental scale, with only few results on a reactor-scale [10]. Further study of heat and particle transport at reactor-scale is therefore necessary. The island divertor is formed by intentionally including a rational surface at the plasma edge, where a radial resonant magnetic field component naturally creates a large island chain at this location. These islands are then intercepted by segmented target plates, forming the plasma scrape-off layer (SOL) and divertor region. While this concept has been experimentally demonstrated on both the Wendelstein 7-AS (W7-AS) and Wendelstein 7-X (W7-X) stellarators, the observed heat and particle exhaust performance has not yet proven that it will perform satisfactorily at reactor-scale. In particular, W7-X thus far does not adequately address particle exhaust [1]. While there are ongoing activities in improving particle exhaust in W7-X, such as possible installation of closed divertors [12], it is not yet clear if such a closed divertor geometry is required at reactor-scale. For example, in the tokamak community, there are indications that at reactor-scale in normal aspect-ratio devices, such closed configurations may not be needed [15]. This is because the distance between the divertor and the LCFS becomes so large that the neutral ionization is very well localized in front of the target plates and thus the plasma “baffles” itself. However, these studies are largely missing in the stellarator community, where very few reactor-scale predictions have been performed [10]. Therefore, this work elucidates the role of device size on divertor performance in the stellarator island divertor configuration. This is done by linearly up-scaling W7-X by two and four times (termed “x2” and “x4” respectively in this work) as shown in table 1 with major radius RR and minor radius aa. To examine the effect of size scaling on divertor performance, we keep the geometry of the island divertor in this study. Rather, the focus of this work is to understand how the current island divertor geometry performs with increasing device size.

W7-X is a 5 field-period stellarator where each half-field period features 5 non-planar and 2 planar coils. This results in 50 non-planar coils and 20 planar coils across the entire device. The divertor geometry is split up into 10 separate identical modules throughout the device. Each module is comprised of a horizontal and vertical target. In W7-X, the island divertor can be operated across different edge rotational transform ι=nm\iota=\frac{n}{m} values where nn and mm are the toroidal and poloidal mode numbers respectively. This ranges from the “low iota” configuration with ι=56\iota=\frac{5}{6} to “high iota” configuration with ι=54\iota=\frac{5}{4}. The results presented here are for only one magnetic configuration in W7-X, namely, the standard magnetic configuration with edge rotational transform ι=55\iota=\frac{5}{5}. We simulate only the “standard” configuration as this the most widely simulated and understood [3, 4, 6, 18].

This paper examines the plasma edge and divertor performance of the island divertor across different device scalings in two parts. The first part in section 2 discusses the density build-up achieved with increasing machine size and its implications. This is done by first introducing the EMC3-EIRENE code and simulation set-up for all size scalings followed by a discussion of the target (or “downstream”) density and temperature behavior. The second part in section 3 analyzes the heat and particle exhaust where we calculate and compare the target deposition pattern for all three size scalings. Finally, conclusions and future work are provided in section 4.

papers.title: Multiscale Quantum-Classical Simulation of Protein Autoproteolysis in a Million-Atom Membrane Environment
papers.abstract: Predicting chemical reactions in biomolecules is challenging because reactive centers are embedded within complex environments that strongly influence their energetics and mechanisms. Here, we present a hybrid quantum-classical workflow that combines molecular dynamics, density functional theory, and correlated wavefunction methods, tightly integrating CPUs, GPUs, and quantum processing units (QPUs) to enable simulations across multiple length and accuracy scales. We apply this approach to ADGRG1 autoproteolysis, a maturation reaction in an adhesion G protein-coupled receptor that has not previously been studied using correlated electronic-structure methods. Our simulations treat a biologically realistic system containing more than one million atoms, including the full-length uncleaved receptor embedded in an endoplasmic-reticulum membrane, while incorporating a 54-qubit IQM quantum processor and up to 1,200 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. These results demonstrate how quantum computers can serve as accelerators within scalable scientific workflows, extending correlated electronic-structure methods to biologically relevant systems.

papers.intro:
G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are among the most pharmaceutically important protein families, targeted by approximately 36% of approved drugs, with 516 approved agents and 337 candidates currently in clinical trials Sánchez Lorente et al. (2025). Adhesion GPCRs (aGPCRs) constitute the second largest family within the GPCR superfamily Hamann et al. (2015), yet no aGPCR has been targeted for drug development, despite an association between several aGPCRs and human disease Sánchez Lorente et al. (2025). Distinguished by their exceptionally large extracellular regions, most aGPCRs undergo a process called cis-autoproteolysis, in which the protein cuts its own backbone at the GPCR proteolysis site (GPS) located within the GAIN (GPCR autoproteolysis-inducing domain), without the help of an external enzyme Araç et al. (2012); Hamann et al. (2015). A precise understanding of the molecular mechanism of this cleavage may provide the basis for targeting this receptor family therapeutically.

ADGRG1 is an aGPCR that undergoes autoproteolysis and has been implicated in several human diseases. Autoproteolysis is a self-cleavage process in which a protein catalyzes the breaking of its own peptide bonds. The autoproteolytically cleaved N-terminal fragment (NTF) of ADGRG1 has been detected in human blood plasma, and ADGRG1 knockout mice undergo prolonged bleeding, defective platelet plug formation, and delayed thrombotic occlusion, suggesting an important role for ADGRG1 in human platelet physiology Yeung et al. (2020). Mutations in ADGRG1 have been found to cause bilateral frontoparietal polymicrogyria (BFPP), a rare genetic disorder that causes cortical malformation Bahi-Buisson et al. (2010) and, recently, high ADGRG1 levels in breast cancer patients have been shown to be significantly associated with an aggressive pathology in triple-negative breast cancer. In breast adipose tissue, ADGRG1 acts as a signaling hub to create an immunosuppressive and pro-metastatic niche in the tumor microenvironment (TME), making ADGRG1 a compelling therapeutic target with which to reprogram the TME and overcome resistance to immunotherapy in breast cancer Zhou et al. (2026).

Understanding ADGRG1 autoproteolysis requires modeling a chemical reaction occurring within a complex biomolecular environment. The quantities that govern the mechanism are the energy barriers separating reactants, intermediates, and products, as these determine reaction rates and reaction pathways. Precise prediction of such barriers demands an accurate description of electronic structure, yet a fully quantum-mechanical treatment of systems of this scale remains computationally intractable, even for large fault-tolerant quantum computers.

Multiscale electronic structure methods address this challenge by applying different levels of theory to different regions of a system. Approaches such as projection-based embedding (PBE) Manby et al. (2012); Goodpaster et al. (2014); Ralli et al. (2024) and quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) Warshel and Levitt (1976); Senn and Thiel (2009) enable the chemically active region to be treated at high accuracy while representing the surrounding environment at reduced cost. PBE has previously been combined with QM/MM to study enzymatic reactions through a correlated wavefunction (WF) description embedded within density functional theory (DFT), itself embedded in a classical environment Bennie et al. (2016). In this work, we adopt a related hierarchical WF-in-DFT-in-MM framework, in which the reactive center is treated explicitly at the wavefunction level, the local environment is described by DFT, and the wider biomolecular surroundings are represented through electrostatic embedding derived from a larger QM/MM model.

Although related approaches have been applied to aGPCR autoproteolysis, they have relied on substantially simplified structural models. Previous QM/MM studies of uncleaved rat ADGRL1 employed constructs containing the isolated N-terminal fragment and part of the tethered agonist solvated in water, without the transmembrane region Seufert et al. (2025). However, cleavage is believed to occur during biosynthesis in the endoplasmic reticulum, and studies of ADGRE2 suggest that the full seven-transmembrane architecture and membrane environment facilitate GAIN-domain autoproteolysis Chung et al. (2025). Furthermore, significant differences exist between human and rodent receptors Salzman et al. (2016), so mechanistic conclusions do not transfer directly between them.

Quantum computers are promising accelerators for the electronic structure components of such multiscale simulations. While a rigorous quantum advantage remains unproven, algorithms such as quantum phase estimation (QPE) Aspuru-Guzik et al. (2005) are widely expected to exhibit more favorable scaling than classical approaches. Hybrid quantum-classical workflows are particularly attractive because they restrict quantum resources to the chemically most challenging regions of a system. Recent fragment-based studies have demonstrated calculations on increasingly large biomolecular systems. A subset of authors in this work developed a three-layer WF-in-DFT-in-MM framework incorporating quantum computing to demonstrate proton transfer in a solvated Zundel cation Bickley et al. (2025). Other work on multiscale QPU-HPC biochemistry has included the 303-atom Trp-cage miniprotein Shajan et al. (2026) and protein-ligand complexes containing up to 12,635 atoms while needing quantum circuits of fewer than 100 qubits Merz Jr et al. (2026).

papers.title: Light-induced local control of magnetic anisotropy and domain pattern in Co/Pt multilayers
papers.abstract: Control of magnetic anisotropy is essential for the fabrication of next-generation devices in spintronics and magnetic memory. While conventional approaches such as material composition, thermal annealing, and ion bombardment are widely used, achieving spatially resolved, continuous control remains a challenge. Herein, we demonstrate a dual-regime, localized control over both transient magnetic states and permanent intrinsic properties in perpendicularly magnetized Co/Pt multilayers using ultra-short laser pulses. By employing a multi-scale approach combining Kerr microscopy, magnetic force microscopy, and vibrating sample magnetometry, we reveal that low-fluence irradiation enables a reversible, helicity-dependent accumulation of magnetic phases without altering the intrinsic quasistatic properties. Conversely, high-fluence exposure acts as localized thermal annealing that permanently hardens the magnetic system. This structural relaxation leads to a substantial enhancement of the effective perpendicular magnetic anisotropy, driving a twofold increase in the local coercive field and expanding the equilibrium stripe domain width. By offering both reversible spin manipulation and deterministic engineering of 2D magnetic landscapes, this work paves the way towards flexible, lithography-free anisotropy structuring for advanced spintronic applications.
