papers.title: Extended J-band spectroscopy of red supergiants: parameter identifiability and metallicity robustness
papers.abstract: Red supergiants (RSGs) provide a near-infrared metallicity diagnostic complementary to optical hot-supergiant spectroscopy, but their low-resolution extragalactic use requires tests of parameter identifiability and modelling robustness. We quantify the information content of extended J-band RSG spectra at R=2000 over 1.155-1.340 um and assess recovery of effective temperature, surface gravity, microturbulence, and metallicity. Using MARCS/TURBOSPECTRUM spectra and an emulator, we perform a six-node Fisher analysis and controlled mock experiments, and analyse 21 SpeX spectra of 20 RSG candidates towards Per OB1. All four parameters produce measurable responses, but only 8-10% of the raw metallicity information and 4-7% of the gravity information are independent of the other parameter directions. Extending beyond 1.22 um provides median fractions of 60% of the raw and 66% of the nuisance-orthogonal metallicity information. Gravity dominates the weakest Fisher mode, while its prior choice shifts association means by at most 0.03 dex. Matched mocks recover metallicity with an rms error of 0.04 dex. Standard continuum treatment biases solar-metallicity mocks by about -0.23 dex, reduced to about -0.01 dex by our adopted treatment. Plausible CNO mismatch adds a zero-point sensitivity of 0.04-0.05 dex, and regularised covariance changes association means by at most 0.03 dex. The preferred analysis gives a mean [Z] = -0.10 dex with a star-to-star dispersion of 0.09 dex. Extended low-resolution J-band spectra therefore yield recoverable metallicity and temperature constraints once continuum placement and weak parameter directions are controlled, although the absolute scale remains conditional on the adopted atmosphere and line-formation framework.

papers.intro:
The chemical composition of young stellar populations traces the present-day enrichment of star-forming galaxies. Quantitative spectroscopy of luminous supergiants extends such measurements beyond the Local Group while retaining the physical insight provided by individual stars. Optical analyses of blue supergiants have established this approach as a powerful means of measuring stellar metallicities and abundance gradients in external galaxies (Urbaneja et al., 2005; Kudritzki et al., 2008; Kudritzki et al., 2024; Bresolin et al., 2025, e.g.). Red supergiants (RSGs) provide a complementary diagnostic because they are among the brightest stars at near-infrared wavelengths and dominate the near-infrared light of young stellar populations (Lançon et al., 2008; Gazak et al., 2013, e.g.). Their spectra can therefore be studied individually (Patrick et al., 2015; Gazak et al., 2015, e.g.) or, at greater distances, through the integrated light of RSG-dominated young massive and super star clusters (Lardo et al., 2015; Davies et al., 2017, e.g.). The capabilities of James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) Near-Infrared Spectrograph (Jakobsen et al., 2022, NIRSpec,) and future Extremely Large Telescope instruments, including Multi-Object Spectrograph (Hammer et al., 2021, MOSAIC,), make it increasingly important to establish how reliably such spectra can constrain extragalactic metallicities.

Among the near-infrared windows available for RSG spectroscopy, the JJ-band offers a particularly promising route. The classical diagnostic interval introduced by Davies et al. (2010), approximately 1.151.15–1.22​μ​m1.22\,\mu\mathrm{m}, contains strong atomic features associated principally with Fe, Ti, Si, and Mg, while avoiding some of the stronger molecular contamination found elsewhere in cool-star spectra. These features retain useful abundance sensitivity at resolving powers of only a few thousand (Gazak et al., 2014), making the technique attractive for observations of individual RSGs and unresolved young stellar populations. Previous studies have demonstrated that such spectra can provide metallicity estimates well beyond the distances accessible to conventional high-resolution stellar spectroscopy (Gazak et al., 2015; Patrick et al., 2017, e.g.). A complementary question has received less attention: which parameter combinations are independently constrained at this resolution, and which parts of the spectrum carry metallicity information that remains distinguishable from the responses to other atmospheric parameters?

An acceptable spectral fit does not by itself establish that all inferred parameters are independently identifiable. At R≃2000R\simeq 2000, individual transitions are blended and the pseudo-continuum is difficult to define, while changes in effective temperature, surface gravity, microturbulent velocity, and metallicity can produce partially similar spectral responses. A strong response to a parameter therefore does not necessarily imply that the spectrum can distinguish its effect from those of the other parameters. Continuum distortions can be projected onto the inferred line strengths, while the assumed carbon, nitrogen and oxygen (CNO) abundance pattern can modify the molecular background and local pseudo-continuum. The treatment of correlated residuals and limitations of the adopted line-formation framework can introduce further shifts. Consequently, neither an acceptable fit nor small formal uncertainties alone demonstrate robust parameter recovery.

Additional wavelengths are most valuable not merely when they increase the total parameter sensitivity, but when they supply responses that differ from those already present and thereby improve parameter separation. Spectral derivatives and Fisher information provide a direct means of examining this local response geometry, identifying the constrained parameter combinations, and locating the wavelengths that carry independent metallicity information. Because these diagnostics are local and model based, they must be complemented by full inference experiments that test global recoverability and sensitivity to systematic assumptions.

papers.title: Self-Reflective Chain-of-Thought (SRCoT): Evidence-Based Text Generation via a Closed-Loop Retrieve--Reflect--Revise Pipeline on Edge LLMs
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent outputs that lack source support or conflict with local operational constraints. We introduce Self-Reflective Chain-of-Thought (SRCoT), a modular architecture that organizes generation as a closed Retrieve--Reflect--Revise loop. SRCoT separates environment state, persistent knowledge, accumulated experience, and short-term memory into provenance-labeled stores. BM25 retrieval supplies local context; subsequent passes expose intermediate drafts, missing-information markers, follow-up queries, and optional claim--evidence mappings. These artifacts inform retrieval, revision, clarification, or abstention decisions. We examine the architecture through qualitative, trace-based case studies in two fully synthetic settings: emergency medical services and Munich-Sim, an emergency-operations simulation. Local prototype runs on an Apple M4-family laptop with 128 GB memory illustrate source-labeled documentation, explicit gap marking, and structured dispatch-style outputs. The traces also reveal provenance-assignment errors, incomplete evidence coverage, and unsafe assumptions that remain possible despite prompting constraints. These cases demonstrate report-level inspectability and local execution, not comparative superiority, hallucination reduction, clinical validity, or operational safety. The architecture separates retrieval and control from the model interface, but behavior across different models remains to be evaluated. SRCoT is a research proof of concept requiring human review, with its principal contribution lying in an inspectable control procedure rather than a new model.

Guided by this perspective, a central design principle of our system is the explicit separation of different types of knowledge and state into distinct, machine-readable representations. We maintain dedicated structures for persistent knowledge and constraints, environmental state, accumulated experience, and short-term memory. Rather than interpreting these components as a biological model, we treat them as a system-level analogy: specialized information stores that are selectively integrated into a shared, task-relevant representation through a controlled coordination step. This design enables transparent state tracking, supports iterative verification against evidence, and allows the system to adapt its actions without conflating long-term knowledge with transient experiences.

papers.title: Beyond Success Rate: Interventional Evaluation of Memory in Vision-Language-Action Systems
papers.abstract: When we say that a robot uses memory, does that memory actually play a role? Success-rate ablations alone cannot establish the use of task-relevant facts: they change information and computation together, while aggregate rates can hide offsetting gains and losses. We propose an Interventional Memory Evaluation Protocol (IMEP) for vision-language-action (VLA) systems to address four questions: (1) Does memory provide a net benefit? (2) Under what conditions does memory help? (3) Do changes to memory alter task outcomes? (4) Are these effects specific to task-relevant facts? At the retrieval interface, we compare target-fact substitutions with fact-preserving replacements, minimal numerical perturbations, and exact replicas, while assessing decision correctness separately from motor execution success. We evaluate within-episode, cross-episode, and agentic memory. In cross-episode learned-bank experiments, a one-unit-in-the-last-place (ULP) intervention, including its installation procedure, changes 11.9% of seed-paired outcomes, while changing key facts produces no clear additional effect over fact-preserving replacements. To examine when memory helps, we introduce ChainBench, where correct decisions require historical information unavailable in current observations. The full memory configuration raises task success from 39.1% to 74.3%, matching the oracle-decision condition under shared recorded executions. These results show that correct history can support robot decisions, but establishing whether a memory system realizes this benefit requires fact-specific evidence beyond aggregate success rates.

A robot’s current observation may omit information needed to act: an earlier visual cue, a previous episode’s experience, or a fact retained across tasks. Vision–language–action (VLA) systems therefore augment policies with memory banks, event keyframes, or temporal representations (Shi et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026; Koo et al., 2026), experience retrieval (Sridhar et al., 2026), and external text records (Zhang et al., 2026b). These mechanisms aim to turn history into useful evidence for current decisions. Their value is often evaluated through memory ablations and task success (Shi et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026). Such gains show improved performance, but do they establish use of task-relevant stored facts (Figure 1a)?

Three distinctions prevent that inference. First, enabling memory can change both information and computation. Second, an unchanged success rate can hide gains on some trials and losses on others (Milani Fard et al., 2016). Third, changing memory can alter behavior even when a replacement preserves the target fact or introduces only a small numerical perturbation. History can also support shortcuts, as shown by causal confusion and copycat behavior in imitation learning (de Haan et al., 2019; Wen et al., 2020). Behavioral sensitivity alone does not establish use of task-relevant facts. Conversely, an undetected net gain does not imply that memory has no effect. Interpretation also depends on whether current observations already reveal the answer, whether an intervention reaches the reader, and whether stored facts remain valid.

papers.title: PONDER: Learning to Generate in the Right Order
papers.abstract: We introduce PONDER, a method that learns in which order an image generator should fill in content and which of its earlier predictions to revise. Masked generative models construct a sample by repeatedly filling in subsets of missing variables. The order of these partial predictions determines the context available in subsequent steps and therefore affects the quality of the final sample. Common strategies are to choose the order randomly or based on local confidence estimates. Conditioned on the partially generated sample and the generator's features, our policy chooses which positions to fill next and/or which previously filled positions to mask for later regeneration, a mechanism we call rethinking. In this way, the generation process is able to adapt to the evolving context and also to revise earlier predictions. We optimize the policy using group-relative policy gradients, with rewards that measure constraint satisfaction, human preference, or distribution quality. For the latter, we introduce FIDgrad, an image-level reward derived from the (first-order) change in Fréchet Inception Distance caused by adding a generated sample to the current feature distribution. With the generators frozen, learned ordering reduces MAR-B ImageNet FID from 4.09 to 2.78 and raises the accuracy on hard visual Sudokus from 3.9\% to 56.6\%, surpassing uncertainty-based greedy ordering (38.7\%). Rethinking further improves these results to 2.70 FID and 96.7\% accuracy, while increasing the rethinking budget of a fixed policy yields continued improvements at inference time.

papers.intro:
Standard diffusion models generate images by iteratively denoising all spatial locations jointly (Ho et al., 2020; Lipman et al., 2023; Karras et al., 2022; Rombach et al., 2022). An alternative is to factorize generation over spatial locations, using a diffusion model to predict individual patches or subsets conditioned on content that has already been generated (Li et al., 2024). In this setting, the generation order becomes consequential because each prediction determines the context available for subsequent ones. It has been shown that such conditional generation is capable of high-quality image synthesis and spatial reasoning (Fan et al., 2025; Wewer et al., 2025), but also that its performance depends substantially on the chosen patch ordering (Fan et al., 2025; Wewer et al., 2025).

If all conditionals were known exactly, different orderings would yield equivalent factorizations. However, the conditionals that are actually learned do not preserve the equivalence. In practice, generation order substantially affects sample quality (Wewer et al., 2025; Li et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2025). This observation leads to a natural question: Can we learn to adapt the ordering in a sample-dependent way, such that the complete, final sample has the best possible quality?

There are three common strategies to define the order: Fixed schedules, most often in raster-scan order, are independent of the generated content (Esser et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2026; Z.ai, 2026). Random schedules sample a permutation per roll-out, as in masked autoregressive models (Li et al., 2024). These decorrelate training from any particular order but provide no mechanism for exploiting context during inference. Greedy schedules prioritize positions according to confidence or (predicted) difficulty: MaskGIT (Chang et al., 2022; Li et al., 2026) unmasks the tokens the generator is most confident about, SRM (Wewer et al., 2025) selects the ones with the lowest predicted uncertainty, and Patch Forcing (Schusterbauer et al., 2026) estimates a per-patch difficulty score and advances easy regions first, so as to obtain more context for harder ones. All three families share the same limitation: either the order of generation is completely independent of the sample being generated, or it is determined by a greedy one-step proxy.

Among those strategies, only greedy confidence-based schedules adapt the ordering to the intermediate, partial state at all. However, the decision is based on an extremely local proxy: it prioritizes positions that are easy to predict given the current context. Such a strategy does not consider how complex future steps will become based on that decision. Thus, a local prediction that is made with high confidence does not, by itself, mean that it will greatly improve the global sample quality. A highly predictable position may provide little useful context, whereas a less certain one may establish useful structure that constrains further patches.

We introduce Ponder (Policy for Ordering, Next-element DEcisions and Rethinking), a scheme for learning a policy that controls the sequence order during generation, including removal of earlier predictions for subsequent regeneration. To that end, we make the following contributions: • Learned ordering for continuous generators. A policy trained with final-sample rewards that decides where a frozen generator fills content next. It requires only the policy’s own action probabilities, not the generator’s likelihoods, which makes it the first such approach applicable to continuous-token generators with diffusion heads. • A rethinking strategy, where the policy learns which earlier predictions to discard and regenerate as new context becomes available. This enables adaptive revision during sequential generation with a controllable rethinking budget that can be varied at inference time. • FIDgrad, a reward function that turns a distribution-level objective into an image-level reinforcement learning signal. By estimating each sample’s first-order effect on Fréchet Inception Distance, FIDgrad enables a generation policy that directly targets quality at the distribution level. A suite of experiments demonstrates the generality of Ponder across class-conditional generation, text-to-image synthesis, and visual constraint solving. With learned ordering alone, it reduces MAR-B ImageNet FID from 4.09 to 2.78, improves MaskGen-KL-XL HPSv2 from 24.50 to 26.50, and raises hard-Sudoku accuracy from 3.9% to 56.6%. Rethinking further improves these results, to 2.70 FID, 27.80 HPSv2 at R=32R=32, and 96.7% accuracy. Moreover, performance continues to improve as the inference-time budget increases while the policy and generator remain fixed (Figure 1).

papers.title: From Adult Renal Masses to Pediatric Wilms Tumors: Evaluating Cross-Domain Generalization of Kidney Lesion Segmentation on MRI
papers.abstract: Deep learning segmentation models for pediatric oncology are often trained on small, single-center cohorts, whereas much larger datasets exist for adult diseases, such as kidney cancer. Whether models trained on adult renal lesions generalize to pediatric Wilms tumors remains unclear. We trained a segmentation model on single-sequence T1- or T2-weighted adult kidney MRI and evaluated it on a held-out adult test set and a pediatric Wilms tumor cohort, where it was compared with a pediatric-specific nnU-Net. Segmentation performance was quantified using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance. On the adult test set, the model achieved a median DSC of 0.86 for renal lesions. On the pediatric cohort, the adult-trained model achieved a median DSC of 0.85 compared with 0.90 for the pediatric-specific model. Despite differences in age, anatomy, and tumor type, the adult-trained model showed promising performance on pediatric Wilms tumors, with only a modest difference in median DSC compared with the pediatric-specific model. However, non-inferiority could not be shown, highlighting the value of pediatric training data. In future work, a fine-tuning strategy could be explored.

papers.intro:
Deep learning-based segmentation is increasingly used to support tumor volume assessment, treatment planning, and response monitoring in pediatric oncology. However, pediatric imaging datasets are inherently small because of the low incidence of pediatric cancers and the practical limitations in assembling multi-center datasets with expert annotations. Although Wilms tumor is the most common pediatric renal malignancy [12], research remains constrained by the scarcity of large, annotated imaging datasets [4], in contrast to the substantially larger cohorts available for adult renal diseases.

Deep learning-based segmentation is increasingly used to support tumor volume assessment, treatment planning, and response monitoring in pediatric oncology. However, pediatric imaging datasets are inherently small because of the low incidence of pediatric cancers and the practical limitations in assembling multi-center datasets with expert annotations. Although Wilms tumor is the most common pediatric renal malignancy [12], research remains constrained by the scarcity of large, annotated imaging datasets [4], in contrast to the substantially larger cohorts available for adult renal diseases.

Whether models trained on much larger adult datasets can generalize effectively to the pediatric setting remains an open question. For CT-based abdominal organ segmentation, Chatterjee et al. showed that an adult-trained model (TotalSegmentator [13]) achieves significantly lower Dice similarity coefficients (DSCs) on pediatric than on adult CT (0.73 vs. 0.81), with the largest performance drops in smaller anatomical structures [5]. These findings motivate investigating whether a similar generalization gap exists for adult-to-pediatric lesion segmentation on MRI. To the best of our knowledge, this has not been previously investigated. Moreover, the lack of a publicly available adult MRI model for kidney cancer segmentation has so far limited direct assessment of adult-to-pediatric transfer.

In this work, we train a segmentation model on adult kidney lesion MRI and evaluate it on the pediatric Wilms tumor cohort previously used by Buser et al. [4]. Specifically, we (1) quantify the generalization gap between the adult model’s performance on an adult hold-out test set and its performance on pediatric data, and (2) directly compare the adult model with a pediatric-specific nnU-Net, on a per-case basis. To enable further evaluation of adult-to-pediatric transfer alongside existing public pediatric models [3], we release our adult model at https://github.com/DIAGNijmegen/oncology-kidney-abnormality-segmentation.

papers.title: Random Sampling of Almost Periodic Stochastic Processes
papers.abstract: We study the effect of random sampling on stochastic processes whose finite-dimensional distributions are Bohr almost periodic under time shifts. The sampling times are generated independently by a two-sided random walk with positive increments or by a two-sided subordinator. Under a non-degeneracy condition we show that the shifted finite-dimensional distributions of the sampled process converge to those of a strictly stationary process. Consequently, if the sampled process is itself almost periodic in distribution, then it must already be strictly stationary. We further prove an $L^2$-law of large numbers for sampled averages under covariance decay and a uniform second-moment bound, and identify its limit with the mean of the stationary limit process. Finally, for $m$-dependent, $L^2$-uniformly integrable almost periodic processes, we establish a central limit theorem for the centered sampled sums, whose asymptotic variance is given by the autocovariance series of the stationary limit.

The basic question is whether almost periodicity survives under random evaluation, and what asymptotic distributional properties emerge after sampling. The classical theory of periodically and almost periodically correlated processes, introduced by Gladyshev [13] and developed further by Hurd [17], requires the mean and covariance function to be almost periodic in time. We work with a different distributional formulation, which has been studied and characterised by Berger and Mohamed [1]. Definition 2.1 and 2.7), where ℒ⁡(⋅)\mathcal{L}(\cdot) denotes the law of a random vector. Thus, our stationarisation result concerns the full finite-dimensional laws, rather than only first- and second-order characteristics. Random translations have previously been used to obtain stationary processes from nonstationary ones. Hurd [16] showed that an independent shift uniformly distributed over one period stationarises a process with periodic finite-dimensional distributions. Iksanov, Kabluchko and Marynych [18] obtained stationary limits from increasingly spread-out uniform translations of deterministic Besicovitch almost periodic functions, including finite-dimensional convergence under additional spectral assumptions. Our law of large numbers is related to this estimation problem: since M⁡(fX)M(f_{X}) is the zero-frequency Fourier-Bohr coefficient of the mean function, Theorem 4.2 establishes mean-square consistency of the sampled average for this coefficient. For second-order characteristics, Monsan [22] and Dehay and Monsan [9] constructed consistent spectral density estimators from random observations. Dehay and Monsan [10] established consistency and asymptotic normality of spectral covariance estimators under jittered periodic sampling, while Dehay and Dudek [12] studied bootstrap methods for second-order analysis under Poisson sampling. These works concern inference for covariance and spectral characteristics. In this paper, we instead identify the limiting covariance structure of the sampled process and use it to determine the variance in our central limit theorem. Central limit theorems for randomly sampled sums have been established in several stationary settings. Guillotin-Plantard and Prieur [14] prove a central limit theorem for weakly dependent sequences sampled by a transient integer-valued random walk. Brandes and Curato [3, Theorem 3.2] proved a central limit theorem for the sample mean of a stationary Lévy-driven moving-average process observed at independent renewal times. Brandes, Curato and Stelzer [4] obtained inheritance results for strong mixing and weak dependence under renewal sampling of strictly stationary processes. Our Theorem 4.5 needs the original process to be almost periodic in distribution, but not necessarily stationary. We assume mm-dependence and L2L_{2}-uniform integrability, and establish a Gaussian limit for the centered sums. The asymptotic variance is identified through the stationary limit from Section 3. Other works on central limit theorems of processes, which are almost periodic in distributional sense include Berger and Mohamed [1], who obtained a central limit theorem for unsampled, L2L_{2}-uniformly integrable, mm-dependent processes, which are almost periodic in distributional sense. The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 collects the required almost periodicity and sampling tools. papers.title: Integer Reachability in Data VASS
papers.abstract: Data Petri nets are an extension of plain Petri nets where, intuitively speaking, tokens carry data values, and transitions may perform equality tests on data values involved. Likewise, data vector addition systems with states (data VASS) are an extension of plain VASS, and equivalent to data Petri nets. The decidability status of the reachability problem in this model is an established and long-standing open question. In this paper we perform a major step towards resolving this question: we show decidability of the integer reachability problem, where the counters can drop below zero. Contrarily to plain VASS, where integer reachability reduces to integer linear programming, the setting of data VASS is significantly more complex, mostly due to the fact that the state spaces are not finite but orbit-finite (like in register automata). Our decision procedure combines an iterative refinement, resembling the KLM decomposition in plain VASS, with a termination argument via a novel way of bounding the number of data values appearing in the refinement. As corollaries, we deduce decidability of a number of decision problems concerning register automata and data Petri nets.
papers.intro:
We investigate the data extension of vector addition systems with states (data vass, or dvass), a model equivalent to data Petri nets, where tokens carry values from some fixed data domain, and executability of transitions is conditioned by relations between data values involved. We concentrate on equality data domain (𝔸,=)(\mathbb{A},=), i.e., a countably infinite set 𝔸\mathbb{A} of data values (atoms) with equality as the only relation [22, 26, 15]. Richer data domains have been also studied, for instance ordered data [22], i.e., a countably infinite, densely and totally ordered set, or an abstract setting of Petri nets with an arbitrary fixed data domain [21].

The most fundamental decision problem for dvass, the reachability problem, asks, given a dvass together with source and target configurations, if there is a run from the source to the target. The decidability status of the reachability problem in case of equality data is a well known and intriguing open question. The problem becomes quickly undecidable for extensions, e.g., for ordered data [22], or with global freshness [26]. On the other hand, the coverability problem (where we ask if there is a run from the source to a configuration that possibly extends the target by some extra tokens) is decidable for both equality and ordered data, and even for every data domain admitting a certain wqo property [21]. The seminal algorithm for vass reachability, the so-called KLM decomposition [23, 19, 20] invokes, as subroutines, decision procedures for coverability and integer reachability. The latter problem is a relaxation of reachability allowing counters to drop below zero, and again reduces to the reachability problem. Up to now, the integer reachability problem was only known to be decidable in the stateless case, i.e., in data vas [16]. On the other hand, any reasonable adaptation of the KLM decomposition to the data setting necessarily has to use states, and thus indispensably needs an integer reachability subroutine for data vass.

We now briefly discuss the main obstacles towards decidability of dvass integer reachability, and our way of overcoming them. Integer reachability in the stateless case of plain vass, namely in vas, reduces to integer linear programming (ilp). Likewise, integer reachability in the stateless case of data vass, namely in data vas, reduces to orbit-finite ilp [11, 12, 17]. The latter problem, although undecidable in general [11], was shown to be decidable in the special case corresponding to integer reachability [16]. The situation changes dramatically when one moves from the stateless to the stateful setting, and the main reason is that the states of a data vass, similarly to its counters or transitions, are an infinite (but orbit-finite) set (like in register automata [2, 3]). In words, data vas with states are exactly data vas with registers. The precise definition of orbit-finite sets, which provide the mathematical foundation of data-enriched models, is given later. Here it is enough to say that these sets have finite (symbolic) representations (they are definable [5]) and are effective, namely can be processed by (symbolic) algorithms [1, 2, 5].

Solving integer reachability in the stateful setting seems to be a more serious challenge than one might expect. In the stateless (plain or data) case, integer reachability is equivalent to solvability of an instance of ilp called the state equation of a (data) vas. The variables of this ilp are all transitions of a (data) vas, and its equations enforce Kirchhoff input-output balance plus the right total effect of all transitions appearing in a solution. In stateful case, mere solvability of the state equation is not sufficient, since an ilp solution should be connected, as a graph, to guarantee integer reachability. This issue is easily solved in plain vass by guessing a connected subset of transitions, and requiring all the transitions from the set to appear in a solution. A similar approach cannot work in data vass for two reasons. First, the set of transitions is orbit-finite, and consequently the set of its subsets is orbit-infinite and hence not effectively guessable (enumerable). Second, we cannot require all transitions in a chosen subset to appear in a solution since the subset is infinite in general.

As our first key observation we notice that solvability of the state equation implies integer reachability, assuming that the data vass is connected, and the effect 𝐯\mathbf{v} of every transition is reversible, namely the vector −𝐯-\mathbf{v} is a positive linear combination of effects of (other) transitions. (Reversibility is strongly related to the Θ1\Theta_{1} step of the KLM decomposition.) Relying on this observation, we design our decision procedure as an iterative refinement which alternately invokes two reduction steps; one reduction step removes transitions which are currently not connected, while the other removes those which are currently not reversible. As we prove that both reduction steps preserve integer reachability, the iterative refinement becomes a correct algorithm once we know that it terminates.

papers.title: A precessing AGN with S-shaped morphology discovered in MALS
papers.abstract: We present J1221$-$1354, a precessing AGN discovered in the MeerKAT Absorption Line Survey (MALS) using deep L-band (0.9--1.6\,GHz) radio data. Its `S'-shaped morphology, revealed by the excellent surface brightness sensitivity of MeerKAT, is consistent with jet precession. Ancillary optical and infrared data establish the source as a Type 2 AGN in a moderately overdense environment. The approaching (southern) jet is brighter but shorter than the receding jet, with the northern edge of the receding jet showing a significantly younger spectral age. These features are peculiar, but consistent with a jet reorientation event in an asymmetric ambient medium, in which the jet re-enters a cavity of previously deposited plasma. A simple ballistic model yields a precession period of $P=290\pm30$\,Myr, consistent with geodetic precession in a supermassive black hole binary (SMBHB) with a binary separation of less than 1.1\,pc. We expect that deep radio continuum surveys in the near future will uncover many more such systems, helping to further strengthen the connection between jet precession and SMBHBs, and the latter's implications for the gravitational-wave background detected with pulsar timing arrays.

papers.intro:
The study of active galactic nuclei (AGN) yields important insights into the formation and evolution of galaxies and their central black holes. At radio wavelengths, many AGN show powerful jets; while most radio galaxies show symmetric opposing jets, peculiar morphologies are also common, arising from jet interaction with the surrounding medium, most prominently in galaxy clusters, or from jet precession. Precessing jets are identified by their inversion-symmetric morphology, which, depending on precession angle and viewing inclination, ranges from subtle jet bending to ‘S’- and ‘Z’-shaped radio galaxies (Nolting et al., 2023, e.g.,). A number of these were already discovered in early radio surveys (Gower and Hutchings, 1982; Condon and Mitchell, 1984; Hunstead et al., 1984; Taylor et al., 1990, e.g.,). Though the exact cause of precession cannot always be determined, geodetic precession of the black hole spin axis is predicted to arise in a supermassive black hole binary (Begelman et al., 1980; Roos, 1988, SMBHB,), making jet precession a possible indicator of a SMBHB. Indeed, for a number of precessing AGN, the precession is consistent with that induced by a binary companion to the central black hole (Roos, 1988; Krause et al., 2019), or the orbital motion of the binary itself (Roos et al., 1993).

Modern radio interferometers with a large number of antennas concentrated in a central core, such as MeerKAT (Jonas, 2016), the LOw-Frequency ARray (van Haarlem et al., 2013, LOFAR,), and the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (Hotan et al., 2021, ASKAP,), offer excellent sensitivity to faint diffuse radio emission. Surveys with these telescopes are already providing important insights into the physics behind a variety of jet morphologies. A well-known example is the ‘X’-shaped radio galaxy PKS 2014–55, where MeerKAT data indicated a clear preference for hydrodynamical backflow over jet reorientation (Cotton et al., 2020). Other studies have revealed the influence of the cluster environment (Chibueze et al., 2021, e.g.), jet precession (Nandi et al., 2021; Sethi et al., 2024; Misra et al., 2025, e.g.), and in some cases, both simultaneously (Koribalski et al., 2024; Kumari et al., 2024, e.g.). Ancillary optical and radio data, in particular very long baseline interferometry (VLBI), have revealed that some AGN with precessing jets show double-peaked optical emission lines and multiple compact components associated with the core at milli-arcsecond (mas) scales (Nandi et al., 2021). These present strong arguments for the SMBHB origin, however, definitive proof remains elusive.

papers.title: Video Diffusion Avatars: Taming Video Diffusion Models into Controllable 3D Avatars
papers.abstract: Video diffusion models (VDMs) trained on internet-scale data encode a rich prior on appearance, motion, and physics that is difficult to replicate with explicit 3D rendering and costly 3D data capture. We introduce Video Diffusion Avatars (VDAs), a method that creates photo-realistic, multi-view consistent avatars from a single image by fine-tuning a VDM for precise control over camera viewpoint, facial expression, and upper-body pose. Departing from 3D morphable models (3DMMs), VDAs use a learned expression space that lifts the expressiveness ceiling of 3DMMs, e.g., for the tongue and mouth interior. However, learned expression codes exhibit heavy viewpoint bias, as our DISTRACT benchmark reveals. We show that this bias can be removed through disentanglement, enabling their use as driving signals for multi-view consistent avatars. Camera and upper-body pose are controlled jointly via proxy-mesh renderings, giving independent control over expression, pose, and viewpoint. A camera-triplet training strategy makes the approach efficient: our models train for 34 hours on a single A100 using only public multi-view data. VDAs outperform state-of-the-art single-image 3D avatars on novel-view reenactment, reducing face LPIPS by 29% and improving perceptual quality (JOD) by 66% on BecomingLit. A static 3DGS reconstruction probe further confirms that our generations are the most multi-view consistent. Built on a video prior, VDAs produce effects beyond the reach of explicit renderers, including physically plausible hair dynamics, shadows, reflections, and refractions.

papers.intro:
Virtual avatars promise to reshape communication, gaming, and visual effects. Many applications demand exact control over facial expression, upper-body pose, and camera viewpoint, and the smallest artifacts read as uncanny. In-the-wild use raises the bar further: accessories, complex lighting, and hair dynamics must be handled convincingly from a single reference image. The dominant paradigm builds explicit volumetric avatars, typically 3DGS (Kerbl et al., 2023) or voxels (Lombardi et al., 2021; Cao et al., 2022), with expressions driven by 3DMMs (Blanz & Vetter, 1999; Li et al., 2017). This approach faces two fundamental limits. First, no large-scale 3D training data exists, and, additionally, effects such as shadows, reflections, refractions, and physically plausible hair dynamics are hard to render explicitly. Second, 3DMM-driven expression control suffers fidelity loss from 2D-to-3D registration. Alternatively, learned expression spaces (Drobyshev et al., 2022; Cheng et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025) avoid this ceiling but, as our proposed DISTRACT benchmark reveals, carry a heavy viewpoint bias that must be addressed before they can drive multi-view consistent avatars. Video diffusion models (VDMs), trained on internet-scale data, offer a rich prior on 3D geometry, photo-realistic appearance, motion, and physics. However, existing VDM-based avatar methods either build 2D avatars without camera control (Tian et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025), or use the VDM only to synthesize multi-view images that are then distilled into a 3DGS avatar (Taubner et al., 2025b; Taubner et al., 2025a), trading off rendering quality against speed. We introduce Video Diffusion Avatars (VDAs), and depart from the two most common building blocks for virtual avatars: 3DMM-control and 3DGS rendering. Following DH-STAR (Zielonka et al., 2026), we define an avatar as a model that, conditioned on a single identity image, renders that person under any requested facial expression, upper-body pose, and camera viewpoint. In our approach the VDM is the avatar: no 3D asset is ever built, and the prior is fully preserved. VDAs rests on three cornerstones. Expression control: we remove the viewpoint bias from learned expression encoders with an explicit disentangler, obtaining higher expression fidelity than FLAME-driven control. Camera and pose control: a proxy mesh combining a FLAME head with a SAM-3D-Body (Yang et al., 2026b) torso jointly encodes camera viewpoint and upper-body pose, while exposing separate control for both. Training: camera triplets from curated multi-view data (Kirschstein et al., 2023; Martinez et al., 2024), with reference, driver and target from different cameras, teach multi-view consistency in 34 hours on a single A100. VDAs outperform all state-of-the-art single-image 3D avatars on BecomingLit (Schmidt et al., 2025), Multiface (Wuu et al., 2022), and VFHQ-test (Xie et al., 2022), improving LPIPS by 29% and JOD by 66% over the strongest baseline. A 3DGS optimization against our generations outperforms prior diffusion-based avatars (Taubner et al., 2025b; Taubner et al., 2025a), camera-controlled VDMs (Lyu et al., 2026), and 3DGS-based avatars (Kirschstein et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026). Our contributions are: (a) VDAs replace the explicit 3D asset with a camera- and expression-controlled VDM, inheriting shadows, reflections, refractions, and hair dynamics from its prior. (b) We expose viewpoint bias in learned expression encoders with the DISTRACT benchmark, debias it, and obtain higher expression fidelity than FLAME-driven control. (c) Camera and pose conditioning via a Plücker-colored proxy mesh, that separates control over camera viewpoint from neck pose. (d) Affordable training strategy on public multi-view data using camera triplets in 34 hours on a single A100, which preserves performance on challenging in-the-wild inputs.

papers.title: Revisiting separators in string graphs, region intersection graphs, and induced-minor-free graphs
papers.abstract: String graphs are intersection graphs of continuous curves in the plane. In 2010, Fox and Pach proved that string graphs with $m$ edges admit balanced vertex separators of size $\mathcal{O}(m^{3/4}\sqrt{\log m})$ and conjectured that this bound can be improved to $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{m})$, which would be optimal. After partial progress, Lee claimed in 2017 to prove this conjecture, and more generally to prove analogous separator theorems for region intersection graphs over minor-closed graph families. A key intermediate step in Lee's approach was a padded decomposition scheme for region intersection graphs. In 2024, Korhonen and Lokshtanov extended Lee's approach to the broader setting of graph classes excluding a fixed graph as an induced minor. These results have since found applications in a wide range of works. Later in 2024, a flaw was discovered in the construction of Lee's padded decomposition scheme, invalidating Lee's as well as Korhonen and Lokshtanov's separator results, and many works relying on them. In this work, we prove that string graphs with $m$ edges admit balanced separators of size $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{m})$, and more generally obtain analogous $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{m})$ bounds for region intersection graphs over fixed minor-closed graph families and for graphs excluding a fixed graph as an induced minor, thereby repairing the vast majority of the affected works. Furthermore, our balanced separators can be found in polynomial time. Our proof uses a different approach from Lee's and does not rely on padded decompositions. Since padded decompositions have also found applications independent of the separator theorems, particularly for string graphs, we also prove a padded decomposition result for region intersection graphs that is optimal for string graphs. We have formalized both the balanced separator and the padded decomposition results in Lean 4 with mathlib.

papers.title: Beyond SAEs: Consistent Concept Discovery with Sparse Coding
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) explain foundation model representations by decomposing activations into sparse combinations of learned dictionary atoms. However, the learned dictionaries can vary across training runs, limiting the reliability and reproducibility of SAE-based analyses. We propose Consistent Sparse Dictionary Learning (ConSDL), which replaces the standard linear encoder with per-sample sparse coding. This is motivated by our synthetic analysis showing that coefficients from a single linear encoder pass are suboptimal compared with those obtained by per-sample optimization, suggesting that sparse coding is a reliable mechanism for dictionary learning. Across 16 synthetic settings, ConSDL achieves near-perfect dictionary and coefficient recovery. These gains translate to state-of-the-art cross-seed consistency across four vision and language settings, where ConSDL improves dictionary and coefficient consistency by 17.6% and 35.9%, respectively, over the average of six SAE baselines.
papers.intro:
Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) (Cunningham et al., 2023) have become a widely used approach for analyzing the internal representations of foundation models. SAEs decompose each model activation into a sparse linear combination of vectors from a learned overcomplete dictionary. Empirically, these dictionary vectors often align with human-interpretable concepts, such as colors, textures, and objects in vision models (Thasarathan et al., 2025) or characters, words, and syntactic patterns in language models (Elhage et al., 2022; Bricken et al., 2023). Importantly, these concepts can be learned without a predefined vocabulary, enabling scalable explanations of model behavior in vision (Lim et al., 2025; Pach et al., 2026) and language (Templeton et al., 2026), audits of hidden biases in models and datasets (Ahsan and Wallace, 2025; Choi et al., 2026), and identification of candidate factors in scientific and medical data (Dasdelen et al., 2025; Nerrise et al., 2026).

Yet, a critical limitation remains before SAEs can serve as practical tools for analysis. SAEs trained on the same data with the same configuration can learn substantially different dictionaries across random seeds (Paulo and Belrose, 2025). This limits reproducibility and reliability. More fundamentally, it raises the question of whether the features learned by SAEs genuinely reflect the model’s internal representations or are artifacts of the training procedure. Recent work has further heightened this concern by showing that SAEs can fail to recover known ground-truth features in controlled synthetic settings (Korznikov et al., 2026; Pacela et al., 2026).

To this end, ConSDL replaces the linear encoder of SAEs with per-sample sparse coding. The algorithm design is motivated by prior work showing that coefficients predicted by a single encoder pass can be suboptimal compared with those obtained by per-sample optimization (O’Neill et al., 2024). We hypothesize that updating the dictionary with these suboptimal coefficients contributes to inconsistency across training runs. ConSDL therefore uses per-sample sparse coding throughout training to obtain coefficients before each dictionary update. To make this procedure stable in practice, we additionally use coefficient refitting to correct shrinkage from the sparsity penalty and a co-active similarity regularizer to reduce dictionary redundancy.

papers.title: MOSS: Multimodal Origami Swamp Robot System
papers.abstract: Robotic systems for environmental monitoring and ecological surveying in wetlands and swamps must operate across diverse terrestrial and aquatic conditions. Conventional fixed-geometry wheels cannot adapt their contact geometry to these varying conditions. This work presents MOSS (Multimodal Origami Swamp Robot System), a compact amphibious robotic platform with 3D-printed origami wheels. The compact crank mechanism switches the wheel between contracted and expanded configurations, changing its width, body diameter, and fin orientation simultaneously. The contracted configuration is better suited to efficient rolling on firmer ground, whereas the expanded configuration provides greater contact and terrain engagement on softer surfaces. MOSS was evaluated on soil, sand, mud with varying water content, and water, in addition to in-motion morphing and terrestrial-aquatic transition tests. The more energy-efficient wheel configuration depended on terrain. The contracted configuration achieved a lower cost of transport on firmer soil and mud, whereas the expanded configuration performed better on wetter mud, sand, and water, reducing the cost of transport by up to 29%. Expanded wheels also reduced slip in wet mud and reduced both slip and hub sinkage in sand. MOSS successfully completed configuration changes in $1.95 \pm 0.11$ s and demonstrated continuous locomotion across soil-mud-water transitions. Outdoor trials further demonstrated operation across natural deformable terrain and water. These results show that adaptive wheel geometry provides terrain-dependent locomotion benefits and enables a single compact platform to traverse substantially different terrestrial and aquatic conditions.

Environmental change and habitat loss motivate long-term, low-disturbance ecological monitoring for conservation and ecosystem management [1, 2]. Swamps support diverse communities, regulate water, and store carbon [3]. Yet biodiversity observations remain spatially and temporally uneven, while seasonal changes in water level and soil condition make repeated surveys difficult [4]. Robotic platforms can reduce the need for repeated human access while collecting observations in challenging environments [5, 6, 7, 8, 9].

Environmental change and habitat loss motivate long-term, low-disturbance ecological monitoring for conservation and ecosystem management [1, 2]. Swamps support diverse communities, regulate water, and store carbon [3]. Yet biodiversity observations remain spatially and temporally uneven, while seasonal changes in water level and soil condition make repeated surveys difficult [4]. Robotic platforms can reduce the need for repeated human access while collecting observations in challenging environments [5, 6, 7, 8, 9].

However, swamp environments often combine firm ground, sand, soil, mud, and water. These surfaces differ in how they support the robot and provide traction, and soft ground can also lead to wheel sinkage [10]. Firm ground favours low rolling resistance, whereas deformable terrain requires sufficient contact area and shear engagement to limit slip and sinkage. Fixed-geometry wheels cannot change their diameter, width, or contact geometry as these requirements change. Previous studies have shown that transformable and origami-inspired wheels can reconfigure their geometry to adjust ground contact across different terrains [11, 12, 13, 14, 15]. Although these studies establish the feasibility of wheel morphing, integrating axial reconfiguration, terrain-interacting fins, and drive-torque transmission into a single compact mechanism remains challenging. More importantly, the locomotion performance of such multimodal morphing wheels remains insufficiently characterised across swamp-relevant terrestrial and aquatic conditions. To address these gaps, this work presents MOSS (Multimodal Origami Swamp Robot System), an origami wheel mobile platform developed for locomotion across swamp-relevant deformable terrains. With MOSS, a systematic experimental evaluation is conducted across representative terrestrial and aquatic environments to determine how morphing between contracted and expanded configurations alters wheel–surface interactions and delivers terrain-specific locomotion benefits.

papers.title: ENFR: Evidence Networks with Flow-Matched References for Amortized Simulation-Based Model Inference
papers.abstract: The evidence, $\mathcal{Z} = p(x | \mathcal{M})$, of a data-generating model $\mathcal{M}$ is a powerful tool in Bayesian frameworks: it enables model inference, model misspecification tests, and goodness-of-fit assessment as an alternative to standard discrepancy statistics, e.g. $χ^2$. While versatile, the evidence is notoriously difficult to compute, even when the likelihood is available. In both likelihood-based and simulation-based inference, estimating $\mathcal{Z}$ provides an immediate solution to high-dimensional goodness-of-fit or model misspecification tests: using $\mathcal{Z}(x)$ as the test statistic induces a minimum-volume level-$α$ test. Such tests are essential to assess model fidelity, which is necessary to trust simulation-based parameter inference. Existing learned approaches largely target Bayes factors, which only measure evidence ratios. Instead, we provide accurate, fast, and amortized estimates of the absolute evidence. We present ENFR: Evidence Networks with Flow-matched References. Building on the Evidence Network framework of Jeffrey & Wandelt (2024), the proposed method first learns Bayes factors with respect to a flow-matched reference, from which the absolute evidence is recovered. We show improvement in estimation of $\mathcal{Z}$ over the flow-based baseline in all applications considered and the best performance of all density estimation methods considered in our benchmarks. We furthermore introduce and provide the proof for an architecture that jointly learns the individual evidences of a set of models $\{\mathcal{M}_i\}$. We demonstrate the performance and scaling behavior of these approaches on data from a variety of scientific applications.

papers.intro:
Science is fundamentally tasked with modeling nature from first principles, and increasingly this modeling is done with high-fidelity simulators that produce samples from a likelihood that cannot itself be evaluated (Agostinelli et al., 2003; Mesinger et al., 2011; Villaescusa-Navarro et al., 2021, e.g.). Simulation-based inference (SBI) has changed how such models are confronted with data: instead of requiring a tractable likelihood, it enables likelihood-free inference directly from simulator samples (Papamakarios and Murray, 2016; Alsing et al., 2018; Brehmer et al., 2020; Cranmer et al., 2020). These methods have already unlocked information in the data that was previously inaccessible (e.g. von Wietersheim-Kramsta et al., 2025; Thomsen et al., 2026, for recent scientific applications), and are being readily adopted across scientific disciplines.

Traditionally, computing the evidence has been a daunting task as the naive estimation of the integral is quickly intractable in high dimensions. papers.title: Waiting Buys Exactly Two Moments: Endogenous Identification in Prediction-Driven Allocation
papers.abstract: A planner with a fixed budget of preventive help must decide whom to help and when. Waiting reveals risk but removes intervention opportunities as higher-risk individuals leave first. We characterize this tradeoff under repeated noisy signals and risk-dependent attrition: in the canonical model, a length-$τ$ observation prefix identifies exactly the latent risk moments $m_j=\mathbb E[p^j]$ for $j=0,\ldots,2τ-1$, buying two new moments per additional period. These identify average next-period attrition among survivors but need not identify allocation welfare or attrition among those prioritized for treatment. Our observationally equivalent constructions establish unavoidable timing regret at any sample size for a fixed observation length, while exact certificates determine whether all compatible populations share a unique optimal date. Matched experiments separate the effects of estimation, bootstrap averaging, and regret weighting. Longer observation often resolves timing ambiguity, but the optimal date may already have passed. In our experiments, bootstrap averaging and early stopping improve decisions, while regret weighting adds no improvement in pooled mean squared regret: better statistical fit need not yield better allocation welfare. The code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/waiting-buys-two-moments.
papers.intro:
Prediction-driven allocation models, such as Novissi [1], HPU [2], and DEWS [3], guide decisions about who should receive support when resources are insufficient to help everyone. For example, consider a hospital with more seriously ill patients than beds equipped to provide close monitoring and life-saving treatment. Doctors can use the information already available to decide who receives those beds, or wait for more test results to better identify who would benefit most. During that wait, however, some patients may become too ill to be saved. Choosing when to act therefore requires weighing the value of additional information against the opportunities to help that disappear during the delay.

This work closes this gap by establishing what a limited observation period reveals about the population’s risks and whether that information is enough to choose the best intervention date. We show that the observations can reveal how many people are expected to lose their opportunity for help during the next period and establish when these observations determine the best intervention date versus when they leave the decision unresolved.

Furthermore, we find that uncertainty about the best time to intervene can persist even when the number of people observed becomes arbitrarily large. This raises a practical question: how do estimation, averaging, and decision criteria affect allocation performance on selected reference populations in this partially identified model? To investigate this question, we compare risk estimation, bootstrap aggregation, and ambiguity-aware decision criteria using simulated populations with known welfare curves. Procedures recommend dates for a future population with the same risk distribution. Comparisons within a common information set isolate the effects of fitting, averaging, and selecting a date.

Our contributions are: 1. Information and timing limits. We characterize the moments revealed by observation, distinguish identified attrition from potentially unidentified welfare, and derive a regret floor that persists at every sample size. 2. Exact decision identification. We reduce comparisons of nonlinear allocation welfare over an infinite-dimensional moment class to two-parameter branch-and-bound with polynomial certificates verified on [0,1][0,1]. This certifies a common optimal date or produces an exactly compatible counterexample, for both unrestricted and still-available dates. 3. Decision performance under limited information. We compare risk estimation, bootstrap aggregation, and ambiguity-aware rules. Comparisons holding information fixed show that early stopping can outperform a converged likelihood fit, while regret weighting offers no improvement over ordinary averaging in the reported pooled results.

papers.title: ModeCast: One-Shot Prediction of Linear MHD Eigenmodes and Growth Rates in Tokamaks
papers.abstract: Large-scale magnetohydrodynamic instabilities break plasma confinement, can trigger disruptions, and constrain fusion reactor design; modeling a single configuration against them takes hours with a reference solver such as JOREK, and a design study requires thousands of hours. ModeCast is the first learned surrogate to return the complete linear stability assessment for MHD modes. Trained on a comprehensive dataset of over 45,000 JOREK simulations across thousands of equilibria, it screens stability across toroidal mode numbers n=1-4 and predicts the full spatial structure and growth rate of unstable modes. With a second network of the same architecture replacing the equilibrium solve, the full pipeline from design parameters runs on one GPU up to 1,000,000x faster than JOREK's equilibrium and linear stability runs. The gain comes from building the linear-phase physics into the formulation, objective, and inputs, yielding up to six times more training data. ModeCast misses none of the unstable held-out cases, and its predicted fields reproduce the simulation's measured physics, from magnetic island topology to resistivity trends. On a fixed-geometry resistivity scan outside its training distribution, refitting only the 22k-parameter growth rate head of the 145M-parameter network on four simulation halves the held-out internal kink growth rate error, and fine-tuning the whole network adds little. Because it is differentiable and returns full fields, ModeCast could in the future assimilate experimental measurements, providing a bridge to real devices and accelerating progress toward commercial fusion. Project page: zenithon.ai/research/modecast.
papers.intro:
Tokamaks are the leading confinement concept for fusion power, and large-scale magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) instabilities, growing from small perturbations of the plasma equilibrium, degrade confinement and set hard operational limits on any design (Zhu et al., 2023). Assessing a configuration’s stability is a central, recurring task, and the reference method is expensive: initialize a nonlinear MHD code such as JOREK (Hoelzl et al., 2021; Pamela et al., 2020; Artola et al., 2021), perturb, and evolve for hours on tens of cores per linear run, for thousands of configurations and modes.

Assessing a configuration’s stability is a central, recurring task, and the reference method is expensive: initialize a nonlinear MHD code such as JOREK (Hoelzl et al., 2021; Pamela et al., 2020; Artola et al., 2021), perturb, and evolve for hours on tens of cores per linear run, for thousands of configurations and modes.

Existing methods trade speed against completeness. Reduced models and analytic criteria are fast but partial (Haverkort et al., 2016). Learned scalar surrogates, trained one instability family at a time, return only a growth rate or a stability label, leaving the identity and location of the mode unknown (Piccione et al., 2020; Bruncrona et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Kumar et al., 2026). Field-level surrogates resolve the fields, but target neighboring regimes and forecast evolution in time rather than one-shot linear stability (Carey et al., 2025; Paischer et al., 2025; Gopakumar et al., 2023). The closest prior work (Chang et al., 2025) covers a single-mode family in cylindrical geometry and reports accuracy only on scalar targets. No existing surrogate answers the question a designer asks of a configuration: which mode is unstable, where it sits, and how fast it grows.

papers.title: CLARO: Clutter Aware Robot Orchestrator for Open-Vocabulary Grasping using VLM Agents
papers.abstract: Robots that follow natural-language instructions unlock a wide range of autonomous applications in households, warehouses, and labs. Real-world environments are diverse and often heavily cluttered, requiring robots to plan over multiple steps, act, and replan as they work toward a goal. We present CLARO (CLutter-Aware Robot Orchestrator), a VLM agent that orchestrates a set of perception and manipulation skills: open-vocabulary object detection, segmentation, 6-DoF grasping, and non-prehensile pushing to locate and retrieve a language-specified target in clutter. CLARO maintains a memory of its past actions to support long-horizon execution, and emits manipulation targets (grasp poses/3D waypoints) allowing transfer across robot arms without task-specific training. We evaluate CLARO against a range of methods on a dynamic simulation environment and standard image-based benchmarks, demonstrating strong generalization across object classes, lighting, and clutter levels. CLARO attains an average success rate of 89.1%, a relative improvement of over 16% on the strongest competing method in high cluttered scenes. We further analyze performance along grounding and grasping axes to characterize where each method succeeds and fails. Finally, we deploy CLARO on a robot arm across diverse cluttered scenes, achieving a success rate of 88.8%, and demonstrating strong sim2real generalizability.

papers.intro:
Grasping objects specified by natural-language is a long-standing goal of robotics and embodied AI [8]. An instruction like “hand me the small screwdriver behind the mug” requires grounding an open-vocabulary referred object and reasoning about its spatial position in the scene. Vision Language Models (VLMs) have brought this goal within reach: by jointly reasoning over images and language, they form a perception backbone that grounds free-form text instructions to the robot’s visual observations [7, 28]. VLMs have been adapted for Language-Driven Robot Manipulation (LDRM) in tasks such as pick-and-place and articulated-object manipulation [2, 22].

An instruction like “hand me the small screwdriver behind the mug” requires grounding an open-vocabulary referred object and reasoning about its spatial position in the scene. Vision Language Models (VLMs) have brought this goal within reach: by jointly reasoning over images and language, they form a perception backbone that grounds free-form text instructions to the robot’s visual observations [7, 28]. VLMs have been adapted for Language-Driven Robot Manipulation (LDRM) in tasks such as pick-and-place and articulated-object manipulation [2, 22].

Recent works use two frameworks for LDRM. Referring Grasp Synthesis (RGS) methods finetune VLMs to predict grasp poses directly from an image and a task instruction, which are then executed by a controller [29, 2, 23]. These methods are trained on large datasets comprising static RGB-D scenes in which the target is assumed to be visible and graspable from the camera view. This assumption breaks down in dynamic environments when objects are occluded and the robot must intelligently search through multiple manipulation steps. The second framework uses end-to-end Vision Language Action (VLA) models that learn a mapping from pixels and language to motor actions, and are deployed closed-loop in both simulation and real hardware [22, 14, 9]. VLAs enable fine-grained robot control and adaptability to a wide range of embodiments but are often evaluated in-distribution: on objects, scenes, and instructions close to the training data. VLAs report poor performance on unseen and open-vocabulary objects, making them unsuitable for deployment in novel environments [1, 32]. Neither framework suffices: RGS cannot search through clutter, and VLAs do not generalize beyond their training distribution, yet retrieving a target in practice requires both. Real environments such as homes, labs, and warehouses are noisy and cluttered, with targets frequently occluded, so a robust system must actively declutter the scene through a multi-step, closed-loop process of planning, grounding, and execution, all while remaining open-vocabulary and deployable without retraining.

Grounding novel objects and decluttering over multiple steps requires a system that perceives, plans, and acts in a closed loop. Tool-calling VLM agents, which show strong spatial reasoning beyond conventional VLMs, are naturally suited to this: rather than learning a monolithic policy, they invoke skills, observe outcomes, and re-plan [5, 26]. A VLM agent in robotics can use a set of skill APIs within a closed loop safety-bounded rulebook, to invoke perception and manipulation functions, observe the environment, and re-plan [11]. Such methods are suitable for clutter manipulation precisely because robot environments are dynamic, the scene changes after every action, demanding iterative grounding, occlusion reasoning, and re-planning (Fig. 1).

We present CLARO (CLutter-Aware Robot Orchestrator), a VLM agent that turns a set of perception and manipulation skills into a general-purpose, open-vocabulary object grasper. Given a cluttered workspace and a language-specified target, CLARO generates planning traces, reasons about occlusions, and executes motion that actively declutters the scene while searching for the target. Once the object is sufficiently exposed, it executes a feasible grasp to retrieve it. CLARO requires no environment-specific finetuning and is the only system to combine open-vocabulary grounding, closed-loop planning, long-term memory, 66-DoF grasping, and non-prehensile decluttering (Tab. 1).

papers.title: Benchmarking and Improvement of Artifact Segmentation Methods in H&E-Stained Whole Slide Imaging
papers.abstract: Technical artifacts introduced during tissue preparation or slide scanning remain a major obstacle to developing robust computational pathology algorithms for hematoxylin and eosin (HE)-stained whole-slide images (WSIs). Despite the growing number of quality-control tools, their real-world utility remains hard to assess because of the limited number of publicly available implementations and the lack of systematic, multi-dataset comparisons. This paper presents a benchmark of artifact segmentation methods for HE-stained WSIs. After a literature review, six publicly available algorithms were selected and compared in terms of their ability to segment artifact-free tissue and selected artifact classes. Two publicly available datasets and a newly introduced dataset released to support further research were used for evaluation. Tissue samples from multiple medical centers and different organs are included, enabling evaluation across heterogeneous data sources. Segmentation performance was assessed using Dice Index, pixel-level recall, and false discovery rate for artifact-free tissue segmentation. For algorithms supporting multiclass artifact segmentation, class-wise Dice Index and inter-class misclassification were evaluated. In addition to segmentation quality, processing time was assessed. Statistical analysis revealed significant differences in segmentation performance between methods. HistoKit, which incorporates a modified version of the GrandQC, was identified as the best-performing algorithm, while HistoQC was the worst. In terms of artifact types, dark spots and out of focus regions were harder to segment than others. Finally, a simple post-processing step was introduced for HistoKit, which further improved segmentation performance. The benchmark establishes a reference for evaluating and developing artifact segmentation methods for HE-stained WSIs.

Tissue-level artifacts arise during tissue preparation, a stage that requires significant precision and expertise in both laboratory procedures and sample collection [29]. The final appearance of the tissue specimen is influenced by numerous variables. Minor variations in preparation protocols, such as fixation time, temperature, tissue thickness, or reagent volumes, are almost inevitable in routine laboratory practice. Therefore, establishing a universal protocol for all laboratories is nearly impossible [52]. Several types of tissue-level artifacts can occur during slide preparation. For example, excessive dehydration of the tissue can cause it to shrink. Cracks in tissue may also be seen, most often resulting from a dull knife or an improperly performed cut. Another common finding is tissue folding. Unfortunately, artifacts from this group are often challenging or even impossible to repair. In most cases, this would require repeating the sample collection process or even performing a new biopsy [25].

papers.title: ToolRosetta: Surface-Form Invariance of Tool-Call Guards
papers.abstract: Step-level guards for tool-using agents are evaluated on tidy JSON tool calls, but deployed coding agents act through execute_bash and execute_code tools whose payloads are strings. We introduce ToolRosetta, which re-renders every candidate action in the AgentDojo and AgentHarm splits of TS-Bench as a Python call, as a shell command, and without the agent's rationale. The renderings are produced by code and verified by round-trip parsing, so the user request, the history, the label and the action's effect stay fixed while only the surface form changes. Across eleven guards with two placebo controls, frontier and strong open-weight guards are stable: no frontier error rate moves by more than 3.4 points. Four of five specialized agent guards are not: under the shell form their false-positive rates rise by 21 to 47 points on AgentDojo, and TS-Guard's by 38 points on its own home benchmark, blocking between a third and nine in ten benign actions; the fifth, StepGuard, does not move. A small open guard drifts five points more permissive. Removing the agent's rationale moves most guards whose input carries it, in guard-specific directions. A request-blind control on one guard shows that the rationale is where intent is read from. A parser that restores the canonical call in front of the guard removes the effect for these renderings, by construction. Benchmark accuracy on JSON calls does not predict a guard's operating point behind a code-acting agent.

Runtime guards that approve or block an agent’s tool call before execution are the most direct defense for tool-using agents (Mou et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026; Chennabasappa et al., 2025). Code-acting agents (Wang et al., 2024; Wang and others, 2025) route most actions through one or two generic tools, execute_bash and execute_code, and the action the guard must judge is a string inside the argument. The same reservation, transfer or deletion arrives as reserve_hotel(hotel=...) inside a code block or as reserve-hotel --hotel ... inside a shell command.

papers.title: Managing complexity for integrated fusion reactor design using a differentiable graph-based MDAO framework: PROCESS as a case study
papers.abstract: Integrated design of nuclear fusion reactors requires combining an increasingly large number of models from different disciplines self-consistently, with model selection and parametrisation changing between design studies. Manual definition of execution order and solvers for cyclic dependencies is error-prone, inefficient, and inflexible. We propose to use a generic graph-based coordination and execution core that enables automated execution order, cycle detection, and solver architecture specification for any set of models or parametrisation. To this end, a computational dependency graph of purely functional models is extended by a conditional node and nesting edges, treating solvers and optimisers in the same way. A minimal set of graph operations then allows for fine-tuned control on feedback resolution, making both optimiser and solver architectures easily reconfigurable. Existing monolithic multidisciplinary design analysis and optimisation (MDAO) architectures can be recovered by sequentially applying these operations. The cottax package implements this extended dependency graph, graph operations, executability checks, and a JAX-based execution layer. This execution layer eliminates runtime overhead and provides native gradient computation through the whole graph. As a proof of principle, cottax is then applied to the PROCESS systems code. Graph sequencing shows that for PROCESS only three small coupled components need to be solved every optimiser iteration. Monolithic MDAO architectures are then assigned to seven different PROCESS configurations, demonstrating the ease of (re)configuring its architecture. Compared to PROCESS, the sequencing and execution back-end together yield a two to three orders of magnitude reduction in model runtime during optimisation. cottax is currently being considered as the basis for developing an integrated stellarator MDAO framework.

Nuclear fusion reactors are complex to design, requiring highly specialised teams of experts working on interdependent subsystems. A complete engineering design may take years, which precludes the many evaluations required for design space exploration and optimisation. In practice, exploration and optimisation are thus carried out with a reduced parametrisation of the reactor (a small set of high-level decisions such as major radius, magnetic field strength, net electric power, blanket type and thickness) and with reduced-fidelity models of its behaviour [1].

Fusion systems codes [2, 3, 4] integrate a set of low- or medium-fidelity models self-consistently to compute system-level design objectives (e.g. cost of electricity) and engineering constraint satisfaction as a function of these high-level decisions. With an optimisation algorithm [5] these models are then executed iteratively to find an optimal design candidate within this parametrisation — an approach more generally known as multidisciplinary design analysis and optimisation (MDAO) [6, 7, 8]. The resulting optimum serves as the starting point for detailed engineering design.

However, the behaviour predicted by the low-fidelity models often turns out to be inconsistent with that obtained in detailed engineering design [9, 10] (e.g. the breeding blanket might not produce its target tritium breeding ratio when 3D effects are taken into account). Since the optimality and engineering constraint satisfaction of the design candidate were established with respect to the low-fidelity models, such inconsistencies imply it is at best non-optimal and at worst unviable, in which case the high-level decisions must change. This is expensive: the strong coupling between subsystems [1] means such a change rarely stays local. For example, a thicker blanket also affects the coil geometry, vacuum vessel, and support structure, which then all require a detailed redesign.

papers.title: Empirical Insights from AI-Powered Software Engineering in Practice
papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is becoming indispensable in future software engineering. Its application spans a wide spectrum - from assisted development to autonomous software engineering, requiring organizations to address associated risks and challenges. This paper investigates these issues through three case studies, highlighting practical problems encountered during GenAI integration. Based on these findings, it provides targeted recommendations for managing risks and ensuring reliable outcomes. This paper provides guidance for effective and responsible GenAI adoption in software engineering based on empirical insights.
