papers.title: Hidden Disruption in Milky Way-like Satellite Galaxy Populations
papers.abstract: Determining whether a satellite galaxy is tidally disrupting from photometric observations alone remains a fundamental challenge in near-field cosmology. Cosmological simulations of Milky Way-mass galaxies predict that satellite populations should be highly disrupted, yet the observed Milky Way satellite population appears largely intact. Understanding this tension requires either uncovering disruption that has gone undetected in Milky Way satellites, or identifying limitations in the simulations themselves. We use the Auriga suite of cosmological simulations to evaluate several commonly used indicators of disruption. We find that, in the simulated satellite population, the shape, size, and proper motion alignment of a satellite's bound component are unreliable indicators of its present-day disruption state despite their widespread use in the literature. In contrast, the extended stellar distribution, specifically the ratio of stellar mass between $3r_{1/2}$ and $10r_{1/2}$ to that within $r_{1/2}$, is strongly correlated with disruption. We introduce the extended mass ratio $μ_{\rm EMR}$ as a metric for comparing extended stellar distributions across satellites of varying masses and exploring their connection to disruption in Milky Way observations. Applying this metric to a sample of Milky Way satellites with measured extended stellar distributions, we find that many are consistent with significant ongoing disruption, even among systems traditionally classified as intact. These results suggest that tidal disruption may be substantially more widespread in the observed Milky Way satellite population than currently recognized, and establish extended stellar distributions as a promising new tool for uncovering this hidden disruption.

Cosmological baryonic simulations are among the most powerful tools for studying galaxy formation and evolution [49]. Within a Λ​CDM\rm\Lambda CDM framework, such simulations reproduce observations of large-scale structure, galaxy clusters, and individual galaxies [126, 138, 143]. In these simulations, structures assemble hierarchically – dark matter halos merge over time, and stars and gas follow the underlying potential [171, 170]. Galaxies form within the dark matter halos and subsequently merge. Smaller galaxies can orbit a more massive host galaxy as satellites, and are disrupted by the tidal field of the host galaxy [16, 69, 28]. This process of tidal disruption produces features such as streams and shells [37, 127, 96, 47, 158] that may persist in the stellar halo of the host galaxy.

Satellite galaxies provide some of the most powerful tests of Λ​CDM\rm\Lambda CDM on small scales. Early comparisons between observed and simulated populations of low-mass galaxies revealed a number of apparent discrepancies [see 15, for a review], which have largely been resolved by simulations with higher resolution and more complete baryonic physics [169, 52, 50, 136, 74, 13, 126] together with deeper and wider surveys of the Milky Way (MW) halo [38, 39, 146]. Current simulations of MW-mass galaxies reproduce the abundance, radial distribution, and internal properties of the observed satellite population reasonably well. However, recent comparisons of disrupting satellites and stellar streams reveal a new discrepancy: these same simulations predict far more tidal disruption than is observed among the MW satellites [132, 124, 133]. This raises the question of whether simulated satellite populations match the real MW as well as their successes elsewhere suggest.

A. H. Riley et al. [124], hereafter Auriga Streams 1 (124), found roughly twice as many massive streams as intact satellites of similar mass around simulated MW-mass hosts, considering systems with M∗≥5×105M_{*}\geq 5\times 10^{5}M⊙\mathrm{\,M_{\odot}}. In contrast, the MW has only a sixth as many known streams as intact satellites above this mass limit [107, 81]. Similarly, the Feedback In Realistic Environments (FIRE-2) suite of zoomed cosmological-baryonic simulations of MW-mass galaxies [167, 168] shows roughly four times as many massive streams as are observed around the MW [113, 2, 61]. In N. Shipp et al. [133], hereafter Auriga Streams 2 (133), the disruption of satellite galaxies is closely tied to orbital history, with smaller pericenters correlated with greater tidal disruption. While the overall distances and pericenters are consistent with the MW, the disruption in the Auriga simulations can occur at larger distances than it does within the MW: the simulated streams have pericenters up to roughly three times the largest pericenter of a MW stream and have much larger apocenters. Meanwhile, intact MW satellites exist at far smaller distances than their simulated counterparts. As with previous small-scale structure discrepancies, the apparent disagreement in disruption rates is likely shaped by both simulation and observational limitations.

Because many stream features are predicted to be too faint for current telescopes, attention has turned to the stars surrounding the bright, detectable cores of satellites. In photometric observations without velocity information, a satellite lacking a visible tidal tail or other disruption feature is typically considered intact, and disruption must be inferred from structural parameters – the 2D projected morphology (shape) and physical extent (size) – of the apparently undisrupted component. In large-scale surveys with radial velocity or proper motion measurements – for example from Gaia – individual member stars can be kinematically associated with their progenitor satellite even at large projected distances, revealing the extended stellar component. Tidal disruption analyses combine these approaches along with backward orbit integration to quantify the orbit and the tracks of possible tidal debris.

Boötes III, often associated with the Styx stream, is likely tidally disrupted, though its connection to the Styx stream remains uncertain [18, 82, 67]. A. Chiti et al. [21] identified members of Tucana II out to ∼9​r1/2\sim 9r_{1/2}, and subsequent membership analyses have identified stars well beyond the central bound region of ∼\sim12 MW satellites, in some cases reaching out to 12​r1/212r_{1/2} [66, 147]. papers.title: An ALMA view on molecular complexity: water, methanol, and methyl formate in the HD 100546 and IRS 48 disks
papers.abstract: Water and methanol are the fundamental constituents of interstellar and cometary ices: understanding their abundances in disks is therefore of high importance to reveal how this ice reservoir evolves across the timeline of star and planet formation. We present ALMA band 5 line emission observations of water and methanol in the warm Herbig disks of HD 100546 and IRS 48. While the IRS 48 disk is methanol-rich, water vapor is not detected, implying a high methanol-to-water column density ratio >0.2, possibly reflecting a distinct ice composition. Methanol and water are both detected in the HD 100546 disk, leading to a CH3OH/H2O ratio of ~0.02, consistent with the median of the cometary distribution and with the lower edge of the distribution of Young Stellar Objects. We suggest that the gas-phase methanol-to-water ratio in the HD 100546 disk directly reveals the ice reservoir subsequently sublimated in the warm disk stage. Moreover, we report a methyl formate-to-methanol ratio in the IRS 48 disk of ~0.2, consistent with the upper edge of the distribution of Young Stellar Objects. The methyl formate-to-methanol ratio in the HD 100546 disk is ~2, much higher than in younger and older sources, possibly reflecting a chemical enhancement of gas-phase methyl formate. We additionally constrain non-LTE conditions, optical depths, and emitting regions of the methanol lines in both disks. These results offer a new opportunity to probe the chemical trail of molecular complexity in the intermediate disk stage, bridging early and late phases of the star and planet formation history.

papers.intro:
Water and complex organic molecules (COMs) are basic ingredients for the development of pre-biotically relevant molecules detected in comets and meteorites, and they are primary components of interstellar ices [56, 86, 10]. Probing the relative abundance of water and COMs encapsulated within these icy grains is thus fundamental to tracing the evolution of molecular complexity across the star and planet formation history [88, 30], starting from the simplest COM, i.e. methanol. A rich statistics on the methanol-to-water ratio has been collected in clouds, Young Stellar Objects (YSOs), and comets from both ice and gas measurements [see e.g. 13, 65, for a review]. While CH3​OH/H2​O\text{CH}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}\text{OH}\text{/}\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O} ratios are largely consistent among clouds and YSOs, cometary values are slightly lower. This could be indicative of either a variation in the abundance of primordial ice in the solar nebula itself, or of a different degree of ice reprocessing in the protosolar disk [89]. Tracing the intermediate protoplanetary disk stage is thus of primary importance to build a bridge between early and later stages of star formation. In this context, the ice reservoir of water and/or methanol has been suggested to be inherited from early stages of star formation for a few sources [15, 118, 1, 75, HD 100546, V883 Ori, L1551 IRS5].

In this picture, methanol is known to form only in the ice phase, primarily from hydrogenation of CO-rich ice, while it cannot efficiently form through gas-phase reactions [132, 51, 53, 50, 102, 105]. Observations of gas-phase methanol thus reveal the ice content that is released through thermal and/or non thermal processes [130, 15, 120, 115, 42]. This offers a window into the methanol ice budget in protoplanetary disks, an intermediate stage between young protostellar systems and evolved planetary and cometary objects. Combined with observations of sublimated water vapor, these gas-phase methanol observations uniquely allow to reveal if the methanol and water ice content in disks is inherited from early stages of star formation.

papers.title: Maximal efficiency of geometric beaming and polarization of highly super-Eddington X-ray sources
papers.abstract: Geometric beaming is an often invoked explanation for the apparent super-Eddington luminosities of ultraluminous X-ray sources. It is a natural consequence of the geometrically thick envelope that is expected to surround the inner accretion disk in the super-Eddington accretion regime; as the radiation can only freely escape through a narrow funnel-shaped cavity, the flux along the funnel axis is enhanced. A fraction of the photons will nevertheless escape the funnel cavity at larger angles, reducing the effectiveness of the beaming. To explore the limits of geometric beaming, we performed Monte Carlo simulations of conservative radiative transfer in an infinitely optically thick funnel while accounting for polarization. We discovered that the beaming becomes inefficient when the funnel opening angle is small $(\lesssim15^\circ$) because the photons tend to remain trapped within the cavity until they reach the upper edge of the funnel where they can escape at larger angles. For most of the photons to escape a narrow funnel through a small solid angle, the funnel has to be unrealistically long. Consequently, geometric beaming could at most boost the apparent luminosity by a factor of a few dozen in our idealized simulations. While larger boost factors on the order of $\sim$100 are possible for funnels with a length of $\gtrsim10^5$ Schwarzschild radii, this requires very narrow opening angles of $\lesssim3^\circ$. Additionally, we found that aberration due to mildly relativistic velocities does not significantly change this result. The maximal polarization degree of light reflected by the funnel remained on the order of a few percent for face-on sources and $\lesssim10\%$ for edge-on sources.

papers.intro:
Ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs) are extragalactic X-ray binaries (XRBs) that appear to exceed the Eddington luminosity for stellar-mass (∼\sim10M☉M_{\sun}) compact objects (Kaaret et al. 2017; King et al. 2023, for reviews, see e.g.). Following the discovery of pulsating ULXs (PULXs) evidently harboring neutron stars, it has become clear that the inferred isotropic luminosity can be greater than the Eddington limit of the compact object by a factor of ∼\sim100 (Bachetti et al. 2014). ULXs offer insight into the poorly understood physics of accretion in the super-Eddington domain, which is also key for understanding the growth of supermassive black hole seeds on cosmic time scales. The extreme apparent luminosities of ULXs cannot, however, be explained by classical accretion disk models, since the radiation pressure is expected to drive powerful outflows that limit the accretion rate (Shakura and Sunyaev 1973). Greater accretion rates may still be possible due to advection of radiation trapped in the accretion flow, leading to a reduction of the radiative efficiency (Begelman 1979; Abramowicz et al. 1988).

Greater accretion rates may still be possible due to advection of radiation trapped in the accretion flow, leading to a reduction of the radiative efficiency (Begelman 1979; Abramowicz et al. 1988).

A number of effects can enhance the observed luminosity of ULXs beyond the expected Eddington limit (see Middleton et al. 2026, for a review). Firstly, the true limiting luminosity may be higher. If ULXs feature magnetars, the extremely strong magnetic field (≳\gtrsim1014​G10^{14}\penalty\ \mathrm{G}) can sufficiently reduce the electron scattering opacity of the accreting gas to raise the Eddington limit (Canuto et al. 1971; Mushtukov et al. 2015). This has been used to explain the most luminous PULXs discovered, which exceeded the Eddington luminosity by a factor of ∼\sim1000 (Israel et al. 2017). Nonetheless, the number of accreting magnetars is expected to be small, as none are observed in the Milky Way. Additionally, if some non-pulsating ULXs feature intermediate-mass black holes, they can produce large luminosities while remaining in the sub-Eddington regime (Colbert and Mushotzky 1999; Farrell et al. 2009).

Secondly, the radiatively driven outflow or geometrically thick accretion disk of an ULX may allow light to escape only through a funnel-shaped cavity. This causes the source to be geometrically beamed akin to a searchlight, enhancing the flux along the funnel axis. Even if the source luminosity is Eddington-limited, the beaming would make the inferred isotropic luminosity appear much greater (King et al. 2001). In contrast, these sources would appear highly obscured when viewed away from the funnel axis. Obscured XRBs such as SS433 may thus represent ULXs viewed edge-on (Fabrika 2004; Koljonen and Tomsick 2020). The recently discovered little red dots (LRDs) have also been suspected as highly obscured super-Eddington sources (Pacucci and Narayan 2024; King 2025; Kritos and Silk 2026).

In the idealized case for geometric beaming, all of the emitted radiation is assumed to escape through the solid angle subtended by the funnel opening from the central source. However, this approximation can overestimate beaming efficiency. General relativistic radiative magnetohydrodynamical (GRRMHD) simulations of super-Eddington accretion show a varying degree of collimation, but a significant fraction of the luminosity escapes away from the funnel opening (Jiang et al. 2014; Kitaki et al. 2021; Zhang et al. 2025a, see, e.g.,). This is in part explained by the finite opacity of the outflow allowing radiation to “leak” beyond the funnel cavity. Moreover, a fraction of the radiative luminosity is lost to the kinetic luminosity of the outflow (Sądowski and Narayan 2015).

papers.title: Expand-and-Prune: Test-Time Candidate-Space Adaptation for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Candidate-based end-to-end driving planners reason over a finite set of trajectory hypotheses. However, for sparse planners, a limited candidate set may provide insufficient support for scene-relevant maneuvers, while fixed downstream candidate budgets do not account for prediction uncertainty. To address these challenges, we introduce Expand-and-Prune, a test-time framework that jointly adapts candidate support and capacity without updating learned parameters. The framework expands the native candidate set using semantic driving intent and temporally propagated predictions and then uses uncertainty in intermediate trajectory scores to adaptively prune the resulting candidates. Across four heterogeneous candidate-based planners and four benchmarks, Expand-and-Prune consistently improves planning performance. It achieves state-of-the-art results on LangAuto, increasing the Driving Score from 68.2 to 75.9, while providing further improvement on Bench2Drive, Fail2Drive, and NAVSIMv2, with particularly strong improvements in out-of-distribution scenarios. Moreover, in its full instantiation, 72.5% of selected trajectories originate from the newly introduced intent-guided or temporal candidates, confirming that candidate-space expansion provides useful hypotheses beyond those generated natively by the planner. The code is available at https://github.com/iis-esslingen/Expand-and-Prune.

Rather than predicting only a single trajectory, many recent planners capture multimodal driving behavior through a finite set of motion hypotheses. These candidates may originate from offline precomputed trajectory vocabularies or clustered anchors [14, 17, 34, 27], or be generated and refined online through learned queries, diffusion, or related generative mechanisms [13, 5, 18, 41, 22]. The planner subsequently scores or refines these hypotheses before selecting a trajectory for execution [17, 34, 27].

Despite advances in candidate generation, how motion hypotheses are constructed and how many are propagated downstream remains largely prescribed by the planner’s inference design. First, for sparse anchor- or proposal-based planners [18, 19], a limited number of hypotheses must cover a broad motion space and may therefore provide only limited support for the maneuver currently favored by the scene. For example, a generic candidate set may contain only a few hypotheses matching a sharp turn even when the current semantic belief strongly favors that maneuver. Second, a fixed downstream candidate budget, often implemented through static Top-KK selection, treats confident and ambiguous scenes alike, propagating the same number of hypotheses regardless of how many plausible alternatives remain [34, 27]. Such limitations may become particularly consequential over longer closed-loop horizons and under distribution shift, where the planner may encounter scene configurations and maneuvers that are poorly represented by its training distribution and native candidate set.

papers.title: A Hectospec Spectroscopic Census of Kinematic Members in the Orion Nebula Cluster
papers.abstract: We present a comprehensive spectroscopic census of the Orion Nebula Cluster (ONC), based primarily on low-resolution optical spectroscopy obtained with MMT/Hectospec. We derive spectral types, youth indicators, and accretion diagnostics for 1513 stars located in the ONC region, enabling the identification and characterization of pre-main-sequence stars. We combine these measurements with a kinematic membership analysis based on Gaia Data Release 3 astrometry to identify and confirm cluster members. Using these combined diagnostics, we identify and characterize 780 bona fide T Tauri stars associated with the ONC. In addition, we construct a census of protoplanetary discs using infrared photometry obtained with the IRAC and MIPS instruments aboard the Spitzer Space Telescope. We further derive stellar masses, ages, and extinctions using the MassAge code, which combines photometric and spectroscopic inputs with stellar evolutionary models, and employs a Monte Carlo approach for uncertainty propagation. The resulting homogeneous catalogue of ONC members provides spectroscopic characterizations, kinematic membership constraints, disc diagnostics, and self-consistent estimates of stellar physical parameters. This dataset offers a refined view of the stellar population of the ONC and provides a robust foundation for investigating its kinematic structure, age distribution, and protoplanetary disc population.

papers.intro:
The Orion Nebula Cluster (ONC) is one of the nearest and youngest regions of high-mass star formation, with an age of ∼\sim1-5 Myr and located at a distance of ∼\sim400 pc (Hillenbrand, 1997; Hillenbrand et al., 2013; Jeffries et al., 2011; Muench et al., 2008; Kounkel et al., 2018; Briceño et al., 2019, e.g.,). Its proximity and high stellar density make it an ideal laboratory for studying the early stages of stellar evolution, including disc evolution, accretion processes, and the dynamical assembly of young clusters. Despite decades of study, fundamental questions regarding its star formation history, dynamical state, and age spread remain open (Muench et al., 2008; Jeffries et al., 2011; Getman et al., 2014; Jerabkova et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019; Fujii et al., 2022; Megeath et al., 2022; Theissen et al., 2022; Alzate et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2024, e.g.,).

Optical spectroscopy provides a robust, direct diagnostic of pre-main-sequence (PMS) stellar populations by leveraging well-characterized spectral features sensitive to stellar youth. Low-mass PMS stars (M∗ ≲\lesssim 2 M⊙\mathrm{M}_{\odot}), commonly known as T Tauri stars (TTS), are traditionally classified into classical T Tauri stars (CTTS) and weak-lined T Tauri stars (WTTS). CTTS are stars undergoing active accretion from their circumstellar discs, whereas WTTS show little or no evidence of accretion. Strong Hα\alpha emission is one of the primary diagnostics used to distinguish CTTS from WTTS, although it may also serve as an indicator of stellar chromospheric activity. In addition, the presence of the Li i λ​6708\lambda 6708 Å absorption line (hereafter Li i) serves as a robust youth diagnostic in low-mass stars (Jeffries, 2006; Soderblom et al., 2014; Briceño et al., 2019; Hernández et al., 2023).

papers.title: SN 2025wiu: A Type Ib Supernova with Post-Peak Optical Rebrightening
papers.abstract: We present optical photometric and optical/near-infrared spectroscopic observations of SN 2025wiu, a Type Ib supernova (SN) at z = 0.046927. The r-band light curve exhibits an initial maximum of approximately -18.2 mag, followed by a weaker optical rebrightening reaching approximately -17.8 mag at +38 days in the rest frame relative to the first maximum. However, the reconstructed bolometric light curve does not show a distinct second peak, but instead exhibits a reduced decline rate during the corresponding phase. The spectra consistently show Type Ib features without narrow emission components associated with circumstellar material. The late-time bolometric decline rate of 0.054 +/- 0.008 mag/day is faster than expected for complete trapping of 56Co decay. A radioactive-decay model for the first peak requires nickel mass = 0.47 solar masses, above the range typical of SNe Ib. A combined radioactive-decay and circumstellar-interaction model reproduces the full bolometric light curve with nickel mass ~ 0.38 solar masses, ejecta mass ~ 4.7 solar masses, and an effective circumstellar mass of ~ 0.10 solar masses, with the interaction contributing from the first peak onward. The lack of interaction signatures in the spectra favours an aspherical, disk-like circumstellar structure engulfed by the ejecta, in which the interaction energy is thermalized below the ejecta photosphere; the fitted circumstellar parameters are therefore effective values rather than direct measurements of the circumstellar geometry. SN 2025wiu demonstrates that optical rebrightening does not necessarily imply a genuine bolometric secondary maximum and highlights the importance of multi-band observations for identifying the powering mechanisms of double-peaked stripped-envelope supernovae.

Several mechanisms have been proposed for this stripping, including strong stellar winds from massive single stars [24, 85] and mass transfer or common-envelope evolution in binary systems [72, 106, 86]. SESNe are further subdivided according to the degree of stripping: objects that retain their helium layers are classified as Type Ib, while those in which helium has also been removed are classified as Type Ic [30].

While typical SESNe show a single-peaked light curve followed by a smooth decline onto the radioactive tail, double-peaked SESNe show a rebrightening after the first peak, which is difficult to explain with 56Ni decay alone; Y. Sharma et al. [81] provide a systematic comparison of the possible mechanisms. Interaction with CSM offers considerable flexibility: depending on the density profile, geometry, and location of the material, it can produce a wide variety of light-curve morphologies [18], ranging from a single luminous bump [50] to multiple undulations arising from a clumpy CSM distribution [74]. Delayed energy injection from a magnetar has likewise been invoked, either through variations in the thermalization of the spin-down energy [63], through evaporation of a companion star [108], or through magnetar flaring activity [28]. A third possibility is a double-peaked 56Ni distribution, in which nickel is present both in the inner and outer ejecta. Because this scenario invokes no additional energy source, the total luminosity is bounded by the synthesized nickel mass and the separation between the two peaks is tightly constrained by the spatial distribution of the nickel, restricting the range of light-curve morphologies it can reproduce; SN 2005bf [32], PTF11mnb [94] and SN 2019cad [68] have been interpreted in this way. Other mechanisms, including fallback accretion onto the compact remnant [60, 14, 69, 11] and pulsational pair instability [3], have also been proposed.

In this paper, we present SN 2025wiu, a double-peaked Type Ib supernova (SN Ib) at z=0.047z=0.047. Its well-sampled Zwicky Transient Facility [8, 37, 26, 57, ZTF;] and Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System [96, 84, ATLAS;] light curves show a second peak ∼\sim38 days after the first, followed by a decline considerably faster than expected from 56Co decay with full γ\gamma-ray trapping. papers.title: Isomer-resolved ion-molecule reaction kinetics of HCO+ and HOC+
papers.abstract: The HCO$^+$/HOC$^+$ abundance ratio has been observed to vary significantly in different astrophysical environments, making it an important diagnostic tool for exploring the interstellar medium. However, uncertainties in the reaction rates and branching ratios of key chemical reactions involving these ions affect the conclusions drawn from observations of either these species or other species that are derived on their basis. Here, we present isomer-resolved ion-molecule reaction rate coefficients of reactions involving HCO$^+$ and HOC$^+$ using a cryogenic ion trap experiment. We measured the rate coefficients of the isomerization reaction of HOC$^+$ to HCO$^+$ with H$_2$ and CO, as well as three different reactions producing both isomers: CO$^+$ + H$_2$ , H$_3^+$ + CO, and ArH$^+$ + CO. Our results show that the reaction of CO$^+$ with H$_2$ predominantly produces HCO$^+$ with a negligible yield of HOC$^+$ . This result is in agreement with recent theoretical predictions, but in major contrast to the generally accepted branching ratio based on previous experimental results. We also find that the isomerization reaction of HOC$^+$ to HCO$^+$ is efficient with both H2 and CO. We were able to assess the impact of our new measured reaction rate coefficients on the predicted HCO$^+$/HOC$^+$ abundance ratio using a state-of-the-art astrochemical model.

papers.title: Linearization in nonlocal elasticity via Gamma-convergence
papers.abstract: Linearization is a classical tool in continuum mechanics that connects nonlinear models of solids to their linear counterparts through the small-strain limit, as in the passage from finite to linear elasticity. Here, we study a nonlocal analogue of this limit process in the context of state-based peridynamics, starting from a class of models in nonlocal hyperelasticity subject to nonlocal Dirichlet boundary conditions. Recent formal calculations in the literature indicate that the linearized versions of these models are closely related to the widely used Eringen models. The main purpose of this note is to make this connection rigorous by establishing $Γ$-convergence of the associated energy functionals and a corresponding compactness result that together imply strong convergence of minimizers. Our proof relies on a local-to-nonlocal transfer argument that reduces the problem to a well-known local linearization result.

papers.intro:
Linearization is an integral concept in continuum mechanics. While nonlinear models are needed to capture the response of a body under large deformations, their simpler linearized versions can be efficiently applied to describe the regime of small strains. In the mechanics literature, linearized models are commonly deduced by formal calculations based on Taylor expansion. The first mathematical derivation via Γ\Gamma-convergence was achieved by Dal Maso, Negri & Percivale [18] in the context of elasticity. These results have since been extended in several directions, for instance, by weakening the coercivity conditions [1], by allowing for energy densities with multiple wells [2] and, more recently, with infinitely many wells [3], by removing restrictions on the traction forces [28], or by accounting for surface energy terms [27]. Similar results are also available for other material models, e.g., in plasticity [30], fracture mechanics [24, 23], magnetoelasticity [4]. While this shows that linearization is by now well understood for a wide range of local models, much less is known in the nonlocal setting; see, e.g., [29] for a recent result in bond-based peridynamics.

papers.title: Control design for a class of nonlinear convection-reaction systems with storage effects and relative degree one
papers.abstract: This article addresses the control design for systems of several convection-reaction equations distributively coupled to a reaction equation. In typical applications, input and output are associated exclusively with the convection-reaction subsystems. Along the common characteristics of the transport processes, the system can be reduced to a single delayed evolutionary ODE. Based on the latter representation, an inversion-based feedforward control is proposed, whose properties depend on the coupling structure of the original system. While the relative degree of the output is zero in many cases, a relative degree of one is of particular interest for practical applications. To compensate for uncertainties and disturbances, the feedforward control is extended by a tracking controller with a predictor based on the transformed system to account for the resulting delays.

papers.title: ExHaLe-jet: Modeling blazar jets with an extended hadro-leptonic radiation code
papers.abstract: Blazars - active galaxies with the jet pointing at Earth - emit across all electromagnetic wavelengths. As the one-zone model becomes increasingly inadequate to describe blazar emission, more elaborate models are needed. In order to self-consistently describe the entire electromagnetic spectrum, extended jet models are necessary. Notably, kinetic descriptions of extended jets can provide the temporal and spatial evolution of the particle species and the full electromagnetic output. ExHaLe-jet is a lepto-hadronic, extended-jet code allowing for in-depth studies of the particle and radiation evolution on all scales. Here, we present our ongoing study regarding acceleration scenarios of particles within the large-scale jet structure. A single acceleration of particles at the jet base (or elsewhere) is insufficient to produce sufficient photon flux. Thus, re-acceleration through, e.g., consecutive shocks along the jet is needed. We explore two possible scenarios for this.

Relativistic jets – with blazars as a prominent example – are among the most energetically extreme environments in the Universe. They are relativistically moving entities containing particles, which are themselves accelerated to relativistic energies in the comoving frame of the jet. In turn, jets can be extremely luminous with rapid and powerful flares – with the most extreme ones belonging to γ\gamma-ray bursts.

Relativistic jets – with blazars as a prominent example – are among the most energetically extreme environments in the Universe. They are relativistically moving entities containing particles, which are themselves accelerated to relativistic energies in the comoving frame of the jet. In turn, jets can be extremely luminous with rapid and powerful flares – with the most extreme ones belonging to γ\gamma-ray bursts.

Jets emit radiation across the entire electromagnetic spectrum. In most cases, the spectral energy distribution (SED) shows two broad components, where the low-energy one is attributed to synchrotron emission of electrons (incl. positrons). The high-energy component is generally assumed to be inverse-Compton emission of electrons scattering ambient photon fields such as synchrotron (the so-called synchrotron-self-Compton process, SSC) from within the jet, or thermal fields from outside the jet (the so-called external-Compton process) including the accretion disk, the broad-line region, the dusty torus or the cosmic microwave background [4]. However, if the association of neutrinos with jets is confirmed [7], the presence of relativistic protons is highly probable, enabling additional processes to produce γ\gamma rays, such as proton synchrotron or secondary cascades [3].

The rapid, and in many cases correlated flares have given rise to the one-zone model, where practically the entire electromagnetic output is attributed to a small region somewhere in the larger jet structure. While this can be used to explain (some) flares [13, 5, 1], it already faces problems with others [6], and is most certainly inadequate to explain the long-term evolution of jets [11, 12, 15]. Hence, multi-zone and extended-jet models, such as ExHaLe-jet, are required to properly describe the emission of relativistic jets.

papers.title: Optimal approximation of smooth functions by ReLU neural networks
papers.abstract: We study uniform approximation of the Hölder ball $\mathcal H_1^s([0,1]^D)$ by fully connected ReLU networks. Except in the one-dimensional Lipschitz case, existing constructions remain separated from the information-theoretic efficiency limit. This article closes the gap for every $s>0$ and $D\ge1$: networks with width $O(N)$, depth $O(L)$, and parameter magnitude $O(1)$ attain uniform approximation error of order $(N^2L^2\log N)^{-s/D}$. No relation between width and depth is required. The construction uses new encoding and decoding mechanisms that exploit higher-order finite-difference bounds for local Taylor coefficients of the target function. As a statistical consequence, empirical risk minimizers over the corresponding clipped network classes attain the minimax regression rate $n^{-2s/(2s+D)}$ without additional logarithmic factors. The paper also gives a detailed exposition of the key approximation techniques, covering both established and new mechanisms.

papers.intro:
Approximation theory for neural networks has a long history. The universal approximation theorems of Cybenko (1989) and Hornik et al. (1989) show that shallow neural networks can approximate every continuous function on a compact set, but they are qualitative. They do not determine how the network size must grow to achieve a target accuracy or, conversely, what accuracy can be achieved with a given architecture. Such quantitative bounds have become one of the central problems in neural-network approximation (DeVore et al., 2021; Dahmen et al., 2022).

papers.title: An Error Taxonomy for Property Graph Data
papers.abstract: Graph data are increasingly used in applications where relationships and topology matter. Yet, compared to tabular data, the notions of data quality and error types for graphs are less established. Tabular error concepts often fail to capture structural properties and context inherent in graph data, hindering systematic quality assessment in graph-based systems. We focus on property graphs (PGs) in graph databases. PGs are often managed without a prescriptive schema, enabling data insertion without explicit validation, while still exhibiting an implicit schema of recurring structural patterns. Irregularities in these patterns may indicate errors, but their interpretation depends on the surrounding graph context. To address these challenges, we provide a systematic view of errors in graph data by proposing a comprehensive graph-specific taxonomy of error types. To position these errors with respect to established work on tabular data quality, we derive a mapping between graph errors and corresponding error notions in tabular data. This mapping highlights which concepts transfer across data models and where structural properties of graphs introduce fundamentally different challenges requiring extensions. Overall, the taxonomy and mapping provide a shared vocabulary for describing, characterizing, comparing, and studying graph data errors, and they lay the groundwork for future work on error detection and repair in graph data.

These include social networks, recommender systems or fraud detection, as they naturally capture highly interconnected data. As graph-based systems become more pervasive (Sakr and others, 2021), ensuring the quality of their data grows in importance. Errors in graph data can significantly alter the reliability of applications, leading to misinterpretations and wrong decisions (Wang and others, 2021).

Several data quality challenges, such as connectivity or heterogeneity, directly influence the design of our taxonomy (Step 5). papers.title: Joining Large String Collections with Jaro-Winkler Similarity
papers.abstract: The Jaro-Winkler measure, originally developed for U.S.\ Census record linkage, captures similarities between strings and accounts for common typographical variations. Despite its widespread use, finding all string pairs that exceed a given Jaro-Winkler threshold remains challenging as the string collection grows large. Existing algorithms for computing the Jaro-Winkler similarity between two strings are either slow for short strings or require quadratic time and fail to scale to long strings. To reduce the number of string comparisons, state-of-the-art techniques perform an index-nested-loop join on trie-based indexes; however, they have only been evaluated on small datasets and high similarity thresholds. For lower similarity thresholds that are relevant in practice, these techniques incur an excessive number of costly Jaro-Winkler computations. We present a novel approach for efficient Jaro-Winkler similarity joins on large string collections. Our solution is based on three key techniques: (1) JUMP is a fast algorithm for computing the Jaro-Winkler similarity between two strings that runs in linear time for bounded alphabets. (2) Dual-bound intersection bitmaps encode strings -- represented as character sets -- into fixed-size bitmaps, which are used to prune candidate string pairs by providing effective bounds on their character overlap; unlike prior bitmap techniques, our bitmaps are equipped with a cost model and adapt to the input data. (3) Our PUMA framework groups strings by prefix to tighten filter conditions, thereby reducing the number of similarity computations. Extensive experiments on large string collections demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms the state of the art, achieving speedups of up to three orders of magnitude.

Data is generated at an unprecedented rate, and the ability to process and correlate it becomes increasingly important. Thus, similarity joins have become a fundamental operation in database management systems. A similarity join between two collections of objects, RR and SS, returns all pairs of objects (r,s)∈R×S(r,s)\in R\times S whose similarity exceeds a user-defined threshold. Similarity joins have been extensively studied across various domains (Mann et al., 2016), and prominent industry applications include Google’s near-duplicate web page detection (Henzinger, 2006), Celonis’ advanced process mining and invoice deduplication (Kocher et al., 2021; Inc., 2024), and Uber’s fraud detection system (Metwally and Shum, 2024).

We identify three main challenges that make Jaro-Winkler joins difficult: (1) Computing the Jaro similarity between two strings is expensive: Each character in one string must be compared to a window of linear size in the other string. Therefore, most state-of-the-art algorithms run in quadratic time in the string length. While linear algorithms exist (Basak et al., 2023; Basak et al., 2026), optimized quadratic implementations (Bachmann, 2025) consistently outperform them even for the longest strings in our evaluation (>100{>}100 characters). (2) Candidate filtering is challenging: Although – like for Jaccard and Cosine similarity – the character overlap of two strings provides a lower bound on the Jaro-Winkler similarity, this bound is hard to exploit. The required overlap is lower than for other normalized similarity measures, which makes this bound less effective. Furthermore, the number of distinct elements in the character sets is small, which renders common join techniques such as prefix filtering less effective (Schmitt et al., 2023). (3) Pairwise prefix dependency: The required character overlap that two strings must satisfy for a given Jaro-Winkler threshold depends on the length of their common prefix. This inherent pairwise dependency makes it difficult to apply state-of-the-art set similarity join techniques. Conservatively assuming the maximum prefix length weakens the overlap bound and leads to even more candidates. Figure 1 shows how we address these challenges at three levels.

papers.title: TriSAR-3D and PaintFusion: A Novel Trimodal LiDAR-RGB-Thermal Dataset and Method for 3D Person Detection in Search and Rescue
papers.abstract: Reliable 3D person detection is important for rescue robotics to give first responders situational awareness. Yet most multimodal 3D detection research targets automotive scenarios in which pedestrians mostly appear in a narrow range of upright, near-road poses. It is therefore unclear how much of the reported performance transfers to rescue settings, as a person may be lying, partially occluded, or in unstructured indoor and outdoor environments. To investigate this gap, we introduce TriSAR-3D, a multimodal person detection dataset recorded with a high-resolution 128-channel LiDAR, an RGB camera, and a thermal camera. It captures varied poses in indoor as well as outdoor locations at different times of day to study their influence on 3D object detector performance. Furthermore, we propose a novel trimodal 3D detection pipeline, PaintFusion, that fuses PointPainting-based evidence using a simple MLP. We show that the derived method reaches 65.4 AP@50 and thereby outperforms strong LiDAR-only (CenterPoint, 53.4), RGB+LiDAR (BEVFusion, 60.5), and adapted trimodal (Tri-BEVFusion, 60.7) baselines on the dataset. At the same time, it is substantially faster than other fusion-based methods such as BEVFusion, with a per-frame latency of 51.6 ms compared to 101 ms. Additionally, we test how the performance of different 3D object detectors generalizes to unseen pose categories. Removing lying instances from training data collapses the lying-pose AP@50 to near zero across all evaluated detectors. The results indicate that dataset diversity exerts a large effect on 3D object detection performance. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/MarkusKramer1/3D-Trimodal-People-Detection.

Fusion of a LiDAR with an RGB and a thermal camera thus covers a wider range of conditions.

papers.title: Momentum: Persistent Dynamics for Video World Models
papers.abstract: Video world models must capture how a scene evolves beyond the current camera view to generate consistent observations when its content reappears. Existing approaches rely on observation history, static point clouds, or image caches constructed from past frames. These representations are often expensive and, more importantly, cannot update dynamic scene content outside the field of view: generated vehicles and pedestrians may be forgotten after leaving the field of view or reappear in physically inaccurate states. We represent an evolving scene through synchronized videos from reference-camera rigs, each comprising eight cameras that jointly cover the surrounding scene. We connect these rigs in a graph and propagate video generation between neighboring rigs to coordinate scene dynamics across locations and time. We introduce Momentum, a two-stage pipeline: WorldUpdate jointly generates reference-camera videos as a shared memory of scene dynamics, and WorldInteract grounds camera-controlled video generation in this evolving memory, allowing moving content to remain represented outside the target view and reappear consistently. To support training and evaluation, we develop a CARLA pipeline that captures synchronized videos from reference camera rigs and a moving target camera, together with an evaluation framework measuring consistency within the generated world state and the target observations.Experiments on generated street scenes show that grounding target videos in scene dynamics generated by Momentum improves dynamic scene consistency by 126.2% in unseen scenes over static image conditioning, while also improving visual fidelity. Our models and source code will be made publicly available.

papers.intro:
Video world models simulate how visual environments evolve over time and respond to actions, supporting applications in game generation (Team et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2025b; Qian et al., 2026), robotic learning and control (Gao et al., 2026a; Ye et al., 2026), autonomous driving simulation (Wayve, 2026; Basant et al., 2026), and virtual-world exploration (Ball et al., 2025; Team et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2025). In these settings, the generated video reveals only a partial view of an environment whose contents and dynamics extend beyond what is currently visible. As the viewpoint changes, the generated observations should remain consistent with both the scene’s spatial structure and the motion of objects within it. A vehicle approaching an intersection should follow the same course whether the generated video follows it, shows it from another viewpoint, or turns away and later shows it again. This requires grounding generation to a world representation that evolves through time.

Existing memory mechanisms provide part of this grounding through observation history or persistent spatial representations. Conditioning on past frames preserves local continuity, but a finite context limits how much of the environment remains accessible (Zhang et al., 2026; Savov et al., 2026; Cai et al., 2026). Image caches (Xiao et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b; Yu et al., 2025a), depth maps (Ren et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2026), and reconstructed point clouds (Ren et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025c) extend spatial memory by retaining information from previously observed locations. However, stored observations describe the scene at the time they were captured. Without a mechanism for advancing their contents, they cannot provide temporally updated grounding for a moving camera. The challenge is therefore to maintain a representation that specifies both what exists at a location and how its state changes over time.

Seoul World Model (SWM) offers a useful foundation through image-based spatial grounding (Seo et al., 2026). It conditions camera-controlled video generation on retrieved street-view images, using geometric reprojection and semantic referencing to anchor generated observations to a particular environment. These references ground the scene’s spatial structure and appearance, while motion is synthesized within the generated video. We extend this principle to spatiotemporal grounding: synchronized videos from spatially distributed reference cameras provide a shared account of both scene appearance and motion. The target camera is thus grounded in the scene at the corresponding location and time, allowing different camera trajectories to observe the same unfolding dynamics.

We introduce Momentum, a two-stage pipeline in which WorldUpdate generates an evolving world state and WorldInteract uses it to ground camera-controlled video generation. The method is presented on Fig. 1. The state is organized as a graph of panoramic rigs, each comprising eight reference cameras. WorldUpdate jointly generates videos for the eight cameras of each rig and propagates generation through the graph, conditioning each rig on geometrically reprojected video from an already generated neighbor. This couples the evolution of scene content across reference viewpoints. WorldInteract then generates video along a target camera trajectory using the resulting world rollout as spatiotemporal grounding. The reference videos therefore serve both as the simulation of scene dynamics and as their persistent representation, enabling motion outside the target camera’s view to remain part of the state used to generate subsequent observations.

With ground-truth reference videos, the Dynamically Grounded WM improves visual fidelity, camera control, and scene consistency over static grounding across single- and multi-rig settings. End-to-end, Momentum generates its own reference videos and improves dynamic scene consistency by 130.2%130.2\% in seen towns and 126.2%126.2\% in an unseen town compared with the Dynamically Grounded WM conditioned on static images.

papers.title: Predicting Privileged Information Effectiveness for On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) enables large language models (LLMs) to learn from privileged information (PI) without a separate teacher model. However, prior work largely treats PI as a fixed design choice, leaving the effects of its content and construction poorly understood. This challenge is particularly important in multi-turn agentic settings, where trajectories contain actions, observations, and reasoning that can be transformed into PI in many ways. We systematically evaluate 16 PI configurations across three multi-turn agentic benchmarks and three student models that vary in scale and reasoning mode. We find that PI effectiveness depends on its content, generation source, and the student model. Information-dense trajectories and PI produced by more capable generators generally yield larger gains, whereas thinking models benefit less consistently. To assess PI before training, we compare PI utility with two KL-based metrics: sampled-token reverse KL ($D$) and error-step KL contrast ($Δd^{-}_{\mathrm{err}}$). The KL-based metrics track post-training performance more consistently than PI utility, which can be distorted by information leakage. Empirically, selecting each task's PI by $Δd^{-}_{\mathrm{err}}$ also improves post-training performance over random selection, most when the PI candidates differ widely. Finally, effective PI remains beneficial when combined with GRPO, allowing the combined objective to outperform a strong GRPO baseline. Overall, our results provide practical guidance for constructing and evaluating PI in OPSD training.

On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) enables LLMs to iteratively improve by turning successful solutions, environment feedback, and experience from their own interactions into training signals without a separate teacher model [19, 35, 7, 22]. Related self-distillation methods have already been used to train coding agents such as Composer 2.5 and agents for long-horizon professional tasks [4, 8]. In OPSD, the model learns from its own trajectories by matching the same model conditioned on PI, thereby internalizing information unavailable at inference time.

The effectiveness of OPSD, however, depends on what the teacher is allowed to see. In general, PI can take many forms, including ground-truth answers [35], demonstrations from prior tasks [22], environment feedback [7], actions from successful trajectories [19], or hints derived from gold solutions or trajectories, such as summaries [19], skills [26], checklists, structured criteria such as rubrics [20, 6], and targeted feedback [33, 4]. These choices determine both the information available to the teacher and how that information changes its distribution relative to the student. However, especially on multi-turn agentic tasks, existing studies evaluate only a limited range of PI formats across a small set of models and tasks [16, 29, 26, 33, 30]. It remains unclear what makes PI produce useful learning signals for the student policy, whether the same choices work across agentic domains and model types, and, critically, whether PI quality can be assessed before training. Reliable offline metrics would allow candidate PI formats and sources to be compared before training, avoiding a separate costly OPSD run for every candidate and focusing compute on the most promising PI.

papers.title: Inductive Learning of Concept Embeddings from Cross-Linguistic Colexification Patterns with Textual Attributes
papers.abstract: The advent of distributional semantics as a framework for computational semantics marked a paradigm shift in the nature of representations, by which meanings are represented as dense vectors commonly known as word embeddings. Computational approaches to historical or typological language comparison, on the other hand, still mostly rely on discrete representations, while the potential of embedding-based methods remains largely untapped in this context. Recent studies have proposed concept embeddings as a language-independent, onomasiological counterpart to word embeddings, based on networks of cross-linguistic colexification patterns. While the resulting concept embeddings reflect meaningful semantic properties and relations, they suffer from a lack of scalability, since they rely on transductive embedding approaches which only learn embeddings for nodes present in the training data. In this study, we present an inductive framework for learning concept embeddings, combining the structural properties of full and partial colexification networks with semantic information from short concept descriptions. This framework allows the embedding of unseen concepts based on a short definition. We show that the resulting concept embeddings correlate with various cross-linguistic measures of similarity or relatedness, while generalizing well to new concepts that were absent from the training data.

papers.intro:
Techniques for word embeddings laid the foundation for the current success of embedded vector representations, building the backbone of Large Language Models and the accompanying technology using them in industrial and scientific applications. Their capability of modeling multifaceted semantic relations and properties has made them a popular tool for investigating lexical semantic change in various domains and languages (Tahmasebi et al., 2021; Schlechtweg et al., 2019; Periti and Montanelli, 2024). However, since word embeddings reflect the semasiological perspective of modeling the meaning of individual words, their application is primarily directed towards the investigation of lexical semantics in individual languages. Approaches in this context are therefore not widely applicable and not suitable for the historical comparison of the majority of the world’s languages: diachronic training corpora only exist for a fraction of languages and cover a much lower time depth than problems in historical linguistics usually reach.

Concept embeddings can be seen as the onomasiological counterpart to word embeddings (Harvill et al., 2022; Rubehn and List, 2025). Drawing inspiration from word embeddings, they learn dense vector representations for abstract concepts which can be defined language-independently. This facilitates semantic modeling across languages. As part of the comparative method, historical linguists need to take semantic shift into account to identify cognates with different, but often related meanings. Consider the English words deer, stool and starve, which are respectively cognates to German Tier ‘animal’, Stuhl ‘chair’ and sterben ‘to die’ (McMahon, 1994, 177). While all of these cognate pairs differ in meaning, their meanings are clearly related – yet, most methods in computational historical linguistics fail to take this semantic similarity into account and are therefore unable to uncover cognates under semantic shift. Drawing inspiration from word embeddings, they learn dense vector representations for abstract concepts which can be defined language-independently. To turn concept embeddings into a reliable tool which computational models in comparative linguistics can build upon, a scalable model is required that can embed any concept, so that semantic properties can be modeled reliably in downstream applications. In this study, we therefore shift to an inductive paradigm (Hamilton et al., 2017) for learning concept embeddings from cross-linguistic colexification patterns. In an inductive setting, embeddings are not learned directly for each node, but based on features attributed to the nodes. In our model, node features are derived from a short semantic description of the concept – therefore, all concepts can be embedded, as long as a brief definition is provided. This scalability overcomes the major limitation of the transductive embeddings presented by Rubehn and List (2025) and turns them into a robust tool for computational approaches in language comparison.

papers.title: Designing for Imperfect Prompts: A Simulation-Based Evaluation of an LLM-Based Enterprise Data Assistant Using Knowledge Graphs
papers.abstract: Enterprise data assistants using large language models (LLMs) promise democratized data access in organizations. Yet in our real-world deployment within the CFO unit's data lake at an industry partner, we observed that business users frequently pose imperfect prompts that include domain-specific vocabulary and lack schema references or structural information. This Design Science Research study examines automatic resolution using a semantic mediation layer. We design and evaluate two design variants: schema-based mediation via semantic similarity, and knowledge graph-based mediation leveraging an automatically constructed knowledge graph from the data lake. Our simulation-based evaluation using real-world data, supported by LLM-as-a-Judge assessments and human validation, shows that knowledge graph-based mediation outperforms the schema-based approach in Precision, Recall, F1, and preserving user intent. We propose a design principle for knowledge graph-based mediation, demonstrating that structured knowledge representation bridges user intent and database structure and guides the design of enterprise data assistants across skill levels.

papers.title: Online Conditional Vine Copulas: Forecasting Electricity Demand
papers.abstract: We propose an online multivariate distributional forecasting model in which we condition the parameters of a vine copula on covariates. An online algorithm updates the parameters sequentially using only the most recent observations. Existing approaches require full batch re-estimation using all available data at each update step, which makes them computationally slow in large-scale forecasting applications and less suitable for settings in which dependence structures change over time. Simulation results show that the online procedure achieves forecasting performance comparable to that of the batch estimator, while reducing computation time substantially. We illustrate the method in a forecasting application to electricity net-demand across five regions of Great Britain and show that (i) the conditional vine copula model outperforms unconditional Gaussian and vine copula benchmarks and (ii) that online estimation improves forecast accuracy when batch re-estimation is not available. The algorithm is implemented in the Python package ondil.

papers.title: From GAN-Based Models to GPT-5: A Taxonomy-Guided Study of Human Performance in Detecting Deepfake Face Images
papers.abstract: Generative models for deepfakes have rapidly evolved from GAN-based architectures to diffusion models and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, empirical research on human performance in detecting deepfake face images has not kept pace. It remains unclear if (and how) detection performance varies across generative models and whether model-specific training improves detection more effectively than general-purpose training. In this paper, we propose the \emph{Deepfake Face Artifact Taxonomy} (DFAT), a cross-model taxonomy of human-recognizable visual artifacts in deepfake face images, based on which we build both general-purpose and model-specific training materials. Through an online experiment ($n = 524$), we examined human performance in detecting deepfake face images and evaluated training efficacy across five representative generative models: three GAN-based, one diffusion-based, and one MLLM (GPT-5). Our results show that participants' detection accuracy was strongly model-dependent and that images generated by more recent and advanced models were not necessarily harder to detect. After training, participants achieved significant performance gains across most conditions, and their improvement varied by model. Notably, model-specific training generally yielded greater numerical gains than general-purpose training. In a five-month follow-up test ($n = 342$), we observed no significant decline in detection accuracy and no significant increase in perceived stress. Overall, our findings provide actionable insights for designing effective, sustainable, and targeted training programs to counter the growing threat posed by deepfakes.

Deepfake face images are frequently exploited for malicious purposes, including disinformation campaigns [1], non-consensual pornography [2, 3], online fraud [4], and cyberbullying [5]. The recent development of generative AI techniques, particularly multimodal large language models (MLLMs) [6, 7] and large vision models (LVMs) [8], has significantly escalated such threats. These modern deepfake generation models have lowered the technical barriers substantially, allowing adversaries to generate highly realistic deepfakes from textual and multimodal prompts, without the need for extensive expertise or computational resources.

papers.title: Oxygen on Rh(100) revisited with ultra-high precision
papers.abstract: We have reanalyzed the 0.25 and 0.50 monolayer (ML) phases of oxygen on the catalytically important Rh(100) surface by quantitative low-energy electron diffraction (LEED), variable-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and density functional theory (DFT). For both phases, the crystallographic structure could be determined by LEED structure analyses with single-digit picometer precision enabled by ultra-low Pendry R factors of R$_\mathrm{P}$ $\approx$ 0.07. For the (2$\times$2)-O phase at 0.25 ML we find oxygen adsorbed at fourfold hollow sites in accordance to earlier results [Surf. Sci. 207 (1988) 55], however, with a pronounced buckling within the second layer of the otherwise unreconstructed substrate. For the 0.50 monolayer phase, we recently identified a (2$\sqrt{2}$ $\times$ 2$\sqrt{2}$)R45$^\circ$-4O ground state structure [Phys. Rev. Res. 8 (2026) 023296], which decomposes into a large number of nano-domains already at temperatures below 100 K. In this paper we provide a detailed analysis of the atomic structure and the ordering behavior of this phase and resolve long-standing discrepancies with the original (2$\times$2)pg model [Phys. Rev. Lett. 82 (1999) 4874]. We further prove by short-range order simulations that the coherent superposition of scattering contributions of the nano-domains leads to a virtual extinction of diffraction spots, which has concealed the true periodicity and symmetry of this phase for so long.

Hereby, one monolayer (ML) refers to the number of atoms within a Rh(100) bulk layer. The restructuring of Rh(100) induced by oxygen adsorption, eventually leading to oxide formation, has therefore attracted considerable experimental and theoretical interest [33, 29, 8, 45, 4, 7, 5, 32, 21, 9, 48, 47]. In particular, for the 0.5 ML oxygen phase the formation of a non-bond-breaking “clock” reconstruction of the topmost Rh layer is well confirmed [4, 5, 32, 7], while at slightly higher oxygen coverage the surface layer breaks up to form one-dimensional RhO2 sub-oxide chains (“shifted-row reconstruction”). In a previous publication [19], we were able to show that the ground state of the 0.5 ML phase, observable only at temperatures well below 100 K, does not exhibit a (2×2)(2\times 2) periodicity, as is commonly observed in experiment, but rather a (2​2×2​22\sqrt{2}\times 2\sqrt{2})R45∘ [or c⁡(4×4)c(4\times 4)] periodicity (called “2​22\sqrt{2}” for short in the following). papers.title: The GAGE survey. I. Deep multi-band stellar variability characterization and automated classification toward Baade's window
papers.abstract: Context. Long-term photometric surveys of the Galactic bulge are vital for characterizing its stellar populations and structure, providing a foundation for next-generation facilities. Aims. We present initial results of the GalActic bulGe with plEiadi (GAGE) project, focusing on variable star discovery in Baade's Window. Methods. Using archival DECam (ugriz) data on the Blanco 4-m Telescope spanning six years, we applied high-precision PSF photometry. We developed a pipeline combining Generalized Lomb-Scargle analysis and polynomial light-curve modelling to derive mean multi-band magnitudes and amplitudes. Results. Quality cuts yield 6,304 high-confidence variable sources. We expand multi-band coverage for 4,568 sources in common with OGLE IV and uncover 1,736 (~28%) new candidates absent from OGLE IV. Using a Random Forest classifier, we categorize these sources, finding that 1,391 were also missing from both Gaia DR3 and VVV. This population is concentrated at the fainter end (i >= 17.5 mag), enabled by our deeper detection limits. Conclusions. Our pipeline effectively probes deep, highly crowded fields, expanding the variable star inventory of the inner Galaxy as a benchmark for Rubin-LSST.

papers.intro:
The Galactic bulge is one of the most massive and structurally complex stellar components of the Milky Way (MW), containing roughly a quarter of its total stellar mass within the innermost few kiloparsecs (Valenti et al. 2010; Licquia and Newman 2015; Valenti et al. 2016; Portail et al. 2017; Simion et al. 2017; Cautun et al. 2020). Its stellar populations and kinematics provide critical constraints on early Galaxy formation and evolution (Cao et al. 2013; Valenti et al. 2016; Portail et al. 2017; Simion et al. 2017). Despite decades of study, the relative contributions of early rapid formation processes versus secular evolution through disk instabilities remain debated (Kormendy and Kennicutt 2004). Recent observational and theoretical work has emphasized the role of clumpy, in situ star formation at high redshift, suggesting that stellar clumps may contribute significantly to the build-up of MW bulge mass and structure (Guo et al. 2015; Guo et al. 2018).

The Galactic bulge is one of the most massive and structurally complex stellar components of the Milky Way (MW), containing roughly a quarter of its total stellar mass within the innermost few kiloparsecs (Valenti et al. 2010; Licquia and Newman 2015; Valenti et al. 2016; Portail et al. 2017; Simion et al. 2017; Cautun et al. 2020). Its stellar populations and kinematics provide critical constraints on early Galaxy formation and evolution (Cao et al. 2013; Valenti et al. 2016; Portail et al. 2017; Simion et al. 2017). Despite decades of study, the relative contributions of early rapid formation processes versus secular evolution through disk instabilities remain debated (Kormendy and Kennicutt 2004). Recent observational and theoretical work has emphasized the role of clumpy, in situ star formation at high redshift, suggesting that stellar clumps may contribute significantly to the build-up of MW bulge mass and structure (Guo et al. 2015; Guo et al. 2018).

Pulsating variable stars are especially powerful probes of galactic structure and stellar populations. These objects are easily identified thanks to their variability and provide robust distance estimates via well-calibrated period–luminosity (PL) and period–luminosity–metallicity (PLZ) relations, enabling three-dimensional mapping of the MW bulge and its constituent populations (Walker 1989; Girardi 2016; Marconi et al. 2018; Bono et al. 2019; Bono et al. 2026). However, different classes of variables trace distinct structural and evolutionary components. For instance, RR Lyrae (RRL) stars and Type II Cepheids serve as prime tracers of ancient, metal-poor populations (Dékány et al. 2015, e.g.,). In the crowded and highly reddened fields toward the Galactic center, RRLs are ubiquitous and uniquely map out an un-barred spheroidal structure (Olivares Carvajal et al. 2024, e.g.,), distinguishing themselves from other stellar tracers like Red Clump stars which predominantly track a younger, intermediate-age barred features. Classical Cepheids, on the other hand, are young supergiants that trace active regions of recent star formation and much younger stellar components (Chen et al. 2019; Ripepi et al. 2021; Trentin et al. 2023, e.g.,). Complementarily, δ\delta Scuti (DSCT) stars represent intermediate-to-young populations spanning the main sequence and subgiant branch; due to their high spatial density, they serve as excellent tracers of fine-scale Galactic disk structure and stellar density gradients spanning the solar neighborhood into the outer bulge components (Poleski et al. 2010; Jayasinghe et al. 2020, e.g.,). Consequently, isolating these individual populations provides a cornerstone method for dissecting distinct star formation epochs and structural sub-components that are otherwise difficult to isolate photometrically and spectroscopically (Marconi et al. 2015; Luongo et al. 2024; Muraveva et al. 2025).

The OGLE IV catalogue now contains more than 78,000 RRL stars in the MW bulge and disk, including tens of thousands of fundamental, first-overtone, and multimode pulsators, and provides extensive time-series II–band photometry with exquisite cadence and depth (Soszyński et al. 2019), paired with VV–band data to constrain their positions in the color–magnitude diagram. OGLE IV surveys have also identified vast samples of other variable types, including DSCT variables, long-period variables (LPVs), and eclipsing binaries (ECL), further enriching the census of stellar variability in the inner Galaxy (Pietrukowicz et al. 2021; Soszyński et al. 2013).

Synergistic near-infrared surveys, such as the VISTA Variables in the Vía Láctea (VVV) (Minniti et al. 2010) and its temporal and spatial extension, the VVV eXtended (VVVX) survey (Saito et al. 2024), have pushed variable star studies deeper into highly obscured regions and low Galactic latitudes. By providing multi-epoch infrared light curves, these public surveys effectively mitigate the severe interstellar reddening limitations that hinder optical frameworks, thereby enabling robust, three-dimensional structural and kinematic analyses of the inner Galaxy (Dékány et al. 2013; Zoccali et al. 2024, e.g.,).

Despite the transformative impact of OGLE IV on the study of stellar variability in the Galactic bulge, its photometric depth and filter coverage impose inherent limitations. The OGLE IV survey, reaches a typical limiting magnitude of I∼21I\sim 21 mag in crowded bulge fields, with a peak at I∼18.5I\sim 18.5 mag, beyond which completeness rapidly declines. Moreover, generally only few epochs are available in the VV–band, making follow-up campaigns to be necessary, for example for the studies in which a multi-band characterization of the variable stars is needed.

Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (Rubin-LSST) will provide an unprecedented dataset of multi-band and multi-epoch for the southern sky, including a good fraction of the Galactic disk and all the Galactic bulge. However, the early classification of the different types of variable stars is hampered by the adopted observational cadence. This will put some limitation on the use of the Rubin-LSST data on the pulsating stars science, for the first one or two years of the survey (Di Criscienzo et al. 2023; Di Criscienzo et al. 2024). Moreover, such a complex and ambitious project would surely benefit of the availability of robust datasets, that can be used as benchmark and validation sample of the obtained catalogues, in the same pass-bands. A multi-band light-curve templates are currently missing for the crowded inner Galaxy, despite their necessity for variable classification.

papers.title: Surveying Experimentally-Validated Components for DNA-Based Molecular Communication
papers.abstract: Molecular communication is a novel paradigm for the design of nanonetworks. It uses molecules as information carriers and enables communication between nanodevices. DNA-based molecular communication is a promising approach for medical applications, such as in-body networks for diagnostics and drug delivery. However, the transition from theoretical models to practical experiments is still in its early stages. This survey reviews experimentally validated DNA-tiles, nanocarriers, and biosensors relevant to implementing DNA-tile-based nanonetworks in vitro. We evaluate these components based on their stability, compatibility, cost-effectiveness, and overall suitability for wet-lab implementation. Based on this analysis, we identify promising component combinations and derive a blueprint for a minimal proof-of-concept experiment. The resulting framework provides researchers with both a structured overview of experimentally relevant design choices and a concrete starting point for implementing and validating DNA-based nanonetworks in the wet lab.

The fields of medicine and computer science have long been interconnected. Complex and diverse medical systems have been created or improved over decades, ranging from smartwatches tracking sleep, pulse and blood pressure to magnetic resonance imaging for diagnostics. The persistent miniaturization of computational units over the years led to powerful and miniscule devices that advance not only medicine, but every field of research. Following this trend of miniaturization, the concept of communicational and computational systems at the nanoscale called nanonetworks emerged in 2008 and shaped the nanocommunication sciences since then [1].

Nanodevices formally split into nanosensors, nanomachines, nanonodes and nanorobots with different sizes, shapes and functions [2]. Akyildiz et al. define three approaches for the development of nanodevices [1]: Top-down, bottom-up and bio-hybrid. The top-down approach uses techniques such as electron beam lithography [3] or micro-contact printing [4] to downscale microelectronic devices to nanoscale. papers.title: pymatgen: 15 years of community growth, new functionality, and future prospects
papers.abstract: We present a retrospective on the Python Materials Genomics (pymatgen) library, reflecting on 15 years of community growth and established best practices. The current version of pymatgen builds on its robust, open-source foundation, emphasising its collaborative nature. Over the past decade, pymatgen has thrived as one of the largest open-source materials science codebases. We detail how pymatgen supports advanced computational materials science workflows, how it adapts to changing demands, and the lessons learned from its growing community, providing guidance beyond pymatgen's open-source community. Pymatgen will continue to evolve in response to the current rapidly changing landscape of computational materials science and materials informatics. We discuss the challenges and potential solutions to managing the community-driven evolution of pymatgen and provide an outlook on its future development.

Python Materials Genomics (pymatgen) 55 was launched in 2011 to provide a robust, reusable software foundation for materials analysis in high-throughput density functional theory (DFT) workflows. The predecessor infrastructure, built on Java 33, was showing its age. The ubiquity of Python, its mix of functional and object-oriented design, rapid development cycle, and interoperability established it as an ideal platform for modern computational materials science software. What emerged from that practical need has, over 15 years, grown into one of the most widely used open-source libraries in the field 81. Today, pymatgen is a cornerstone of the Materials Project 34, 30, a dependency for hundreds of downstream packages, and a standard toolkit across research areas spanning battery materials, defect modelling, machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs), and materials informatics6 (Figs. 1 and 2).

Scientific software rarely achieves broad, cross-disciplinary adoption, as exemplified by Fig. 1, combined with persistent long-term development. In this retrospective, we review pymatgen’s design principles and the philosophy of interoperability that enabled its broad adoption. We trace the growth of its contributor community and downstream package ecosystem and examine the technical and organisational challenges that accompany maintaining infrastructure at this scale. Lastly, we outline the directions we believe will matter most in the next phase of its development.
