papers.title: Normalizing Flow Maps
papers.abstract: Scalable approaches to learning neural dynamical systems have placed diffusion, flow matching, and few-step generators in flow maps at the forefront of generative modeling. Such state-of-the-art models have limited access to explicit model densities despite evolving from classical generative modeling approaches that leveraged tractable likelihoods, e.g., Normalizing Flows and Autoregressive models. In this paper, we combine these threads of few-step generation and tractable sample likelihoods and introduce Normalizing Flow Maps (NFM), a class of exactly invertible pushforward maps that generalizes normalizing flows and flow maps. More precisely, NFMs learn the integrator of an underlying dynamical system, but crucially, they provide efficient exact likelihood evaluation by construction. To enable scalable training of NFMs, we derive two complementary axes of consistency inherent to NFMs that yield (self) distillation objectives: (1) pointwise matching, which unlocks $\ell_2$-based flow-map style regression losses, and (2) distributional matching, which matches pushforward distributions to the marginals of a prescribed forward process. On conditional image generation on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-64, NFMs achieve state-of-the-art sample quality among parameter-matched normalizing flows, while supporting likelihood-based RLHF. For equilibrium sampling in Boltzmann Generators, NFMs outperform prior state-of-the-art normalizing flows on both single-system and transferable peptide benchmarks.

papers.intro:
Learning a transport map between a tractable reference distribution and the empirical distribution of complex data has become the de facto paradigm in generative modeling, with varied application domains spanning audiovisual media (Ho et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023a), biomolecular modeling (Abramson et al., 2024; Watson et al., 2023), and scientific simulation (Shu et al., 2023; Du et al., 2024). Driving this widespread adoption is the ability to leverage standard alignment techniques such as best-of-NN selection (Ramesh et al., 2021), inference-time steering (Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021; Ho and Salimans, 2022; Bansal et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2025), and post-training algorithms (Black et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025a) which effectively sharpen the model distribution—by increasing sample rewards assessed by an oracle. However, each generated sample necessitates computationally expensive numerical integration of an ODE or SDE—producing a substantial inference tax that computationally challenges the steering and post-training pipeline (Wohlwend et al., 2025; Scarpellini et al., 2026).

Driving this widespread adoption is the ability to leverage standard alignment techniques such as best-of-NN selection (Ramesh et al., 2021), inference-time steering (Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021; Ho and Salimans, 2022; Bansal et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2025), and post-training algorithms (Black et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025a) which effectively sharpen the model distribution—by increasing sample rewards assessed by an oracle. However, each generated sample necessitates computationally expensive numerical integration of an ODE or SDE—producing a substantial inference tax that computationally challenges the steering and post-training pipeline (Wohlwend et al., 2025; Scarpellini et al., 2026).

Indeed, while typical Autoregressive LLMs have a mature post-training stack—e.g., PPO (Schulman et al., 2017), GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), etc.—corresponding algorithmic frameworks for diffusion and flow model post-training are both vast and varied (Wallace et al., 2024; Prabhudesai et al., 2023; Clark et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2023). The crucial distinction is that LLMs natively provide tractable sample likelihoods, whereas evaluating exact densities for diffusion and flow-matching models is computationally challenging. Specifically, evaluating sample likelihoods of flow models requires integrating the instantaneous change of variables along the underlying ODE, computing a high-dimensional network Jacobian, and necessitates stochastic trace estimation (Chen et al., 2018; Meyer et al., 2021). Instead, it is computationally more attractive to target the reward-tilted distribution, by modifying the drift of the underlying dynamics through path-space objectives. These objectives, however, crucially rely on high-variance value estimates of the terminal reward. More precisely, value function estimation necessitates propagating terminal rewards through noisy intermediate states, which requires backpropagating through time (Ben-Hamu et al., 2024)–or a noisy single-step denoising approximation (Blasingame and Liu, 2025; Lee et al., 2026b). These algorithmic features combine and give rise to tilting objectives that are inherently high variance, often leading to unstable post-training and mode collapse.

The crucial distinction is that LLMs natively provide tractable sample likelihoods, whereas evaluating exact densities for diffusion and flow-matching models is computationally challenging. Specifically, evaluating sample likelihoods of flow models requires integrating the instantaneous change of variables along the underlying ODE, computing a high-dimensional network Jacobian, and necessitates stochastic trace estimation (Chen et al., 2018; Meyer et al., 2021). Instead, it is computationally more attractive to target the reward-tilted distribution, by modifying the drift of the underlying dynamics through path-space objectives. These objectives, however, crucially rely on high-variance value estimates of the terminal reward. More precisely, value function estimation necessitates propagating terminal rewards through noisy intermediate states, which requires backpropagating through time (Ben-Hamu et al., 2024)–or a noisy single-step denoising approximation (Blasingame and Liu, 2025; Lee et al., 2026b). These algorithmic features combine and give rise to tilting objectives that are inherently high variance, often leading to unstable post-training and mode collapse.

As generative models are deployed at scale, the cumulative cost of repeated sampling for generation, steering, and post-training makes inference efficiency a central design consideration. This practical motivation has led to the emergence of flow maps (Boffi et al., 2025a; Geng et al., 2025; Boffi et al., 2025b), that directly learn the flow integrator, effectively compressing numerical simulation into few network evaluations. Although the exact ODE flow is a diffeomorphism, standard parameterizations are not invertible, nor do they provide tractable Jacobian determinants. While flow maps reduce the inference tax, they do not resolve the crucial likelihood-access gap—limiting their usage in scientific applications like Boltzmann Generators (Noé et al., 2019). As a result, classical Normalizing Flows (NF) (Tabak and Vanden-Eijnden, 2010; Tabak and Turner, 2013; Dinh et al., 2017; Rezende and Mohamed, 2015) trained with MLE remain an attractive exact likelihood-based model class. However, their practical deployment critically relies on noise injection into the clean data distribution for stable training, which unfortunately eliminates the promised access to cheap sample likelihood (Chen et al., 2026). Taken together, these considerations motivate a new generative model that combines few-step sampling of flow maps with exact sample likelihoods for scalable, likelihood-based post-training.

papers.title: A Model Organism for Studying Unverbalized Evaluation Awareness
papers.abstract: Large language models can recognize when they are being evaluated and change their behavior accordingly, undermining the reliability of safety benchmarks. Evaluation awareness (EA) is usually measured by having an LLM judge scan reasoning traces for explicit statements of recognition, but this signal is increasingly unreliable. Recent frontier-model system cards report a drop in verbalized rates between releases, which is indistinguishable from awareness that has gone unverbalized. Interpretability methods could detect such unverbalized evaluation awareness (UEA) in individual interactions, but lack instance-level ground truth. Asking the model alters the input, and dataset labels do not reveal whether it recognized a particular prompt as an evaluation. We address this gap with a model organism. Using synthetic document fine-tuning, SFT, and DPO, we train Qwen3.5-27B to emit a marker (a designated token) in its final response when it recognizes an evaluation, while suppressing the marker and verbalized awareness in its reasoning. The marker largely tracks the evaluation concept as it can be strongly modulated by evaluation framing in the system prompt. When not told whether it is being evaluated, the organism recognizes evaluations from test-question cues, mirroring what its base model often verbalizes. Using the marker as a label, we benchmark linear probes, the Jacobian Lens, and Activation Oracles, built on the base model and blind to the marker. None recovers the label reliably. These results suggest that current interpretability methods are not yet reliable UEA detectors, even when recognition relies on simple cues. Our model organism offers a testbed for improving them.

Evaluations guide deployment decisions, but are only meaningful if a model behaves under evaluation as it would in deployment. Frontier models distinguish evaluation from deployment transcripts significantly above chance (Needham et al., 2025). This Evaluation Awareness (EA) can alter behavior. Steering or editing evaluation-aware reasoning shifts safety-relevant behavior (Abdelnabi and Salem, 2025; Schoen et al., 2025), and models that verbalize awareness or know how evaluations are designed may score safer on benchmarks (Aranguri and Bloom, 2026; Deckenbach et al., 2026).

papers.title: Synthesis of the Transient Behaviour of Optimization Algorithms for Strongly Convex Objective Functions
papers.abstract: We study the transient behavior of first-order optimization methods for unconstrained minimization of smooth and strongly convex objective functions. These methods are modelled as linear systems over finite-time intervals embedded in feedback with the gradient nonlinearity. By characterizing the function class through discrete-time Zames-Falb integral quadratic constraints, we employ a robust $\mathcal{H}_2$ control framework to obtain convex semidefinite programs certifying tight worst-case bounds on the terminal distance to the optimizer. Building on the same formulation, we derive a convex synthesis procedure for a transient-optimal method that achieves the optimal finite-horizon bounds and guarantees error reduction over any prescribed number of steps. The framework naturally extends to delayed gradient measurements, enabling both transient performance analysis and synthesis of optimal algorithms under feedback delays.

papers.intro:
Classical analyses of convex optimization algorithms emphasize asymptotic convergence, whereas many applications are dominated by finite-time, or transient, performance. Model predictive control is a prominent example: the optimization problem must be solved within a fixed sampling interval, meaning only a limited number of iterations are available before a decision must be made. In such settings, the transient behaviour of the algorithm — how quickly and reliably it approaches the optimizer in the first few iterations — is of greater practical relevance than its eventual asymptotic rate.

To address this gap in transient analysis, this paper aims to unify two complementary research streams. The first stream was initiated by the seminal work of Drori and Teboulle, who introduced the Performance Estimation Problem (PEP) framework for analyzing worst-case behaviour of first-order methods applied to smooth convex functions and provided approximate solutions [3]. Subsequent work by Taylor et al. delivered exact analytical PEP solutions and the Performance Estimation Toolbox (PESTO), enabling systematic semidefinite programming–based analysis over a broad range of performance criteria [14, 15]. This line of research culminates in the analytically defined Information-Theoretic Exact Method (ITEM) for smooth strongly convex minimization, which achieves the oracle-complexity lower bound for black-box first-order methods on this problem class [2, 16].

The second research stream, closer in spirit to this paper, adopts a control-theoretic framework for analyzing and designing optimization algorithms. In this view, optimization methods are treated as dynamical systems and studied with tools from control theory. Earlier work has designed continuous-time optimization algorithms as smooth feedback systems, establishing convergence through passivity-based arguments [4], and has extended classical momentum methods, which are naturally described as second-order systems, to higher-order integrator dynamics with convergence guarantees provided by robust control techniques [8]. Robust control techniques such as integral quadratic constraints (IQCs) have proven particularly powerful in this context, as also demonstrated by Lessard et al., who exploit Luré systems and IQCs to analyze the worst-case asymptotic convergence of first-order methods [6]. More recently, convex synthesis approaches based on dynamic IQCs have been developed to automatically design accelerated first-order methods with optimal guaranteed asymptotic rates, even in the presence of nontrivial dynamics such as delays [11, 12].

These results quantify the transient cost of acceleration for given algorithms using a specific notion of transient growth, but does not address algorithm synthesis or additional dynamics such as delayed gradient measurements.

The main contributions of this paper are two-fold. First, we propose a control-theoretic framework, based on discrete-time Zames–Falb IQCs, to analyze the worst-case transient performance of first-order algorithms in the input–output domain, for general finite-horizon quadratic performance objectives. The resulting convex semidefinite programs (SDPs) provide tight finite-horizon upper bounds that coincide with those obtained from exact PEP formulations. Second, we use Zames–Falb multipliers to synthesize a transient-optimal linear time-varying first-order method. Notably, the synthesized parameters recover the information-theoretic exact method (ITEM) as a special case, demonstrating that optimal finite-horizon performance can also be realized via IQC-based synthesis. A key feature of our synthesis is the ability to explicitly model delays in the gradient measurements, which are unavoidable in practical applications due to communication latencies or computation times and can severely degrade the critical first few iterations of an algorithm.

papers.title: Forecasting Voltage Time Series under Anomalies Using a WGAN Model With Lipschitz Control and Progressive Kernel Critic Strategy
papers.abstract: In time-series forecasting tasks, the use of recursive forecasting on high-dimensional data substantially increases the complexity of the prediction process. The main challenge is that long-term dynamics becomes harder to model, since the sequences show greater temporal variability. To counteract this limitation and improve the modeling of long-term dynamics, and more importantly, address high-dimensional recursive forecasting, this paper uses a Wasserstein GAN equipped with a progressive Lipschitz penalty and an adaptive kernel. This model is capable of taking a window of the data stream and forecasting the next values, subsequently reconstructing the time-series stream and dynamically adapting its kernel to each new window. The proposed model is a deep learning framework based on a Wasserstein GAN (WGAN-CLP) with an adaptive kernel to model alterations in streaming voltage time series. To establish the methodological foundation, we review the WGAN-LP formulation another variant model in this class and extend its framework through an adaptive kernel critic model. We then evaluate this extended model using power ratios, correlation coefficient (CC), and relative root mean squared error (RRMSE). The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms benchmark methods in both accuracy and robustness. The evaluation shows promising performance of the WGAN-CLP with an adaptive kernel framework in forecasting sequence alterations across the voltage and energy time-series datasets.

papers.intro:
A time series is a sequence of observations collected over time that has core properties of sequential structure, temporal ordering, dependence across time, and patterns such as anomalies. Time-series prediction relies on understanding temporal dependencies, and its control tasks require accurate modeling of evolving patterns. Peculiarities such as representation techniques, distance measures, and indexing methods support these tasks [37]. Other functionalities in terms of data mining include distance measures for comparing sequences, temporal analysis for long-term patterns, and stream analysis for real-time data. Together, these characteristics underlie key operations in the mining of the time series - [19]. Time-series data often exhibits high dimensionality and complicates temporal dependency modeling and representations. Digitization has led to massive, high-resolution data inputs which challenge processing capacity [4]. Classical forecasting models in this paradigm are exponential smoothing and ARIMA, known as probabilistic frameworks. Bayesian methods, in contrast, provide a general probabilistic framework applicable across diverse time-series settings [32, 54]. Earlier research primarily emphasized foundational theoretical developments that shaped modern forecasting methods. Previous contributions concentrated on establishing core principles that later models built upon. In this regard, much of the prior literature focused on methodological advances that significantly influenced the evolution of time-series modeling [34]. At the time, SES was widely used in practice but underdeveloped theoretically [33]. As state-space models expanded, researchers established a formal statistical foundation. This led to renewed academic interest. The transition to state-space formulation revived interest in developing unified error models. One core reason is that state-space approaches typically rely on a single-source-of-error assumption, which simplifies estimation and interpretation. Exponential smoothing methods can be expressed in state-space form using either additive or multiplicative error specifications. Earlier work provided initial formulations, and [34] formalized the additive and multiplicative error formulations, building on earlier outlines by [13]. Linear exponential smoothing is mathematically equivalent to an ARIMA(0,1,1) model. Non-linear time-series relationships can be approximated using finite Volterra series, which motivates the use of a non-linear model structure. This is mainly because non-linear formulation complicates estimation and inference; these aspects have received comparatively limited attention. The main issue is that Non-linear time-series models often suffer from over-parametrization [52]. Because of this, increasing model complexity can reduce interpretability and heighten the risk of overfitting.

This is mainly because non-linear formulation complicates estimation and inference; these aspects have received comparatively limited attention. The main issue is that Non-linear time-series models often suffer from over-parametrization [52]. Because of this, increasing model complexity can reduce interpretability and heighten the risk of overfitting.

Exponential smoothing is a foundational forecasting method developed in the mid-20th century by [11, 30, 56]. Later [34] showed that exponential smoothing can outperform ARIMA models when data exhibit non-Gaussian characteristics. Some exponential-smoothing variants re-normalize seasonal indices to reduce bias in level and seasonal estimates. Notably, certain ARIMA models give equivalent forecasts to the linear exponential smoothing methods. More recent work explores neural architectures such as CNNs, fully connected networks, and RNNs for structured time-series data [33, 34, 18]. Additionally, motif discovery, which identifies recurrent subsequences, represents another important application of time-series analysis tasks. Because motif identification is inherently probabilistic, exact solutions are often not guaranteed [25]. Certain ARIMA formulations are mathematically equivalent to linear exponential smoothing. This provides identical one-step-ahead forecasts under specific parameter settings, which allows exponential smoothing methods to be interpreted within a statistical modeling framework. This equivalence enables researchers to construct prediction intervals by using ARIMA-based error distributions to derive uncertainty measures for smoothing forecasts [34, 33]. This results in more rigorous interval estimation for exponential smoothing models. Distributional forecasting aims to estimate the full probability distribution of future observations, and the smoothing methods often provide tractable approximations for these distributions. This makes them beneficial when probabilistic forecasts are required.

In multi-step forecasting, performance depends on several modeling choices. These factors include model order selection, forecast horizon, error propagation, and the characteristics of the underlying time series. These collectively determine the reliability of long-range forecasts [32, 24]. Another method is seasonal decomposition, which separate trend, seasonal, and residual components. In this method, the choice of decomposition approach can influence forecast accuracy, particularly when seasonal patterns are strong or irregular. Deterministic seasonality repeats with fixed amplitude and timing, whereas stochastic seasonality varies over time. This makes deterministic seasonal structure less common in real-world data. Consequently, this influences whether exponential smoothing or ARIMA-type seasonal models are appropriate. A double-loop Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm has been employed to classify epileptic seizures from electroencephalogram (EEG) signals. This work has addressed the challenge of detecting seizure patterns within highly noisy and variable biomedical time-series data. Ghiassa et al. [20] evaluated a dynamic ANN architecture, comparing its forecasting performance with traditional ANN and ARIMA models to address the problem of capturing evolving dependencies that static models often miss. Han and Kamber (2006) [28] investigated clustering methods for time-series data mining, describing partitioning, hierarchical, density-based, grid-based, and model-based approaches [20, 28], addressing the challenge of grouping patterns in streaming data where cluster structures evolve. For instance, time-series prediction is a widely studied application aimed at modeling market behavior, addressing the difficulty of forecasting highly volatile and non-stationary signals. In this regard, Bai and NG [7] introduced hard and soft thresholding to construct targeted predictors, addressing the problem of irrelevant factors that degrade forecast accuracy in high-dimensional financial models. [40] proposed a 2D deep convolutional auto-encoder that learns representations directly from raw data, addressing the problem of time-consuming manual feature extraction in complex time-series applications. Together, these studies highlight the diverse methodological landscape of time-series analysis, ranging from probabilistic EM algorithms [15] and dynamic neural networks to clustering frameworks, targeted predictors, and deep auto-encoders [29]. Each of these addresses distinct challenges such as noisy biomedical signals, evolving data streams, non-linear dependencies, and automated feature extraction.

papers.title: Explaining Chess and Go in Natural Language
papers.abstract: Modern chess engines play far beyond human ability, often choosing moves whose underlying ideas are difficult for humans to understand. We propose an automatic metric for evaluating chess explanations, grounded in chess-engine evaluations. Evaluating state-of-the-art language models using this metric, we find that they perform surprisingly poorly, often relying on surface-level board observations rather than robust, transferable chess concepts. We then introduce BinProp, a training-free method that enables these same models to discover reusable chess concepts and use them to explain moves in natural language. BinProp improves explainability for every model tested, nearly tripling the average score compared with direct prompting. Beyond chess, the same method discovers useful concepts in Go, draughts, and shogi without additional tuning.

papers.intro:
Modern chess-playing algorithms, called chess engines, are vastly superior to human players, but their decisions are often difficult to understand. Since Shannon’s formulation of computer chess (Shannon, 1950), engines have followed the same basic paradigm: search through possible continuations, evaluate the resulting positions, and choose the move whose continuation looks best using MiniMax (v. Neumann, 1928). papers.title: Are Single-Leader-Multi-Follower Problems Particular Cases of Bilevel Optimization?
papers.abstract: For more than 20 years, single-leader multi-follower (SLMF) problems have been treated as a more difficult class of problems in comparison to bilevel optimization. In this work we challenge this common belief, studying whether SLMF problems can be reformulated as equivalent bilevel optimization problems. We consider both optimistic and pessimistic formulations. For the optimistic case the answer is positive: We derive an equivalent bilevel problem by representing the followers' equilibria as fixed points of the solution mapping of a single optimization problem. For pessimistic problems, the situation is different. We show that every optimistic trilevel problem admits an equivalent pessimistic SLMF formulation with two followers. Conversely, for every pessimistic SLMF problem verifying a mild attainability assumption we establish an equivalent optimistic trilevel reformulation. The reformulations are easy, readily tractable, and they preserve convex and linear data. Thus, unless $\text{NP}=Σ_2^p$, we deduce as byproduct that multiple followers induce an unexpected complexity gap between optimistic and pessimistic approaches, which is not the case when considering one follower alone.

papers.intro:
Bilevel optimization deals with optimization problems in which some variables are required to solve another optimization problem. These problems model hierarchical interactions between two decision makers, the leader and the follower. The leader makes a decision first and anticipates the optimal response of the follower, whose problem depends on the leader’s decision. If several followers interact non-cooperatively at the lower level, one obtains a single-leader multi-follower (SLMF) problem. Each follower then solves an optimization problem that also depends on the strategies of the other followers. The resulting lower-level problem is a Nash equilibrium problem or, if the followers’ feasible sets depend on the other followers’ strategies, a generalized Nash equilibrium problem (GNEP). Hence, SLMF problems extend the usual single-leader single-follower (SLSF) setting of bilevel optimization.

While simply quoted by [17] in his pioneering work, such combinations of hierarchical optimization and equilibrium problems have been studied in the seminal work of [14], and can be traced back to [15]. For an overview of single- and multi-leader-follower games, including existence results, reformulations, and solution methods, we refer to [2]. A tutorial on solving SLMF problems using SOS1 reformulations is given in [1]. A central issue of these models is that the followers’ equilibrium need not be unique. In the optimistic case, the leader selects the most favorable equilibrium among those satisfying the upper-level constraints. In the pessimistic case, the leader accounts for the worst equilibrium outcome and requires the coupling constraints to hold for every equilibrium. This distinction already arises in bilevel optimization [7, 3] and is equally relevant for SLMF problems.

SLMF problems appear more difficult than their SLSF counterparts because the leader must anticipate a system of mutually dependent optimization problems. In general, minimizing the sum of the followers’ objectives over their jointly feasible strategies does not characterize the equilibria of the game. Moreover, convexity of each follower’s problem does not ensure convexity of the equilibrium set, and even uniqueness of each individual best response does not ensure uniqueness of the equilibrium. These properties make the analysis and solution of SLMF problems challenging. However, they do not settle whether SLMF problems are actually harder than bilevel problems. In particular, the question remains whether an SLMF problem can be reformulated as a bilevel problem while preserving properties such as convexity or linearity of the data.

In recent years, several papers have shown that problem classes that are usually studied separately can be related by suitable reformulations. [19] develops a scheme for pessimistic bilevel optimization based on a tight optimistic bilevel relaxation and a procedure for recovering a feasible optimal solution. This allows one to apply methods for optimistic bilevel optimization to pessimistic problems. For solvable bilevel problems with rational linear data, [9] show that coupling constraints can be removed while preserving linearity and the globally optimal solutions after projection onto the original variables. [10] prove corresponding results for pessimistic linear bilevel problems and also derive optimistic reformulations without coupling constraints. Finally, [12] show that, under suitable assumptions, GNEPs can be reformulated as Nash equilibrium problems by adding one player. These reformulations preserve linear or convex structure for the respective problem classes. The common idea of these works is to use additional variables or players to obtain a formulation that allows one to apply theory and methods from another problem class.

In this paper, we study whether SLMF problems with a lower-level GNEP can be reformulated as bilevel optimization problems. We first consider the optimistic case. Inspired by the use of copied follower variables in [19], we represent the followers’ equilibria as fixed points of the solution mapping of a single optimization problem. We then introduce a copy of the followers’ strategy vector at the upper level and link both copies by equality constraints. This yields an equivalent optimistic bilevel problem without any assumption on the structure of the problem. We show that the reformulation preserves convex and linear data. For explicitly encoded rational linear data, the reformulation can be constructed in polynomial time and has polynomial encoding length.

This yields an equivalent optimistic bilevel problem without any assumption on the structure of the problem. We show that the reformulation preserves convex and linear data. For explicitly encoded rational linear data, the reformulation can be constructed in polynomial time and has polynomial encoding length.

For pessimistic SLMF problems, we derive an equivalent optimistic trilevel optimization problem under an attainability assumption on truncated constraint-violation functions. The truncation allows us to handle unbounded constraint violations, and we show that the attainability assumption always holds under linear data. We also prove the reverse result: every optimistic trilevel problem can be reformulated as a pessimistic SLMF problem. To this end, we encode the feasible region of the middle- and lower-level problems through a two-player GNEP and impose optimality by robust comparisons with its equilibria. Both reformulations preserve linear data and can be constructed in polynomial time with polynomial encoding length for rational linear data. We also discuss the assumptions and modifications needed to preserve convex data.

The truncation allows us to handle unbounded constraint violations, and we show that the attainability assumption always holds under linear data. We also prove the reverse result: every optimistic trilevel problem can be reformulated as a pessimistic SLMF problem. To this end, we encode the feasible region of the middle- and lower-level problems through a two-player GNEP and impose optimality by robust comparisons with its equilibria. Both reformulations preserve linear data and can be constructed in polynomial time with polynomial encoding length for rational linear data. We also discuss the assumptions and modifications needed to preserve convex data.

Finally, we analyze the complexity of SLMF problems with rational linear data. Using the results of [11, 4, 16], we prove that the decision problem for optimistic SLMF problems with rational linear data is NP-complete, whereas its pessimistic counterpart is Σ2p\Sigma_{2}^{p}-complete. The latter result continues to hold without coupling constraints, already for a two-follower game. We prove this by reducing the DeNegre bilevel knapsack problem, whose complexity was established by [5]. We further give a linear example showing that direct exact penalization of the robust coupling constraints can fail. Thus, unless NP=Σ2p\mathrm{NP}=\Sigma_{2}^{p}, there is no polynomial-time reduction of the general pessimistic SLMF decision problem with rational linear data to the corresponding optimistic linear bilevel decision problem. The optimistic and pessimistic SLMF formulations therefore have different relationships with bilevel optimization even when all data are linear. This contrast was unexpected because our starting point was the scheme of [19] for solving pessimistic bilevel problems through optimistic bilevel optimization.

papers.title: Bad Diagnosis: Analyzing Consent and Data Collection Practices of Mobile Medical Apps
papers.abstract: Mobile health (mHealth) apps collect personally-identifiable information while handling uniquely sensitive medical data, ranging from mental health records to real-time glucose or heart rate monitoring -- yet they remain poorly understood at scale. We present the first comprehensive analysis of consent and data collection practices across 10,000+ mHealth apps on the Google Play Store, combining static analysis and privacy policy examination. We develop a rigorous operational definition to distinguish health apps from general wellness programs, and design a measurement framework to detect misuse of permissions and violations of consent. Our analyses reveal a troubling ecosystem: 69.15% of apps request at least one permission unrelated to their stated purpose, with over 52.9% apps requesting location data, and 50.5% and 34.9% apps requesting camera and microphone access, respectively -- despite no functional justification based on app descriptions and stated purposes. Most alarmingly, nearly 93% of apps fail to provide users with a consent form, directly violating regulatory requirements such as GDPR; and even among the remaining 7%, 1 in 14 demonstrate a gap between the obtained consent and collection of personally identifiable information. These findings demonstrate an urgent need for stronger enforcement of privacy regulations in mHealth apps. We plan to release our dataset and measurement tools for continued monitoring of this critical space.

papers.title: Between Spoilers and Guesswork: Avoiding Over-Specification in Coding Benchmarks
papers.abstract: Benchmarks drive AI progress, but are hampered by task under-specification and over-specification. Task under-specification causes guesswork, where solutions have to make things up, or worse, resort to contamination or reward hacking. Task over-specification causes spoilers, where solutions can bypass some of the harder steps the benchmark was supposed to measure. Since future-looking benchmarks should be difficult, over-specification reduces a benchmark's shelflife of community adoption. Repository-level coding benchmarks have helped the field progress but experience unnecessary churn due to both over- and under-specification. For instance, SWE-bench Pro, FEA-bench, Doc2Feat-bench, and Multi-SWE-bench all tackle under-specification by augmenting task statements with hints derived from ground truth. We show that leaking ground-truth information into the task statement causes over-specification in some of these benchmarks. We experiment with various specification levels, trying to thread the needle between spoilers and guesswork. Based on these results, we recommend techniques for deriving parsimonious hints. Repository-level coding benchmarks have contributed to great advancements in coding agents by evaluating them via executing held-out tests against their proposed patches (Jimenez et al., 2024). For these evaluations to measure implementation ability, the task description and available repositories have to communicate the requirements enforced by the tests. Achieving this alignment has proven difficult. OpenAI introduced SWE-bench Verified to reduce underspecification and unfair testing (OpenAI, 2024). It later recommended SWE-bench Pro after finding test flaws and contamination in Verified (OpenAI, 2026c), then withdrew that recommendation after finding underspecified prompts and overly restrictive tests in Pro (OpenAI, 2026b). This churn is evidence for both the importance and difficulty of this problem. An agent can then implement the requested behavior correctly yet fail solely because it chose a different name. Recovering these unstated interface choices introduces guesswork into an evaluation intended to measure software implementation ability.

papers.title: Inducing Extraordinary-log Criticality through a Quantum Spin Chain
papers.abstract: We demonstrate the emergence of extraordinary-log criticality in a quantum many-body system by coupling a spin-$1/2$ Heisenberg chain to a two-dimensional quantum critical Heisenberg bilayer. Under the quantum-to-classical mapping, the chain acts as a plane defect in a three-dimensional critical environment for which the extraordinary-log universality class has recently been predicted. Using large-scale sign-problem-free quantum Monte Carlo simulations, we directly probe the renormalization-group flow of the effective defect coupling through the spin stiffness. We observe the characteristic logarithmic growth with linear system size $L$, corresponding to a stable weak-coupling fixed point and a running coupling $g(L)\sim 1/\log L$. Furthermore, the extracted step-scaling function quantitatively follows the universal renormalization-group flow predicted for the extraordinary-log universality class, including the leading and subleading universal coefficients. Our results establish extraordinary-log criticality in a genuine quantum many-body setting and show that its universal behavior persists despite the topological $θ$-term present in the low-energy field theory of the isolated spin chain.

papers.title: Three-dimensional spatial modelling of nuclear de-excitation lines
papers.abstract: Galactic cosmic rays (GCRs) are thought to originate from shock acceleration in supernova remnants, but interstellar ionization rates suggest an additional low-energy cosmic-ray (LECR) component. LECRs excite nuclei in the ISM, producing MeV gamma-ray line emission through subsequent de-excitation. Observations of this emission can constrain the LECR flux, morphology, and acceleration mechanisms. We construct all-sky maps of Galactic de-excitation emission using three-dimensional (3D) CR distribution models. By comparing them with the Galactic diffuse gamma-ray emission, we assess the detectability of the de-excitation line components against the underlying continuum. We calculate the emission by combining 3D CR distributions from GALPROP and gamma-ray production cross sections from TALYS. We also model an additional LECR component motivated by the high ionization rates measured in the ISM. The predicted de-excitation emission is relatively weak when integrated over the broad regions commonly adopted in MeV gamma-ray analyses ($|l|\leq30^{\circ}$ and $|b|\leq15^{\circ}$), contributing only $\lesssim 1\%$ above the leptonic continuum even considering the additional LECR component. The all-sky maps reveal that, in the standard scenario, the de-excitation-to-leptonic flux ratio remains low over the entire sky, reaching at most ${\sim}20\%$ toward the Galactic anticenter. In contrast, models including an additional LECR component exhibit a pronounced enhancement toward the GC, where the ratio exceeds $100\%$, indicating favourable prospects for detection through spatially resolved analyses. The 6.1-to-4.4 MeV intensity ratio is particularly sensitive to the maximum energy of the injected LECR spectrum, varying by up to ${\sim} 30\%$. Future MeV gamma-ray observatories could thus identify a distinct LECR population and constrain its acceleration and transport.

papers.intro:
The origin of cosmic rays (CRs) has remained a mystery for more than a century (Hess, 1912). Low-energy CRs below 1 GeV (hereafter, LECRs) are strongly affected by the heliospheric magnetic field, making it challenging to constrain their spectra at the source using only direct particle measurements within and around the heliosphere, including those obtained by Voyager (Cummings et al., 2016). In the standard paradigm, CRs up to PeV energies are thought to be accelerated mainly by shock waves in supernova remnants (SNRs), but there is still no conclusive evidence for this scenario (see, e.g., Blasi, 2013; Gabici et al., 2019, and references therein). From the viewpoint of astrochemistry, LECRs are considered to be a major source of ionization of hydrogen and helium in dense gas, and thus an important driver of chemical evolution in star-forming regions and protoplanetary disks (Padovani et al., 2013). However, measurements of the ionization rate toward the Galactic plane and the Galactic Center (GC) region indicate that the inferred LECR intensity is more than an order of magnitude higher than predicted by the standard CR propagation model, suggesting the presence of an additional LECR source (Indriolo et al., 2009, e.g.,). As for the origin of the additional LECR component, several scenarios have been proposed, including astrosheaths (Scherer et al., 2008, the shocked stellar-wind regions between the termination shock and the astropause;), superbubbles (Tatischeff et al., 2021), and stochasticity effects in SNRs (Phan et al., 2023). However, the existence and properties of a distinct Galactic LECR component remain uncertain (Gabici, 2022, for a review, see). Observational constraints on the LECR spectrum are therefore essential for establishing the presence of such a component and, if present, for investigating its origin and propagation in the Galaxy.

Two main indirect methods have been proposed to probe LECRs: one is to detect X-rays produced when LECRs ionize inner-shell electrons of atoms in the gas, followed by their de-excitation; the other is to detect γ\gamma-rays produced when LECRs excite atomic nuclei in the gas, followed by their nuclear de-excitation. Observations using the former method have mainly been based on the 6.4 keV line emission from neutral iron. Several detections of 6.4 keV line emission potentially associated with LECRs have been reported (Tatischeff et al., 2012; Nobukawa et al., 2015; Nobukawa et al., 2018); however, since this line emission can be produced not only by LECR ions but also by X-rays and electrons, it is challenging to place stringent constraints on the LECR flux. The latter method, based on MeV γ\gamma-ray observations, overcomes this limitation because the excitation processes are caused predominantly by LECRs.

To date, no LECR-induced MeV line emission has been detected from the Galactic plane, or even the GC. Although a number of studies have predicted this γ\gamma-ray emission, the calculations have generally been limited to one- or two-dimensional spatial models and focused primarily on spectral predictions (Indriolo et al., 2009; Dogiel et al., 2009; Benhabiles-Mezhoud et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2021; Liu and Yang, 2024, e.g.,). In this study, we extend previous calculations to a three-dimensional framework and present the first skymap models of LECR-induced nuclear γ\gamma-ray line emission. This skymap-based approach facilitates comparisons between nuclear line emission and leptonic continuum emission, the latter of which constitutes a major background for nuclear-line observations. Physically motivated all-sky models are also crucial for comparisons with MeV γ\gamma-ray observations, since most current MeV instruments employ Compton-camera or coded-mask techniques, whose spectral analyses rely on assumed source distributions. In addition, we investigate LECR source models motivated by ionization-rate measurements. We construct LECR source models with parameters constrained by current CR observations and evaluate their expected γ\gamma-ray emission.

papers.title: Scaling of entanglement with distance between subsystems: detection of phase transitions in the $t'$-$π$-flux model
papers.abstract: The system-size scaling of bipartite entanglement can be used to detect phase transitions. We develop a related approach for strongly correlated electron models where large density matrices or large system size scaling are inaccessible. To this end, we demonstrate that phase transitions of various kinds are signaled by a sharp signature in the first- or second-order logarithmic derivatives of the negativity measuring entanglement between small clusters at varying distances. Crucially, we show how to mitigate the effect of quantum Monte Carlo noise at large distances when computing the negativity. Our focus is on the $t'$-$π$-flux Hubbard model using auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo simulations. It has the particular advantage of showing three distinct phase transitions in a single model: semimetal to band insulator, semimetal to antiferromagnetic Mott insulator, and a magnetic order-disorder transition belonging to the Gaussian, Gross-Neveu, and O(3) Wilson-Fisher universality classes, respectively.

A key challenge in condensed matter theory is the detection and classification of phase transitions when the Ginzburg–Landau theory for first- and second-order phase transitions [1] is not applicable. Order-parameter-free approaches can be based, among others, on the fidelity (ground-state overlap) [2, 3], machine learning [4, 5, 6] or tensor network properties [7], and, most prominently, on entanglement. For the latter, the quantum Fisher information [8] can be used [9] , and has been used for detecting quantum criticality [10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15] as well as multipartite entanglement in cuprates [16, 17, 18]. Even more often, at least for theoretical calculations, bipartite entanglement measures are considered [19]. For example, a phase transition can be detected through the system -size scaling of the entanglement entropy [19, 20, 21, 22, 23], an approach that can be extended to finite-temperature entanglement measures [24, 25].

However, this need not necessarily be the case.

Small subsystems at a finite distance have been considered before, but with different scaling variables. Correlations between two distant clusters, captured by the correlation density matrix [36], were recently sampled with QMC and analyzed by finite-size scaling at maximal separation [37]. The negativity between separated regions has been studied as a function of distance at criticality [38, 39], including with QMC in the π\pi-flux tt-VV model [40]. In one-dimensional free fermions, the negativity between separated blocks distinguishes symmetry-protected topological phases and topologically distinct critical points [41]. Entanglement between small subsystems has also been used to construct measures of genuine multipartite entanglement, employed to detect phase transitions in the quantum Ising model [42], and recently extended to fermions and studied as a function of temperature and separation in the Kitaev chain [43]. In all these works, the separation is either kept fixed or tied to the system size, or varied at a fixed coupling, typically at the critical point to extract universal exponents. Here, we instead follow the coupling dependence of the negativity at a sequence of distances dd, so that dd plays a role analogous to that of the system size. This is motivated, for example, by the distance scaling of the negativity observed in Ising chains with defects [44].

papers.title: Thermalization-induced self-polarization of temporally incoherent light: A nonequilibrium wave turbulence kinetic approach
papers.abstract: Conservative nonlinear waves generally undergo an irreversible process of thermalization toward the Rayleigh--Jeans (RJ) equilibrium state. Light thermalization has recently been experimentally investigated in the two-dimensional transverse spatial dynamics of multimode waveguides. Here, we consider the one-dimensional temporal dynamics of incoherent light propagating in a weakly birefringent single-mode fiber. We show that light thermalization is responsible for a self-polarization of the incoherent wave during its propagation. Within the framework of wave turbulence theory, we show that this phenomenon originates from a nonequilibrium process of adiabatic cooling: polarization fluctuations are continuously transferred toward the high-frequency tails of a local RJ equilibrium state, whose effective temperature decreases during propagation, thereby increasing the degree of light polarization. Moreover, in the absence of a high-frequency cut-off that would regularize the ultraviolet catastrophe in the temporal domain, the optical wave exhibits an ever-increasing degree of polarization, ultimately approaching unity. These results show that it is thermodynamically advantageous for the optical field to evolve toward a polarized state, which provides new insight into spontaneous self-organization phenomena in conservative Hamiltonian systems operating far from thermodynamic equilibrium.

Non-integrable Hamiltonian systems of random waves generally undergo thermalization – an irreversible evolution toward thermodynamic equilibrium, characterized by a state of maximum entropy. In the weakly nonlinear regime, this process is accurately described by the wave turbulence (WT) theory [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], which has been successfully applied to various physical systems [8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13], including optical waves propagating in liquid crystals [14], or in optical fibers [15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22]. In spite of the formal reversibility of the Hamiltonian system, the wave turbulence kinetic equation describes the actual irreversible evolution to the Rayleigh-Jeans (RJ) equilibrium distribution, as expressed by a HH-theorem of entropy growth.

Optical systems provide a natural setting for exploring the emergence of collective phenomena from nonlinear wave interactions. In this context, there is increasing interest in the study of so-called ‘fluids of light’ with effective photon-photon interactions, which constitute the photonic analogue of atomic Bose gases [23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28]. The notion of a fluid of light arises from a mathematical correspondence between the propagation of light through a nonlinear medium and the conservative time evolution of a quantum fluid of interacting photons [29]. Propagating fluids of light have consequently provided a versatile platform for investigating a broad range of fascinating phenomena, including the generation of superfluid Bogoliubov sound waves [30, 31], complex vortex dynamics [32, 33, 34, 35, 36], binary fluids [37], spin-orbit-coupled fluids [38, 39], analogue gravity and cosmology [40, 43, 44, 41, 42, 45, 46], turbulent cascade regimes [47, 48], and the dynamical emergence of prethermalized equilibrium states [49, 50, 51, 52].

Nevertheless, because collisional scattering processes between single photons are exceedingly rare in standard media, these phenomena were expected to require impractically long propagation distances. In contrast, for classical fields, thermalization and condensation are predicted to occur much more rapidly owing to bosonic stimulation effects, as discussed in [54, 55, 56, 57, 4, 21].

In this context, the thermalization of classical optical waves toward the RJ equilibrium distribution has become a topic of significant interest in recent years. In particular, by considering quasi-monochromatic optical beams – thus neglecting temporal dynamics and restricting the analysis to the transverse spatial degrees of freedom – the problem reduces to a two-dimensional (2D) spatial thermalization process. Within this framework, thermalization toward the classical 2D RJ distribution has been predicted for optical waves propagating in multimode fibers [58] using the framework of wave turbulence theory [1, 2, 4, 5, 21]. The finite number of guided modes in a multimode fiber not only accelerates the convergence to the RJ equilibrium, but also regularizes the ultraviolet catastrophe that is intrinsic to classical-wave systems [58]. It is precisely in this guided-wave geometry that RJ thermalization has recently been investigated experimentally through the transverse 2D spatial dynamics of a quasi-monochromatic speckle beam propagating in a multimode fiber [59, 60, 61, 62, 63, 64, 65]. This phenomenon is closely connected to the spatial beam self-cleaning effect [66, 67], whose underlying physical mechanism has been analyzed in several theoretical studies [59, 68, 69, 70, 71, 72, 73, 75, 74]; see also the review articles [76, 77]. More broadly, this sustained research activity has contributed to the emergence of the field of optical thermodynamics [70, 79, 80, 78, 81, 82, 83, 84, 85, 86]. From a different perspective, temporally incoherent light waves propagating in single-mode fibers have been considered for a long time to study optical turbulence [15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21]. papers.title: Validating LLM-generated political networks with survey-reported partisan exposure
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior in social science research, including decisions, interactions, and social relationships. However, in network formation tasks, existing evaluations often focus on aggregate network properties, while networks with plausible structural properties may still fail to reproduce individuals' social and political environments. Here, we generate LLM-based political networks using personas sampled from the nationally representative ANES 2020--2022 Social Media Study and use respondents' survey-reported partisan exposure as an empirical benchmark for the political environments generated for the corresponding personas. We first characterize the structural properties and political assortativity of the generated networks, and then compare ego-level partisan exposure with the survey. We find that the structure and political assortativity of the generated networks vary across experimental configurations. More importantly, when comparing generated partisan exposure with the survey, some models generate stronger separation between Democratic and Republican egos than reported in the survey, with higher same-party and lower cross-party exposure, while others mainly underestimate Republican exposure across ego groups. Moreover, networks with similar political assortativity can still generate different partisan environments around the same personas, including among networks with plausible structural properties. Finally, generated networks show group-specific errors, under- or overestimating exposure to either Democrats or Republicans for specific social groups. These findings show that evaluating LLM-based social simulations only through aggregate outcomes can hide errors in the local environments through which those outcomes emerge, highlighting the importance of validation at both aggregate and individual levels.

papers.title: A configurational numerical viscosity for thermodynamically compatible finite volume schemes of compressible multiphase flows
papers.abstract: We consider the fluid subsystem of a variationally derived hyperbolic thermodynamically compatible (HTC) model of compressible multiphase flows. Its total energy is in general not convex in the natural state variables, so a scalar numerical viscosity acting on them need not produce non-negative entropy. Reformulating the equations in terms of the volume fractions separates changes in the amount of each phase from changes in its intrinsic state. This guides the construction of a configurational numerical viscosity in phase variables, in which the energy is convex, while the scheme retains the structure of the HTC model. At the semi-discrete level, the new schemes satisfy: I) local conservation of the phase masses, the mixture momentum and the total energy; II) a cell entropy inequality whose production is non-negative face by face and phase by phase, with no convexity assumption in the evolved variables and no clipping; III) positivity of the partial densities and volume fractions under explicit time-step conditions; IV) exact preservation of contact equilibria; V) equivalence with a scheme for the density-weighted volume fractions. The key ingredients are: i) an exact decomposition of the jump of each phase across a face into a configurational part, dissipated with the material speed, and an intrinsic part, dissipated with the acoustic speed; ii) an exchange form of this dissipation between neighbouring cells, with non-negative weights; iii) a side-wise transfer of the dissipation to the evolved variables through the chain rule of each cell, which turns the energy defects into Bregman divergences of the single-fluid energies; iv) a thermodynamic correction of the reversible part built in the phase variables. Properties I)-V) are proved and verified numerically, including a shock tube in which the Rusanov viscosity produces negative entropy and a shock-water column interaction.

papers.intro:
Compressible flows of several immiscible fluids separated by material interfaces, such as bubbles or droplets in a liquid, shocks interacting with liquid columns or cavitating flows, are often computed with diffuse-interface models [8, 57, 6, 59, 58]. For models of Baer–Nunziato type, the literature ranges from their mathematical analysis and the solution of the Riemann problem [33, 7, 60, 26] to path-conservative and pressure-based schemes [28, 50] and to models with more than two phases [39, 40, 49, 34]. Each phase is described as a continuum with a volume fraction, and an interface is the thin region in which the volume fractions change. A numerical scheme for such models has to regularize shocks without diffusing the interfaces more than necessary, while preserving the conservation properties and the thermodynamic structure of the model. With a scalar numerical viscosity applied uniformly to all variables, these goals can conflict. In Rusanov-type schemes, and more generally in scalar parabolic numerical regularizations based on characteristic speeds, the dissipative scale is set by the fastest waves. In a liquid, the acoustic speed can exceed the material velocity by an order of magnitude or more. The same acoustic scale then controls the numerical diffusion of an interface, even though the interface is transported with the material velocity: in water-air computations, this can lead to substantial interface smearing.

The models considered here belong to the class of symmetric hyperbolic thermodynamically compatible (SHTC) systems introduced by Godunov and Romenski [36, 37]. Their two-phase and multiphase versions [55, 54, 53, 64] evolve the relative velocities of the phases as state variables and combine conservative fluxes with non-conservative terms reflecting the geometric structure of the model. Interfacial friction and pressure relaxation are described by algebraic source terms with non-negative entropy production. Numerical schemes for these models include high-order ADER discontinuous Galerkin, all-Mach-number and implicit–explicit finite volume methods, and exactly curl-free schemes [52, 43, 42, 23, 51]. The unified HTC multiphase model of [34] extends this description to elastic and heat-conducting media, in the spirit of the unified first-order formulation of continuum mechanics [31], for which structure-preserving semi-implicit schemes have recently been developed [27]. In this work we consider its fluid subsystem, with relative velocities, interfacial friction and pressure relaxation, but without elastic and heat-conducting effects.

Their two-phase and multiphase versions [55, 54, 53, 64] evolve the relative velocities of the phases as state variables and combine conservative fluxes with non-conservative terms reflecting the geometric structure of the model. Interfacial friction and pressure relaxation are described by algebraic source terms with non-negative entropy production. Numerical schemes for these models include high-order ADER discontinuous Galerkin, all-Mach-number and implicit–explicit finite volume methods, and exactly curl-free schemes [52, 43, 42, 23, 51]. The unified HTC multiphase model of [34] extends this description to elastic and heat-conducting media, in the spirit of the unified first-order formulation of continuum mechanics [31], for which structure-preserving semi-implicit schemes have recently been developed [27]. In this work we consider its fluid subsystem, with relative velocities, interfacial friction and pressure relaxation, but without elastic and heat-conducting effects.

The thermodynamic structure of the continuous model should also be reflected in its numerical approximation: the discrete evolution should satisfy both an energy balance and an entropy inequality. Entropy-conservative and entropy-stable schemes provide a systematic framework for enforcing discrete entropy relations, following the work of Tadmor [62, 63], also for non-conservative systems [20]; recent developments include discontinuous Galerkin formulations [21, 22]. For fluid systems, these methods typically discretize the conservation laws, including total energy, and enforce an additional discrete entropy relation. Hyperbolic thermodynamically compatible (HTC) schemes [1, 2, 18, 17, 14, 15, 16] reverse this choice: they evolve the entropy densities and construct the discretization so that the total-energy balance follows as a consequence. Their convergence towards dissipative weak solutions has been proved for the Euler equations [29], semi-implicit variants whose time step is restricted only by the material velocity have recently been proposed [32], and structure-preserving HTC schemes for nonlinear SHTC systems with involutions have been developed in [41], together with exactly div–curl–grad compatible and energy-conservative discontinuous Galerkin schemes [3]. They have been applied, among others, to a two-fluid model with two entropy inequalities [65] and to Lagrangian gas dynamics and continuum mechanics [11, 10], and a space–time discontinuous Galerkin method that uses the state and the dual variables together has recently been proposed in [30]; see also [4] for structure-preserving continuous–discontinuous Galerkin schemes. In the finite volume HTC framework mentioned so far the numerical flux has two parts. The reversible part is made exactly compatible with the energy conservation law, either through a path integral in the dual variables or by correcting a central flux along a prescribed direction with one scalar coefficient per face, the so-called Abgrall correction [1], which has also been reinterpreted and extended to residual distribution and discontinuous Galerkin schemes [5, 35]. The dissipative part is a numerical viscosity with non-negative entropy production. A common choice is a scalar viscosity acting on the evolved variables, whose production is proportional to the pairing between the jumps of the state and of the thermodynamic forces. This pairing is non-negative when the energy is convex in the evolved variables [2]. A viscosity written directly in the forces, in the spirit of [62], has a non-negative production by construction.

The thermodynamic structure of the continuous model should also be reflected in its numerical approximation: the discrete evolution should satisfy both an energy balance and an entropy inequality. Entropy-conservative and entropy-stable schemes provide a systematic framework for enforcing discrete entropy relations, following the work of Tadmor [62, 63], also for non-conservative systems [20]; recent developments include discontinuous Galerkin formulations [21, 22]. For fluid systems, these methods typically discretize the conservation laws, including total energy, and enforce an additional discrete entropy relation. Hyperbolic thermodynamically compatible (HTC) schemes [1, 2, 18, 17, 14, 15, 16] reverse this choice: they evolve the entropy densities and construct the discretization so that the total-energy balance follows as a consequence. Their convergence towards dissipative weak solutions has been proved for the Euler equations [29], semi-implicit variants whose time step is restricted only by the material velocity have recently been proposed [32], and structure-preserving HTC schemes for nonlinear SHTC systems with involutions have been developed in [41], together with exactly div–curl–grad compatible and energy-conservative discontinuous Galerkin schemes [3]. They have been applied, among others, to a two-fluid model with two entropy inequalities [65] and to Lagrangian gas dynamics and continuum mechanics [11, 10], and a space–time discontinuous Galerkin method that uses the state and the dual variables together has recently been proposed in [30]; see also [4] for structure-preserving continuous–discontinuous Galerkin schemes. In the finite volume HTC framework mentioned so far the numerical flux has two parts. The reversible part is made exactly compatible with the energy conservation law, either through a path integral in the dual variables or by correcting a central flux along a prescribed direction with one scalar coefficient per face, the so-called Abgrall correction [1], which has also been reinterpreted and extended to residual distribution and discontinuous Galerkin schemes [5, 35]. The dissipative part is a numerical viscosity with non-negative entropy production. A common choice is a scalar viscosity acting on the evolved variables, whose production is proportional to the pairing between the jumps of the state and of the thermodynamic forces. This pairing is non-negative when the energy is convex in the evolved variables [2]. A viscosity written directly in the forces, in the spirit of [62], has a non-negative production by construction.

Two observations motivate the present work. The first is that, for the model considered here, the convexity on which the classical scalar viscosity relies is not available. The energy is convex in suitable phase variables, but not in the variables in which the scheme is written as soon as the phases slip with respect to each other (Section 3.4); the pairing between the jumps of the state and of the thermodynamic forces, and with it the entropy production of the scalar viscosity, can therefore be negative. Section 7.3 shows that this happens in a shock tube, in the regions where one of the phases is present only in traces, and that clipping the negative production breaks the conservation of the total energy.

papers.title: Termination-dependent surface Fermiology in the intercalated altermagnet CoNb$_4$Se$_8$
papers.abstract: Altermagnets have recently gained attention for hosting symmetry-enforced spin-split bands despite zero net magnetization. Angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy (ARPES) offers direct access to their electronic structure. However, the intrinsic surface sensitivity of this technique complicates the identification of the observed features: Surface states can be misinterpreted as the spin-split counterpart of bulk bands. This issue becomes particularly relevant for layered intercalated systems, where micrometer-sized domains with distinct terminations often coexist on a cleaved surface. We discuss this scenario for CoNb$_4$Se$_8$, one of the first established layered altermagnets. Supported by density functional theory calculations, we employ micro-ARPES to probe individual domains and reveal two contrasting surface terminations. We identify Co- and Se-terminated domains with characteristic surface states arising from bulk-surface connectivity of the material. Our work shows that termination-dependent surface contributions are essential for the reliable spectroscopic identification of altermagnetism and for assessing its presence across the family of layered materials.

papers.title: Logic-Guided Graph Denoising Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Graph diffusion models are competitive approaches for generating complex graph-structured data. However, when such distributions have strict structural constraints, diffusion models may fail to capture them exactly, resulting in the generation of invalid graphs. In this paper, we propose a method for grounding graph diffusion models in domain-specific knowledge via First Order Logic (FOL), leveraging its expressive and interpretable formalism to impose structural constraints on the generative process. We incorporate domain knowledge using classifier guidance, a technique that conditions the diffusion model's distribution on external variables to exert control over the sampled data. During the generative process, classifier guidance steers the denoising trajectory to optimize an objective function, which we define as a fuzzy and differentiable relaxation of the logical rules. Our methodology requires only the specification of constraints in FOL, whose satisfaction is encouraged at inference time to guide a pre-trained generative model. We evaluate our approach by comparing the unconditional generation of knowledge graphs with our logic-guided framework, which incorporates domain ontologies as structural constraints during inference. This approach significantly increases the proportion of generated graphs that satisfy the ontological constraints.
papers.intro:
Graph generation involves learning an underlying data distribution to facilitate the synthesis of novel, realistic graph structures. Graph diffusion models (Jo et al. 2022; Vignac et al. 2023; Huang et al. 2023; Cognolato et al. 2026a; Cognolato et al. 2026b) and flow-matching models (Eijkelboom et al. 2024; Qin et al. 2024) can model distributions over graphs with discrete labels and continuous attributes. In some applications, such as biology, graphs need to satisfy domain-specific rules (Rigoni et al. 2020) that define whether a graph is well-formed. However, neural generative models lack a mechanism to explicitly enforce structural constraints, which requires specialized techniques to tackle them. Thus, the problem of constrained graph generation, i.e., sampling graphs from a subspace of elements satisfying a set of constraints, has gained traction (Liu et al. 2018; Rigoni et al. 2025; Madeira et al. 2024).

First Order Logic (FOL) (Barwise 1977) may serve as a unified approach to encode and combine heterogeneous constraints. FOL can be used to formalize properties in graphs, where node and edge labels are represented as unary and binary predicates, respectively (Cai et al. 1992). The rules may act on single nodes, their neighbors, and the type or direction of the relations, e.g., bipartiteness and transitivity. FOL rules may also act considering the whole graph structure, e.g., requiring the presence of a specific node type. The ability to operate both locally and globally provides a tool for controlling the structure and content of graphs. This setup has enabled the definition of ontologies for knowledge graphs, providing a schema for otherwise unstructured data (Gruber 1993).

In this paper, we propose LTN-guidance, a methodology for injecting domain knowledge as FOL constraints into the generative process of graph diffusion models (Vignac et al. 2023), without any additional training. Our aim is to increase the probability of sampling valid graphs. First, we propose a graph signature, i.e., the collection of symbols defining the vocabulary of the first order language, enabling the definition of logical formulas over labeled graphs. During generation, we use classifier guidance (Dhariwal and Nichol 2021) to steer a pre-trained diffusion model toward optimizing rule satisfaction (the external objective function). Our method provides the target FOL constraints as Logic Tensor Network (LTN) (Badreddine et al. 2022) differentiable functions. A mechanism based on Focal Loss (Lin et al. 2017) allows adaptive reweighting of constraints, increasing the contribution of less satisfied sentences in the generative process. Finally, we propose cheaper implementations of LTN functions, e.g., for implementing cardinality constraints over edges.

Our main contributions are: 1. A graph signature that allows the definition of logical rules over labeled graphs. We integrate the signature with axioms to ensure label exclusivity; 2. A plug-and-play method for steering graph diffusion models with knowledge in FOL. During inference, FOL constraints are translated to differentiable functions through Logic Tensor Network, and used to steer a pretrained unconditional model with classifier guidance. 3. We evaluated a popular graph diffusion model, DiGress (Vignac et al. 2023), with and without our technique, for the generation of small knowledge graphs from the IntelliGraphs benchmark (Thanapalasingam et al. 2023) against knowledge graph embedding and LLM-based approaches. We observe an improvement in validity, achieving >95%>95\% in most datasets. 4. We performed generation with new rules, compatible and conflicting with the data, to evaluate the conditional in-distribution and out-of-distribution validity, respectively. LTN-guidance consistently shows responsiveness to input formulas by producing a high fraction of valid graphs.
