papers.title: High average flux positron sources driven by a mJ-class laser
papers.abstract: We report on the production and characterisation of MeV-scale positron populations driven by a high-repetition-rate, mJ-class laser system. The positrons are generated via a two-step Bethe--Heitler process driven by laser-wakefield-accelerated electron beams propagating through a mm-scale lead converter. At 10 Hz, approximately 1000 positrons in the 0.8--1.7 MeV energy range were measured over 100 accumulated shots. Stable electron acceleration was demonstrated at 10 Hz, 100 Hz, and 1 kHz using approximately 9 mJ of laser energy in the focal spot, indicating the potential for substantially higher average positron fluxes for laser systems operating at kHz repetition rates and energies of 10s of mJ. Such a positron source allows generating sufficiently high average fluxes of MeV-scale positrons while maintaining low positron yields per pulse and narrow temporal distributions, a regime of particular interest for novel applications in material science and fundamental physics. The measured positron yields and spectra are in good agreement with Monte Carlo simulations, supporting the modelling of the positron-production process and magnetic transport system.

papers.intro:
Laser–plasma accelerators have emerged as compact and highly tuneable sources of relativistic particle beams capable of producing electrons, ions, and photons with energies ranging from the MeV up to the multi-GeV scale. In particular, laser-wakefield acceleration (LWFA) [1] enables the generation of high-energy femtosecond-scale electron beams within cm-scale plasmas driven by ultrashort, high-intensity laser pulses. These electron beams have been widely explored as drivers for secondary radiation sources, including X-rays, γ\gamma-rays, and particle beams [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9].

These systems enable laser–plasma particle sources to operate at substantially higher average flux while retaining the ultrashort temporal characteristics of laser-driven acceleration [12, 13, 14]. In particular, high-repetition-rate LWFA can provide femtosecond-scale electron beams for applications including ultrafast imaging [15, 16] and the generation of secondary sources [17, 18, 19, 20, 21].

In this process, relativistic electrons interact with a high-ZZ converter target, producing bremsstrahlung photons which subsequently generate electron–positron pairs via the Bethe–Heitler process [22]. Justified by these recent developments, plasma-based positron sources have been included as a flagship application of the ESFRI user facility EuPRAXIA [28, 29].

In materials science, a particularly important application is Positron Annihilation Lifetime Spectroscopy (PALS), a non-invasive technique capable of identifying sub-nanometre defects in materials [27]. An ideal positron source for PALS should combine a high average flux, allowing sufficient statistics to be accumulated within practical acquisition times, with a low positron yield per pulse to minimise detector pile-up. Short positron bunch durations are also desirable in order to minimise the beam-related contribution to the instrument response function and maximise the temporal resolution of the measurement. Furthermore, a tuneable positron energy is required for depth-resolved studies, with increasing positron kinetic energy enabling probing at greater depths within a material. Current high-intensity variable-energy PALS facilities typically deliver monoenergetic positrons with energies from approximately 0.1 to 20 keV, enabling depth-resolved measurements only within microns of the surface of the sample. The width of their instrument response function is typically of the order of 180–250 ps, with contributions from both the temporal spread of the positron pulse and the detector response [30, 31]. Laser-driven sources offer the prospect of extending precision PALS measurements into the MeV energy range, enabling substantially greater implantation depths. Their short intrinsic bunch duration, combined with appropriate energy selection, could also reduce the beam-related contribution to the timing response, while high-repetition-rate operation offers the potential for rapid accumulation of PALS spectra.

In this scheme, the laser generates super-thermal electron populations within the target, which subsequently drive positron generation while propagating through the remainder of the converter. These experiments generally require high laser pulse energies and therefore operate at low repetition rates, limiting the achievable average positron flux and typically requiring large-scale high-energy laser facilities. [27] numerically proposed an alternative approach in which positron generation is driven by laser-wakefield-accelerated electrons produced using mJ-class, high-repetition-rate laser systems. Provided that the converter can sustain high-repetition-rate operation, this approach offers a route towards more compact sources with high average positron flux.

In this work, we report on the first experimental demonstration of laser-driven positron production using a table-top mJ-class laser system. The experiment was conducted at the Extreme Light Infrastructure–Attosecond Light Pulse Source (ELI-ALPS) using the eSYLOS beamline, driven by the SYLOS2 laser system, delivering 25 mJ, 14 fs pulses with a repetition rate tuneable from 10 Hz to 1 kHz [33]. Approximately 9 mJ of laser energy was contained within the focal spot on a 300 micron gas jet, generating multi-MeV electron beams that subsequently propagated through a mm-scale lead converter. The generated positrons were captured by a quadrupole doublet and magnetically dispersed onto a scintillator screen. These results demonstrate the possibility of producing high flux and tuneable MeV-scale positrons using a table-top high repetition rate laser, with characteristics of relevance to material science applications.

papers.title: Universal operators: topology and consequences of ISP failure
papers.abstract: Assuming a negative answer to the invariant subspace problem for separable complex Hilbert spaces, we prove that every universal operator has a continuum of minimal infinite-dimensional invariant subspaces with pairwise trivial intersections. These subspaces can be chosen so that the restrictions are invertible and their powers decay at any prescribed geometric rate. For an affine composition operator on the Hardy space $H^2(\mathbb{D})$, we derive restrictions on the zeros, inner factors and Hardy regularity of generators, and construct minimal models with radial vanishing of any prescribed finite order. Independently of the invariant subspace problem, we identify the norm interior, closure and boundary of the universal operator class. Its interior is the Caradus--Pozzi class, its closure is the complement of the upper semi-Fredholm class, and its boundary consists of the operators that are neither upper nor lower semi-Fredholm.

papers.title: Strongly Choquet-Deny groups and invariant strictly convex renormings
papers.abstract: We introduce and study a strengthening of the notion of Choquet-Deny groups, which we call \emph{strongly Choquet-Deny groups}. We show that a countable group $G$ is strongly Choquet-Deny if and only if for every uniformly bounded representation of $G$ on any separable Banach space $X$, there exists an equivalent $G$-invariant strictly convex norm on $X$. We provide a full classification of finitely generated strongly Choquet-Deny groups and show that a finitely generated group is strongly Choquet-Deny if and only if it is virtually abelian. This fully resolves a question of Mikael de la Salle for finitely generated groups. As a further application, we show that for every uniformly bounded representation of a compact extension of an abelian topological group on any separable Banach space, there exists an equivalent invariant strictly convex norm.

papers.title: Zeta potential of magnetic-field-controlled silver nanoparticles
papers.abstract: Magnetic-field-dependent nanoparticle size does not by itself determine zeta potential, which also depends on interfacial charge, electrolyte screening, and the location of the slipping plane. We extend the sphere-packing description of silver nanoparticles by distinguishing the structural surface, the effective charge plane, and the hydrodynamic slipping plane. The model uses structural radii of \SI{20}{nm} and \SI{5}{nm} at zero field and \SI{250}{mT}, with reported zeta potentials of \SI{-13.2}{mV} and \SI{-10.0}{mV}. Effective charge is related to the defective-shell atom count. For field-independent interfacial parameters, the linear response without additional charge weighting decreases with decreasing radius. Its normalized form depends on three electrokinetic lengths through only two sums, preventing their independent determination from a field-dependent zeta curve. At \((κ^{-1},t_{\mathrm{lig}},δ_{\mathrm{slip}})=(3,0,1)\,\mathrm{nm}\), nonlinear Poisson--Boltzmann electrostatics changes the fitted shell coefficient from 0.316 to 0.299. Constant total charge still predicts an increase in zeta magnitude, opposite to the observed trend in the evaluated scenarios. Independently calibrated shell and area charge laws differ by less than \SI{0.05}{mV}, so the endpoint agreement does not distinguish these mechanisms. Propagating the initial size frequencies gives a narrower endpoint size distribution than measured. With charge parameters determined from the measured size populations, its predicted mean zeta potential is \SI{-9.131}{mV}, with standard deviation \SI{0.994}{mV}. Imposing the measured mean by charge recalibration does not remove the discrepancy in size width. The combined structural and electrokinetic model thus identifies both the size-dependent contribution to zeta potential and the interfacial information needed to interpret it.

papers.intro:
Nanoparticles provide a versatile means of tailoring material properties through control of size, morphology, and surface structure. At these reduced length scales, changes in electronic structure and the increasing proportion of atoms near the surface give rise to physical and chemical responses that differ from those of bulk materials. These features underpin applications in electronic and photonic devices 12, 29, functional nanomaterials 20, sensing and biomedical technologies 21, 10, 9, and renewable-energy processes 19. Reliable control of particle size and its distribution is therefore an important requirement for obtaining reproducible properties across these applications. The relevance of nanoscale material control also extends to photonics and optoelectronics. Alongside advances in silicon-based platforms for guiding light and controlling polarization 38, 41, 40, 42, 37, 36, 39, 43,semiconductor nanoparticles offer size-dependent optical functionality, including quantum-dot photon–emitter interfaces 34. Their optical properties contribute to a broader landscape of semiconductor approaches that includes superlattices and quantum-well structures 3, 30, 25, 23, 35, 26. For silver nanoparticles, size and the surrounding dielectric environment affect the optical response 16, and controlled size series also show size-dependent antibacterial activity 1. These dependencies motivate methods that control both the characteristic size and the width of the size distribution 31, 33. For particles dispersed in a liquid, however, structural size alone is insufficient to describe their behavior. The charge associated with the interface and the screening produced by mobile ions also influence the interactions between particles 13, 22. Relating size selection to electrokinetic properties therefore requires a description of both the particle structure and the surrounding electrolyte. In addition to electrostatic interactions, the chemical composition of the particle interface can play an important role in colloidal stability and aggregation. For example, the formation of a protein corona around silver nanoparticles was reported to improve their colloidal stability and suppress aggregation over 75 days 2. Experimental studies of functional nanomaterials further illustrate the importance of interfacial chemistry in determining their behavior in liquid environments. Popat and co-workers demonstrated that the functionalization of mesoporous silica nanoparticles with a positively charged chitosan shell produces a pH-responsive system whose behavior depends on the chemical state of the surface coating 28. Related investigations of functionalized gold nanoparticles by Patra and co-workers have shown the relevance of electrostatic interactions and surface characterization to biomolecular attachment 6. In graphene-oxide membranes, Joshi and co-workers examined size-dependent ion adsorption, illustrating the role of the surrounding ionic environment in interfacial processes 14. More recently, work involving Kaushik and Mishra demonstrated the use of zeta-potential characterization alongside particle-size measurements in the development of functionalized, pH-sensitive nanocarriers 24. Although these systems differ in composition and application, they collectively illustrate why structural dimensions alone cannot fully characterize the particle–liquid interface. This distinction motivates the separate treatment of structural size, effective charge, and electrokinetic boundary conditions adopted in the present work.

Magnetic-field-assisted preparation offers a means of varying nanoparticle size through an external experimental parameter 17, 33. A theoretical treatment must connect this parameter to the energetic conditions for particle formation. Classical nucleation theory provides such a starting point: the formation of a new phase is governed by the competition between the free-energy cost of creating an interface and the free-energy decrease associated with the new phase. Their balance determines the nucleation barrier and its critical size 15. For small particles, the conversion between size and atom count is also important, since a uniform bulk-density description does not distinguish the particle interior from its less efficiently packed surface region 31, 32.

In our sphere-packing treatment, we described the nanoparticle as a densely packed core surrounded by a defective shell and used the resulting atom count in the work of formation 31. Including the magnetic contribution produced an analytical relation between particle radius and field strength. For the silver preparations considered there, two characteristic size points determine the structural trajectory. The same relation also connects different initial radii to a family of field-dependent sizes. It therefore provides a basis for examining the response of a size distribution, in addition to that of a single characteristic particle.

papers.title: Hard Instances on Demand
papers.abstract: The conclusions of an experimental study of algorithms are only as good as the instances they are run on. Benchmark libraries for well-studied problems took decades to curate, while evaluations of new problems often fall back on random instances, which are known to be misleading: they may say more about the random generator than about the algorithmic question at hand. We treat instance generation as an optimization problem: parameterize the instance space, take the solver's running time as the objective, and let a black-box optimizer search for hard instances. We develop a widely applicable workflow built on the Nevergrad optimization platform and demonstrate it on four NP-hard problems: satisfiability, traveling salesperson, Hamiltonian cycle, and non-permutation flow-shop scheduling. The search needs only the solver, an instance encoder, and a compute budget. Our evolved instances beat the hardest instance of a budget-matched random draw in all four case studies, by an order of magnitude or more in three. They are often competitive with long-curated benchmark sets: our SAT champion is harder (for a three-solver portfolio) than 78% of the 498 SAT Competition formulas in its size class; our 20-city TSP champions take several times longer than the hardest measured classical TSPLIB instance (229 cities); and our flow-shop champion takes 238.6 seconds of CP Optimizer time to solve to proven optimality (versus 4.5 seconds for the hardest of 100,000 random draws) while denying CP-SAT an optimality proof. The optimizer even recovers known structure from running time alone: it locates a SAT clause/variable ratio near the phase transition and finds structurally different champions for the two scheduling engines.

papers.intro:
Good test instances can be scarce. For a handful of classical problems, decades of community effort have produced benchmark libraries: the SAT competitions [34, 19], TSPLIB [48], MIPLIB [21], and the Taillard instances for shop scheduling [59] are all good examples. Each of these serves an NP-hard problem whose solvers are exact (i.e., they prove the answers they return) and, even there, curation is a running concern: the SAT competitions solicit new benchmarks every year and MIPLIB is in its sixth edition, with both collections requiring re-curation as solvers improve and once-challenging instances become easy.

Good test instances can be scarce. For a handful of classical problems, decades of community effort have produced benchmark libraries: the SAT competitions [34, 19], TSPLIB [48], MIPLIB [21], and the Taillard instances for shop scheduling [59] are all good examples. Each of these serves an NP-hard problem whose solvers are exact (i.e., they prove the answers they return) and, even there, curation is a running concern: the SAT competitions solicit new benchmarks every year and MIPLIB is in its sixth edition, with both collections requiring re-curation as solvers improve and once-challenging instances become easy.

The situation is worse away from the classics. When Hiermann et al. [28] introduced the electric fleet-size-and-mix vehicle-routing problem with time windows and recharging stations (by now a classical problem warranting reviews of its own [38]), they also had to create its benchmark set. A new problem may have no established instance corpus while a new algorithm for a known problem may face only a thin one. The common fallback is random instance generation, which has well documented dangers. Johnson [35], in his classic essay on experimental algorithmics, lists concentration on unstructured random instances among his named pet peeves, writing that such instances “may actively mislead us as to the difficulty of the problem.” Johnson’s example is random asymmetric TSP distance matrices, which become easy as the instances grow (for the commonly used bounded coefficient ranges). Hooker [29] and McGeoch [44] likewise make test-problem choice central to valid algorithm experiments. Many natural random distributions produce systematically easy instances; for random 3-SAT, the classic observation is that hardness concentrates near the satisfiability threshold [10, 51], a picture since revisited critically [52]. Our own measurements agree that a positive evaluation on such instances says little: in our SAT and TSP experiments, even the hardest instance of a budget-matched, random draw is an order of magnitude easier than the evolved champions (section 3). On the other hand, a new algorithm performing well on a thin, albeit established, benchmark set may not imply good performance in general, merely good tuning to the benchmark.

We propose to attack both problems the same way: search for hard instances directly. We parameterize a space of instances of a given size and let a black-box optimizer maximize the solver’s measured running time over it. We propose to attack both problems the same way: search for hard instances directly. We parameterize a space of instances of a given size and let a black-box optimizer maximize the solver’s measured running time over it. The optimizer plays the role of adversary and needs nothing apart from the ability to run the solver. Hardness found this way is necessarily relative to the attacked solver (section 2). Hardness for a portfolio of solvers is a stronger property, and our approach finds that as well (subsection 3.1).

Our central proposal is a concrete default toward that goal: alongside performance on standard benchmarks, an experimental paper should also report the hardest instances a fixed-budget adversarial search finds against its own solver. Our paper gives a concrete, easy-to-follow workflow which only requires the solver, an instance encoder, and an evaluation budget (section 5 discusses the cost), ingredients every experimental paper already has. Adversarial testing tells the reader what benchmark averages cannot: where the solver breaks, and how badly.

A platform like Nevergrad plausibly supplies the adversary, but it offers several hundred optimizers with no guidance on which of them can attack a solver’s running time. Whether the found instances are impressive or trivial can only be judged against strong existing benchmarks, which new problems (those that most require this sort of analysis) do not have. papers.title: Framing Spatial Hearing within the Free Energy Principle: A Hierarchical Model of Perceptual Learning
papers.abstract: Spatial hearing relies on dynamic internal representations to decode spatial information from ever-changing acoustic conditions. A fundamental example is sound localisation, where listeners infer the direction of an invisible sound. Bayesian inference provides a computational account of such a localisation process; however, modelling efforts are largely limited to static listening scenarios. Instead, the free energy principle (FEP) describes perception, learning, and action as joint minimisation of variational free energy (VFE), providing a principled framework to account for dynamic conditions. Here, we take a first step toward applying the FEP to spatial hearing. We characterise how listeners' beliefs evolve across trials, in which they estimated sound direction and received subsequent visual feedback on each trial. Listeners are described by a hierarchical generative model where visual feedback drives gradient descent on VFE, updating beliefs over three independent quantities: lateral and polar localisation precisions and hemifield disambiguation. The model captures individual learning trajectories and reveals components with different dynamics: lateral precision improves, as does hemifield disambiguation, consistent with increased sensitivity of the auditory pathway in decoding vertical direction. Notably, polar precision also increases, most for listeners with the lowest initial precision, suggesting that the observed vertical improvement is driven by both hemifield disambiguation and polar precision. This work establishes spatial hearing as a tractable domain for FEP and motivates future closed-loop experiments with full action-perception cycles.

papers.title: Relations between optical spectral parameters and the (far-)infrared continuum in Type~1 active galactic nuclei
papers.abstract: This study combines multi-wavelength continuum data with optical spectral properties for a far-infrared (FIR)-selected sample of Type 1 active galactic nuclei (AGNs) from AKARI data. We explore the relation between AGN physics and concomitant star formation processes using empirical correlations of optical and multiwavelength data. We measured spectral parameters including full widths at half maximum (FWHMs) and velocity shifts of broad and narrow optical emission lines, as well as continuum luminosities from GALEX FUV to AKARI 160 microns. The sample contains 88 AGNs observed at both optical and FIR wavelengths. About 50% are Seyfert 1s with both broad H$β$ and H$α$ lines; almost all remaining objects are S1.9s with only broad H$α$. The FWHMs of broad H$β$ and H$α$ are anti-correlated with luminosity in most bands. Shifts of narrow H$β$, H$α$, and [O III] 5007 lines and FWHM of [O III] 5007 correlate with optical and IR luminosities. Luminosities at 65 and 90 microns are more strongly connected with optical and other spectral properties than those at 140 and 160 microns. These trends extend the well-known Eigenvector 1 (EV1) correlations into the MIR and FIR domain. The anti-correlation between broad-line FWHMs and NIR and MIR luminosities is probably caused by the inclination of the torus and accretion disc: higher inclinations see less AGN radiation. However, most objects fall into Population A along the quasar EV1 main sequence, where narrower broad H$β$ profiles and FIR excess emission are commonly linked to higher Eddington ratios.

papers.intro:
Understanding the connection between active galactic nucleus (AGN) spectral properties in different spectral ranges is essential for unraveling the AGN complex structure and governing processes in emission regions. The spectra of Type 1 AGNs are distinguished by the presence of both broad and narrow emission lines, which provide insights into the dynamics of the gas in the vicinity of the supermassive black hole (SMBH) at their centres (Osterbrock and Ferland 2006). According to the standard model (Urry and Padovani 1995), around the black hole lies an accretion disc, which is surrounded by the broad-line region (BLR) and, farther out, by the narrow-line region (NLR). These regions are enclosed by the infrared (IR)-emitting dusty torus extending out to ∼\sim2-10 pc (Tristram et al. 2013; Almeyda et al. 2020).

These regions are enclosed by the infrared (IR)-emitting dusty torus extending out to ∼\sim2-10 pc (Tristram et al. 2013; Almeyda et al. 2020).

Infrared observations provide an insight into the AGN environment, such as the dust composition, temperature, and physical structure, and the contribution of star formation (SF) and the AGN’s energetic processes. Mid-infrared (MIR) radiation covers ∼\sim5-25 μ\mum range, while far-infrared (FIR) includes wavelengths from 25-300 μ\mum and near-infrared (NIR) radiation covers wavelengths of ∼\sim0.8-2.4μ\mum (Lamperti et al. 2017). The MIR emission from active and star-forming galaxies arises mostly from H II regions, photo-dissociation regions and hot dust heated by energetic X-ray to UV photons from AGNs (Hernán-Caballero and Hatziminaoglou 2011; González-Martín et al. 2013; Hernán-Caballero et al. 2015). The NIR emission arises primarily from hot dust surrounding the AGN and from SF in the host galaxy, with a possible contribution from jets (Fazeli et al. 2019; Dumont et al. 2019). Attempts to connect MIR and optical spectral parameters of AGNs, to better understand AGN physical characteristics, have been made in many studies (Sani et al. 2010; Lacy et al. 2013; Lakićević et al. 2017; Lakićević et al. 2018; Feltre et al. 2023). In Lakićević et al. (2022) positive correlations of the full width at half maximum of the broad Hβ\beta line (FWHMBHβ\beta), and optical and MIR luminosities were discussed in relation to the model of dusty cone. Strong correlations have been found between optical and MIR starburst diagnostics (Veilleux 2002; LaMassa et al. 2012). Lakićević et al. (2018) investigated narrow- and broad-line Seyfert 1 galaxies at MIR and optical wavelengths and found that some correlations of spectral parameters are different in these two types of objects, possibly due to the different viewing angles.

Far-infrared luminosity is often used as an indicator of star formation, since the FIR emission may come from starburst regions in the host galaxy, although FIR radiation can also come from the AGN-heated dust component (Netzer 2009; Mullaney et al. 2011; Matsuoka and Woo 2015; Dai et al. 2018). A large fraction of the IR emission in AGNs comes from polar outflows in the narrow-line region (NLR; at least 40 pc from both sides) from AGNs, observed at MIR continuum (Zhang et al. 2013; Stalevski et al. 2019; Alonso-Herrero et al. 2021; Isbell et al. 2025). These features provide a unique signature of the AGN’s geometry and orientation relative to the observer. The problem of separating the IR emission (1-1000μ\mum) into an AGN and a star-forming host component is still extant, although various efforts have been made to estimate these components (Mullaney et al. 2011; Kirkpatrick et al. 2015; McKinney et al. 2021). Usually, it is assumed that AGNs contribute negligibly to FIR emission at wavelengths ≳100,μ\gtrsim 100,\mum, and that the emission at these wavelengths is dominated by star formation in the host galaxy (Mullaney et al. 2011). In galaxies with strong star formation, the host galaxy can outshine the AGN at FIR wavelengths (Shao et al. 2010; Magdis et al. 2013), while AGN-heated dust can dominate the IR emission at shorter wavelengths (Mullaney et al. 2011).

Feltre et al. (2013) did not find evidence that the presence of an AGN affects the star formation process in the host galaxy, but rather that the two phenomena can occur simultaneously over a wide range of luminosities. Ramasawmy et al. (2019) found no clear evidence that AGN activity significantly affects SF in host galaxies. A correlation between SF and AGN luminosities is found by Netzer (2009) and Stanley et al. (2015); the relation between AGN luminosity and FIR luminosity has been investigated by Rosario et al. (2012). This study explores correlations between optical parameters and FIR (and other) luminosities in Type 1 AGNs, a comparison rarely addressed in the literature. These relations probe the link between central engine activity and the dusty environment. Optical spectral properties (e.g. FWHM, line luminosities, and shifts) trace gas kinematics and may be connected to IR emission through processes such as outflows, turbulence, and dense molecular gas. We further investigate how these sources differ from other optically visible AGNs.

A subset of Type 1 AGNs exhibits strong broad Hα\alpha emission, while the broad Hβ\beta component is significantly weaker or even absent despite clearly detected narrow lines. This behaviour is commonly interpreted as a consequence of dust reddening within the BLR or along the line of sight, since shorter-wavelength emission such as Hβ\beta is more strongly attenuated than Hα\alpha (Goodrich 1989; Maiolino et al. 2001). The effect is consistent with large Balmer decrements indicative of substantial internal extinction and is frequently observed in intermediate Seyfert subclasses (types 1.8 and 1.9; Osterbrock 1981; Maiolino et al. 2001; Kovačević-Dojčinović et al. 2022).

papers.title: Local Projected Controllability of Nonlocal Continuity Equations
papers.abstract: We formulate and study the problem of local projected controllability (LPC) for characteristic solutions of controlled nonlocal continuity (transport) equations on the space of probability measures over a separable Banach space. The task is motivated in particular by self-interacting models in machine learning, whose action can be represented as controlled dynamics of the probability distribution over input data, while the actual output is given by a finite-dimensional vector of features extracted from the terminal distribution by a possibly nonlinear observation map. Given a fixed finite family of velocity fields which may depend on the transported measure, we ask whether the reachable values of the observable vector fill a neighborhood of its reference value. Our approach is to lift the transport equation in the space of measures to an ordinary differential equation on a Banach space of maps. This representation makes it possible to employ the machinery of Lie brackets developed for Banach manifolds, while the resulting sufficient condition for LPC can be formulated directly on the space of measures.

Classical controllability theory asks whether the system at hand has enough degrees of freedom to produce all desired motions Agrachev and Sachkov (2004) — a property which is difficult to verify directly. This theory becomes much more complicated when the state space is infinite-dimensional. At the same time, in practice, one is often interested not in the entire infinite-dimensional state, but in a few numerical characteristics extracted from it. A question which is natural in many applications is the following: given a control system on a Banach manifold ℳ\mathcal{M}, with control inputs uu and the corresponding states xtux^{u}_{t}, along with an “observation map” g:ℳ→ℝNg\colon\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{N}, N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}, does the set {g⁡(xtu)}\{g(x^{u}_{t})\} of reachable observations contain a neighborhood of a fixed reference value?

A problem of this type was addressed in Hermes (1979): the control system was given by an ODE in a Banach space, with a drift and a single control-linear term, and the observation was represented by a continuous linear map. The authors called this property local controllability of the observation along the reference solution and gave a sufficient condition in terms of Lie directions projected by the map gg. Subsequent results remained largely model-specific; various versions of the same task were studied, in particular, for the Euler and Navier–Stokes equations Agrachev and Sarychev (2006); Shirikyan (2007).

A central result of classical geometric control theory is the Rashevskii–Chow theorem Rashevsky (1938); Chow (1939), which relates controllability of a driftless system to the properties of the Lie algebra generated by the controlled vector fields. In ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, one can choose finitely many Lie brackets whose values form a basis of the tangent space and then apply the inverse function theorem to a finite composition of the corresponding flows; see, e.g., Agrachev and Sachkov (2004).

A passage to infinite dimensions changes the situation substantially: the resulting Lie algebra may be dense in the tangent space without spanning it, and this is no longer sufficient for the reachable set to contain a neighborhood of the initial state. One of the first infinite-dimensional counterparts of the classical Rashevskii–Chow theorem was obtained by Dudnikov and Samborski (1980) for systems in Banach spaces; related sufficient conditions for global approximate controllability were established in Ledyaev (2004). Further extensions were made for control systems on Banach manifolds Kipka and Ledyaev (2015) and regular manifolds modeled on convenient locally convex spaces Khajeh Salehani and Markina (2014). Related Lie-algebraic controllability results for ensembles of points and families of mappings can be found in Agrachev and Sarychev (2020); Agrachev and Sarychev (2022).

papers.title: The Strong Total Cover Problem
papers.abstract: The Strong Total Cover Problem (STCP) is a novel covering problem defined on a graph $G = (V, E)$, where the objective is to find a minimum-cardinality subset $T \subseteq V \cup E$ such that every element of $V \cup E$ is covered. In this setting, a vertex covers itself and all its incident edges, while an edge covers itself together with its two endpoints. The STCP resembles classical covering problems such as Vertex Cover and Edge Cover problems, and naturally arises as the dual of the total matching problem. In this paper, we investigate the STCP from algorithmic, complexity, and polyhedral perspectives. We first establish close connections between STCP, the Dominating Set Problem, and the Maximum Induced Matching Problem. These relationships provide structural insights, imply the NP-hardness of STCP, and identify graph classes for which the problem is polynomial-time solvable. We then investigate the weighted version of STCP, showing that it remains NP-hard even on complete graphs with binary weights. On the other hand, we present a 2-approximation algorithm, and a polynomial-time algorithm for complete bipartite graphs. On the polyhedral side, we introduce the Strong Total Cover Polytope and derive several families of valid inequalities, some of which are shown to define facets. Finally, we provide a complete linear description of the associated polytope for triangular cactus graphs, revealing an interesting contrast with the considerably more intricate facial structure of the dominating set polytope on cactus graphs.

papers.title: Fast matrix-vector products in tensor-train format via structured sketching
papers.abstract: We propose a randomized, streamable algorithm that computes a tensor-train approximation of a matrix-vector product without ever forming the full intermediate tensor. We develop three contraction strategies for streaming tensor-train approximation (STTA): sequential, fused, and pre-sketched. We focus on the regime of large operator mode sizes and show that pre-sketching can provide significant speed-ups when a lower-rank approximation of the input is sought, by pre-computing all sketch-related contractions with the operator. The pre-sketched strategy can also accelerate successive randomized compression (SRC), although to a lesser extent since its second sweep depends on the input vector and cannot be pre-computed. We compare the three strategies in terms of computational cost and memory, and demonstrate their performance on synthetic and application-driven examples where rank reduction is relevant.

The TT matvec is a fundamental building block in many modern tensor-based computational workflows, including quantum chemistry [29], quantum many-body simulation [15], large-scale discretizations of partial differential equations [4], and high-dimensional model reduction [22]. Accelerating the matvec routine is therefore of critical importance.

We propose and analyze three distinct approaches: sequential, fused, and pre-sketched. They all compute the same object but differ in the order in which the core of the operator, the core of the vector, and the sketching matrices are contracted at each site. papers.title: Alignment of visual brain encoding models with individual perceptual similarity judgments
papers.abstract: Encoding models that predict brain activation responses to images have traditionally been trained to maximize accuracy when predicting observed brain data. However, their internal representations may not reflect individual human perception. In this work, we investigate whether we can fine-tune brain encoding models to better align their representations with individuals' similarity judgments. Using similarity judgments of 100 images from 8 participants in the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we adapt a generic human similarity judgment model (DreamSim) separately for each participant to obtain personalized perceptual similarity models. These models are then used to obtain subject-specific similarity structure across images in their encoding model training sets. We fine-tune each participant's baseline encoder in two conditions, aligning its representations with either generic or personalized similarity judgments, with the same initialization and objective. We find that baseline brain encoders reflect within-subject perceptual similarity more strongly than measured fMRI responses and preserve intersubject correlations present in measured fMRI, but fail to reflect those of human perceptual similarity judgments. Fine-tuning with generic, population-level perceptual similarity information results in better alignment with human judgments than baseline encoders, but these models still fail to capture intersubject correlations of human judgments. However, fine-tuning with personalized perceptual similarity information results in models that are the most aligned with human perceptual similarity judgments and also reflect intersubject correlations of human judgments. Our framework provides an approach for bootstrapping human similarity judgment data into more individualized, human-aligned brain encoding models of vision.

papers.intro:
Visual brain encoding models aiming to predict brain responses elicited by images and video clips have become increasingly accurate as new vision models have been developed in adjacent fields. These visual brain encoding models are typically optimized to accurately predict measured brain activity (Mitchell et al., 2008; Huth et al., 2016; Gu et al., 2022; Gifford et al., 2025; Conwell et al., 2024; Naselaris et al., 2011). However, a visual brain encoding model that accurately predicts measured brain activity may not necessarily have internal representations that reflect an individual person’s perceptual similarity, i.e. how similar two images are to a particular person. Such alignment of brain activity models and human perceptual similarity would be particularly useful for downstream tasks - for example decoding, i.e. reconstructing seen or imagined stimuli from brain activity patterns. In decoding, having a model whose brain activity representations for any two images reflect those images’ perceived similarity would allow reconstructing images with better fidelity to human similarity judgments (Scotti et al., 2023; Ozcelik and VanRullen, 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Rajabi et al., 2025; Takagi and Nishimoto, 2023).

How a person perceives the similarity of two images, or human perceptual similarity, is a popular area of study in the broader field of psychophysics. Behavioral similarity experiments in these areas ask individuals to organize stimuli according to their perceived relationships. Representational similarity analysis (RSA) is a statistical approach that provides a framework for comparing similarity structures across various , multi-modal spaces (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008; Sucholutsky et al., 2024; Nili et al., 2014; Kriegeskorte and Kievit, 2013; Simkova et al., 2026). RSA can be applied in this context to perceptual similarity, measured brain activity via fMRI, and encoding model predictions of brain activity to enable comparison of how image similarity spaces are conserved across the modalities. Analysis of these representational spaces can also allow quantification of either the similarity of representations across modalities within an individual or how the across-subject correlations of similarity spaces are preserved. A brain encoding model trained on individual participant data may be subject-specific in the sense that it predicts that participant’s neural activity in an identifiable way (compared to other subjects’ data), while still failing to reflect that person’s perceptual relationships between stimuli.

Incorporating human similarity judgments into brain encoding models has several practical challenges. Human similarity measurements are onerous to collect for the thousands of image stimuli usually contained in high-quality vision neuroscience fMRI datasets (Allen et al., 2022; Zerbe et al., 2026; Hebart et al., 2023; Chang et al., 2019). Therefore, when they are collected, it is only for a small subset of the images drawn from the stimuli set. Machine learning models have been used to estimate human similarity judgments, but are normally trained on data drawn across a cohort of many individuals and thus represent population-level averages rather than individual-level perceptual judgments (Marjieh et al., 2023; Fu et al., 2023; Muttenthaler et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2018). Incorporating human similarity judgments into brain encoding models has several practical challenges. Human similarity measurements are onerous to collect for the thousands of image stimuli usually contained in high-quality vision neuroscience fMRI datasets (Allen et al., 2022; Zerbe et al., 2026; Hebart et al., 2023; Chang et al., 2019). Therefore, when they are collected, it is only for a small subset of the images drawn from the stimuli set. papers.title: Counting and Sampling Manufacturable Stacking Sequences
papers.abstract: Designing the stacking sequence of a composite laminate is a discrete optimisation problem: each ply takes one of a few orientations, each evaluation may cost a finite-element solve, and the design must obey manufacturing rules and design guidelines, which optimisers enforce by penalty, repair or rejection. We describe the admissible set exactly. The two manufacturing rules forbid a finite set of factors, so the sequences they admit form a regular language, recognised by an automaton that tracks the last orientation and the length of its run; balance and the ten per cent rule constrain the Parikh vector and are carried by a dynamic program over automaton state and counters. One table, polynomial in N, counts the admissible sequences without producing them, draws them uniformly, and tells whether a partial sequence can still be completed. We give pseudocode, exact counts for three orientation sets, closed-form ceilings on the composition, and four of the five single-rule entries a published table left uncomputed. At 48 plies, 99.8% of the nodes of a layer-wise search tree checking the rules locally have no admissible completion on eight orientations; the completion test removes them. A one-point crossover that cuts two admissible parents only where they share an automaton state and their child closes the counters returns admissible children by construction.

papers.intro:
A composite laminate is a stack of NN plies, each a sheet of parallel fibres laid at one of a finite set of orientations, and its stacking sequence lists those orientations from one surface to the other. We borrow the vocabulary of formal languages: the allowed orientations form an alphabet Σ\Sigma, a stacking sequence is a word over it, one letter per ply, and a set of stacking sequences is a language. The orientations determine the in-plane and bending stiffness of the laminate, hence its buckling load, natural frequencies and deflection under load, and the design problem is to maximise one of these responses, or to minimise NN subject to targets on them. It is a discrete optimisation problem over ΣN\Sigma^{N}, and each evaluation of the objective may cost a finite-element solve. It has been searched with genetic algorithms since the early 1990s [10, 39], with permutation encodings [40, 30], particle swarms [13], scatter search [49] and ant colonies [6], and with branch and bound: layer by layer from the outer surface inwards [34], in a modified form that starts from “ideal” layers and keeps one branch per level [12, Sec. 2], or in the space of lamination parameters, where the admissible laminates form a fractal set [56], non-symmetric laminates included [42]. It has been extended to blending across panels [52, 60], to lamination parameters as a continuous relaxation [41, 4], to variable-stiffness laminates [1, 50], to strength as well as buckling [6, 5], to multiple objectives [2], and to structures other than flat panels: cylindrical panels [2], laminated grid plates [20], a wind-turbine blade [3] and an aero-engine fan-blade-like structure [11].

Not every word is a laminate that can be built or certified. Two manufacturing rules are local: consecutive plies must not differ by more than 45∘45^{\circ} of orientation, and no more than three consecutive plies may share one. Designers add guidelines that are not local, namely mirror symmetry, balance between +θ+\theta and −θ-\theta, and a minimum share of ten per cent for each principal direction; symmetry and balance are dropped where a directional stiffness or a coupling is wanted, as in aeroelastic tailoring [51]. Each of these methods spends part of its effort on candidates outside the set these rules define: a genetic algorithm penalises the rules it does not build into its encoding [39] or repairs them [55], a sampler builds candidates and rejects the non-compliant, a branch and bound checks each partial sequence against the rules and learns only at the leaves that a branch had no admissible completion. The rules enter as a filter: as design rules to respect [27, 33] or to relax [57], as constraints on the fibre paths of tow-steered plies [9, Sec. 5], or as a coupled ply-order and ply-drop problem [3]. We describe the admissible set exactly and derive from the description algorithms that produce admissible sequences, and only those.

papers.title: Diagnosing GNN Failure Modes with Layer-Wise Probe Entropy
papers.abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are typically evaluated only at their final layer, obscuring how task-relevant information evolves during message passing. We introduce a post-hoc diagnostic that freezes a trained GNN, fits an independent linear probe to each layer, and tracks probe accuracy alongside normalized predictive entropy. Across real and synthetic graph settings, layer-wise probe entropy distinguishes beneficial, neutral, and harmful smoothing, a capability not demonstrated by existing geometric measures. Moreover, by comparing shallow and deep models, we show that the onset of entropy degradation separates the two main GNN failure modes: structural mismatch under heterophily, which appears from the earliest layers even in shallow models, and excessive-depth oversmoothing, which emerges only as propagation depth increases. These results establish probe-entropy trajectories as a tool for analyzing information flow in GNNs and motivate future work on adaptive depth selection and early-exit mechanisms.

papers.intro:
Message-passing GNNs update node representations by aggregating information from neighbouring nodes [1, 2]. Across layers, task-relevant information may accumulate, remain stable, or degrade. Two distinct failure modes can cause this degradation. First, excessive propagation can oversmooth representations and erase discriminative information [3, 4, 5, 6]. Second, structural mismatch can arise under heterophily, where low-pass aggregation can mix incompatible label signals and become harmful from the first layers [7, 8, 9]. A drop in final-layer accuracy can reveal that a failure has occurred, but it cannot distinguish between these cases. This distinction is important because the two failures require different remedies: oversmoothing may be addressed by limiting propagation depth, whereas structural mismatch may require changing the aggregation operator.

A drop in final-layer accuracy can reveal that a failure has occurred, but it cannot distinguish between these cases. This distinction is important because the two failures require different remedies: oversmoothing may be addressed by limiting propagation depth, whereas structural mismatch may require changing the aggregation operator.

Existing approaches to identifying the source of failure have largely focused on detecting oversmoothing through changes in representation geometry [10, 11, 12, 6]. These measures show that representations are becoming smoother, but changes in these smoothness measures alone do not establish whether smoothing improves, preserves, or degrades task performance. When smoothing is harmful, these measures alone also cannot determine whether the failure arises from excessive-depth oversmoothing or from aggregation that is harmful from the first layers under heterophily.

papers.title: Acquisition Function-Guided Generation for Bayesian Optimization over Discrete Spaces
papers.abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) over discrete spaces is challenging due to missing gradients and the sparsity of valid solutions. Latent-space BO sidesteps both issues by fitting a surrogate in the latent space of a generative model, which however substantially complicates the direct incorporation of domain knowledge that is naturally expressed in the original discrete space. In this work, we instead combine a pretrained generative model with a surrogate defined directly in data space, where inductive biases such as domain-specific kernels can be readily incorporated. Rather than maximizing the acquisition function over the discrete design space, our method samples candidates from the generative model under a distribution tilted by the acquisition function. To recover useful gradients for sampling, we embed this tilted distribution into a diffusion bridge that yields a smooth, posterior-averaged acquisition function. This leads to \emph{acquisition function guided generation} (AFGG), which we instantiate with a categorical diffusion model and an autoregressive normalizing flow. Across a broad suite of molecular benchmarks, the diffusion model variant performs on par with leading BO methods, while the flow model variant outperforms state-of-the-art methods in most cases and remains highly competitive otherwise. Our implementation is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/afgg.

papers.intro:
Bayesian optimization (BO) offers a sample-efficient approach to problems such as molecular and protein design, where objective evaluations are costly and the search space is discrete and structured (Garnett, 2023; Yang et al., 2025). Unfortunately, direct optimization over such spaces is hard because valid designs are sparsely populated in a combinatorial space and standard continuous optimizers have no useful gradients to follow (Moss et al., 2020). Latent-space Bayesian optimization (LSBO) addresses both challenges by training a generative model over the discrete space—thereby capturing the sparse structure of valid designs—and by performing BO in its continuous latent space, where gradients for acquisition optimization are readily available (Gómez-Bombarelli et al., 2018).

Latent-space Bayesian optimization (LSBO) addresses both challenges by training a generative model over the discrete space—thereby capturing the sparse structure of valid designs—and by performing BO in its continuous latent space, where gradients for acquisition optimization are readily available (Gómez-Bombarelli et al., 2018).

However, domain knowledge is harder to incorporate in an abstract latent space, while in data space, such knowledge can often be encoded directly through inductive biases such as domain-specific kernels (Rogers and Hahn, 2010). Furthermore, the latent space must also “do two jobs at once:” support faithful generation and provide a geometry in which the objective is easy to model by a surrogate. These goals need not align, which motivates many LSBO methods to adapt the latent representation during BO (Maus et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2023; Chu et al., 2024; Tripp et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2025; Deshwal and Doppa, 2021), despite the small-data regime in which such adaptation can overfit (Ober et al., 2021). Moreover, even a strong generative model only approximates the sparse set of valid designs, so acquisition optimization can move into poorly supported regions of latent space where decoding becomes unreliable (Moss et al., 2025; Bodin et al., 2025).

In this paper, we propose acquisition function guided generation (AFGG), which replaces acquisition function maximization with sampling from a distribution that tilts a frozen pretrained generative model toward designs favored by the acquisition function. The construction is generic in both components: it requires only a generative model that supports guided sampling and any non-negative acquisition function that can be evaluated pointwise; the latter need neither be differentiable nor define a probability. Since the discrete, combinatorial design space makes direct sampling from the tilted distribution difficult, we embed it into a diffusion process over the generative model’s continuous space. At each noise level, this yields a smooth posterior-averaged acquisition function that provides the gradients needed for guided sampling. The resulting gradients can then guide sampling in the same spirit as guidance in diffusion models (Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021; Ho and Salimans, 2022), which gives the method its name.

Our contributions are threefold: • Acquisition function guided generation. We formulate the BO inner loop as sampling from an acquisition-tilted distribution that combines a frozen pretrained generative model with a surrogate defined directly in data space (Section 3.1). We show that this target can be recovered exactly in the generative model’s continuous space and that the resulting guidance term reduces to replacing the model’s posterior mean by its acquisition-weighted counterpart (Section 3.3). • A unified construction for different generative models. We derive AFGG from a common diffusion-bridge construction and show how it applies to both categorical diffusion models and autoregressive normalizing flows (Section 3.4). The generator remains frozen throughout BO, while the surrogate and acquisition function stay in data space. • State-of-the-art empirical performance. Across a broad suite of molecular design benchmarks under tight evaluation budgets, AFGG with the categorical diffusion model performs on par with leading BO methods. More strikingly, AFGG with the flow model achieves state-of-the-art performance on most benchmarks and remains highly competitive on the rest (Section 4).

papers.title: Domain-specific language alignment of multimodal embeddings towards explainable predictions
papers.abstract: Multimodal data are commonly fused into latent representations that improve downstream task performance but are not interpretable, limiting their application in domains that require explainable model decisions. Vision-language alignment has made image embeddings interpretable through language, but requires vast image-caption training data. However, captioned data are typically not available for multimodal embeddings, as relevant features cannot directly be observed and annotated from embeddings alone. Here, we propose a framework to language-align any embedding space that can be linked to interpretable auxiliary data. Captioning functions convert auxiliary data into partial captions; a soft contrastive loss weights pairs by the similarity of their properties that each caption describes; and a rank-based concept retrieval task evaluates alignment against the auxiliary data rather than the captions. We apply this framework to multimodal Earth embeddings to facilitate explainable predictions for two species distribution modelling tasks: S2BMS and SatBird. AlphaEarth embeddings beat previous state-of-the-art models on 6/7 metrics, while our framework language-aligns domain-specific concepts of the embedding space, outperforming previous Earth observation vision-language models on average concept retrieval for both datasets. Finally, aligned concepts recover species-habitat associations ($ρ$=0.44) and relate habitat descriptions to species predictions, showing that abstract embeddings can be interrogated in the language of domain experts.

One avenue is to attribute predictions to the different data modalities (zbinden2026masksdm), however, if the data modalities are not interpretable (as for example with fused or latent representations), attribution-based methods are not able to explain SDM predictions.

Specifically, three challenges arise when aligning multimodal embeddings to language. First, embeddings need to be captioned, even though humans (or multimodal LLMs) inherently cannot textually describe features of an abstract embedding space. We address this by weakly annotating embeddings using linked auxiliary databases to construct multiple, partial text captions. Therefore, we define a soft contrastive loss objective that computes similarity for each (partial) caption separately, as well as introduce a rank-based retrieval task that granularly tests the language alignment of the embedding space using concepts grounded in auxiliary data, rather than the caption data.

papers.title: A prime isoartinian ring that is not noetherian
papers.abstract: A right module is isoartinian (resp., isonoetherian) if every descending (resp., ascending) chain of submodules is eventually constant up to isomorphism, and a ring R is right isoartinian (resp., isonoethe- rian) if RR is isoartinian (resp., isonoetherian). Facchini and Nazemian proved that a semiprime right isoartinian ring is right noetherian if and only if it is right isonoetherian if and only if it has finite Goldie dimen- sion and that every commutative semiprime isoartinian ring is noether- ian. We construct, over an arbitrary field K, a (non commutative) prime (right and left) isoartinian ring that is neither right nor left noetherian.

papers.intro:
Throughout, rings are associative with identity and modules are unital right modules. Following Facchini and Nazemian [3], a module MRM_{R} is called isoartinian if for every descending chain M⊇M1⊇M2⊇⋯M\supseteq M_{1}\supseteq M_{2}\supseteq\cdots of submodules of MM there is an index n≥1n\geq 1 such that Mi≅MnM_{i}\cong M_{n} for every i≥ni\geq n. A ring RR is right isoartinian if the module RRR_{R} is isoartinian. Every right artinian ring is right isoartinian, and a domain is right isoartinian if and only if it is a principal right ideal domain [3]. Semiprime right isoartinian rings are studied in [3, Section 4]. Such rings are right non-singular and satisfy the ascending chain condition on annihilator ideals [3, Lemmas 4.3 and 4.5]. Moreover, by [3, Theorem 4.6], for a semiprime right isoartinian ring RR the following are equivalent: RR is right noetherian; RR is right Goldie; RRR_{R} has a finite Goldie dimension; RRR_{R} is a sum of the isosimple right ideals. The semiprime right isoartinian right noetherian rings are exactly the finite direct products of matrix rings over principal right ideal domains [3, Theorem 4.7]. In the commutative case the noetherian hypothesis is automatic: a commutative semiprime isoartinian ring is a finite direct product of principal ideal domains [3, Corollary 4.8]. It is therefore natural to ask whether every semiprime right isoartinian ring is right noetherian, that is, whether the finiteness of the Goldie dimension in [3, Theorem 4.6] is automatic, as it is for commutative rings. This question has been open for years and since the definition of isonoetherian (isoartinian) rings in [3], isoartinian rings and modules have been studied in various sources; for example [5, 11, 8, 6, 7, 1, 10, 4, 2]. The purpose of this note is to show that the answer is negative.

papers.title: Bridging the Language Gap in Scholarly Data II: Enhancing Gender Inference for Chinese Names
papers.abstract: Perceived gender inference from names is important for inclusive scientometrics research, yet existing methods perform poorly on non-Western scholars. We address this gap for Chinese names, which appear in two forms, Hanzi and Pinyin, its Romanized form (e.g., Zhang Wei, Li Na). In international bibliographic records, names are often available only in Pinyin. However, a single pinyin name can correspond to multiple distinct hanzi characters with different gender associations, so gender inference from Pinyin alone is intrinsically ambiguous. To address this, we first develop two hanzi models, a regression model that produces a continuous gender score from 0 (male) to 1 (female), and a classification model that outputs one of three labels (\em{male}, \em{neutral}, \em{female}). We train them on a sample of hanzi names from Chinese-language physics publications, rated by 11 native Chinese speakers. On this sample, the models achieve an RMSE of $0.09$ and an R$^2$ of $0.85$ (regression), and macro-AUC of $0.97$ and a Cohen's $κ$ of $0.81$ (classification), demonstrating high performance that is robust to class imbalance. For pinyin names, we propose a pipeline that aggregates hanzi predictions via transliteration and frequency weighting, together with an ambiguity score that flags names whose gender cannot be resolved from Pinyin alone. Benchmarked against three off-the-shelf tools (Namsor, GPT, and Claude), our models achieve the highest agreement with human annotations for both gender scores and gender labels, in both scripts. Applied to an independent sample of Chinese-named authors in APS journals, our models assign a gender to every name, whereas existing Pinyin-based methods leave between 20\% and 100\% of names unclassified. These findings demonstrate the importance of hanzi-level information for reliable gender inference of Chinese names. Code and data are publicly available.

papers.intro:
Scientometrics and science-of-science research often rely on inferring socio-demographics such as gender to understand central dynamics: who collaborates with whom [36, 6], who cites whom [43, 80], and how recognition and resources flow across communities [34, 74, 51]. The goal is not only to describe patterns but to detect biases—for example, in hiring, citation, or funding—and to design interventions that make research more equitable [46, 50, 9, 77]. However, for large-scale studies, individual attributes are often unavailable, making other observable but noisy proxies, such as names or bibliometrics, necessary to infer gender [41, 47], ethnicity [16, 45], or geographic origin [35, 60].

Most existing gender-inference tools are developed and evaluated using data from English-speaking or well-resourced populations, where census data and labeled name lists are readily available [84, 17, 73, 78]. As a result, many non-Western naming conventions remain poorly supported [41, 64, 76, 78]. Chinese names are a prominent example. Prior work reports substantially lower accuracy for Chinese names, which are often excluded from streamlined analyses [41, 76]. This exclusion introduces systematic bias in studies of collaboration, citation, and diversity. Addressing this gap is therefore essential for representative scientometric and science-of-science research.

Names may appear in Hanzi, the logographic Chinese script, or in a Romanized form (i.e., Latin alphabet to represent pronunciation). For logographic names, we use Simplified Chinese to ensure consistency with mainland Chinese naming conventions. For Romanized names, we adopt Hanyu Pinyin, the official Romanization system for Standard Mandarin [19], the most widely spoken variety of Chinese [14]. The mapping between the two representations, known as transliteration, is asymmetric. Each hanzi character typically corresponds to a single pinyin syllable (with rare exceptions [48]), but a single pinyin syllable may map to many Hanzi—a well-documented characteristic of Mandarin [58, 21, 18]. In our corpus, 8,094 distinct single hanzi characters collapse into only 408 pinyin syllables, and the three most frequent pinyin syllables (yi, ji, yu) each map to over 120 hanzi characters (146, 130, 123, respectively). This transliteration ambiguity compounds with a second source of uncertainty. Each hanzi character carries both meaning and sound, and parents typically select one or two characters, rarely three, guided by semantics, phonetics, and family tradition rather than strict gendered conventions [13, 40]. As a result, the association between any hanzi character and gender is statistical rather than deterministic. Consider the pinyin name “Deng,” which may represent 澄, 登, or 灯—typically found in male names therefore perceived as masculine—but also 等 or 邓, can be found in both genders. When only “Deng” is observed, the underlying hanzi character is unknown, and even if it were known, its gender signal can only be probabilistic. Gender inference from Pinyin alone is therefore inherently ambiguous, see Figure 1a.

We first train two independent models that infer gender directly from hanzi character names: (i) a regression model that predicts a continuous gender score between 00 (mostly male) and 11 (mostly female), and (ii) a three-class classification model that infers a categorical label (male, neutral, female). Each hanzi name is represented by features derived from three existing gender-inference tools, which provide complementary gender signals at the character level. For regression outputs, we aggregate hanzi scores using four strategies that vary in their weighting schemes (uniform vs. frequency-weighted) and reference populations (our corpus vs. national statistics). For classification outputs, we aggregate predictions via majority voting, assigning male or female when one label dominates, and neutral when the labels are tied.

papers.title: EKT-Router: Expert-Evidence Alignment for Embodied Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Embodied vision-language models must answer questions from partial, evolving observations. Their success depends on both the reasoning capability selected and the evidence available to it. Expert routers adapt internal computation, while tool-augmented systems acquire external evidence; choosing these independently can leave a suitable expert without the evidence it needs. We introduce EKT-Router, a bounded framework that jointly selects a capability expert, optional knowledge, and perceptual tools. Outcome-derived signatures represent the overlapping strengths of General, Spatial Reasoning, and Spatiotemporal experts. A joint utility scores complete expert-evidence routes under a call budget. After acquisition, a packet verifier admits valid evidence with positive predicted expert-conditioned gain. The selected expert then answers once, reverting to the unchanged observation if all packets are rejected. Across 6 embodied QA benchmarks, EKT-Router achieves a mean score of 61.4, the highest among the compared systems, and averages 74.7 on 10 general vision-language benchmarks. With all external evidence disabled, question-conditioned expert selection alone improves over the best fixed expert by 1.75 points. Ablations show that learned routing is the dominant component and that knowledge and perception are complementary.

papers.intro:
Embodied vision–language models (EVLMs) answer questions about evolving scenes from partial observations. Such grounded understanding supports language-guided robotic planning and interaction (Liang et al., 2025). Queries require semantic knowledge, precise geometry, or temporal state tracking; decisive cues may occupy only a few pixels or span several frames (Majumdar et al., 2024; Sermanet et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025). Success depends on both the selected capability and the evidence it receives. A relative-position question may benefit from localization, whereas an event-order question requires temporal context; neither source is useful merely because it is available. The route must therefore account for what the question demands, what each expert can infer from the original observation, and what an external provider can add. We study expert–evidence alignment under partial observability: matching a reusable capability with query-specific evidence, while retaining a generalist path and avoiding an unbounded agent loop.

Existing methods address different parts of this problem. Embodied generalists such as LEO and RynnBrain integrate perception, language, and action capabilities, whereas SpatialVLM, SpatialRGPT, and RoboSpatial use geometric supervision to strengthen spatial reasoning (Huang et al., 2024; Dang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2024a; Cheng et al., 2024; Song et al., 2025). Mixture-of-experts methods provide conditional parameter paths for efficient specialization (Wu et al., 2024; Shen et al., 2024); ViperGPT and LLaVA-Plus instead compose external vision modules to recover information that a backbone cannot reliably infer (Surís et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024a). These expert routers focus on selecting a parameter path, whereas the cited tool-augmented systems acquire evidence for a fixed or implicit reasoner. Jointly choosing the capability path and its external evidence makes their dependence an explicit part of the routing decision.

These coupled choices pose two challenges. (i) Evidence value is expert-dependent. Expert strengths overlap, and the same knowledge or tool output can provide different gains to different experts. papers.title: TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Advances in frontier coding agents have sharply increased the token costs of AI-assisted software engineering. Their token efficiency is typically evaluated on isolated tasks, whereas real-world developers use them to continuously build, update, and maintain large-scale projects. This mismatch motivates us to evaluate agents over sequences of realistic coding tasks, where we find that agents exhibit recurring environment-dependent token costs that existing methods struggle to reduce. To minimize these costs, we introduce TokenEconomizer, an external controller that cuts environment-specific token costs over a sequence of tasks. These cuts come from determining (i) which operational micro-skills to inject, (ii) which persistently irrelevant tools to prune, and (iii) when to intervene in unproductive failure loops. Across Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot CLI paired with frontier models, TokenEconomizer reduces the average token cost by 18.4-30.9% with comparable task success. Savings hold in every repository under every tested agent-model setting and generalize to diverse domains such as sequential web development and security auditing, where costs fall by 6.4-21.2% depending on task structure. Our work establishes adaptive black-box cost control as a promising direction for reducing token costs of coding agents in realistic settings.

Frontier large language models (LLMs), coupled with agent harnesses that support tool use (Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2025a), have become increasingly capable of completing realistic, long-horizon software engineering tasks (Jimenez et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025; Merrill et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026). These components are commonly packaged as commercial products, including Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot CLI. These agents are designed primarily for generic task success, but their increased capability comes at a substantial token cost. As shown in Fig. 1(a), the billed context at each turn includes persistent system and user instructions together with an expanding history of model outputs and tool interactions, causing earlier content to be charged repeatedly across the trajectory.

Token efficiency has primarily been studied and optimized at the level of individual tasks. Model-level controls such as lower reasoning effort save tokens at a cost in task success (Table 1), while harness-level controls such as tool availability and auxiliary instructions typically require manual configuration. More targeted approaches to trajectory compression, observation filtering, and specialized repository exploration often require agent-loop modifications or additional trained components (Xiao et al., 2025; Kovács, 2026; Li et al., 2026b), limiting their plug-and-play deployment. More importantly, task-local optimization overlooks the continuity of software development, where successive changes occur within an evolving codebase (Xu et al., 2025; Joshi et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2026). Such continuity creates an opportunity for cost control: within a shared environment, such as a code repository, completed executions can provide reusable experience for future tasks. We therefore optimize cumulative cost across a sequence of tasks in that environment, rather than treating each execution in isolation.

We first test whether fixed, externally applied cost-control strategies can deliver consistent token savings. Our cost profiling covers 60 SWE-Bench tasks across 6 repositories (Jimenez et al., 2024) and evaluates three representative fixed strategies from popular open-source plugins: command-output compression with Rust Token Killer (RTK), semantic code navigation with Serena, and structural context injection with Aider’s repository map. Empirically, we find that no fixed strategy reduces cost consistently: each has both positive and negative repository-level effects, and their pooled effects are small (Fig. 2). Meanwhile, the default traces reveal three recurring sources of headroom: operational knowledge is repeatedly rediscovered, most loaded tools remain unused, and failed trajectories consume disproportionate cost. Taken together, these findings point to strategies that adapt to each environment from its accumulated traces, rather than fixed strategies applied uniformly.

Motivated by these findings, we introduce TokenEconomizer, an experience-driven external controller for coding agents. It treats each agent as a black box: it acts through exposed prompt and tool settings, monitors execution events, and does not modify model weights or agent-loop code. At its core, a controller applies general cost-control meta-strategies to continually refine environment-specific policies from completed execution traces. These policies adaptively determine (i) which one-line operational facts about the environment to activate as micro-skills, (ii) which loaded but irrelevant tools to prune, and (iii) when to intervene in unproductive failure loops. papers.title: Characterization, ageing and post-mortem dataset of commercial 58Ah prismatic NMC cells
papers.abstract: This paper provides an extensive dataset for commercial 58 Ah prismatic NMC cells. The dataset comprises three types of data: characterization, ageing, and cell teardown. Characterization data include tests such as GITT, HPPC, and EIS, among others. Ageing data were obtained from 41 cells subjected to 38 distinct ageing conditions, including application-surrogate drive cycles. Recurring reference performance tests and EIS measurements track the evolution of each cell. Teardown data were obtained from pristine and aged (post-mortem) cells. They include material analyses and half-cell measurements. This single dataset supports analytics, model development (both machine-learning and physics-based), benchmarking, and techno-economic analysis. Several example analyses are carried out to show the usability of the data. For instance, the paper shows how lithium stripping can be detected from the voltage response of a short discharge applied after each charge. The data and the processing and analysis scripts are openly provided alongside this paper.

papers.intro:
Lithium-ion batteries are the fastest-growing energy-storage technology: they provide sufficient energy density for stationary and mobile applications and already support the decarbonization of transport and industrial energy storage (IEA, 2026). Batteries in Electric Vehicles (EVs) provide zero local emissions (Kelly et al., 2023), and utility-scale batteries provide grid-scale flexibility and grid services (IEA, 2024). When installed behind the meter alongside rooftop solar, coupled to large industrial loads, or co-located with large generation sites (utility-scale solar or wind farms), batteries can reduce the need for fossil-fuel-based energy by reducing curtailment, improving self-consumption, and increasing the penetration of renewables (Prakash et al., 2022).
