papers.title: Model Checking for Noisy Toric Words
papers.abstract: Toric words have recently gained attention as a means to model the behaviour of dynamical systems such as linear loops. This work is concerned with describing when the toric model is precise enough to decide whether the trace of a system is contained in an omega-regular language. Our contributions are threefold. (i) We use topological means to generalise a class of toric words by defining noise-robust dynamical systems and their sets of noisy traces. We prove that all noisy traces of a system are almost-periodic, and have the same set of recurrent factors. (ii) We apply the abstract techniques above to concrete sequences obtained as sign descriptions of real algebraic linear recurrence sequences (LRS), and show that the language-membership problem for sign descriptions of LRS with few dominant roots is decidable. (iii) We show that noisy traces of noise-robust dynamical systems are indistinguishable to a prefix-independent omega-regular language, and inclusion is decidable provided the common language of their recurrent factors is recursive. We incidentally obtain properties of prefix-independent omega-regular languages that may be of independent interest.

papers.title: How Finite-Rank Bottlenecks Shape the Low-Rank Adaptation Landscape
papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. Most existing analyses rely on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime, which linearizes the network around the pretrained weights. In this work, we take a different approach that requires no linearization: our key observation is that, once the backbone is frozen, the loss sees each adapted weight matrix only through a finite-rank linear map induced by the frozen activations. Trace-norm regularization then forces the optimizer to pick a low-rank matrix among all matrices that produce the same observed output. This yields global minimizers whose ranks are controlled by the rank of this map, which we call the \emph{bottleneck rank}, rather than the sample size. For multi-head attention, we obtain tighter rank upper bounds by exploiting two additional invariances: row-wise softmax is insensitive to additive row constants in the score matrix, and value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. For the factorized LoRA objective with weight decay, we prove a complementary result on the nonconvex side: after an arbitrarily small generic positive semidefinite perturbation, every first-order stationary point is rank-deficient once the LoRA rank exceeds a threshold determined by the bottleneck rank. Finally, we show that global minimizers of the perturbed objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm problem, and we provide uniform generalization bounds governed by the spectral structure of the frozen features.

papers.title: Distributional signatures of computation: inferring mechanisms from computation time distributions
papers.abstract: Computational complexity theory provides a framework for analysing abstract models of computation, whereas computational systems operate as finite physical implementations whose behaviour is shaped by their architecture and physical substrate. In such systems, computational organisation cannot be directly characterised from algorithms or internal representations. Building on the use of reaction time distributions to constrain mechanisms in cognitive science, we introduce an empirical framework for investigating computation in physical systems by inferring computational mechanisms from observable computation time distributions. The framework combines empirical benchmarking, which characterises computational efficiency through the scaling of computation time with problem size, with distributional analysis, which treats computation time distributions as signatures of the stochastic dynamics generated by different computational mechanisms. We demonstrate the framework using a scalable visual search paradigm, comparing human performance with three computational models that employ distinct mechanisms of evidence accumulation. Benchmarking reveals broadly similar scaling behaviour for the models and human observers, whereas distributional analysis distinguishes between these models. We show that computation time distributions provide an empirical level of description linking observable computational behaviour to underlying computational mechanisms. This framework complements computational complexity theory by extending the empirical study of computation from measuring computational performance to characterising computational organisation. It provides an empirical approach for comparing finite computational systems across diverse physical implementations, including biological, classical, neuromorphic, and quantum systems, without requiring access to their internal algorithms or architectures.

papers.title: Upper bounds on the number of causal pieces in spiking neural networks
papers.abstract: The input space of single-spike neural networks decomposes into causal pieces, and the number of causal pieces has been shown to provide a lower bound on the approximation error for some spiking neural networks. While this decomposition is applicable to a wide range of spiking neuron models, the limits of how many causal pieces can be realised by spiking neural networks are still unknown. In this work, we derive two complementary upper bounds on the number of causal pieces in feedforward single-spike neural networks. First, we establish a combinatorial bound given by the poly-Bernoulli numbers, which applies to a broad class of spiking neuron models. The bound is of order $e^{2(L-1)N\log N+\mathcal{O}(N)}$, with network depth $L$ and maximum layer width $N$. Second, for a specific set of neuron models, we derive a bound based on hyperplane arrangements. Applying the latter framework, we obtain bounds of order $\mathcal{O}\!\left(N^{(4L-3)(N_0-1)}\right)$ for the non-leaky integrate-and-fire model with exponential synapses and the ReLU-type spike response model, and $\mathcal{O}\!\left(N^{L(N_0-1)}\right)$ for the leaky integrate-and-fire model with Dirac-$δ$ synapses, where $N_0$ is the input dimension. For the non-leaky integrate-and-fire model with Dirac-$δ$ synapses, additional temporal structure allows us to sharpen the general combinatorial bound to one that depends only on $N_0$, independently of the network depth and widths.

papers.title: Local proxies for memory-efficient training
papers.abstract: Local learning algorithms can reshape resource requirements of artificial intelligence. The memory bottleneck of standard end-to-end backpropagation lies in the need to store all network activations until the loss gradient has been propagated back through. Local learning avoids this, but typically at a cost in accuracy. We study how to achieve accurate and memory efficient local learning in transformers. For each transformer block, we train a local proxy network to predict the global network output via distillation. Gradients can be independently propagated through this local proxy while estimating well the backpropagation gradients. In theory, this approach is exact for deep linear networks; in non-linear residual models, the gradient error can be bounded when using the appropriate residual proxy. We verify this numerically and demonstrate that optimizing the distillation loss improves gradient estimation. Evaluating the performance of proxy propagation on CIFAR-100 in vision transformers, we find that it achieves a better accuracy/memory trade-off compared to other local algorithms. Finally, we show that the method is further relevant for fine-tuning large language models on a small memory budget. Our method trains faster and achieves higher performance than memory-efficient zeroth-order learning algorithms with comparable memory cost.

papers.intro:
Conventionally, intelligence emerges in neural network models from end-to-end training with backpropagation (Rumelhart et al., 1986). By design, backpropagation induces a backward locking problem (Jaderberg et al., 2017). A forward pass first computes the network activations from inputs to outputs and then the backward pass propagates gradients in reverse order. In the meantime, network activations need to be stored, increasing memory requirements with network depth. The large memory consumption is a major manufacturing cost and increases the energy consumption of training datacenters (Gholami et al., 2024). When training large language models (LLMs) under a limited memory budget, the network depth and sequence length that fit in memory therefore constrain the range of tasks and the reasoning capability of the model.

When training large language models (LLMs) under a limited memory budget, the network depth and sequence length that fit in memory therefore constrain the range of tasks and the reasoning capability of the model.

Historically inspired by neuroscience research (Hebb, 1949; Markram et al., 2011; Gerstner et al., 2018), local learning is one way of avoiding the backward locking problem. Since the brain appears to be a distributed network without a precise backward gradient communication pathway, it is natural to suppose that biological sub-networks mainly learn from their immediate inputs and internal representations (Lillicrap et al., 2020). Yet few local learning algorithms have been scaled to transformers, and attempts so far have had limited success (Filipovich et al., 2022). Most of these algorithms were not designed to approximate the backpropagated gradient, so they struggle in deep architectures; on top of this, those designed for biological plausibility often come with an increase in training time. Within the scope of local learning, we seek an alternative to backpropagation that is mathematically grounded and memory efficient without compromising training time.

Since the brain appears to be a distributed network without a precise backward gradient communication pathway, it is natural to suppose that biological sub-networks mainly learn from their immediate inputs and internal representations (Lillicrap et al., 2020). Most of these algorithms were not designed to approximate the backpropagated gradient, so they struggle in deep architectures; on top of this, those designed for biological plausibility often come with an increase in training time. Within the scope of local learning, we seek an alternative to backpropagation that is mathematically grounded and memory efficient without compromising training time.

Towards this goal, we define locality by partitioning a large transformer into blocks, with the gradient computation in each block decoupled in the sense of Jaderberg et al. (2017): block parameters are updated immediately after the forward pass of the block. Hence, we say that learning is “local” if it needs to store activations from only one block at a time in memory. Additionally, when the block updates are fully independent, we say that the training algorithm is “unlocked”, making possible an efficient form of model parallelism (Belilovsky et al., 2020). Here, we follow a principled approach to estimate global gradients locally. To each block we equip a local proxy network with the objective of predicting the global network output via distillation. Gradients of each block are then computed with local backpropagation through the proxy instead of the downstream blocks. This way, proxy propagation (ProxyProp) offers theoretical insights that translate into a practical algorithm: • Theory: ProxyProp is an approximation of the global backpropagation. Despite the locality and the simplicity of the prediction objective, a linear proxy implicitly estimates the expected network Jacobian, and is therefore exact in deep linear networks. • Theory: For non-linear residual networks, when the proxy follows a residual parameterization, the local gradients are exact at initialization and can achieve a bounded gradient estimation error when the skip connections of the network are dominating. • Simulation: For supervised classification in vision transformers (ViT), across various network partitionings, ProxyProp offers a better trade-off between memory and accuracy over other local algorithms. • Simulation: ProxyProp enables memory-efficient fine-tuning of LLMs, achieving higher performance than zeroth-order optimization techniques (MeZO) at comparable memory cost (even when MeZO uses 8x more compute time).

papers.title: Nearly Linear Private Learning of Littlestone Classes
papers.abstract: Differentially private learning aims to learn from data while protecting individual training examples. For binary classification, finite Littlestone dimension characterizes approximate private PAC learnability (Alon et al., JACM 2022). Understanding how this dimension controls private sample complexity remains a central question. For classes of Littlestone dimension $d$, the first general upper bound was doubly exponential in $d$ (Bun, Livni, and Moran, FOCS 2020). Subsequent work improved this to $\widetilde O(d^6)$ (Ghazi et al., STOC 2021) and then to $\widetilde O(d^5)$ (Lyu, STOC 2026). We prove a nearly linear upper bound of $O(d\log d)$. Our main algorithmic contribution is a structural exponential mechanism for data-dependent candidate sets equipped with a rank satisfying suitable stability conditions. For natural Littlestone classes such as subspace indicators, this rank has a simple geometric interpretation: it is the codimension. This yields a private PAC learner for subspaces of dimension at most $d$ over any field, with tight linear dependence on $d$ and no dependence on the ambient dimension, improving the quadratic dependence of Kaplan et al. (STOC 2025). Our second contribution is combinatorial: drawing on model-theoretic ideas, we construct a suitable rank for general Littlestone classes and establish the counting bounds required by the mechanism.

In the classical PAC model, a learner receives labeled examples drawn from an unknown distribution and should produce a predictor that is accurate on new examples from the same distribution; see, for example, [16]. papers.title: Graphlet-based Decentralized Finance Transaction Method Classification
papers.abstract: Decentralized Finance (DeFi) transactions involve complex interactions among accounts, smart contracts, and tokens. We investigate whether network topology can identify transaction methods that describe DeFi operations. We extract directed graphlet features to classify the 30 most frequent methods. Our results show that graphlet features complement event log counts in improving classification performance. Using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), we further derive model explanations that reveal method-specific graphlet structural patterns.
papers.intro:
Decentralized Finance (DeFi) provides financial services such as lending, borrowing, and trading without intermediaries through programmable smart contracts. Users interact with DeFi protocols through transactions that invoke methods implemented in smart contracts. Such methods may involve multiple tokens and contracts, while sequences of methods can be composed into more complex strategies Kitzler et al. (2023). For instance, a transaction calling an aggregator contract may route trades through several decentralized exchange protocols to obtain a more favorable exchange rate.

For instance, a transaction calling an aggregator contract may route trades through several decentralized exchange protocols to obtain a more favorable exchange rate.

Transaction methods provide a semantic description of the operations performed, but human-readable labels rely on public contract interfaces, which do not cover all transactions. Inferring transaction methods from observed execution behavior can help identify, inspect, and validate on-chain financial activities, particularly when explicit method information is unavailable or uncertain.

papers.title: LocalIntent: Outcome-Specific Structured Generation for Backend-Compatible Smart Building Automation with Local LLMs
papers.abstract: Locally deployed large language models (LLMs) can reduce reliance on remote cloud services for natural language smart building automation, but backend-facing processing requires correct outcome selection, alignment with local capabilities, and valid structured outputs. We investigate whether a complete outcome-specific prompting design improves compact-model outputs beyond generic route-then-generate prompting. The proposed LocalIntent approach routes requests to ordinary or persistent-rule branches: the former produces commands, clarifications, or rejections, while the latter generates trigger-action rules, followed by deterministic validation. We evaluate four locally executed Gemma and Qwen models spanning 2B-9B parameters on 101 non-persistent and 54 persistent-rule records, comparing Monolithic prompting, generic two-stage prompting, LocalIntent, and validation-guided repair. Across the evaluated datasets, LocalIntent achieves higher intent understanding, device identification, and action/parameter correctness than generic two-stage prompting, while clarification/mode correctness remains model-dependent. The largest gains occur for rules, where LocalIntent improves intent understanding from 26.4% to 80.6%, device identification from 59.3% to 84.7%, rule-mode correctness from 49.1% to 98.6%, and action/parameter correctness from 5.6% to 44.9%. For non-persistent requests, pooled gains are smaller: intent understanding increases from 39.6% to 53.2%, and action/parameter correctness from 30.7% to 42.8%.

We introduce LocalIntent, which routes requests to an ordinary or persistent-rule branch. The rule branch generates a predicate-bearing trigger and action. The ordinary branch produces a target–action–parameter command, clarification, or rejection under non-execution guardrails. A deterministic validator tests structure, registered entities, supported actions and parameters, and mechanically testable rule consistency. We compare LocalIntent with Monolithic prompting and TwoStageGeneric, a generic route-then-generate design. The methods differ in routing labels, prompts, schemas, context presentation, and fallbacks; thus, we compare complete designs without isolating individual mechanisms. We also assess validation-guided repair and local inference latency. LocalIntent’s clearest differences occur on persistent rules; non-persistent differences are smaller and model-dependent, and repair adds little aggregate benefit.

papers.title: BMuon: Budgeting Muon's Spectral Geometry for Structured Compressibility
papers.abstract: Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer for neural network training and admits an interpretation as steepest descent under a spectral-norm geometry. Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply when their MLP hidden channels are pruned after training. To reconcile Muon's optimization performance with structured compressibility, we introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which modifies Muon's spectral geometry so that hidden channels across blocks compete for a shared allocation budget. The resulting oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under a family of norms that interpolate between Muon's geometry and structured sparse geometries. Our principal sparsity control is an interpretable global channel-allocation budget, rather than a setting-dependent sparsity-penalty coefficient. For linear factorization models, we show that Muon admits minimum-cost exact representations with redundant hidden width, whereas under the BMuon oracle geometry and a sufficiently scarce budget, every minimum-cost representation is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a minorization-maximization surrogate for the exact allocation problem. On ImageNet-1K with ViT-S/16, BMuon improves over Muon under gradual structured MLP pruning, and its learned allocations provide a more effective pruning criterion than weight magnitude. On a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb, BMuon improves over Muon under post-training MLP channel pruning.

papers.intro:
Modern Transformer models incur substantial memory and computational costs at inference time, motivating compression for more efficient deployment (Kwon et al., 2022). Pruning is a natural approach to this problem, but practical gains depend on the sparsity structure: unstructured sparsity often requires specialized kernels or hardware, whereas structured pruning removes entire computational units and translates directly into efficiency gains (Wen et al., 2016; An et al., 2024). Feed-forward modules can account for roughly two thirds of Transformer parameters (Geva et al., 2021), making their hidden channels a natural target for structured compression. Global pruning ranks channels across layers jointly, allowing different layers to retain different numbers of channels (Lee et al., 2021; An et al., 2024). Post-pruning fine-tuning adds computational cost, especially for large models (Kwon et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2024), motivating compressibility to emerge during training so that pruning requires little or no recovery.

Post-pruning fine-tuning adds computational cost, especially for large models (Kwon et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2024), motivating compressibility to emerge during training so that pruning requires little or no recovery.

Muon has demonstrated strong training efficiency across model scales, from small vision and language-model benchmarks to billion-parameter language models (Jordan et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025; Shah et al., 2025). Its matrix update can be viewed as a linear minimization oracle over a spectral-norm ball, giving Muon a steepest-descent interpretation in spectral-norm geometry (Pethick et al., 2025). Prior work has shown that implicit bias can depend on optimization geometry (Gunasekar et al., 2018). For Muon, recent theory identifies a spectral-norm margin bias in linear and smooth homogeneous models (Fan et al., 2025; Gronich and Vardi, 2026). Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers degrade rapidly under structured MLP pruning, suggesting that Muon’s spectral geometry does not by itself encourage structured compressibility. As shown in Figure 1, a Muon-trained ViT-S/16 on ImageNet-1K collapses after only 30%30\% global MLP channel pruning, with Top-1 accuracy falling from 75.23%75.23\% to 3.17%3.17\%. In contrast, our proposed Budget Muon (BMuon) algorithm retains 74.08%74.08\% Top-1 accuracy after 70%70\% pruning, nearly matching its 74.17%74.17\% accuracy before pruning, with no post-pruning recovery. This raises the central question: can Muon’s spectral geometry be modified to encourage structured compressibility?

BMuon chooses the allocation globally, intuitively asking where the update budget should be spent to obtain the greatest first-order decrease in the loss.

NuMuon (Dolatabadi et al., 2026) is the closest prior compression-aware variant of Muon. It imposes a nuclear-norm constraint on Muon’s update direction to improve low-rank compressibility. BMuon instead targets structured compressibility over hidden channels by introducing a global channel budget into Muon’s spectral-norm geometry. Prior work has also incorporated compressibility into training. Lu et al. (2022) train networks for unstructured pruning with Frank–Wolfe under fixed layerwise constraints on the weights, while Zimmer et al. (2025) use Frank–Wolfe under fixed norm constraints for convolutional filter pruning and low-rank compression. BMuon instead leaves the weights unconstrained and modifies Muon’s spectral update geometry for global hidden-channel compression. Resource-constrained structure learning and global structured pruning have been studied across CNNs and Transformers (Gordon et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023; An et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026a). GRASPrune (Wang et al., 2026b) learns gates post hoc on a frozen LLM to select MLP channels and attention KV-head groups under a single global parameter budget, while DABP (Laroui et al., 2026) jointly trains CNN weights and continuous channel gates under a global resource budget. BMuon uses no forward gates; its budget instead controls the channel-wise reweighting of Muon’s spectral update constraint during training.

Theoretically, we show that the BMuon oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under an induced norm Ωα,K\Omega_{\alpha,K}, where α\alpha controls the strength of channel reweighting and KK is the global budget over the NN hidden channels. This family recovers Muon when α=0\alpha=0 or K=NK=N. At α=1\alpha=1, its unit ball is the convex hull of operator-norm-bounded updates supported on at most KK coupled hidden channels. This is related to group kk-support norms through the use of structured support (Argyriou et al., 2012; Rao et al., 2017), but its atoms are bounded in operator norm rather than Euclidean norm. It is also related to spectral kk-support norms (McDonald et al., 2014; McDonald et al., 2016), but differs in the notion of sparsity: spectral kk-support uses sparsity in singular values, whereas BMuon uses MLP-channel sparsity. (2021), this is the minimum parameter-space cost among exact two-matrix factorizations that realize the same linear predictor. We prove that, under an explicit budget-scarcity condition, every minimum-cost BMuon factorization is width-minimal, whereas Muon’s minimum cost can also be attained by factorizations with redundant hidden width.

papers.title: Dissipative solutions for fibred Wasserstein gradient flows of Cahn-Hilliard-type energies
papers.abstract: We study fourth-order evolution equations with a fibred Wasserstein gradient-flow structure, describing spatial transport of finitely many or a continuum of types. The driving Cahn-Hilliard-like energy combines a diagonal gradient contribution with nonlinear interactions between types. We prove subsequential convergence of the fibred Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto scheme to solutions satisfying an energy-dissipation inequality. For general type distributions, the absence of compactness in the type variable is addressed through defect-based solution concepts. On $\mathbb R^d, d\le 3$, we construct dissipative solutions satisfying an additional entropy-dissipation inequality. On smooth bounded domains in any space dimension, a coercivity estimate for the metric slope allows us to construct energy-dissipating solutions without relying on flow interchange, thereby covering non-convex domains endowed with the intrinsic length distance. In both cases, a variational comparison of the piecewise constant and De Giorgi interpolants yields a common limiting energy and strong convergence of the difference to zero without requiring strong compactness. For finitely many types, the defects vanish and the construction yields weak solutions. We further establish weak-strong uniqueness of dissipative solutions in every space dimension and of energy-dissipating solutions in dimensions $d\le5$. Combined with the respective existence results, this yields strong convergence of the variational approximations whenever a sufficiently regular, strictly positive solution exists.

papers.intro:
We study fourth-order evolution equations describing the spatial transport of interacting populations with a fixed distribution of types. The dynamics are driven by a common Cahn–Hilliard-like energy and formally have the structure of a gradient flow with respect to a fibred Wasserstein distance. This framework allows for mixtures of finitely many species, populations with continuously distributed traits, and, more generally, combinations of singular and continuous type distributions. A motivation comes from continuum descriptions of cell adhesion, sorting and segregation. The type variable y∈Yy\in Y may encode cell type or adhesion-molecule expression [32], a differentiation status or a gene expression profile [34, 11], or a collection of intracellular regulatory variables [5]. We here treat these characteristics as fixed labels and assume that the mass of each type is conserved. Our model thus describes spatial rearrangement in regimes where changes in cellular state and population size can be neglected.

In [15], Falcó, Baker and Carrillo formally derive a local fourth-order system from nonlocal adhesive interactions in a short-range limit. Their numerical simulations show that the local model reproduces a range of cell-sorting patterns associated with differential adhesion. A related phenomenological fourth-order model of tissue growth was proposed earlier by Chertock, Degond, Hecht and Vincent [13], where repulsive interactions induce segregation of initially mixed cell populations. The model is derived by a Wasserstein gradient-flow ansatz for the conservative part, with the growth terms being incorporated afterwards. For a second-order tumour growth model with continuously distributed phenotypes y∈[0,1]y\in[0,1], where mass transport is driven by the gradient of a common population pressure, we refer to David [14].

papers.title: Fast Distributed $(Δ+ 1)$-Edge Coloring in Bipartite Graphs
papers.abstract: We show that, on bipartite $n$-vertex graphs in the LOCAL model of distributed computation, $(Δ+ 1)$-edge coloring can be solved deterministically in $O(f(Δ) \log n)$ rounds for some function $f$. In particular this implies a deterministic $O(\log n)$-round upper bound for $(Δ+ 1)$-edge coloring on bipartite constant-degree graphs. Our results improve on the previous state-of-the-art bounds (which hold already on general graphs) whose $n$-dependencies are $\widetilde{O}(\log^5 n)$ rounds deterministically and $\widetilde{O}(\log^2 n)$ rounds randomized [Bernshteyn and Dhawan, J.\ Comb.\ Theory 2025]. In fact, we obtain the aforementioned results already for a more restrictive version of $(Δ+ 1)$-edge coloring that corresponds to a \emph{local-palette} strengthening of Vizing's theorem shown recently to hold [Christiansen, STOC 2023]. In this version, every edge $\{u, v\}$ has to be colored with a color from $\{1, \dots, \max(\operatorname{deg}(u), \operatorname{deg}(v))+ 1\}$. For all of our results, the vertices do not need to know on which side of the bipartition they lie---the structural promise of bipartiteness suffices.

papers.intro:
Edge coloring is one of the classical problems in graph theory, studied for many decades. One of the cornerstone results on edge coloring, Vizing’s theorem [49], states that every simple graph of maximum degree Δ\Delta admits a proper edge coloring with Δ+1\Delta+1 colors, and this is best possible in general: odd cycles, for example, require three colors although Δ=2\Delta=2. Since Vizing’s discovery, (Δ+1)(\Delta+1)-edge coloring has been examined across many models of computation, with substantial progress especially in recent years (see, e.g., [12, 29, 13, 14, 11, 15, 4, 2, 28, 3] for the most recent progress in sequential, dynamic, and distributed algorithms). In this work, we study the deterministic complexity of (Δ+1)(\Delta+1)-edge coloring in the standard LOCAL model of distributed computation.

In the LOCAL model [45], the input graph is considered as a communication network with the vertices (or nodes) of the graph representing computational entities: computation proceeds in synchronous rounds, and in each round every vertex may send an arbitrarily large message to each neighbor, receive the messages sent to it, and perform arbitrary local computation. Each vertex has to terminate at some point and then output its local part of the global solution to the considered problem; for (Δ+1)(\Delta+1)-edge coloring, each vertex has to output a color from {1,…,Δ+1}\{1,\dots,\Delta+1\} for each of its incident edges such that endpoints of the same edge agree on the color of the edge. The runtime of a distributed algorithm governing the behavior of the vertices is simply the number of rounds until the last vertex has terminated. For a full definition of the LOCAL model, we refer the reader to Section 2.

papers.title: DeDiCa: A Scalable Deconfounding Discrete Causal Generative Model
papers.abstract: We introduce DeDiCa, a practical framework for efficient causal inference with discrete variables and hidden confounding that revisits classical probabilistic modeling through a tensorized parameterization of causal Bayesian networks, enabling tractable inference. Given a causal graph, DeDiCa is trained once on observational data by maximum likelihood, exactly marginalizing over hidden confounders, and can then estimate any (proxy-)identifiable interventional query. Despite this deliberately simple parameterization, DeDiCa matches state-of-the-art neural causal generative models in ATE estimation, while supporting memory-efficient CPU training and exact interventional inference in milliseconds. Compared with causal foundation models, DeDiCa scales more effectively with additional observational samples and achieves competitive accuracy at substantially lower inference time and memory. DeDiCa provides a tractable, accurate, and scalable approach to causal inference in discrete settings with hidden confounding.

papers.title: Humanity's Last Choice: A Common Evaluation Standard for Generative Engine Optimization
papers.abstract: Humanity's Last Choice describes the idea that the last choice people need to make is which AI system they entrust with the decisions that follow. These systems rely on external sources that content providers can edit through generative engine optimization (GEO) to increase source visibility and influence recommendations. Choosing among these systems therefore requires comparable evidence of how well they carry out user requests when exposed to GEO. Benchmarks have made progress in standardizing tasks, models, and metrics, but they often define their own spaces of GEO strategies and use different editing constraints. These differences can conflate gains from better optimization algorithms with those from greater freedom to edit sources, while making evaluation coverage difficult to compare across benchmarks. We therefore call for a common evaluation standard and propose a meta-taxonomy that describes where sources are edited, how they are edited, and what signals those edits target. Drawing on representative literature, we map existing strategies into a searchable space and outline a protocol for controlled comparisons with explicit coverage reporting. This provides a foundation for common leaderboards that can inform which systems people choose to rely on.

papers.title: Lipschitz Bounds for Neural Networks Using a Two-Copy Linear Fractional Transformation
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a new method to bound the global Lipschitz constant of a neural network (NN). Our formulation uses a two-copy linear fractional transformation (LFT) representation of the NN with stacked signals. We use biased quadratic constraints (QCs) to bound the input/output behavior of the nonlinear activation functions. We then formulate a linear matrix inequality condition, using these biased QCs, to bound the Lipschitz constant of the NN. The best (smallest) Lipschitz bound is computed via a convex, semidefinite program. There are two key distinctions of the proposed two-copy formulation in comparison to existing methods that rely on a single incremental representation with incremental signals. First, the NN bias terms are eliminated in the standard incremental representation, but appear in our formulation. Second, there is a larger class of QCs that can be expressed for the nonlinearities in our formulation than in the incremental representation. We show that our proposed formulation yields less conservative Lipschitz bounds due to these two differences. We illustrate these points via several simple, motivating examples. We also demonstrate the proposed method using a benchmark problem with a NN controller for an inverted pendulum.

This paper proposes a new method to bound the global Lipschitz constant of a neural network (NN). Such bounds are useful for certifying robustness properties of neural networks (NNs). A variety of methods have been proposed for computing Lipschitz bounds and here we focus on SDP-based methods. Existing approaches, e.g., LipSDP [1], rely on an incremental formulation for the NN. The input/output behavior of the nonlinear activation functions are characterized by quadratic constraints (QCs) or integral quadratic constraints (IQCs) [2, 3, 4]. These constraints are then incorporated into a linear matrix inequality (LMI) condition that yields a global Lipschitz bound. The best (smallest) bound can be computed via a semidefinite program (SDP). Extensions address non-slope-restricted activations [5] and local Lipschitz and other incremental input/output properties [6]. Related QC- and IQC-based methods have been developed for stability analysis of neural-network feedback systems [7, 8] and for constructing recurrent neural networks with certified properties [9]. A recent overivew is given in [10].

More recently, [14] presented examples for which common SDP-based verification methods fail, including ReLU networks with dead neurons. These observations motivate a unified formulation that retains bias information and permits richer QCs on the activation functions.

papers.title: Direct Conditional Parameterization for N-Dimensional Splatting
papers.abstract: N-dimensional splatting extends 3D Gaussian Splatting with view direction and time to model view-dependent and dynamic effects. Each primitive is lifted into a joint distribution over position and conditioning variables, then conditionally sliced at each rendering query. N-DGS and UBS share this step across Gaussian and Beta kernels: recovering the conditional mean, opacity, and covariance requires per-primitive matrix inversions and regression products in every forward pass. We introduce direct conditional parameterization, replacing this covariance-derived readout with explicit per-effect parameters: a Cholesky precision factor for opacity and a factorized query-to-position regression operator with learnable per-dimension coupling. Unrestricted conditional coordinates recover a valid joint covariance; our factorization adds spatial-scale and coupling priors. Applied to both kernels, the parameterization yields dGS (Gaussian) and dBS (Beta). Across five static and dynamic benchmarks, they match or exceed their covariance-derived counterparts on quality, with gains up to +1.26 dB in the main MCMC evaluation. Production slicing is 6.9-7.7 times faster than on-the-fly covariance-derived conditioning; complete-render profiling gives 1.25-1.91 times speedups on four trained scenes. Direct conditioning provides a structured, kernel-agnostic alternative for N-dimensional splatting. Project page: https://gaozhongpai.github.io/dgs/.

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) (Kerbl et al., 2023) achieves photorealistic novel-view synthesis at real-time speeds through explicit 3D Gaussian primitives. Static primitives, however, struggle with specular reflections, temporal dynamics, and view-dependent geometry.

Recent work extends 3DGS along two orthogonal axes. The first is kernel shape: alternatives to the Gaussian kernel include Beta kernels (Liu et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2026), generalized exponentials (Hamdi et al., 2024), and Student-t distributions (Zhu et al., 2025). The second is dimensionality: N-dimensional Gaussians (N-DG) (Diolatzis et al., 2024), refined as 6DGS (Gao et al., 2025a) and 7DGS (Gao et al., 2025b) (collectively N-DGS), lift each primitive into a joint distribution over 3D position and conditioning variables (view direction with C=3C{=}3, view+time with C=4C{=}4). At render time, the (3+C)(3{+}C)-dimensional primitive is conditionally sliced at the current query (a view direction or timestamp) using the conditional Gaussian formulas: the mean shifts, the opacity is modulated by a kernel evaluated at the query, and the spatial covariance receives a correction term. Universal Beta Splatting (UBS) (Liu et al., 2026) combines the two axes by replacing the Gaussian opacity decay with an anisotropic Beta kernel while inheriting the same conditional-slicing structure. N-DGS and UBS together represent the leading N-dimensional splatting formulations across Gaussian and Beta kernels.

Opacity uses a directly parameterized Cholesky precision factor, and position uses a factorized regression operator with learnable per-dimension coupling that decouples position from opacity by default and recovers full coupling on demand. papers.title: MIXSim: A multiclass first order traffic model with composition-dependent dynamics for mixed-autonomy urban networks
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel multiclass first order macroscopic traffic model for mixed-autonomy in signalized urban networks, called MIXSim. Human driven vehicles (HDVs) and Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) are represented as separate classes while origin-destination information is retained through commodity specific states. The local vehicle class composition and class specific driving behaviour characteristics determine the parameters of a composition-dependent triangular fundamental diagram. At signalized intersections, the composition of movement demand additionally determines the saturation flow rate, while the realized movement flow is constrained by demand, effective green time, and downstream receiving capacity. Numerical experiments investigate different CAV penetration levels and CAV time gaps, together with alternative signal control strategies. The numerical experiments illustrate how changes in CAV penetration and CAV time gap affect network performance under the tested conditions, and demonstrate the use of MIXSim for comparing signal control strategies across different mixed traffic regimes.
papers.intro:
Urban traffic congestion remains a persistent societal problem and a major challenge for mobility systems, as recurrent demand peaks and finite road and intersection capacities produce delays, queues, spillback, unreliable travel times, and inefficient use of the network [1]. This challenge is becoming increasingly complex with the gradual introduction of Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs), which are expected to coexist with human driven vehicles (HDVs) during a prolonged transition period. CAVs may differ from HDVs in their car following behavior, longitudinal spacing characteristics, discharge behavior, and routing capabilities. Consequently, traffic flow characteristics and effective capacity may depend on the local vehicle composition [2, 3, 4]. The analysis and management of mixed-autonomy urban networks therefore require traffic models capable of representing such composition-dependent dynamics rather than relying exclusively on uniform and fixed traffic flow parameters.

Consequently, traffic flow characteristics and effective capacity may depend on the local vehicle composition [2, 3, 4]. The analysis and management of mixed-autonomy urban networks therefore require traffic models capable of representing such composition-dependent dynamics rather than relying exclusively on uniform and fixed traffic flow parameters.

Traffic simulation is widely used to evaluate traffic management and control strategies before field deployment. The appropriate modeling resolution depends on the strategy being investigated, the objectives of the study, and the performance indicators of interest [5, 6]. Microscopic packages such as PTV Vissim, Aimsun, Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO), and CityFlow represent individual vehicle behavior and detailed controller interactions, making them particularly suitable when trajectories, lane level effects, safety, vehicle interactions, or other disaggregate measures are central [7, 8, 9, 10]. When the quantities of interest are instead aggregate network measures, such as travel time, accumulation, queue discharge, spillback, throughput, or controller performance, first order macroscopic models can provide a computationally parsimonious environment for repeated network scale experiments.

The Cell Transmission Model (CTM) is an established first order macroscopic traffic flow model that describes traffic evolution through conservation equations together with sending and receiving functions [11, 12]. Its discretized link representation naturally captures queue formation, propagation, and spillback, while flows across signalized junctions can be constrained by upstream demand, effective green time, movement saturation, and downstream receiving capacity. Discrete first order kinematic wave models have subsequently been extended to represent heterogeneous and multiclass traffic, such as the FASTLANE model [13], as well as multilane traffic with lane changing and overtaking [14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20], and class specific flow interactions [21].

Mixed-autonomy traffic introduces a further source of heterogeneity because the traffic flow characteristics of a road segment may vary with the local proportion of HDVs and CAVs. Multiclass CTM formulations have therefore been developed to represent mixed human driven and automated traffic and the resulting composition-dependent traffic flow properties [22, 23, 24]. In signalized urban networks, however, vehicle composition is relevant not only to traffic propagation along links but also to the discharge capability of individual intersection movements. A network level mixed-autonomy model should therefore be able to represent composition-dependent behavior at both the link and signalized movement levels while preserving the interactions among congestion propagation, routing, and traffic signal control.

papers.title: Non-Adiabatic Spin-Induced Currents in Magnetic Weyl Semimetals
papers.abstract: We theoretically study dc electric currents induced by rapid spin precession in noncentrosymmetric magnetic Weyl semimetals using the Floquet--Keldysh Green's-function formalism. The spin dynamics act as a time-dependent chiral gauge field and the geometric structure of electric currents is expressed in terms of the Berry curvature, the quantum metric, and the shift vector. For an isotropic Weyl cone, only an injection current is generated. This current scales quadratically with the driving frequency and linearly with the relaxation time associated with coupling to a fermionic bath. We further show that a finite Weyl-cone tilt modifies the available interband-transition phase space, smooths the frequency dependence of the current, and allows for a shift current and another type of injection current, both of which flow in directions determined by the tilt and the direction of the precession. A finite net current can remain after summing contributions from Weyl nodes of opposite chiralities when their transition phase spaces are inequivalent.

papers.title: Triangle Covers of Polygons: Approximation Algorithms and Complexity
papers.abstract: We study the geometric set cover problems of covering and partitioning a polygon into a minimum number of triangles. While the decision version of the covering problem is known to be APX-hard and $\exists\mathbb R$-complete (even for polygons without holes and vertices in general position), the computational complexity of partitioning a simple polygon into a minimum number of triangles is open. Our main result refutes a 40 year old conjecture by Asano, Asano, and Pinter stating that the triangle vertices of a minimum partition lie on intersection points of special lines, which are iteratively generated by the polygon vertices and the intersection points. In particular, we show that there exist polygons where all minimum triangle partitions need Steiner points with irrational coordinates. This indicates that the problem might be more complex than previously expected. Complementarily, we provide a simple constant factor approximation to compute a minimum triangle partition of a given polygon (possibly with holes). In the context of coverings, we devise the first constant factor approximation for computing a minimum triangle cover of a simple polygon. For general polygons, an $O(\log n)$-approximation follows by close inspection of previous work.
papers.intro:
Representing complex objects as a union of much simpler geometric objects is a fundamental problem and may facilitate processing, rendering, and analysis across many disciplines, e.g., computational geometry, data compression, pattern recognition, and image processing. Natural geometric primitives include simple polygons of small complexity, star-shaped polygons, and convex polygons. In this work, we study the problem of covering a polygon with arguably the simplest primitives that combines all these properties, namely triangles. papers.title: Contracting with an Agent under Model Mismatch
papers.abstract: In the classical principal-agent setting, the principal delegates some task to the agent, who receives a payment conditioned on the outcome of the task, which in turn benefits the principal. To align their objectives, the principal designs a contract that incentivizes the agent to take actions beneficial to the principal. In practice, however, the agent may act under misspecified beliefs about the underlying environment, leading to systematically suboptimal decisions. In this work, we study this problem through a principal-agent Markov Decision Process (PAMDP), in which the principal repeatedly interacts with an agent whose transition model may differ from the true environment dynamics. The principal has access to the true transition model and designs contracts that account for the agent's belief and incentives. We characterize contract design under model mismatch and develop a framework that enables the principal to induce desirable long-term benefits even though the agent has a potentially inaccurate understanding of the environment.

papers.intro:
The incentive alignment between two parties has long been described through the principal-agent framework, in which a principal delegates a task to an agent by offering a contract that specifies an outcome-based payment. The design of optimal contracts has been explored by economists and computer scientists [5, 6, 13], where it plays a fundamental role in understanding strategic interactions and incentive mechanisms in both macro- and micro-economic settings.

The design of optimal contracts has been explored by economists and computer scientists [5, 6, 13], where it plays a fundamental role in understanding strategic interactions and incentive mechanisms in both macro- and micro-economic settings.

In the era of increasing human-AI cooperation, the contract design problem has become more relevant than ever before. When delegating tasks to AI systems, we must account for the potential misalignment of the environment dynamics, where one party cannot always assume that the other possesses an accurate model of the environment and may act according to a misspecified understanding of the environment dynamics. This form of model disagreement has been studied in a two-agent sequential stochastic game, where agents may use different models of the world while sharing the same reward structure [8]. Existing formulations of the principal-agent Markov Decision Process (PAMDP) [3, 26] assume that both parties share the same model of the world. We, however, consider a case where the agent acts according to an unknown, potentially suboptimal misspecified model. Under this model misalignment, the principal’s goal is to design contracts that maximize its utility while remaining incentive compatible with respect to the agent’s transition model.

Under this model misalignment, the principal’s goal is to design contracts that maximize its utility while remaining incentive compatible with respect to the agent’s transition model.

We study the problem of contract design under uncertainty about the agent’s environment model. Our approach is based on balancing exploration, in which the principal proposes contracts that reveal information about the agent’s model, and exploitation, in which the principal leverages the information to offer approximately optimal contracts. Exploration is crucial because the agent’s dynamics influence both the actions induced by a contract and the decision to accept it. Consequently, a principal who ignores these belief misalignment risks may design suboptimal contracts, resulting in suboptimal utility or even contract rejection.

We propose a Bayesian learning approach for contract design in PAMDPs with misspecified agent beliefs, where the principal knows the true transition dynamics and the agent uses a different model. We assume that the principal has access to a finite set of possible agent models. The principal maintains a posterior distribution over this set and updates this belief through their repeated interactions. Using the estimated agent’s transition model, the principal computes least payment contracts using backward induction and linear programming. We analyze how mismatched transition dynamics in a PAMDP setting influence contract design and the resulting incentive mechanism. Our main contributions are reformulating the optimal solutions for this setting and validating our approach through empirical experiments. We further investigate how the choice of the candidate model set influences the learning process, including the accuracy of the agent’s transition model estimation, the convergence of the posterior and the resulting contract design.

Principal-agent problems, which formalize settings in which a principal delegates a task to an agent under moral hazard, have been extensively studied in economics and computer science as a fundamental framework [5, 13, 17, 18, 23]. [5] has provided an extensive overview of standard contract theory and incentive mechanism design. Recently, algorithmic contract design has been widely studied in the literature to investigate how contracts can be designed using computational methods [1, 7, 12, 13, 14, 20]. The complexity of finding optimal contracts has been studied in [2, 15, 19, 27]. Moreover, [6, 11] have considered multi-agent settings where the principal designs contracts for multiple agents by extending the single agent contract design approaches.

Optimal contract design is closely related to online learning when the principal does not have perfect information about the agent. Furthermore, [4, 19, 25] have focused on the settings where the agent learns over time, investigating how to design suitable contracts by incentivizing the learning agent.

papers.title: Hydrogen Ion-Cut Single-Crystal Diamond Membranes for Wide and Ultrawide Bandgap Semiconductor Heterointegration
papers.abstract: Single-crystal diamond membranes (SCDms) were created using a hydrogen ion-cut process combined with a two-step post-implantation annealing, electrochemical etching, and micro-transfer printing. Monte Carlo simulations comparing H, He, C, and O implantation predicted a narrower vacancy-distribution profile for hydrogen under the implantation conditions examined. Raman spectroscopy was used to evaluate implantation-induced lattice damage and its recovery during annealing and membrane release, while optical bandgap analysis provided further evidence of restoration of the diamond lattice structure. After delamination and removal of residual graphitic material, freestanding SCDms with improved crystalline quality were obtained. The SCDms were subsequently transferred to GaN, SiC, AlGaN, and AlN substrates without an adhesive layer. The successful formation of diamond/WBG and diamond/UWBG heterostructures demonstrates the feasibility of integrating the SCDms with a range of semiconductor platforms. Overall, these results establish hydrogen implantation as an effective route for producing high-quality SCDms for future diamond-based heterogeneous integration applications.

papers.title: TAN: A Size- and Form-Adaptive Masked-Convolution Encoder for Tissue Graphs
papers.abstract: Tissue graphs represent histology images as graphs over tissue-conforming superpixels, which keeps homogeneous tissue regions intact instead of cutting them into rectangular patches. To embed superpixels, current encoders crop them to bounding boxes and then pad, resize, or mask them, so background or fill values can leak into the node features. This matters in practice, and especially in medical imaging, where a prediction should depend on the tissue and not on an arbitrary preprocessing choice: on BACH, changing only the fill of the masked region shifts the accuracy of frozen encoders by up to 6 percentage points, larger than the differences among the four best encoders under mean fill, and the preferred fill differs between datasets, so it cannot be fixed once and for all. We present TAN (Tissue-Aware Network), a compact convolutional encoder (0.41M parameters) that processes each superpixel at its native shape and extent and excludes background from every operation, which makes its embeddings exactly invariant to the fill by construction. Under identical masks and an identical graph classifier, TAN's accuracy on BACH is not significantly different from that of the 303M-parameter foundation model UNI (81.1% vs. 80.7-82.6%, depending on the fill), with ~740x fewer parameters, ~1,190x fewer FLOPs, and no pretraining. On BRACS, TAN is close to a ResNet18 trained under the same protocol and trails the histopathology foundation models. An ablation with TAN's architecture but standard processing of fill-padded crops shows that masking keeps accuracy similar (nominally higher on BACH, lower on BRACS, within noise) at less than half the FLOPs.
papers.intro:
Whole Slide Images (WSIs) span gigapixel dimensions and are therefore usually cut into rectangular patches and classified with Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) [1, 2, 3]. MIL treats the patches as independent instances and ignores where they lie, so it cannot represent how tissue regions are arranged and connected [1]. Tissue graphs address this by encoding local microenvironments and global tissue architecture [4]: nodes, commonly superpixels, represent tissue regions, and edges their spatial relationships. This work targets node-feature encoding.

Tissue graphs address this by encoding local microenvironments and global tissue architecture [4]: nodes, commonly superpixels, represent tissue regions, and edges their spatial relationships. This work targets node-feature encoding.

Current formulations struggle with non-rectangular nodes. Node features come from handcrafted color and texture descriptors [5], which lack the expressive capacity of deep representations, or from deep-learning backbones restricted to rectangular grids, e.g., applied to fixed-size patches centered on each region [6]. Forcing an irregular entity into such a grid requires cropping, resizing, padding, or masking a rectangular crop, which can introduce artifacts, distort scale, and mix surrounding content into the node features; for standard convolutions over masked regions filled with substitute values, artifacts are well documented in inpainting [7].

papers.title: The Compactness Theorem for Enriched Logic
papers.abstract: The framework of enriched logic extends positive logic (also known as coherent logic) from sets to structures internal to a symmetric monoidal closed category $\mathcal{V}$. This framework was developed by Rosický and the second-named author. The main novelty of this logic is that the arities of the function and relation symbols are now objects in $\mathcal{V}$. We prove the compactness theorem for this enriched logic. That is, a set of $\mathcal{V}$-enriched sequents has a model (internal to $\mathcal{V}$) if every finite subset has a model. To achieve this, we define ultraproducts of enriched structures and prove enriched versions of Łos' theorem. We then develop some model-theoretic applications. We start with an enriched version of the model-theoretic method of diagrams, establishing a correspondence between homomorphisms whose domain is some enriched structure $A$ and models of the set $\operatorname{Diag}(A)$ of all enriched atomic formulas with parameters from $A$ that are true in $A$. Combining this with our compactness theorem, we prove amalgamation results, laying the foundations for enriched syntactic types (in the model-theoretic sense). We finish the paper with a collection of examples of $\mathcal{V}$ that our results apply to. Besides recovering the classical case when $\mathcal{V} = \mathbf{Set}$, these include many presheaf toposes, categories of monoid acts, the category of abelian groups and related additive categories, categories of (small) enriched categories, and the categories of posets and pseudometric spaces.

papers.title: Beyond the Benchmark: Conditioning, Domains and Failure Modes of Qwen3-TTS
papers.abstract: Qwen3-TTS reports state-of-the-art zero-shot voice cloning, but its technical report leaves open how the model should be conditioned, how it behaves outside read speech, and how it fails. We characterise its two cloning interfaces, in-context learning (ICL) and X-Vector, against Chatterbox, XTTS-v2 and F5-TTS on read, meeting, emotional and air-traffic-control (ATC) speech, using eighteen objective measures, an LLM judge, a spoofing countermeasure and a listening test. Neither interface dominates: ICL clones timbre more closely from correctly transcribed references, X-Vector clones timing, and ICL degrades sharply when a short reference transcript is wrong. Domain explains four times more variance than system choice. Qwen3-TTS leads on intelligibility and pitch register but trails on prosody, and the objective measures rank systems differently from listeners. An off-the-shelf countermeasure flags its clones no more often than genuine recordings, and on ATC radio it fails for every system. Code and audio are released.

Since neural codec language models made speaker-conditioned synthesis practical [1], zero-shot voice cloning has become a crowded field of open systems such as XTTS-v2 [2], F5-TTS [3], Chatterbox11 1 github.com/resemble-ai/chatterbox and, most recently, Qwen3-TTS [4], several reporting human parity on read-speech benchmarks [5, 6]. papers.title: Can We Use Saliency Maps for the Evaluation of Generative Image Models?
papers.abstract: Evaluating generative image models remains challenging, as commonly used metrics depend on fixed pretrained feature extractors optimized for different tasks that do not always align with human realism perception across datasets and model families. To address this limitation, we investigate a human-inspired evaluation framework that avoids representations learned for unrelated tasks. Specifically, we train a generator-specific classifier to distinguish real images from samples produced by a given model and analyze its decisions using saliency maps. Across diverse benchmarks, we observe that these classifiers learn generator-specific artifacts rather than a universal notion of "fakeness", exhibiting strong accuracy and limited cross-generator transfer. This makes saliency analysis particularly informative: the resulting attribution maps highlight visual cues and structural irregularities characteristic of each model's outputs. By combining classification accuracy and saliency information, we obtain a composite score aligned with human judgments, without relying on large pretrained backbones and using only real and generated samples from the evaluated model.

papers.intro:
In recent years, generative image models have achieved remarkable progress, producing synthetic images that are often hard to distinguish from real ones [11]. This progress has been driven by several families of generative models, including explicit-likelihood models such as variational autoencoders (VAEs)[45, 16], adversarial models such as GANs [14] and their large-scale variants (e.g., BigGAN [5] and StyleGAN/StyleGAN-XL [25, 38]), as well as diffusion and score-based models (DDPM [18], LDM [37]), which currently provide strong fidelity–coverage trade-offs. Despite these advances, evaluation methodologies have not progressed at the same pace. Ideally, evaluation should rely on human studies, which are, however, expensive, difficult to scale, and sensitive to experimental design, thus motivating research towards the definition of algorithmic evaluation metrics that are aligned with human judgment.

These metrics typically follow a two-stage design: images are first embedded into a feature space using a pretrained neural network, and distances between the distributions of real and generated samples are then computed in that space. While effective and widely adopted, this design makes evaluation strongly dependent on the chosen feature extractor.

With the advent of self-supervised learning (SSL), recent protocols often replace Inception-V3 [43], trained on ImageNet-1k [10], with more general-purpose feature extractors such as DINOv2 [34], SimCLRv2 [8], and CLIP [36]. This shift mitigates known limitations of Inception-based features, as quantified in the benchmark reported in [41], which spans multiple real-image datasets and relies on extensive human evaluations. In that paper, DINOv2 is reported to be the feature extractor that best correlates with human ability to distinguish real from generated images for almost all the aforementioned metrics. At the same time, these results highlight a key limitation: evaluation performance strongly depends on the chosen feature extractor. For instance, using SimCLRv2 features shows almost no correlation with human judgments for all metrics.

Alongside replacing Inception-V3 with large unsupervised or self-supervised models, recent work has questioned FID itself, arguing that its underlying multivariate Gaussian assumption is generally invalid for neural feature representations. Jayasumana et al. [19] address this issue with CMMD, replacing the Fréchet distance with non-parametric maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) and using CLIP rather than DINOv2 for feature extraction. Thus, the choice of feature extractor remains critical, and metric-human correlation strongly depends on it, as we show in the remainder of this paper.

A further potential limitation of these evaluation protocols is that representations learned for classification, SSL, or multimodal alignment are assumed to be suitable for measuring generative realism. Yet, these objectives differ fundamentally from real-versus-fake discrimination [27]. Classification and SSL models are typically trained to be invariant to low-level perturbations (subtle texture inconsistencies, high-frequency artifacts, or minor geometric distortions) so long as semantic identity is preserved. Yet, generative artifacts often appear exactly as such low-level irregularities, meaning that semantically oriented feature spaces may suppress the most informative cues for detecting fakes.

As the goal of generative modeling is often perceptual, i.e., producing images that appear realistic to humans, a key question is how well automatic metrics align with human judgments. To quantify realism directly at the perceptual level, the HYPE benchmark was introduced in [55]. In particular, the HYPE∞ protocol models realism assessment as a two-alternative forced-choice real-vs-fake task: at each trial, a participant is shown either a real image sampled from the training distribution or a generated sample from a specific model, and must decide whether the image is real or fake. Models are then scored by human error rate (HER), defined as the fraction of incorrect judgments. Large-scale benchmarks such as [41] adopt HYPE∞ to evaluate the human-alignment of automatic metrics across datasets and model families, making HER a practical reference signal to assess perceptual realism.

Motivated by the above-mentioned limitations, in this paper we investigate the viability of novel evaluation strategies that do not rely on external feature extractors but remain aligned to human judgment. Borrowing ideas from HYPE∞, where participants are shown an image and must decide whether it is real or fake, we train a generator-specific classifier (GSC) to discriminate real images from those produced by a given model. We then leverage explainable AI (XAI) techniques to analyze the classifier’s behavior and use this analysis for model evaluation. The key intuition is that humans often rely on the presence of visual artifacts that rarely occur in the real world, such as poorly defined contours, unnatural textures, or repetitive patterns [13]. By explicitly identifying and characterizing these cues via explainability methods, our framework provides a general evaluation strategy that more closely mirrors human perceptual judgments. To this end, we rely on saliency-based attribution methods, which provide tools to localize and quantify the evidence used by a model. In particular, Integrated Gradients (IG) [42] is well suited to our setting, as it attributes a model’s prediction to input pixels by integrating gradients along a path from a baseline image to the actual input. More broadly, saliency and explanation methods such as SmoothGrad [40], Grad-CAM [39], LayerCAM [20], XGrad-CAM [12], and SHAP [30] have been widely used to inspect the evidence behind neural-network decisions. In our case, however, saliency maps are not used merely for qualitative visualization: they become part of the evaluation process, as they are used to quantify how strongly and where a GSC detects artifacts in generated images.

papers.title: Think More or Read More? A Token-Budget Theory of Reasoning with Shared Context
papers.abstract: Reasoning systems increasingly improve answers by incorporating additional context into the model's input, from multi-agent debate, where agents read their peers' responses, to self-refinement, where a model revisits its own drafts. In these systems, communication consumes context as one agent's output becomes another's input. We study the regime where token reading and generation draw on one fixed token window, so every token spent reading is a token that cannot be spent reasoning. We develop a \textbf{token-budget theory} that formalizes this trade-off, modeling accuracy as a function of the reasoning budget remaining after reading and aggregating votes with a Condorcet jury model that permits correlated errors. For multi-agent debate, the theory gives a closed-form prediction for the optimal number of agents. This quantity is estimated from single-agent measurements, allowing the optimal group size to be determined without running debate, and the same accounting extends to a heterogeneous set of different models. We empirically verify our theory and show that, at the predicted group size, our method outperforms strong baselines under the tightest calibration spend, where debate-calibrated rules can afford only one or two questions. Self-refinement obeys the same accounting, with its own draft in place of a peer message. The theory further predicts that communication pays only when the gain in the accuracy ceiling exceeds the reasoning room spent on reading, with this condition tightening as the window shrinks. Across five open models and four reasoning tasks, self-consistency matches or beats deployed debate at $93$\% of $980$ matched window-and-group-size settings, with the gap being largest under tight windows and nearly disappearing at a loose one, consistent with the theory. Under a shared window, how much room a model has left to \textit{think matters more than what it reads}.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in reasoning pipelines that reuse model-generated text as input to subsequent computation. Multi-agent debate exchanges answers among agents (Du et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2024), while self-refinement feeds a model its own previous drafts (Madaan et al., 2023). Such reuse can improve reasoning by providing additional information, but under a fixed token budget, it also raises a fundamental question: not whether added feedback helps, but how much it is worth in terms of the reasoning budget it consumes.

Majority-voting analyses predict that adding agents amplifies a correct majority until correlated errors cap the gain (Ladha, 1992; Liu et al., 2026). However, on multi-hop reasoning tasks, a single long chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022) often matches or outperforms a multi-agent system under an equal thinking budget (Tran and Kiela, 2026). Debate also does not consistently outperform self-consistency on an accuracy-per-token-cost frontier (Smit et al., 2024; Bertalanic and Fortuna, 2026), echoing the broader trade-off between token expenditure and accuracy in sampling and search (Snell et al., 2025; Brown et al., 2024). The token budget deserves separate attention because it corresponds directly to the cost incurred in practice. At current API prices, inference can range from cents to tens of dollars per million tokens, depending on the model and provider (OpenAI, 2026; Google, 2026; Anthropic, 2026). For multi-agent debate, the cost grows further with the number of agents nn (group size): adding agents increases not only the amount of reasoning generated, but also the amount of peer text that must be read and processed. Existing work attacks this cost either by compressing agent communication or by fixing the reasoning budget, but treats communication and reasoning as separate costs, despite both consuming the same token budget (§\lx@sectionsign2). Once the token budget is viewed this way, a trade-off appears: with nn small, more of the budget remains for thinking, while with nn large, most of it is spent on reading peer messages, leaving little room to reason. The question is then how to estimate the best group size n∗n^{\ast} for multi-agent debate under this trade-off. Existing approaches measure nn by sweeping or adaptively searching the design space, for instance, successive halving (Jamieson and Talwalkar, 2016). Both require debate runs to identify the operating point, without explaining why one group size is optimal or when adding more agents stops improving accuracy.

Our model yields a closed-form prediction of an interior optimal group size n∗n^{\ast} that moves with the budget. It is read off single-agent measurements: we measure the ability curve with a cap sweep and estimate one error-correlation parameter at the initial round, then predict group size without running the debate. With a sufficiently large budget, our predictions approach the classical correlation-limited ensemble, where the main benefit comes from aggregating independent evidence. The practical advantage of our approach is therefore greatest in the tight-budget regime, where choosing the group size correctly matters most and our method achieves the best accuracy-budget trade-off. At the predicted size, it incurs only a 1.4%1.4\% accuracy gap from a per-cell oracle, using between 2626 and 7979 calibration questions depending on the cell, where the debate-calibrated rules use only one or two at matched spend. The accounting extends to a heterogeneous model set, where the rule chooses which models to include as well as how many.

Our framework also clarifies the cost of communication relative to self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023). Self-consistency leaves the full window available for reasoning, whereas debate spends part of that budget processing peer responses, so communication must provide sufficient informational benefit to justify this cost. In our experiments, self-consistency matches or beats deployed debate at 93%93\% of the 980980 matched operating points, while a paired test finds debate significantly ahead at only 0.5%0.5\%. The gap is largest under tight budgets and nearly disappears at a loose budget, where communication consumes a smaller share of the available reasoning budget. Self-refinement, which rereads only its own last draft without voting, pays the same fixed reading cost every round with none of the amplification that voting provides, so its accuracy collapses faster than debate’s as rounds accumulate.

papers.title: Identifiability from Moments in Independent Component Analysis Mixture Models
papers.abstract: We study Independent Component Analysis (ICA) mixture models. These models consist of mixtures of ICA densities. An ICA density is associated with a random vector whose coordinates become mutually independent after an invertible linear transformation. ICA mixture models are nonparametric extensions of the celebrated family of Gaussian mixtures. We show that in many cases the ICA mixtures are identifiable from the collection of the observed moment tensors, that is, the mixing coefficients, linear transformations, and source moments of order up to $d$ can be identified from the moment tensors of order up to $d$ for generic parameters. We address the problem by studying the corresponding secant varieties and their algebraic properties such as dimensions and Gauss maps. In particular, for $n$-variate distributions, we establish that generically and up to the trivial scaling and permutation symmetries, when $d\geq 5$, the parameters can be recovered uniquely for asymptotically up to $n^{d-2}/d!$ mixture components. For $d=3,4$, we show identifiability up to a finite equivalence class for asymptotically up to $n^{d-2}/d!$ and $0.5 n^{d-2}/d!$ components respectively, where for $d=4$ the mixing coefficients need to be known a priori. The obtained bounds on the component numbers have the maximum possible orders in $n$, and for $d = 3$ and $d\geq 5$, they are also asymptotically sharp.

papers.intro:
Density estimation is a fundamental problem in statistics with applications in various fields such as machine learning, economics, and genetics [silverman1998density, WangScott2019, DiNardo1996, Segal2001ClusteringOT]. Given independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) samples generated according to an unknown probability distribution, the goal is to estimate this distribution by leveraging the observed samples. To this end, one considers a statistical model, i.e. a family of candidate probability distributions that is believed to contain the true distribution, and seeks the best estimate of the true unknown distribution (or its density function) within this model.

Given independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) samples generated according to an unknown probability distribution, the goal is to estimate this distribution by leveraging the observed samples. To this end, one considers a statistical model, i.e. a family of candidate probability distributions that is believed to contain the true distribution, and seeks the best estimate of the true unknown distribution (or its density function) within this model.

A celebrated statistical model for density estimation is the family of Gaussian mixtures. A Gaussian mm-mixture is a convex combination of mm (possibly different) Gaussian density functions. Gaussian mixtures have been shown to estimate any sufficiently smooth density function [scott1992multivariate], and have received extensive attention, due to their applications in areas such as speech recognition [ZhangAlder1994], geographic modeling [Zhou2020], and modeling the COVID-19 pandemic [SINGHAL2020110023]. In particular, the identifiability of the defining parameters of a Gaussian mixture – namely, its mixing coefficients and the means and covariance matrices of its components – from its moments has been studied from an algebraic viewpoint in [amendola2016moment, amendola2018, Lindberg2025].
