papers.title: In Human Memories. Technology, Creativity and Self-Determination: An Ethical Proposal
papers.abstract: This research investigates the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in modern compositional practices, with a particular focus on two case studies: Convergence (2020/21) by Alexander Schubert, for String Ensemble and AI System, and In Human Memories (2024) by Francesco Vitucci, for four cellos and one electroacoustic player, whose installation was created by the Electronic Music School of the "N. Piccinni" Conservatory of Bari. The initial historical survey traces the evolving use of technology in composition, revealing how the search for new expressive possibilities has driven the development of technological tools through experimentation. The appearance of AI marks a fundamental shift: no longer just a tool, AI now poses questions and challenges to the composer. Engaging with AI becomes an exploration of an unknown entity, whose full capabilities are still largely undiscovered. This new interaction leads composers to confront AI not merely as a passive resource but as a participant in the creative process, outlining an ethical path to reclaim technology as a creative tool. In Human Memories reflects this dynamic, demonstrating how AI can serve as both inspiration and a driving force in shaping contemporary music.

Over the past few decades, artificial intelligence (AI) has ceased to be mere science-fiction speculation and has become a concrete and increasingly pervasive reality in everyday human life. From virtual assistants that answer questions to algorithms that suggest what to watch, read or buy, AI has taken its place alongside human beings, becoming a more or less discreet, yet extraordinarily influential presence in many spheres of contemporary existence.

Paradoxically, from an inclusive perspective, one could speak of ‘integration’ if human beings were able, with full awareness, to distinguish their own way of tackling a given problem from a strategy devised by AI. This ability is becoming increasingly rare, since most AI systems are of the reproductive type,11 1 Cf. Floridi L., La quarta rivoluzione: come l’infosfera sta trasformando il mondo, Raffaello Cortina Editore, Milan 2017. that is, they aim to reproduce human behaviors more quickly, efficiently and effectively. Rather than of integration, in many cases it is more appropriate to speak of ‘substitution’, acknowledging AI’s greater problem-solving capacity, which stems from its enormous computational power. It should be made clear that what is being introduced here is an objective observation about AI. It is a tool that is beginning to unfold its benefits and dangers, just like many other artificial tools (and today no one would dream of “blaming cars for our obesity”22 2 Ibid. The ongoing substitution initially concerned fields such as industrial automation and data management, where the ability to index and process large amounts of information (big data) in extremely short times represented a genuine revolution. However, as technology progressed, AI began to extend its influence into areas that until recently seemed the exclusive preserve of human intellect and sensibility, among them artistic creativity. Art, in all its forms, is traditionally seen as one of the highest expressions of the human mind, a territory in which intuition, imagination, technique and emotion work together to shape works that implicitly pursue one goal: to achieve an understanding, an intelligibility, capable of withstanding time and cultures. The involvement of AI in this domain has sparked considerable debate and controversy, raising fundamental and far from trivial questions about what it means to create and what distinguishes a machine from an artist. The AI question, however, introduces elements of discontinuity: technology, once sought out to serve a creative need, now manifests itself through artificial intelligence as an entity with which the composer comes into contact, in a dialogue whose potential is constantly evolving.

The conscious use of technology, however, is something quite different from its superficial use. The process of digital democratization set in motion by the introduction of the personal computer can be observed from multiple social perspectives, but unconditional access to data-processing tools affects an ever-wider audience of users. This openness has generated a new category of prosumer users, “who ‘produce’ only by consuming tailor-made services and devices”.33 3 Di Scipio A., Circuiti del tempo: Un percorso storico-critico nella creatività musicale elettroacustica e informatica, Libreria Musicale Italiana, Lucca 2021, p. 560 (translation by the authors). Just as the inner workings of a smartphone are unknown to most people, ready-made tools have also taken root in the creative use of technology, giving more prominence to the packaging of a ‘product’ than to the understanding of the underlying ‘process’ – a long-standing dilemma tied to the separation of competences, summarized below.

Starting in the 1970s, some research institutes opened their doors to composers, giving them the opportunity to use the newly developed technologies. Since the composer in residence had, in most cases, followed a traditional course of study and had approached technology out of sheer curiosity, some form of support from an expert collaborator was required. Initially, this professional figure was meant to instruct the composer on the sonic possibilities of the new instruments and to assist with the more technical processes, opening up architectures that would otherwise be difficult to understand. A strong idea began to take hold: the premiere as an “action collective”,44 4 Menger P. M., Les Laboratoires de la création musicale, La Documentation française, Paris 1989, p. 129. the outcome of a collaboration among professionals with different competences. From its earliest years of activity, the French institute IRCAM (Institut de Recherche et Coordination Acoustique/Musique) seems to have formalized the specific role of this collaborator, whose title changed several times between the 1970s and the turn of the millennium before acquiring its current one of RIM, that is, Réalisateur en Informatique Musicale.55 5 Cf. Zattra L., Les origines du nom de RIM (Réalisateur en informatique musicale), “JIM – Journées d’Informatique Musicale”, Saint-Denis, Paris 2013, pp. 113-120. Pierre Boulez’s question of 2001, perhaps a rhetorical one, is well known: “Le compositeur est-il suffisamment avancé pour ne plus avoir besoin d’assistants?”. The various announcements of currently open RIM positions at IRCAM offer an implicit but eloquent institutional answer.

papers.title: How bright can a galaxy be? Extreme value predictions for high-redshift survey observables
papers.abstract: Assessing the significance of extreme galaxy candidates has typically relied on redshifts and stellar / halo masses inferred through inverse modelling, which carries substantial systematic uncertainty. We combine the halo mass function with a conditional model for galaxy emission and apply the Extreme Value Statistics (EVS) formalism to predict the distribution of the observed flux of the brightest galaxy expected in a given survey area, redshift interval and photometric band. We find the choice of parametric star formation history (SFH) dominates the modelling uncertainty, introducing a spread approaching $\sim 1 \, \mathrm{dex}$ by $z \sim 18$, whilst the stellar population synthesis model, initial mass function and metallicity each contribute $\lesssim 0.3 \, \mathrm{dex}$. The luminous $z \gtrsim 9$ candidates in COSMOS-Web cluster about the median prediction for the area they were drawn from, and lie at least an order of magnitude below the $3σ$ limit, a margin comparable to the SFH systematic. Of the observational samples reaching beyond $z \sim 13$, the two spectroscopically confirmed galaxies at $z \simeq 14$ lie close to the median prediction for their area, whereas photometric candidates at $z \gtrsim 16$ reach $+4σ$ (a probability to exceed of $\sim 10^{-5}$), the brightest lying at the limit obtained by converting all halo baryons into stars. Since the prediction bounds the flux far more tightly than the photometry bounds the redshift, such offsets are most naturally resolved by errors in the inferred redshifts. This approach allows extreme candidates to be assessed directly in the observational plane, making explicit the modelling assumptions common to forward and inverse approaches.

JWST has revealed a range of unexpected and exciting galaxy populations, including a number of extremely bright galaxy candidates at very high redshifts (Finkelstein et al., 2022; Naidu et al., 2022; Castellano et al., 2023; Castellano et al., 2025; Labbé et al., 2023; Casey et al., 2024; Robertson et al., 2024; Pérez-González et al., 2025; McLeod et al., 2026). The abundance of luminous sources at z≳10z\gtrsim 10 exceeds the extrapolation of pre-JWST ultraviolet luminosity functions, and the bright end evolves more slowly with redshift than had been anticipated (Donnan et al., 2023; Harikane et al., 2023; Wilkins et al., 2023; Chworowsky et al., 2024; Whitler et al., 2025). Inverse modelling through SED fitting initially suggested that many of these sources had redshifts and stellar masses that were in tension with our models of astrophysics and, in the most extreme cases, the concordance cosmological model itself (Lovell et al., 2023; Boylan-Kolchin, 2023).

Inverse modelling through SED fitting initially suggested that many of these sources had redshifts and stellar masses that were in tension with our models of astrophysics and, in the most extreme cases, the concordance cosmological model itself (Lovell et al., 2023; Boylan-Kolchin, 2023).

Since then, updates to the data calibration and improvements to the modelling procedure have reduced this tension somewhat (Mason et al., 2023; Yung et al., 2024). Spectroscopic follow-up has shown a number of the most extreme photometric candidates to be lower-redshift dusty or evolved interlopers, brown dwarfs, or AGN/LRD candidates (Zavala et al., 2023; Arrabal Haro et al., 2023; Hainline et al., 2026; Bradač et al., 2026), and re-analyses including longer-wavelength constraints typically recovered lower stellar masses than were first reported (Desprez et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Lapasia et al., 2026). A number of astrophysical explanations have also been proposed that accommodate the observed abundances within Λ\LambdaCDM, including feedback-free or otherwise highly efficient starbursts (Dekel et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Somerville et al., 2025), bursty star formation and the associated stochastic variability in the UV luminosity (Sun et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2023; Gelli et al., 2024), reduced dust attenuation in early, compact systems (Ferrara, 2024), and a contribution to the continuum from accreting black holes (Hegde et al., 2024). Whether any tension remains is therefore, to a large degree, a question about the chain of modelling assumptions connecting an observed flux to a dark matter halo mass, and any uncertainties on the redshift estimate.

Rather than asking whether the abundance of an entire population is consistent with a model, EVS gives the full probability distribution of the single most extreme object expected in a given sample (Gumbel, 1958; Katz & Nadarajah, 2000). This makes it well suited to assessing individual record-breaking objects, since a single object detection in excess of the prediction is, in principle, falsifying. The approach has been applied extensively to the most massive galaxy clusters (Davis et al., 2011; Harrison & Coles, 2011; Harrison & Coles, 2012; Holz & Perlmutter, 2012; Waizmann et al., 2012), and more recently to the most massive and most luminous galaxies at high redshift (Lovell et al., 2023; Heather et al., 2024; Enríquez-Vargas et al., 2026).

By assuming a form for the halo mass function, a cosmic baryon fraction and stellar fraction we placed both upper and lower limits on the most extreme mass halo and galaxy. Jespersen et al. (2025a) showed the impact of cosmic variance on these predictions from pencil beam / small area surveys, showing that for a single JWST pointing the median predicted mass can drop by over 1 dex at z>5z>5. The same clustering that drives this variance also implies that the most extreme sources are preferentially found in overdense, protocluster-like environments (Castellano et al., 2023, e.g.), so that conditioning the prediction on the observed density of the field in which a candidate is found can substantially modify its inferred significance (Jespersen et al., 2025b). However, all of these studies use stellar and halo masses inferred through inverse modelling, typically through spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting of the multi-wavelength electromagnetic emission of individual galaxies from photometric and, in more limited cases, spectroscopic data. Inverse modelling necessitates many assumptions that can impact the derived properties to varying degrees (Conroy, 2013; Leja et al., 2017; Iyer et al., 2026). These include the details of the source populations, such as the assumed initial mass function (IMF), and the stellar metallicity, as well as properties of intervening attenuating matter such as nebular gas and dust in the interstellar medium. There are often strong degeneracies between the parameters describing these properties, leading to large uncertainties on their derived properties (Robotham & Bellstedt, 2025; Bellstedt & Robotham, 2025). At high redshift these issues are particularly acute: the templates and priors adopted are calibrated on lower-redshift populations (Steinhardt et al., 2023), and young, luminous stellar populations can outshine older stars, biasing the recovered stellar masses (Tacchella et al., 2022; Narayanan et al., 2024; Harvey et al., 2025). Different codes and parameter choices applied to the same photometry can therefore return masses differing by an order of magnitude, which directly affects any statement of tension.

papers.title: Low-Cost Third-order Algebraic Diagrammatic Construction Method for Excited States Using Tensor Hypercontraction and State-Specific Frozen Natural Orbitals
papers.abstract: We have developed a reduced-cost framework for excited-state calculations by combining the state-specific frozen natural orbital (SS-FNO) approach with the third-order algebraic diagrammatic construction [ADC(3)] method and tensor hypercontraction (THC). This strategy enables a systematic and controllable truncation of the virtual orbital space, while significantly lowering the computational scaling through the THC representation of the electron repulsion integrals. The method allows black-box application via adjustable thresholds and includes a perturbative correction that compensates for the truncation error. We have used the CIS(D) method to generate the natural orbitals for the excited states. The performance of the SS-FNO-THC-ADC(3) method is assessed for valence, Rydberg, and charge-transfer excitations. Benchmark calculations demonstrate that the combined approach achieves excellent agreement with the canonical ADC(3) results. The efficiency of the present implementation is demonstrated by calculating the excitation energy of a molecule containing 31 atoms and more than one thousand basis functions.

papers.title: Anti-synchronized collective rotation in magnetic colloidal particles under rotating magnetic fields
papers.abstract: Collective synchronization is a common response of interacting magnetic particles subjected to rotating external fields. Here we demonstrate a distinct nonequilibrium state in a two-dimensional cluster of magnetic colloidal particles in which the ordered crystalline core rotates, on average, opposite to the direction of the applied rotating magnetic field, while the defect-rich outer region continues to rotate with the drive. We term this state anti-synchronized collective rotation. By combining structural, spectral, bond-resolved, and layer-resolved torque analyses, we show that anti-synchronization is associated with a broader defect-rich interface, enhanced and dynamically heterogeneous bond deformation, and a reorganization of torque transmission between the surface and the crystalline interior. In the synchronized state, steric torques compensate the opposing dipolar contribution in the outer core, maintaining a positive net interaction torque. In the anti-synchronized state this compensation becomes insufficient, producing a negative net torque in theouter core and enabling core-surface rotational decoupling. Increasing the driving frequency restores coherent rotation through a transition characterized by competing positive- and negative-angular-velocity populations and hysteresis, consistent with a discontinuous, first-order-like dynamical transition. These results demonstrate how deformation and spatial redistribution of interaction torques can generate counter-rotating collective states in driven colloidal matter.

papers.intro:
Driven many-body systems provide a broad framework for understanding the emergence of collective behavior in interacting systems maintained away from thermodynamic equilibrium by external forcing. Periodic driving, in particular, can give rise to a rich variety of dynamical phenomena, including synchronization [1, 2, 3], pattern formation [4, 5], dynamical self-assembly and collective motion [6, 7, 8], and transitions between distinct nonequilibrium states [9, 10, 11]. Soft-matter systems provide particularly suitable platforms for investigating such phenomena because their mesoscopic constituents and relatively weak interaction energies allow their structures and dynamics to be readily modified by external perturbations and thermal fluctuations. Colloidal suspensions, in particular, can be driven away from equilibrium through externally imposed mechanical forcing [12] or particle-level self-propulsion [13], leading to a wide range of collective responses. One prominent example is lane formation in mixtures of oppositely driven colloidal particles, which has been observed in Brownian dynamics simulations of both two- and three-dimensional systems [14, 15]. Similar behavior, including local lane formation, has been reported experimentally in oppositely charged colloidal suspensions subjected to steady [16, 17] and alternating electric fields [18]. Beyond lane formation, Reichhardt et al. [19] demonstrated the emergence of moving clump and stripe phases in driven colloidal systems with competing short-range attractive and long-range repulsive interactions on disordered substrates. These examples illustrate how the interplay between external driving, interparticle interactions, and structural rearrangements can generate diverse collective states and interesting dynamical phenomena.

Among externally driven soft-matter systems, magnetic colloidal suspensions provide a versatile platform for investigating nonequilibrium collective dynamics, as their structural organization and dynamical response can be controlled through the strength, frequency, and orientation of applied magnetic fields. These systems have attracted sustained interest over several decades owing to their rich structural and dynamical behavior. A prominent class of magnetoresponsive soft materials is ferrofluids, consisting of magnetic nanoparticles dispersed in a liquid carrier [20, 21]. The application of external magnetic fields can substantially modify their structural and rheological properties by promoting the formation and reorganization of particle aggregates. Owing to the anisotropic nature of dipole–dipole interactions, magnetic particles can assemble into a variety of structures, including linear chains, rings, and branched networks [22, 23, 24]. Beyond static or quasistatic field-induced assembly, time-dependent magnetic fields provide an additional means of controlling particle organization and motion. In particular, rotating magnetic fields can induce dynamical self-assembly, structural reorganization, and collective rotational dynamics through the competition between magnetic interactions, viscous dissipation, and the timescale of external forcing. Early studies by Kopelman and coworkers demonstrated that individual magnetic colloids can rotate synchronously with a rotating field at sufficiently low driving frequencies, whereas above a characteristic threshold, viscous resistance prevents sustained frequency locking [25]. Extending this picture to interacting particles, Tierno investigated the dynamics of dipolarly coupled colloidal rotators, demonstrating how magnetic interactions give rise to coupled rotational responses, including synchronization and beating phenomena [26]. Jäger and coworkers showed through computer simulations that the loss of single-particle synchronization can be accompanied by a collective structural transition from a layered to a disordered state [27]. The connection between synchronization and structural organization was further demonstrated experimentally by Yan and coworkers, who investigated the self-assembly of magnetic Janus colloids under rotating magnetic fields [28]. Subsequently, Yan, Bae, and Granick demonstrated the formation of rotating colloidal crystals exhibiting structural rearrangements, dislocations, and mobile domain boundaries, highlighting the importance of internal deformation in the dynamics of field-driven colloidal assemblies [29]. The role of hydrodynamic interactions, particularly the coupling between rotational and translational motion mediated by the surrounding fluid, has also been investigated theoretically and computationally [31]. These studies highlight the close connection between magnetic synchronization, collective structural organization, and internal particle rearrangements, raising the broader question of how the rotational response of a deformable colloidal assembly is determined by the interplay between external forcing and interparticle interactions.

While the synchronization of individual magnetic moments with an external rotating field has been extensively investigated[27], the collective rotational dynamics of interacting magnetic colloids involve additional degrees of freedom arising from their internal structure and interparticle interactions. In contrast to the rotation of individual magnetic moments, the orbital motion of particles within a colloidal assembly is governed by the interaction forces transmitted through the particle network, which may undergo continuous deformation and structural rearrangement under periodic forcing[29]. An important issue, therefore, is to understand whether the interplay between magnetic interactions, internal deformation, and spatially heterogeneous force transmission can give rise to collective rotational motion opposite to the direction of the applied field.

papers.title: Asymptotic dimension of graphs excluding an induced or fat minor
papers.abstract: Asymptotic dimension is a large-scale invariant of metric spaces that was introduced by Gromov (1993). A major open problem in coarse graph theory asks whether, for every fixed graph $H$, the class of graphs excluding $H$ as a fat minor has bounded asymptotic dimension. A weaker conjecture asserts the same conclusion for graphs excluding $H$ as an induced minor. We substantially expand the range of graphs $H$ for which these conjectures are known to hold. Specifically, we prove bounded asymptotic dimension for the following classes of graphs: graphs excluding a fixed planar graph as a fat minor; and graphs excluding a fixed string graph as an induced minor. All of our results also hold for the stronger notion of Assouad--Nagata dimension, a refinement of asymptotic dimension. These results have a number of applications, two of which we mention here. First they imply that an induced minor-closed class is $χ$-bounded if and only if it does not contain some Burling graph. Second they imply that, in graph classes excluding a fixed planar graph as an induced minor, treewidth is polynomial in maximum degree.

papers.intro:
Every connected graph, finite or infinite, forms a metric space when equipped with the shortest-path metric. This enables the study of metric properties of graphs. For instance, in geometric group theory, the programme established by Gromov [Gro93] postulates the study of finitely generated groups at “large scale” through metric properties of their Cayley graphs. A large-scale metric property should be invariant under quasi-isometries, that is, mappings that preserve metric spaces up to bounded multiplicative and additive distortion. For Cayley graphs, in particular, this guarantees that the property is not influenced by the choice of a finite generating set for the group. An emerging branch of graph theory known as coarse graph theory, popularized mostly by Georgakopoulos and Papasoglu [GP25], aims at providing large-scale analogues of concepts and results from structural graph theory with a motivation of making them potentially useful for applications in geometric group theory and coarse geometry.

Asymptotic dimension is a central quasi-isometry invariant introduced by Gromov [Gro93] as part of the above-mentioned programme. Intuitively, it captures the dimensionality of a metric space when viewed from a large distance, ignoring local details. See [BD08] for a survey of its role in geometric group theory. For graph classes or infinite graphs, it is often considered as a large-scale analogue of chromatic number.

Understanding how asymptotic dimension interacts with structural graph theory is one of the defining themes of coarse graph theory [BBE+24, Dis26, Liu25, Pap23, DN22, Hic25]. A landmark result of Bonamy, Bousquet, Esperet, Groenland, Liu, Pirot, and Scott [BBE+24] asserts that every proper minor-closed graph class has asymptotic dimension at most 22, and at most 11 if it excludes a planar graph. In proving this result, Bonamy et al. A recurring feature of these proofs is that they first establish a quasi-isometric structure theorem for the corresponding class of fat-minor-free graphs, reducing the problem to the well-understood setting of minor-closed graph classes. However, recent work of Davies, Hickingbotham, Illingworth, and McCarty [DHIM26] and of Albrechtsen and Davies [AD25] demonstrates that such quasi-isometric structure theorems fail in general, even when the excluded fat minor is planar. Consequently, this approach cannot be extended to prove Theorem 1.2, and our proof requires fundamentally different techniques.

Our second main result concerns induced minors. A graph HH is an induced minor of a graph GG if it can be obtained from GG by deleting vertices and contracting edges. Induced minors interpolate between minors and fat minors. For hereditary graph classes, excluding a graph HH as a fat minor is essentially equivalent to excluding a subdivision of HH as an induced minor [Hic25]. papers.title: Two-generator presentations with a relation gap
papers.abstract: We exhibit two-generator two-relator group presentations that have cyclic relation modules but do not present one-relator groups; this resolves the relation gap problem. By attaching a single 3-cell to each of the corresponding presentation 2-complexes, one obtains counterexamples to Wall's D2 problem.

papers.title: Do Knowledge and Reasoning Oriented Benchmarks Induce Stable Representation Signatures in LLMs?
papers.abstract: Internal signatures could support monitoring, adaptive computation, and mechanistic analysis, but benchmark prompts can be separable without any shared computational distinction. We test whether a prespecified knowledge/reasoning label defines a reusable internal signature in five contemporary 7B to 31B models. We treat the \textbf{task} as the unit of inference probes hold out complete tasks, labels are permuted across tasks, and the best layer and stream are reselected for every permutation. Raw probes recover an eight-versus-eight-subject MMLU partition in all five models (macro-F1 $0.78$--$0.81$), but prompt text predicts it nearly as well: under an identical probe configuration, the activation advantage is only $0.017$--$0.070$ macro-F1 and is not significant. At the prespecified $0.01$ level, lexical adjustment removes significance while the adjusted states still identify individual subjects, and the selected site changes across task panels and selection rules. Additionally, two released base-training trajectories show no common direction. These pooled layerwise measures recover the task label but identify no transferable knowledge/reasoning signature at the tested sensitivity, which cannot exclude moderate effects. The resulting protocol gives future internal monitors and intervention studies a sequence of tests to pass. Project page: \url{https://parsa-ra.github.io/lmbehave/}.

Decoding a label is not sufficient, however: a model can encode task identity, vocabulary, and format without implementing one shared knowledge or reasoning computation (Hewitt and Liang, 2019; Belinkov, 2022; Kumar et al., 2022; Sahoo et al., 2026).

Behavioral evaluation, observational decoding, and intervention answer distinct questions: they measure outputs, recoverable information, and output sensitivity under manipulation, respectively (Hewitt and Liang, 2019; Belinkov, 2022; Meng et al., 2022; Conmy et al., 2023). Latent-state methods can recover propositions or deployment-relevant labels (Burns et al., 2023; Feng et al., 2025; McKenzie et al., 2025), while probes can also learn dataset regularities (Pimentel et al., 2020). Sahoo et al. (2026) show that format controls weaken a reasoning-mode probe, and they add a causal steering experiment. We test a different binary partition without reproducing their intervention, and we add task-level exchangeability, exhaustive permutation, selection-aware depth inference, five contemporary checkpoints, and two training trajectories. Concurrent contamination-probing work likewise emphasizes nuisance-matched baselines and detection calibration (Braun, 2026).

Task and function vectors make raw task separation plausible (Hendel et al., 2023; Todd et al., 2024). Our narrower question is whether these task differences align with one transferable knowledge/reasoning direction. Intervention studies report shallower dependence for knowledge retrieval and deeper dependence for reasoning (Song et al., 2026), or selective recall-versus-reasoning effects on controlled puzzles (Fartale et al., 2025). These task-specific causal findings motivate our test, but they neither imply nor require a benchmark-independent passive signature. Causal tracing restores a clean hidden state in a corrupted run and measures output recovery; activation patching substitutes a component state between paired runs and measures the output change (Meng et al., 2022; Conmy et al., 2023). Our passive measurements instead generate hypotheses for such interventions.

papers.title: The START mission: Probing the 2029 Apophis Flyby via a Low-Cost Geocentric SmallSat
papers.abstract: The Student-led Threatening Asteroid Reconnaissance of Tsinghua (START) marks the inaugural mission of the Tianxing Program, a deep-space exploration initiative led by students at Tsinghua University. Conceived as a low-cost, rapid-response small-satellite mission, START will investigate the near-Earth asteroid (99942) Apophis during its close approach to Earth in April 2029, when significant terrestrial tidal forces will offer a rare opportunity to observe the physical and dynamical response of a rubble-pile asteroid in real time. The 300 kg spacecraft is scheduled for rideshare launch into low Earth orbit in early 2028 and will then use solar electric propulsion to transfer to a circular mission orbit with a semimajor axis of approximately 38,000 km and an inclination of 55 degrees. START will execute a high-speed flyby of Apophis from a closest distance of 7 km at the asteroid's closest approach to Earth, to capture its tidal response. The payload suite consists of a high-resolution narrow-field camera, a wide-field navigation camera, and three near-infrared multispectral imagers. By acquiring centimeter-scale imagery and meter-scale reflectance spectra, the mission will characterize the asteroid's surface morphology and composition and monitor immediate tidally induced surface modifications. Ultimately, START will provide geometrically complementary, high-cadence datasets to international flagship missions to Apophis, demonstrating a highly scalable and cost-effective architecture for future planetary defense and small-body exploration.

papers.intro:
The near-Earth asteroid (99942) Apophis is currently the focus of unprecedented international scrutiny owing to its exceptionally rare Earth close approach (ECA) on April 13, 2029 [29]. During this event, the ∼\sim340 m340\text{\,}\mathrm{m} diameter stony asteroid will pass within 31 600 km31\,600\text{\,}\mathrm{km} of the Earth’s surface—a distance closer than geostationary orbit. Such a deep penetration into Earth’s gravitational tidal field by an object of this size is a once-in-a-millennium event [8], making Apophis visible to the naked eye for approximately two billion people in parts of Europe, Africa and Western Asia. This historic proximity serves as a powerful catalyst for global public engagement and has led the United Nations to declare 2029 the International Year of Asteroid Awareness and Planetary Defence [42]. For the scientific community, this encounter represents more than a standard reconnaissance opportunity; while previous small-body missions have typically characterized asteroids as static, evolved remnants of the early solar system, the 2029 ECA provides the first-ever opportunity to witness active planetary evolution in real time. By observing this natural experiment, we can transition from analyzing the fossilized results of past processes to directly monitoring the immediate physical and dynamical responses of a rubble-pile body to terrestrial tidal forces. The anticipated tidal torques are expected to induce measurable changes in Apophis’s spin state and orientation, potentially triggering localized surface resurfacing, mass wasting, and seismic activity [22, 64, 35, 5]. Capturing these ongoing transitions will yield an unprecedented scientific output, offering deep insights into the geotechnical properties of potentially hazardous asteroids and clues to their internal structure.

Recognizing this opportunity, the international space community has mobilized a fleet of missions to characterize Apophis across different temporal and spatial scales. The European Space Agency (ESA) is developing the Rapid Apophis Mission for Space Safety (RAMSES), which aims to rendezvous with the asteroid in early 2029—approximately two months before ECA—to conduct a comprehensive “before-and-after” survey [36]. Following the encounter, NASA’s OSIRIS-APEX will rendezvous with Apophis to investigate its post-encounter state and conduct active surface-disturbance experiments [21]. Furthermore, JAXA’s DESTINY+ mission, en route to 3200 Phaethon, is planned to perform a high-speed flyby of Apophis in early 2029, potentially providing the first close-up images to aid the subsequent rendezvous operations [2]. Additional reconnaissance efforts are being explored through NASA’s Request for Information to repurpose the Janus spacecraft for a pre-encounter flyby [54, 55, 10], as well as a growing number of innovative SmallSat concepts such as MIT Project Apophis [9, 1], Caltech’s mission concept [20], Argotec’s ATENA [52], Milo Institute’s Apophis Pathfinder [6], and Apophis Recon Swarm [63].

Unlike traditional asteroid missions that require multi-year deep-space cruise phases and high departure energies, Apophis’s trajectory carries it deep into Earth’s gravity well. This provides a unique window for a minimalist flyby architecture, where a spacecraft can be deployed from Earth-orbiting platforms—such as low Earth orbit (LEO) or geostationary transfer orbit (GTO)—and reach the target within months using modest propulsion systems. This “Earth-vicinity” accessibility effectively lowers the barriers to deep-space exploration, enabling rapid-response mission designs that were previously cost-prohibitive.

Leveraging this window, we propose the Student-led Threatening Asteroid Reconnaissance of Tsinghua (START), a low-cost, rapid-response flyby mission. As the inaugural mission of the Tianxing Program, it is being developed by Tsinghua University in collaboration with the Deep Space Exploration Laboratory and commercial space partners. START is designed to demonstrate a scalable and repeatable model for planetary defense and space exploration. Operating within a budget of approximately 30 million RMB (∼\sim 4.54.5 million USD) and supported by private investment, the mission utilizes a 300 kg300\text{\,}\mathrm{kg} small satellite platform launched as a secondary payload into low Earth orbit in early 2028. START will use solar electric propulsion (SEP) to reach its mission orbit and then perform a high-speed flyby of Apophis near ECA to investigate surface responses under strong terrestrial tidal forcing. The nominal distance at START–Apophis closest approach (CA) is 7 km7\text{\,}\mathrm{km}, balancing imaging performance with operational separation from RAMSES spacecraft (Section IV.1). To achieve high-resolution staring imaging, these payloads are mounted on a two-axis, high-speed tracking mechanism featuring wide-range pointing and closed-loop tracking capabilities. Guided by an integrated data processor, the system utilizes real-time measurement data from the instruments to compute relative line-of-sight kinematics. This enables the tracking mechanism to stably track Apophis during the close-proximity flyby, effectively compensating for the extreme relative velocity, angular velocity, and angular acceleration. These high-cadence observations are specifically designed to characterize the asteroid’s immediate physical and dynamical transitions—such as localized mass flow and spectral change—providing critical constraints on regolith cohesion and evolutionary pathways of rubble-pile near-Earth asteroids while complementing international flagship missions through a distinct observing geometry.

papers.title: GRASP: Global-Local Representation Alignment and Spatial-Physical Grounding for Bimanual Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that directly regress joint-space actions avoid the deployment-time cost of inverse kinematics. However, their training objectives remain misaligned with task success, as joint-space losses ignore the unequal physical consequences of joint errors and visual conditioning lacks explicit focus on hand-object interaction regions. To address these issues, we propose a training-phase prior injection framework for fine-grained bimanual manipulation. First, a physics-grounded flow-matching loss maps the implicit clean-action estimate at every noise level through differentiable forward kinematics (FK) and supervises the resulting Tool Center Point (TCP) pose and inter-arm relative pose, with a bounded noise-level weighting that compensates gradient decay. Second, we introduce a global prediction query group distilled from a frozen DINOv3 teacher through future-frame feature prediction, together with a local interaction query supervised by Grounding DINO at the attention level. Both teachers are removed at inference, and the deployment pipeline is that of a standard joint-space flow policy, adding only the learned query pathway. Simulation and real-robot experiments on long-horizon bimanual tasks show that the two priors are complementary across different deployment settings. The full model excels in in-distribution deployment, while the distilled query branch is preferable under strong visual randomization.

papers.intro:
Vision-Language-Action models have made significant progress in general robot manipulation, with models such as π0.5\pi_{0.5}, OpenVLA, and LingBot-VLA 2.0 [1, 2, 3] demonstrating strong manipulation capabilities. Flow-based policies such as π0\pi_{0} generate continuous action sequences through conditional flow matching [4, 5]. Such models either predict the End-Effector Pose (EEP) in task space, requiring a real-time Inverse Kinematics (IK) solver that may yield unreachable poses and discontinuous trajectories due to the one-to-many mapping [6], or directly regress the joint configuration, which avoids these issues but may misalign the normalized joint-space loss with physical-space task success. Specifically, standard joint-space regression losses do not explicitly account for the configuration-dependent effects of joint errors on end-effector motion. As a result, similar errors in joint space can lead to substantially different task-space deviations after forward-kinematic propagation. Meanwhile, visual conditioning in VLA models is often learned indirectly from the action objective, which may limit consistent attention to fine-grained hand-object interaction regions.

In our evaluation, we conduct both simulation and real-robot experiments, and show that the proposed framework exhibits a number of desirable properties for fine-grained bimanual manipulation: • Simulation benchmark: on 50 bimanual tasks from the RoboTwin 2.0 [9] benchmark, our full model improves the average success rate over the π0.5\pi_{0.5}-SFT baseline by 15.1 percentage points in clean settings, while the π0.5\pi_{0.5}-Global+Local Query variant improves it by 29.0 percentage points under domain randomization. • Real-robot evaluation: on four long-horizon real-world tasks, including make watermelon juice, soda bottle opening, beverage mixing, and clothes folding, our method improves the average success rate by 14.2 percentage points over the baseline. • Physically accurate execution: supervision in physical space reduces TCP position error compared with joint-space-only training, confirming that the geometric loss better aligns the optimization objective with physical execution. • Interaction-aware perception: the decoupled global–local queries improve manipulation performance under randomized scenes and unseen-language instructions by guiding the policy toward task-relevant interaction regions.

papers.title: On the crystalline Artin--Mumford invariant
papers.abstract: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p>0$ and let $W=W(k)$. We prove that the torsion subgroup of $H^3_{\mathrm{cris}}(X/W)$ is a birational invariant of smooth projective varieties over $k$. The proof combines the action of correspondences on Hodge--Witt cohomology and on the first Nygaard piece of the de Rham--Witt complex.

papers.title: Client-Aware Security Adaptive Early Exit Vision Transformers for Heterogeneous Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) trains a shared model across data-owning clients without centralizing raw data, but client data difficulty and compute budgets can differ. We study local early-exit Vision Transformer (ViT) inference, where an intermediate classifier may return a prediction before the final Transformer stage. The proposed method replaces one global acceptance threshold with a client-specific base threshold from label entropy and shallow-exit confidence, then adjusts each input using predictive entropy, confidence, top-two class margin, and exit depth. Aggregation uses only clients that updated a parameter. Security-aware routing reaches 88.70% CIFAR-10 accuracy with 32.0% depth saving and 73.7% ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy with 30\% saving. On matched six-client non-IID CIFAR-100, full-depth accuracy is 72.28% versus 68.20--71.80% for four heterogeneous-FL baselines; robustness-aware routing reaches 70.01% with 32.55% saving.

papers.title: Maximal estimates of the Schrödinger operators with quadratic potential for orthonormal systems
papers.abstract: We establish an equivalence principle for local mixed-norm estimates for generalized Schrödinger propagators acting on orthonormal systems. Under suitable mixed-norm conditions, estimates for generalized propagators follow from the corresponding free Schrödinger estimates for every summability exponent $1\leβ\le2$. Applications include maximal estimates for Schrödinger equations with time-dependent quadratic potentials and for the special Hermite operator, as well as almost everywhere convergence of the associated densities. For the special Hermite operator, we also obtain a single-function maximal estimate that is sharp up to the endpoint. We construct counterexamples for the Schrödinger operator, by combining single particle and many particle constructions in complementary dimensions, yielding new necessary conditions in an intermediate range of summability exponents.

authors.name: Eunhee Jeong
authors.institution: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology

papers.title: Continuous-Phase Frequency-Hopping MIMO Signaling and Processing for ISAC
papers.abstract: Frequency-hopping MIMO integrated sensing and communications (FH-MIMO-ISAC) supports agile multidimensional signaling but faces challenges in phase-continuous transmission, demodulation without channel-phase information, and coherent processing of multi-frequency echoes. We propose a continuous-phase frequency-hopping (CP-FH) MIMO ISAC waveform with matched communication and radar processing. Information is conveyed jointly by frequency combinations and continuous-phase-modulation symbols. CPM phase accumulation and frequency-hopping linear-frequency-modulation phase compensation maintain phase continuity and reduce spectral leakage. We derive exact inter-element orthogonality conditions, residual cross-correlation bounds, and a bound on averaged transmit-beampattern ripple. For communication, projection-energy demodulation requires no channel-phase information and approximates least-squares detection under weak inter-branch correlation. It separates frequency-combination search from CPM-symbol decisions, reducing complexity while retaining direct joint-search decisions. For radar, structure-matched coherent processing combines space-time-frequency matched filtering, velocity-consistent Doppler focusing, and frequency-aperture focusing to form a three-dimensional coarse-range--velocity--fine-range response. It reduces Doppler-mismatch loss and extra detections from periodic range grating lobes in conventional pulse-Doppler processing. We further derive the joint range response, output signal and noise powers, and receive beampattern. The analysis characterizes target-discrimination limits under periodic ambiguity and shows that the proposed processor preserves frequency-aperture range resolution and full-aperture angular resolution, with equal output noise power under the stated conditions.

authors.institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

papers.title: Towards Agentic Proof Harness Engineering
papers.abstract: Formal verification of real-world projects requires substantial manual effort, from specifying correctness properties to constructing the infrastructure needed to check them. We envision verification agents that assist developers throughout this process. Among the many tasks involved, one stands out as both foundational and amenable to automation: proof-harness engineering. A proof harness defines an isolated verification environment for a program unit, such as a function or module, by providing symbolic inputs, initialization code, and models of its dependencies. Today, proof-harness engineering remains largely a manual task performed by verification engineers. To explore the potential of coding agents for this task, we propose an agentic proof-harness engineer that automatically constructs verifier-ready harnesses from a software project and a designated verification target. We combine the agent with formal soundness and precision guards to validate generated abstractions and guide their refinement. We evaluate the feasibility of our approach in an exploratory case study on curl and libuv, using three historical assertion violations already embedded in the source code as verification properties. Our results show that the agent successfully constructs proof harnesses that enable CBMC to detect all three violations. We further demonstrate the potential for reusing these harnesses with other verification tools.

papers.title: A compact, dual-colour chirped-pulse laser system for field-deployable coherent Rayleigh-Brillouin scattering diagnostics
papers.abstract: Single-shot coherent Rayleigh-Brillouin scattering (CRBS) requires dual colour, frequency, and pulse duration agile laser systems, currently available only in laboratory layouts. In this work, we present a compact, portable, and robust next generation laser system that meets all of these requirements. Key features include an integrated master-slave seed laser design for stable frequency chirping, fiber-coupled acousto-optic modulator (AOM) gated pulse shaping for long-term thermal stability, and customized amplification stages in a rugged, portable enclosure which simplifiy the alignment and maintenance process. The system in this implementation can deliver up to $450$~mJ per arm, chirp rates up to $\sim22$~MHz$/$ns, and arbitrary temporal profiles within $\sim25$~ns to $\sim1$~$μ$s. This laser system is validated by measuring the neutral number density of an atmospheric plasma jet, and a two-dimensional temperature map is constructed, demonstrating lab-grade diagnostics for field deployment.

papers.title: HydraLLM: Adaptive Width Slicing for Elastic Text and Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: LLMs and LVLMs are increasingly deployed across heterogeneous hardware, ranging from data-center GPUs to resource-constrained edge devices. Their fixed-size architectures limit the ability to reuse a single model across deployment settings with different compute, latency, and model-size targets. We introduce HydraLLM, an elastic MQA-based architecture. Its number of active attention heads determines the effective widths of the embeddings, attention projections, feed-forward layers, and the output head, forming a nested family of subnetworks within a single parameter set. We introduce a static-to-elastic conversion pipeline that, starting from a pre-trained model checkpoint, includes importance-driven weight reordering and stochastic subnetwork training with knowledge distillation. We extend this principle to multimodal inference through an elastic projection module whose output width follows the active text width. HydraLLM covers a wider range of active parameter configurations than FFN-only elastic architectures. With 75% of heads active, HydraLLM achieves 2.2 percentage points higher TriviaQA accuracy than a state-of-the-art nested baseline configuration which has 17.25% more parameters. With 50% of heads active, our multimodal model achieves a CLIPScore comparable to that of the 7$\times$ larger Gemma 3 4B model. With only 25% of heads active, HydraLLM increases token-generation throughput by 75.3% over the full-width configuration.

papers.title: Presentability of categories of localizations and analytic rings
papers.abstract: We prove that certain categories of Bousfield localizations are presentable and give explicit regular cardinals $κ$ for which they are $κ$-presentable. As an application, we show that the category of analytic rings in the sense of Clausen and Scholze is $(2^{\aleph_0})^+$-presentable.

papers.title: Geometric Viewpoint of $L^\infty$ Estimates for Linearized Monge-Ampère Equations
papers.abstract: We prove a Harnack inequality on Monge--Ampère gradient graphs under suitable geometric bounds, giving us interior $L^\infty$ estimates for the linearized Monge--Ampère equation. The proof combines Moser iteration on extrensic balls with a gradient estimate for the extrinsic distance function. The argument avoids the Caffarelli--Gutiérrez Harnack inequality and the engulfing and covering properties of Monge--Ampère sections.

papers.title: alkhder at ImageEval 2026 Shared Tasks: Constrained Selection and Rotation-Averaged Logit Scoring for Multimodal Hallucination Detection
papers.abstract: We describe our submission to Subtask~1b of ImageEval 2026. The task consists of selecting the single visually valid statement from three candidates paired with an image, and is in both English and Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). Our system uses a pre-trained 7B vision--language model in a zero-shot setting, without task-specific training or fine-tuning. We formulate the task as a constrained selection problem and choose the answer using next-token log-probabilities. To reduce answer-position bias, we apply a Latin-square rotation to the candidate statements. Our system achieves CI scores of 0.0510 on the English test set and 0.0960 on the MSA test set, reducing CI relative to the official 3B baselines reported on devtest by 83.7\% and 80.4\%, respectively.

authors.name: Amro Najjar
authors.institution: Luxembourg Institute of Science and Technology

papers.title: alkhder at AlexandriaX-2026: Context-Aware English-to-Dialectal Arabic Dialogue Translation with QLoRA-Fine-Tuned NileChat-3B
papers.abstract: This paper describes team Alkhder's submission to Subtask 1 of the AlexandriaX-2026 shared task, which asks systems to translate English dialogue turns into thirteen Arabic dialects. We fine-tune NileChat-3B-Base with QLoRA on the Alexandria parallel dialogue corpus, training one set of adapter weights for all dialects. Each turn is translated conditioned on the target country and dialect, the domain, the participant roles, the speaker-addressee gender direction, and the preceding dialogue context. At inference, conversations are translated autoregressively and the model is fed its own previous outputs back as context without using any gold target-side test information. Under the constrained track, using only Alexandria data, it trains in about one hour and translates the private test set in under two hours. The system reaches a country-macro-averaged spBLEU of 20.36 and chrF++ of 36.64 on both tracks.

authors.name: Amro Najjar
authors.institution: Luxembourg Institute of Science and Technology

papers.title: Gravitational Waves as a Probe of Multi-Fluid Cosmologies: General Formalism and the Case of Cosmological Stasis
papers.abstract: Scalar-induced gravitational waves (SIGWs) provide a powerful probe of the expansion history of the universe prior to the Big Bang. Indeed, the production of such gravity waves depends on the evolution of first-order scalar perturbations within the early universe, while their subsequent propagation depends on the background equation of state. In this paper we extend previous discussions by studying SIGWs in cosmologies containing multiple fluids. As we shall demonstrate, the gravitational-wave signal within such multi-fluid cosmologies is modified in two distinct ways: not only are there new velocity effects which have no single-fluid analogues, but there are also significant alterations to the subsequent redshifting of modes that enter the horizon before the multi-fluid era ends. Thus SIGWs provide a probe of not only the overall expansion rate within such cosmologies, but also their internal multi-fluid composition. As an example, we then consider the case of gravitational waves arising during an epoch of cosmological stasis. During such an epoch, the abundances of energy components with different equations of state remain constant, thereby giving rise to a universe with a constant effective equation of state which nevertheless remains genuinely multi-fluid despite cosmological expansion. Despite their constant equations of state, we find that such stasis cosmologies also give rise to tensor power spectra and present-day gravitational-wave abundances which are significantly different from those expected within a standard radiation-dominated universe.

papers.title: Harnack-type inequalities for nonlocal doubly nonlinear parabolic equations
papers.abstract: We establish intrinsic Harnack inequalities for nonlocal doubly nonlinear parabolic equations in the slow-diffusion range: \begin{equation*} (u^q)_t+ \operatorname{P.V.} \int\limits_{\mathbb{R}^N}\frac{|u(x, t)-u(y, t)|^{p-2}(u(x, t)-u(y, t))}{|x-y|^{N+sp}}\,dy=0,\quad s\in(0,1),\quad 0<q < p-1. \end{equation*}

papers.title: Complexity of liveness in ring Petri nets and of halting in chip-firing on simple digraphs
papers.abstract: A ring Petri net (weighted circuit, cyclic weighted T-system) consists of a single directed circuit with arbitrary positive arc weights. We show that deciding liveness of ring Petri nets is coNP-complete, and that coNP-hardness holds in the strong sense already for token-conserving rings, in which every transition consumes and produces the same number of tokens. The proof is a short reduction from the covering problem for systems of residue classes (the complement of Simultaneous Incongruences). Together with a known reduction to circuits, it follows that liveness of weighted T-systems (weighted marked graphs, synchronous dataflow graphs) is coNP-complete, and coNP-hard in the strong sense. As a further consequence, the halting problem for chip-firing on simple directed graphs is NP-complete, which answers a question of Farrell and Levine. On 7 October 2026, the problem of liveness was posed to the AI model Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), which found the reduction, also suggesting the application to the chip-firing problem, and wrote a first version of this paper; the human authors checked it and, together with the model, revised it iteratively into the present form.

papers.title: From quantum emitters to technological platforms: a perspective on semiconductor quantum dots
papers.abstract: Photonic quantum technologies are based on controlled photon states. To generate these, quantum dots have emerged as excellent sources of single and entangled photons. In this Perspective, we briefly review the chronological development of quantum dots as photon sources, from their beginnings as quantum emitters in the early 2000s to the advanced photonic devices being developed today. We highlight the interplay between fundamental research and industrial aspects before discussing the photonic quantum technologies we expect to emerge in the near future.

papers.title: A new proof of equality cases of the Brunn-Minkowski inequality on manifolds
papers.abstract: We give a new proof of equality cases of the Brunn-Minkowski inequality on manifolds, following the work of Balogh-Krisátly. Our proof extends also to equality cases of the strong Brunn-Minkowski inequality, introduced by Magnabosco-Portinale-Rossi.

papers.title: MultiPASE: Shape-Aware Comparative 3D Genome Analysis
papers.abstract: 3D genome structures reconstructed from Hi-C data provide valuable insights into chromatin organization, but comparing them across conditions and time points remains challenging because of noise, variability, and arbitrary orientation. State-of-the-art comparison approaches often rely on contact-matrix-based summaries, which do not preserve the spatial geometry of the reconstructed structures and make integration with gene expression and chromatin accessibility difficult. There is therefore a need for robust structural alignment and spatial abstraction methods that support integrated analysis across conditions and time points. We present MultiPASE, a computational pipeline for comparative analysis of reconstructed 3D genome structures represented as gene-level spatial point clouds. MultiPASE aligns point clouds into a shared coordinate frame using coarse-to-fine rigid registration with PCA-based axis disambiguation and robust ICP refinement, then summarizes spatial organization using two complementary shape abstraction methods that produce stable, nested, multi-scale representations from dense core regions to broader structural extent. Using Hi-C-derived reconstructions from viral infection experiments, we show how the approach reveals condition-dependent structural changes that are difficult to interpret from raw 3D structures alone. By integrating spatial structure with gene expression and chromatin accessibility, MultiPASE supports interactive analysis of spatial organization and gene relocation patterns. A quantitative validation, reported in the Supplementary Materials, shows that the proposed shape abstractions preserve non-convex features, remain stable across samples, and that the alignment pipeline is necessary for meaningful comparison. A usage case and a usability evaluation with eight participants demonstrate the pipeline's effectiveness for comparative structural analysis.

papers.title: Prune the Leaky Neurons: Mitigating Private Data Leakage in Fine-Tuned LLMs via Joint-Embedding-Guided Pruning
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on proprietary records enables domain adaptation but introduces two challenges: (i) privacy leakage of memorized private data, such as personally identifiable information (PII), and (ii) balancing private data removal with utility preservation. Existing defenses, including data sanitization and differential privacy, often degrade performance, while privacy-neuron editing lacks a PII-free reference to distinguish identity-specific neurons from those supporting useful text. We propose JEPA-Prune, a post-hoc neuron pruning framework guided by a model trained exclusively on PII-free views. Alongside the fine-tuned private model, JEPA-Prune, trains a public model on surrogate and masked views of the same records using a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), capturing domain knowledge without identifiers. A cross-model representation probe quantifies deviations between private representations of leaked records and this PII-free reference. Integrated gradients and a scale-invariant specificity score then identify PII-responsive neurons, which are pruned without retraining. Experiments show that pruning just 1.6% of neurons reduces PII inference accuracy by up to 7.4x and PII extraction recall by up to 13.9x, while keeping unseen-text perplexity within 16% of that of the unpruned model for most LLMs. In contrast, privacy-neuron editing increases perplexity by at least 26x.

authors.name: Mohamed Elmahallawy
authors.institution: Deutsches Zentrum für Luft- und Raumfahrt e. V. (DLR)

papers.title: Veil-Then-Reveal: Protecting PII Privacy via Reversible Pseudo-Anonymization in Zero-Trust User--LLM Interaction
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly process sensitive documents and personal information, yet sending prompts containing personally identifiable information (PII) to remote providers exposes data subjects and organizations to risks from logging, retention, model training, and unintended disclosure. Existing anonymization methods often mask or remove PII, while conventional encryption eliminates the lexical and structural cues needed for effective LLM processing. We present Veil-then-Reveal (VtR), a user-side PII pseudo-anonymization framework for privacy-preserving LLM interaction under a zero-trust threat model. VtR treats remote LLM providers as untrusted and sends only pseudo-anonymized prompts, keeping plaintext PII on the user. VtR first detects PII and replaces it with realistic, same-type, in-vocabulary surrogates before prompts leave the user's device, preserving their linguistic and structural properties. It combines format-preserving encryption (FPE) for structured PII, such as phone and credit-card numbers, with a keyed-hash dictionary and secure vault for semantic PII, such as names, locations, and organizations. Session-specific mappings provide cross-session unlinkability, while user-side restoration reversibly replaces surrogates with their original values in LLM responses. We further introduce a rank-class FPE strategy for dates that preserves format and ambiguity while reducing cipher evaluations. Evaluation on three datasets containing 11,322 annotated PII instances achieves 97.9% detection recall, 95.2% protection of detected values, and 99.9% round trip; 100% of echoed surrogates end-to-end round-trip restoration.

papers.title: The effect of oxygen on the surface tension of AlTi metallic alloys
papers.abstract: We perform molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of AlTi metallic alloy melts, with a specific focus on surface properties and the effect of oxygen. The simulations use a machine-learned inter- action potential (MLIP) that has recently been tested through experimental data for the statical and dynamical properties of AlTi melts in the bulk [Kato et al. (2026)]. We find that the surface- tension response to oxygen depends strongly on the AlTi composition. Element-resolved density profiles show that oxygen enrichment near the interface is accompanied by a suppression of the Al surface segregation observed in the oxygen-free liquid. The results are compared to experimental values obtained using levitation techniques in microgravity.

papers.title: Magnetic order in epitaxial (La2/3Sr1/3MnO3)3/(BaTiO3)3 trilayer heterostructures
papers.abstract: The realization of artificial magnetic structures with high epitaxial quality and elevated critical temperatures remains a key challenge for spintronics. Here, we report the fabrication and characterization of epitaxial (La2/3Sr1/3MnO3)3/(BaTiO3)3 trilayer heterostructures grown by layer-by-layer laser ablation. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy, magnetization measurements, and neutron diffraction confirm their exceptional crystalline order and the absence of structural defects. Neutron diffraction reveals no antiferromagnetic at non-zero wavevector Bragg peaks, ruling out most antiferromagnetic configurations with a non zero wave vector Q. Magnetic hysteresis loops instead evidence a ferromagnetic order with a remanent moment of about 0.5 Bohr magneton per Mn atom at room temperature, persisting either in-plane or out-of-plane depending on the applied field. Our findings highlight neutron diffraction as a powerful tool for elucidating the magnetic structure of complex thin films and suggest that weak interlayer coupling through BaTiO3 leads to ferromagnetism with a high critical temperature (about 600 K).
