papers.title: Towards Hyperparameter Transfer for Differentially Private Optimization
papers.abstract: Scaling laws and hyperparameter tuning remain central challenges in training large-scale models, particularly under differential privacy (DP), where optimization is further complicated by noise injection and per-sample gradient clipping. While Maximal Update Parametrization ($μ$P) allows for zero-shot hyperparameter transfer in standard training, we show that it fails under DP constraints due to the distinct spectral properties of high-dimensional noise versus low-rank gradients. In this work, we introduce DP-$μ$P, a theoretically grounded framework that extends $μ$P to the privacy-preserving setting. By analyzing the interaction between gradient clipping, noise injection, and feature learning, we derive a Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) condition that governs layer-wise learning rate scaling. Combining this with our proposed spectral scaling formulation, we provide specific scaling rules for DP-SGD, DP-Adam, and DP-Muon optimizers. Empirically, we demonstrate that DP-$μ$P enables effective zero-shot transfer of learning rates across model widths on diverse architectures (MLP, ViT, GPT-2), matching or exceeding the performance of individually tuned baselines while significantly reducing computational costs.

authors.name: Tianze Wang
authors.institution: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey

papers.title: TransNSNet: A Transformer-Enhanced Multi-Scale Adversarial Framework for CT-to-PET Image Synthesis
papers.abstract: This study investigates CT-to-PET image synthesis using TransNSNet, a Transformer-enhanced multi-scale adversarial framework. A paired CT-PET dataset was curated from the public non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) Radiogenomics collection through patient screening, slice-level matching, preprocessing, and patient-level train-test separation. The proposed framework generates PET-like predictions at multiple spatial scales and applies coarse-to-fine reconstruction supervision, while TransPatchGAN introduces contextual feature interaction into adversarial evaluation. A progressive ablation study compares Pix2Pix, NSNet-Base, NSNet-D, and TransNSNet. Image-level performance was summarized over a fixed convergence window (epochs 80-101) from one training run per model. TransNSNet achieved the best mean value in nine of ten metrics, whereas NSNet-Base achieved the highest visual saliency-induced index. For fixed-fraction high-intensity regions, NSNet-D was marginally higher in slice-level recall and balanced accuracy, but the equal-weight patient-level values were nearly identical and the highest Dice values shifted to TransNSNet. These differences were small relative to between-patient variability. In the separate adaptive patient-level analysis (n=10), no pairwise model difference remained statistically significant after Holm correction. TransNSNet also had a substantially smaller parameter footprint than the original next-scale models. These findings indicate promising image-quality trends, but they do not establish statistical superiority or clinical validity; synthesized PET-like images should not be interpreted as substitutes for clinically acquired PET.

authors.name: Xiaoyu Deng
authors.institution: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey

papers.title: Input- and Feature-Space Correction for Cross-Hospital IHC Grading
papers.abstract: Pathology foundation models (FMs) are trained predominantly on hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images but are increasingly used as frozen feature extractors for immunohistochemistry (IHC), where cross-hospital differences can impair grading. However, systematic comparisons of correction methods for cross-hospital IHC grading remain limited. To address this gap, we benchmark label-free transformations applied to input images before frozen-FM encoding and to features after frozen-FM encoding using UNI and Virchow2, three IHC markers, and six directed cross-hospital transfers, yielding 12 settings. Among the evaluated input-space methods, our proposed method FIX achieved the largest macro-F1 improvement over no correction, outperforming well-known stain normalization techniques. Among feature-space methods, a simple feature-wise standardization achieved the best improvement over no correction, outperforming CORAL. Under patient-averaged tile-level evaluation, combining FIX with feature-wise standardization improved macro-F1 and quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) by 0.181 and 0.208, respectively, and reduced ordinal error by 0.209 relative to no correction. These results show that input- and feature-space transformations can provide complementary benefits for cross-hospital IHC grading with frozen pathology FMs.

papers.title: Commutative Coarse-graining on the Sphere
papers.abstract: Filtering by spatial convolution underlies coarse-graining and Large Eddy Simulation, the analysis of multiscale dynamics, and data processing across the sciences. Yet, as commonly practiced on the sphere, it violates a basic consistency requirement: commutation with differential operators, which is necessary for deriving coarse-grained dynamics and preserving the physics across lengthscales. The root of the problem is nonlocality of filtering, which compares directions in different tangent planes. The same reason underlies the Foucault pendulum's precession, and it is why the commutation failure is intrinsically geometric rather than being due to the coordinate system or numerical grid. A recently proposed generalized spherical convolution is, for a given scalar kernel, the unique linear operator commuting with the radial projection, divergence, and curl. Any consistent linear operator, be it spectral truncation, wavelet transform, diffusion, Green's-function inversion, or a machine-learned convolution, necessarily takes this form. From a simulation of an unstable jet, we demonstrate commutation to within numerical round-off, whereas common filtering that ignores curvature produces significant spurious divergence where none exists and gradient errors comparable to the gradients themselves.

papers.title: A $\mathbb{C}$-motivic $w_1$-self-map of periodicity 1
papers.abstract: Let $\mathrm{DY} = \mathbb{1}/(η, ν) \in \mathrm{SH}(\mathbb{C})$. We construct a $w_1$-self-map of periodicity 1 $w:Σ^{5,3}\mathrm{DY} \to \mathrm{DY}.$ The cofiber is a realization of $DA(1)$, the double of the subalgebra $A(1)$ of the $\mathbb{C}$-motivic Steenrod algebra $A$.

papers.title: Image Moment Estimation for Crowded Datasets
papers.abstract: Single-particle cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is an imaging technique capable of reconstructing high-resolution three-dimensional (3D) structure of biological macromolecules from a set of noisy projection images taken at random viewing directions. The mathematical model for cryo-EM images typically assumes that each image contains exactly one particle, which is centered at the origin. However, many experimental datasets contain particle images which include multiple particles: one central particle and a few crowding particles. This deviation from the model leads to inaccurate estimation of image statistics, such as the low-order image moments. To account for this, we propose a method to estimate image moments while correcting for the effect of crowding particles. This method can be run directly from a set of cryo-EM micrographs with picked particles, and we demonstrate its efficacy on a wide array of synthetic data.

papers.title: LongForge: Measuring and Improving Long-Context Instruction Data via Evidence-Assertion Reasoning Graphs
papers.abstract: Existing quality control for long-context instruction-tuning data is a one-shot judgment inside the generation pipeline that leaves only a scalar, revealing neither which document parts an answer uses nor how many reasoning steps it writes down; the data can thus be neither audited nor controlled. We formalize data quality as a property of the alignment structure among document, question, and answer, and build LongForge, which pairs an analyzer that measures long-context data with a synthesizer that generates it. The analyzer reverse-reconstructs each sample into an evidence-assertion reasoning graph and programmatically computes four dimensions on it: breadth, depth, correctness, and completeness. Every reading traces back to specific evidence spans and reasoning steps, making data auditable. Measuring seven mainstream datasets reveals two previously unquantified defects: breadth barely grows with document length, and depth is generally low, the two being nearly orthogonal. The synthesizer then embeds the analyzer into generation, gating on correctness and completeness and deferring breadth and depth to a training-time mixture over measured values, which makes the training distribution controllable. On two backbones, its two mixtures, LongForge-1 and LongForge-N, outperform the strongest baseline by 2.2-4.7 points on average over six long-context benchmarks, and in a controlled comparison that holds the gate and the candidate pool fixed, raising breadth and depth alone is worth a further 1.16 points, making the structural distribution of training data a lever on downstream quality rather than only a description of it.

authors.name: Xing Wu
authors.institution: State Key Laboratory on Integrated Optoelectronics

papers.title: Reconnection in 2D Inertial Magnetohydrodynamics
papers.abstract: We consider two-fluid equations of inertial magnetohydrodynamics in two spatial dimensions. These equations can be recast as the evolution of two active scalars, with fluid-like interaction kernels. The equations come in two flavors, left-handed and right-handed. They are conservative and have global unique solutions for both smooth initial data and for initial data in Yudovich class $L^1(\mathbb R^2)\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb R^2)$. We prove that the inviscid limit holds in Yudovich class. We prove the persistence of $C^{2,α}$ regularity of patch boundaries through merger events for the left-handed equations. We finally show numerical examples of magnetic reconnection, validating known rigorous results and uncovering new cases.

papers.title: Approximating the Girth of an Undirected, Weighted Graph for Larger Approximation Factors
papers.abstract: The girth of a weighted undirected graph is defined as the length of a shortest cycle in the graph. In this paper, we give a randomized $O\left(m^{1+2/(k-1)} n^{1/(k-1)}\right)$ algorithm to approximate the girth of a graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges to within a factor of $k$ for any real $k$. We assume that all edge weights are non-negative. For sufficiently high approximation factors, our algorithm outperforms the state of the art by polylogarithmic factors. Specifically, for approximation factors $k = c\frac{\log n}{\log \log n}$ where $c>5$, our algorithm gives a runtime of $O\left(m (\log n)^{5/c}\right)$, while instantiating the previous best $k$-approximation algorithms with $k = c\frac{\log n}{\log \log n}$ yields a running time of $O\left( \frac{cn (\log n)^{2 + 4/(3c)} }{\log \log n} + m\log n\right)$ (Kadria, Roditty, and Vassilevska Williams, arXiv:2607.00938). Furthermore, the algorithm presented here is conceptually simple, has relatively small constants, eschews single-source shortest path and sparse spanner algorithms, and employs a new technique, which we call ``random filtering.'' That being said, the basic algorithm returns only a numerical estimate for the girth, rather than a witness cycle.

papers.intro:
The girth of a graph is defined as the length of a shortest cycle. It is a fundamental graph parameter that has been studied algorithmically as far back as the 1970s. A foundational algorithmic treatment of the problem was given by Itai and Rodeh in 1978 [4] in which they gave an O⁡(min⁡(m​n,nω))O\left(\min(mn,n^{\omega})\right) algorithm to compute the girth of an unweighted, undirected graph, where ω\omega is the matrix multiplication exponent. Since then, many advances have been made in computing graph girth. In 2016, Orlin and Sedeno-Noda gave an O⁡(m​n)O(mn) algorithm for computing the girth of a weighted, directed graph [9]. However, the difficulty of exact girth computation and the inability to break the cubic runtime barrier for combinatorial algorithms have prompted researchers to instead explore approximation algorithms. The first truly subquadratic multiplicative approximation for unweighted, undirected graphs was given by Lingas and Lundell, whose randomized O~​(n3/2)\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})-time algorithm achieves an 8/38/3-approximation [8]. Roditty and Vassilevska Williams later obtained the first subquadratic 22-approximation: their deterministic algorithm runs in O~​(n5/3)\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3}) time [13]. For directed graphs, Pachocki, Roditty, Sidford, Tov, and Vassilevska Williams showed that, for every integer k≥1k\geq 1, the girth of a directed graph with nonnegative integer edge lengths can be approximated within a factor of O⁡(k​log⁡n)O(k\log n) in O⁡(m​n1/k​log5​n)O\!\left(mn^{1/k}\log^{5}n\right) time with high probability [10]. Most recently, Kadria, Roditty, and Vassilevska Williams obtained the currently best general time–approximation trade-off for weighted undirected graphs with nonnegative real edge lengths [6]. For every integer k≥2k\geq 2, their algorithm computes a (2​k/3)(2k/3)-approximation in O⁡(k​n1+2/k​log⁡n+m⁡(k+log⁡n))O\!\left(kn^{1+2/k}\log n+m(k+\log n)\right) time. This matches, up to polylogarithmic factors, the corresponding trade-off previously known for unweighted graphs [12, 5]. Lastly, our algorithm is randomized and works by repeatedly drawing randomly sampled subgraphs of our graph. Our algorithm draws inspiration from other well-known randomized graph algorithms, such as Karger’s algorithm [7] and Alon-Yuster-Zwick’s color-coding [2]. Indeed, some of these randomized sampling techniques have even been used as subroutines in cycle algorithms before, such as in [1] where they make use of the observation that if each vertex is retained with probability pp, then a given triangle is more likely to be in a subgraph than a 4-cycle (by precisely a factor of pp).

papers.title: Input-output analysis with a sphere packing approach
papers.abstract: Input-output analysis with linear programming is widely used in the planning of national economies. However, linear programming attains its optimum at a vertex of the feasible set, and a small deviation of the optimal plan in some direction violates a constraint. So far, little attention has been paid to finding sets of production plans which guarantee both the supply-demand balance of an economy and a given level of its gross domestic product (GDP), and the sphere packing approach cannot be applied directly, since the balance equations define a set with an empty interior. In this paper, we introduce the set of $(\varepsilon,δ)$-solutions, in which GDP may be smaller than its optimal value by at most $\varepsilon$ and supply may differ from demand by at most $δ$, and we find a sphere with the maximum radius inscribed into this set by solving a linear programming problem. We prove that the optimal radius is positive for positive tolerances, that it is non-decreasing, concave and piecewise linear with respect to the tolerances, and that it is bounded by the narrowest balance constraint, which is determined by a sales-concentration index of sectors. The approach is applied to the official input-output tables of Mongolia for 2010-2019 and 2024. The classical optimal plan has zero robustness, while the robust plan keeps 99.73% of the maximal GDP and, in a Monte Carlo simulation, tolerates independent deviations of all outputs and final demands of up to $\pm$0.30%. The margin of robust plans is limited by sectors with concentrated sales, mainly education and, increasingly, export-oriented mining, which indicates that a diversification of the users of mining output widens the set of robust plans.

papers.title: AuditKIT: A Unified Evaluation Spine for Benchmarking, Judging, and Comparing Large Language Models and Agentic Systems
papers.abstract: Evaluating language models and agents requires combining benchmark accuracy, judge-based assessment, runtime performance, tool-use behavior, and retrieval quality. Differences in interfaces, metric semantics, and trace formats complicate these comparisons and can hide failures in agentic workflows. We present AuditKIT, a source-available evaluation library that records these measurements in one result representation, with direction-aware metric contracts, configuration fingerprints, and extensible metrics and backends. For agents, it provides turn-aware tool-call matching, separates parallel from sequential execution, and distinguishes verified task outcomes from trajectory-level diagnostics. Missing or unobservable evidence is marked unscored rather than counted as failure. For retrieval-augmented generation, it combines ranked retrieval metrics, judged grounding, and deterministic evidence checks. Seven case studies spanning model comparison, serving runtimes, retrieval, tool calling, and interoperability show how answer extraction, runtime behavior, and metric selection change evaluation outcomes.

papers.title: The Schubert bialgebra
papers.abstract: We introduce a Schubert bialgebra $\mathcal{A}=\bigoplus_{n\geq 0}\mathbb{Z}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, in which polynomials in different numbers of variables multiply to zero and the coproduct splits the variables into two consecutive blocks, and study its graded dual $\mathcal{D}$, whose product is concatenation of weak compositions. The Schubert polynomials $\mathfrak{S}_u^n$ form a basis of $\mathcal{A}$; we give an explicit formula for the dual Schubert basis $Ξ_u^n$ of $\mathcal{D}$ via a transition formula to an elementary symmetric basis, and show that the Schubert structure constants $c_{u,v}^w$ are the coefficients of the coproduct of $\mathcal{D}$ in the dual Schubert basis. The product of $\mathcal{D}$ is then lifted to an associative product $\sqcup$ on the free abelian group $\mathcal{BRC}$ of bounded RC graphs, built from a transition map $\mathcal{Z}$ on RC graphs that realizes the Lascoux-Schützenberger transition formula and generalizes Little's bumping algorithm. Quotienting $\mathcal{BRC}$ by ideals coming from Demazure crystal equivalence, Nadeau-Tewari forest equivalence, and quasi-Yamanouchi equivalence yields manifestly positive Littlewood-Richardson rules for the dual Schubert, dual key, dual forest, and dual slide bases of $\mathcal{D}$. Read on $\mathcal{A}$, these are branching rules: enumerative formulas for splitting a Schubert, key, forest, or slide polynomial across two blocks of variables, and in the Schubert case they compute the Levi branching coefficients of Ressayre-Richmond for $\mathrm{GL}_p\times\mathrm{GL}_q\hookrightarrow\mathrm{GL}_{p+q}$.

papers.title: Sharp Instrumental Variable Bounds under The Marginal Sensitivity Model
papers.abstract: Marginal sensitivity models bound the degree of unmeasured confounding but do not incorporate instrumental-variable restrictions, even when an instrument is available. We develop a framework combining these models with instrumental-variable assumptions to sharpen inference on population treatment effects without requiring treatment monotonicity or treatment-effect homogeneity. For continuous and finite ordered outcomes, we characterize sharp identified sets for potential-outcome means and the average treatment effect, together with observable restrictions implied jointly by the instrumental-variable and sensitivity assumptions. The bounds admit explicit formulas for finite ordered outcomes, while optimization over prespecified threshold classes provides tractable outer bounds for continuous outcomes. We develop cross-fitted one-step estimators that accommodate flexible nuisance estimation. Under suitable conditions, the resulting outward confidence sets asymptotically cover the sharp identified interval without requiring optimal threshold estimation. Stronger conditions yield semiparametric efficient estimation and inference for restricted-class bounds. Numerical experiments show narrower confidence sets when incorporating an instrument and compare the performance of outward inference and inference for individual bounds. We apply the framework to the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment to illustrate how combining instrumental-variable assumptions with restrictions on the degree of unmeasured confounding can strengthen conclusions about the effect of Medicaid coverage on emergency-department use.

papers.title: Stabilizing Illumination Conditioning in SSM-Based Low-Light Image Enhancement with Bottleneck Prompt Sidecars
papers.abstract: Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) requires more than brightness amplification because real low-light images often exhibit spatially varying illumination, amplified noise, color distortion, and local detail loss. Recent SSM- and Mamba-based restorers provide efficient long-range modeling, yet the route for introducing illumination priors into such backbones remains insufficiently studied. This study addresses safe illumination conditioning for SSM-based LLIE through a bottleneck-side PromptAdapter. A lightweight illumination estimator first predicts a single-channel illumination map, which is then converted into prompt tokens and injected through a residual sidecar adapter at the bottleneck, thereby avoiding direct modification of the state-space core. Under a locked three-seed evaluation protocol on LOL-v1, LOLv2-Real, and LOLv2-Synthetic, the PromptAdapter improves over the Base model by 0.94 dB, 1.24 dB, and 0.93 dB in PSNR, respectively, while also improving SSIM, LPIPS, and masked dark-region metrics. The clearest real-data evidence appears on LOLv2-Real. A Learned-Fixed control on LOL-v1 indicates that the present results support the utility of the sidecar conditioning pathway more strongly than a strict claim of illumination-conditioned superiority, and the LOLv2-Synthetic result remains stability-conditioned. These findings suggest that, in SSM-based LLIE, conditioning design can be as important as the conditioning signal itself.

papers.title: Robust Estimation under Spurious Correlation via Statistical Counterfactual Augmentation
papers.abstract: Spurious correlations between nuisance features and outcomes present a fundamental challenge for statistical learning and inference. Counterfactual Data Augmentation (CDA), the practice of resampling nuisance features while preserving features of interest, has emerged as a popular strategy to mitigate such correlations, yet its statistical properties, and its reliance on an untestable validity assumption, remain largely unexplored. We provide a statistical treatment of CDA, termed Statistical CDA (SCDA), with two components. First, casting SCDA as a simulated-moment M-estimator, we establish consistency, asymptotic normality with a sandwich covariance and a finite-augmentation-draw variance correction, oracle efficiency for the target parameter, and the equivalence of iterative and one-shot procedures via stochastic approximation, yielding valid large-sample inference where previously none was available. Second, because the augmentation's validity cannot be tested from the observed data when features are entangled (a fact we prove), we develop a sensitivity analysis that bounds the residual nuisance--outcome dependence by a parameter $Γ$, giving sharp identified intervals for the target with valid confidence intervals and a breakdown frontier; the point-identified theory is the $Γ=0$ special case. Simulations confirm the efficiency gains under validity and the robustness bounds under possible invalidity, placing a widely used augmentation method on a transparent inferential footing.

papers.title: Dynamic Auction Mechanisms in a Closed-Credit Economy: Sequential Slot Reallocation in Air Traffic Management
papers.abstract: Indivisible resources allocated in advance may need to be reallocated when capacity reductions make existing assignments infeasible, yet monetary compensation is often impractical or undesirable. We develop a sequential resource reallocation scheme using reusable artificial credits, where agents hold pre-existing resource rights and have heterogeneous marginal valuations over time blocks. Capacity reductions produce fractional endowments, which our closed-credit scheme resolves into indivisible final allocations. We model agents' intertemporal preferences through a predicted-value-to-go function and characterize conditions ensuring that their optimal demand is non-increasing in price. We propose an ascending-auction mechanism that partitions agents into subgroups and uses the minimum subgroup market-clearing price as a common transaction price. We show that the mechanism preserves non-myopic individual rationality and weak nontrader neutrality. Moreover, we establish Pareto efficiency under optimal-demand clearing in the unified market and bound the expected gain from misreporting by the probability that an agent changes the common price. Simulations of airport slot reallocation demonstrate reductions in total modeled delay and cancellation costs relative to a ground-delay baseline.

papers.title: Foundation-Model Supervision of Distilled Potentials for Million-Atom Molecular Dynamics
papers.abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials distilled from foundation models enable fast large-scale molecular dynamics (MD), but they can fail locally in chemical environments that their training data did not sample. System-averaged error metrics and small random audits often miss such sparse or isolated failures. Here we use an exact equivariant foundation model, MACE-MPA-0, to check every atom of million-atom production simulations. Reorganizing two-layer MACE inference into a receiver-chunked three-pass schedule that keeps no per-edge intermediates resident reduces the marginal memory per atom 340-fold, evaluates up to $2.86\times10^{7}$ atoms on a single H200 GPU, and supervises $10^{6}$-atom trajectories in LAMMPS at 1.3% of the run time. Distilled MACE students run four to nine times slower than NEP89 with 0.95-1.28 times the teacher's force error against density functional theory (DFT). In molten SiO$_2$, whole-system checks uncover a persistent tail of under-coordinated atoms hidden by the system-averaged error and an isolated, unphysical O-O contact that a 1% random audit misses 94% of the time. On-the-fly retraining on teacher-labelled 13-Å clusters, with the force loss restricted to their inner 6 Å, removes three quarters of the failure tail and the kilobar-level pressure biases in SiO$_2$ and compressed water; the repair converges to the teacher, not to DFT.

papers.title: Operations on $G$-sets and the Dress map
papers.abstract: We study versions of binomial and multichoose coefficients for finite $G$-sets, extending a result of Siebeneicher from the 1970s concerning the duality between these operations. If the group $G$ comes from a finite Galois extension of fields, the Dress map provides a bridge from $G$-sets to quadratic forms over the base field. We show that this Dress map is compatible with binomial coefficients of finite $G$-sets and a particular operation on quadratic forms we define. This allows us to extend the definition of Brugallé and Wickelgren's quadratically enriched binomial coefficients to arbitrary Grothendieck--Witt classes. This allows for a new proof that quadratically enriched binomial coefficients depend only on the trace form of the inputted étale algebra, as well as an elegant reproof of a result of Chen and Wickelgren about binomial coefficients over finite fields.

papers.title: Efficient spectral unmixing using endmember variability
papers.abstract: A mixed signal vector composed of a weighted sum of random, unobserved endmember vectors has a mean and a variance that both depend on the unknown weights. This suggests that linear estimates of the weights based on the mean model are likely to be inefficient, and could possibly be improved upon by estimates that also make use of the variance model. In the context of a latent factor model for source variability, we calculate theoretically how much information is available in the variance model, and show how this information may stabilize inference in the case of an ill-conditioned mean model. We show through several data examples that utilization of the variance model is likely to improve parameter estimation in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: Synthetic Image Oversampling for Rare-Class Representation Learning in Deep Facial Phenotyping
papers.abstract: Recent deep facial phenotyping methods can support the recognition of genetic syndromes, but patient images are often scarce and unevenly distributed across disorders. Synthetic facial images offer a way to supplement the training data without collecting additional patient photographs. Their usefulness, however, depends on whether they improve recognition of real patients: generated images may introduce artifacts or repeat features already represented in the training set. It is therefore necessary to examine both how much synthetic augmentation to use and which disorders benefit. We investigate disease-specific synthetic oversampling using images from the Phenotypic Disease Image Database to augment a subset of the GestaltMatcher Database. We compare increasing augmentation levels in an image-based model, GestaltMatcher-Arc, and a multimodal model, GestaltMML, while keeping the real training and patient-disjoint evaluation partitions fixed. Repeated training runs assess overall and disease-specific accuracy, and an exploratory embedding analysis examines changes in class compactness and separation. Augmentation improves mean recognition accuracy in both training setups, although gains remain modest in GestaltMatcher-Arc and continue across the tested levels in GestaltMML. These aggregate improvements are accompanied by uneven disease-level responses, including reduced accuracy for some disorders. In the embedding analysis, disorders with fewer real training images tend to gain more class separation, but geometric changes do not consistently track classification performance. Together, the findings support synthetic oversampling for limited-data facial phenotyping and emphasize the need to assess its amount and benefit for individual disorders within each training setup.

authors.name: Zhanliang Wang
authors.institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

authors.name: Kai Wang
authors.institution: Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania

papers.title: A Neural Network - Based Tool for Rapid Orbital Solution of Contact Binary Systems
papers.abstract: With the rapid growth of large-scale time-domain surveys, vast amounts of photometric and spectroscopic data are continuously being released. A substantial number of contact binaries have been identified, accompanied by both light curves and radial velocity observations. Traditional modeling of these datasets relies on computationally intensive physical models, which limits their applicability to large-scale analyses. To this end, this paper proposes the use of a fully connected neural network and a SIREN (Sitzmann et al. 2020) model to rapidly generate radial velocity curves. After training, the models can rapidly generate radial velocity curves with high accuracy, significantly reducing computational costs and enabling efficient large-scale studies. This method was further integrated with the light curve computation framework developed by Li et al. (2025), allowing simultaneous fitting of radial velocities and light curves. To assess the reliability of the proposed model, synthetic observational datasets were constructed and used for parameter estimation. The deviations between the derived parameters and the ground-truth values were analyzed quantitatively, enabling a comprehensive evaluation of the model's accuracy.

papers.title: mmPencil: Toward Writing-Style-Independent In-Air Handwriting Recognition via mmWave Radar and Large Vision-Language Model
papers.abstract: In-air handwriting recognition based on radio frequency (RF) signals offers a promising solution for human-computer interaction, yet existing methods are often limited by predefined writing planes, constrained writing styles, and small recognition vocabularies. To address these limitations, we propose m^2VLMs, a modality mapping architecture that bridges millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar sensing and large vision-language models (VLMs), and develop mmPencil, a 3D in-air handwriting word recognition system. mmPencil reconstructs 3D handwriting trajectories from mmWave signals using a multi-stage spatial trajectory reconstruction algorithm and maps them into visual representations through a spatial-to-visual mapping algorithm, enabling VLMs to recognize handwriting while reducing sensitivity to writing styles and environmental factors. We collect and release a 3D mmWave handwriting dataset containing 7,664 samples of 200 words from 12 users across 22 writing scenarios. Extensive experiments demonstrate that mmPencil achieves robust word recognition under variations in writing position, range, angle, speed, size, direction, and user movement. It achieves 97.60% accuracy on 200 word classes for seen users and 92.50% zero-shot accuracy on 50 word classes for unseen users, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines.

authors.name: Zhu Wang
authors.institution: Southern University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Chirality-resolved imaging of spin waves with a quantum spin
papers.abstract: Spin waves carry their propagation direction in the handedness of their circularly polarized stray field, a property inaccessible to scalar magnetometers. In the Damon-Eshbach surface wave of an in-plane magnetized film, the dipolar field above the film rotates with a handedness fixed by the direction of travel. The nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centre in diamond is an intrinsic polarization analyser: a right-handed field about the NV axis drives one spin transition, and a left-handed field drives the other, in both the ground and the excited state. Here, we exploit the two excited-state transitions, which lie inside the spin-wave band of yttrium iron garnet (YIG), as a pair of chirality channels and image Damon-Eshbach waves in both directions. Because reflection from an etched boundary reverses the handedness, the incident and reflected waves appear as two lines in one spectrum and are imaged separately. In the ground state, the same rule applies, and the selected field drives Rabi oscillations, a route to chirality-selective control of the NV spin by magnons. Reading the two channels gives the direction of a spin wave at one point, without a phase reference. This advances chirality-resolved quantum sensing and provides insight into chiral spin-wave dynamics.

authors.name: Bo-Yuan Yang
authors.institution: State Key Laboratory of Mechanical Transmission

authors.name: Chengchao Xu
authors.institution: University of Science and Technology of China

papers.title: Probabilistic Fourier extension and the Schrödinger equation
papers.abstract: We give applications of the probabilistic Fourier extension theorem for the paraboloid in d dimensions (see [Saw7] for the sphere, and the proof there holds for a smooth compact piece of the paraboloid) to the global initial value problem for the Schrödinger equation with initial data f, in which we obtain sharp averaged Sobolev regularity results over certain `martingale transforms' of the intial data f. The deterministic analogue in three dimensions has been obtained recently by OpenAI [Ope].

papers.title: Federated Multiagent Soft Actor Critic for IRS Assisted Cognitive Radio Networks under Partial Observability
papers.abstract: Intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRSs) can improve spectrum efficiency and interference control in cognitive radio networks (CRNs) by reconfiguring the propagation environment. This paper presents FMASAC, a federated multi-agent soft actor-critic framework for IRS-assisted CRNs under partial observability, in which distributed secondary users (SUs) jointly select their transmit power and the phase shifts of an assigned subset of IRS elements using only local observations. Primary user (PU) protection is incorporated through an interference-penalized reward, and SUs coordinate by periodically averaging model parameters at a federated server, without exchanging raw observations, channel state information, or replay data. We formulate the problem as a partially observable Markov decision process, specify the local learning and aggregation procedure, and characterize its per-round communication cost. Illustrative performance trends contrast FMASAC with centralized SAC, independent SAC, IRS-fixed multi-agent reinforcement learning, and a heuristic CRN strategy. We also outline the simulation-based evaluation and the open challenges, namely constraint handling, agent heterogeneity, and scalability, that are needed to validate the framework.

papers.title: Initiating Removal from Operational Symptoms in Federated Vehicular Networks
papers.abstract: Connected vehicles train a driving model through federated learning (FL) and drive with it, so a faulty contribution often surfaces only as a delayed symptom on the road. Federated unlearning (FU) assumes that a removal request names what to forget. A symptom names no vehicle or round, and aggregation has already spread its cause across the fleet. We propose \underline{A}ggregation-\underline{T}ime \underline{O}perational-evidence \underline{N}eutralization of \underline{E}ffects (\method{}), which makes unlearning a term of the FL aggregation rule. \method{} projects everyday driving errors and reported symptoms onto a subspace spanned by recent global increments. It propagates the surviving effect of every contribution with curvature estimated from these increments and scores all contributions in one backward pass. A two-tier correction suppresses suspected effects in every round and eliminates confirmed ones after a one-round probe. We prove that backward scoring matches forward scoring and that the elimination is exact when training is flat outside the subspace. On three driving datasets, \method{} leaves 43\% to 61\% less residual harm than the strongest baseline in eight of nine settings while staying within 0.36 points of full retraining in utility.

papers.title: Volterra-Skorokhod Reflection and Fluid Limits of Loss Queues
papers.abstract: In the $G_t/G/n/n$ loss queue, a customer blocked at time $u$ remains missing from the system for as long as it would have been served. A fraction $K(t-u)$ of the blocking at $u$ therefore still affects the occupancy at time $t$, where $K=1-G$ is the service survival function. We show that, for every arrival process satisfying a functional strong law of large numbers, the fluid limit of this queue is a reflection with kernel $K$ of the fluid limit of the associated infinite-server queue. The reflection is defined by a one-sided reflection problem on $(-\infty,1]$ in which the regulator is convolved with a memory kernel. Given a càdlàg input $ρ$ and a kernel $K$ with $K(0)=1$, we seek a pair $(\hatρ,η)$ such that $\hatρ=ρ-\int_0^\cdot K(\cdot-u)\,dη(u)$ takes values in $(-\infty,1]$, $η$ is nondecreasing, and $η$ increases only when $\hatρ=1$. We refer to this problem as the Volterra-Skorokhod problem. We show existence and uniqueness of the solution and that the solution map is Lipschitz continuous in the uniform norm and nonanticipating. It therefore applies to stochastic inputs path by path. Unlike the classical Skorokhod map, this map is not monotone. For nonincreasing kernels, however, the regulator is the smallest admissible one and monotone in the input. In the queue, this orders the cumulative fluid losses under ordered arrival rates. Furthermore, since arrivals enter the queue through the reflection kernel, the regulator is a thinning of the arrivals.

authors.name: Mingrui Wang
authors.institution: Xi'an University of Science and Technology

papers.title: A Plausible Explanation Is Enough to Mislead Multimodal Judges
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly serve as judges in training and evaluation pipelines, often assessing answers together with explanations. Although AI judges are sensitive to textual factors, it remains unclear whether ordinary plausible explanations can sway judgments requiring visual verification. We introduce JUPE, a visual-question-answering (VQA)-style benchmark that fixes answers while varying explanations. Across 14 MLLM judges, ordinary explanations that sound plausible mislead judges, with effects comparable on average to deliberately persuasive arguments. Plain justifications and chain-of-thought rationales reduce rejection of incorrect answers by 12.7 and 13.8 percentage points, respectively. We call this failure plausibility capture. Using signal detection theory, we find a significant mean shift in decision criterion toward acceptance, without a clear change in mean discriminability. Explanations sway judgments across domains, explanation generators, and judging protocols, while tested mitigations offer limited, model-dependent protection. Such shifts can inflate performance estimates when judges evaluate answers with explanations.

authors.name: Yuchen Yang
authors.institution: Beijing Academy of Agriculture and Forestry Sciences

papers.title: String functions and cyclotomic Hecke algebras
papers.abstract: In this paper we study the Kleshchev multipartitions that label simple modules of certain cyclotomic Hecke algebras with parameters $1$ and $-1$. The $2$-residue statistic divides these multipartitions into blocks. We deduce a bivariate generating function for the blocks using representation theory. We also relate the generating functions of multipartitions in a fixed block to string functions associated by Kac and Peterson to irreducible highest weight modules of a type $A_1^{(1)}$ affine Lie algebra. By considering matrices formed by these generating functions, we reprove some results of Kac--Peterson on string functions using the Macdonald identities of Rosengren--Schlosser. As an application, we obtain new infinite product formulas for these generating functions.

papers.title: Structured Perception Representations for Off-road Dynamics Learning
papers.abstract: Autonomously navigating off-road terrain at high speed demands accurate control, which often relies on dynamics models that capture complex interactions between the robot and terrain. In off-road regimes, terrain interaction is a major component of the vehicle's dynamics. Prior work attempts to capture this effect by training learned models of the vehicle's dynamics, conditioned on its perception of the local environment. However, said conditioning is often overly simplistic, ignoring the spatial structure of the dynamics problem. Our approach, SpatialBEV, exploits this spatial structure. At each step, we query the bird's-eye-view (BEV) features around the predicted state, conditioning the next prediction on current geometric and semantic cues. We additionally present a benchmarking approach that mines a dataset's most difficult scenarios. On datasets collected across seasons, SpatialBEV reduces prediction error by 17.1%, compared to physics-based and learned baselines. We further evaluate on hardware on high-speed ($\geq$10 m/s) and geometrically challenging courses with a 25.3% reduction in maximum cross-track error. More details can be found at https://theairlab.org/spatial-bev-dynamics .

papers.title: Graph-Learned Spring SST Evolution and Land-Ocean Synergy Improve Yangtze Summer Rainfall Prediction
papers.abstract: Seasonal prediction of Yangtze summer rainfall is challenged by nonstationary oceanic precursors. Here we demonstrate that accounting for the evolution of spring SST and state-dependent land surface information improves predictability. Graph total variation (GTV) is applied to March-May SST fields over the western Pacific, Niño3.4, and tropical Indian Ocean to identify spatially coherent, month-specific SST coefficients for each grid cell and month to form a scalar GTV index. The learned coefficient patterns capture April-to-May ENSO decay and an opposing Indian Ocean adjustment, consistent with coupled Indo-Pacific variability. During 2008-2022, the GTV index prediction outperforms Niño3.4-based and sparse-regression benchmarks. Further improvement is achieved by including interactions of May Indo-China Peninsula soil moisture with Indian Ocean SST, importantly also correcting several underestimated wet summers. Circulation diagnostics associate the learned index with a summer geopotential-height dipole and Yangtze moisture convergence, while dry-Indochina/warm-Indian-Ocean conditions coincide with stronger westward extension of the western Pacific subtropical high.

authors.name: Haishan Chen
authors.institution: Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology

papers.title: Topological edge and domain-wall phonons in the mass-dimerized diatomic chain: complex band structure, Zak phase, and spectral unfolding
papers.abstract: The one-dimensional chain with alternating masses is the simplest mechanical system with a topological band structure. We give a fully analytical account of its localized vibrations built on the complex band structure. The evanescent Bloch waves available at each frequency are matched directly to force balance at a free end or a domain wall, without transfer matrices, which yields closed-form frequencies and decay lengths for every localized mode. The free-end mode sits at a branch point of the complex band structure, where the acoustic and optical sheets join and the decay is fastest. For uniform springs, a sharp wall between the two mass orderings hosts one in-gap mode, symmetric at the light$\mid$light wall and antisymmetric at the heavy$\mid$heavy wall, and an adiabatic construction shows that these are the same topological mode; the light$\mid$light wall also binds a non-topological mode above the optical branch. Spectral unfolding makes this classification visible in momentum space: the sign of the Bloch factor sets the zone-center or zone-boundary character of each mode, and its magnitude sets the width. The Zak phase, quantized by inversion, identifies the modes of topological origin and fixes a half-integer mode count per band at a wall, while the chiral symmetry known to be hidden in strain coordinates explains which frequencies are pinned.

papers.title: Truth in Contrast: Calibrated Factual Evidence from Language Model Likelihoods
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode substantial factual knowledge. Yet, estimating confidence in factual claims reliably remains challenging. We study likelihood-based factual confidence from the complementary perspectives of discrimination and calibration across multilingual factual statements. Specifically, we instantiate contrastive generative likelihoods as Contrastive Factual Evidence (CFE), which compares the likelihood of the same claim under competing factual and non-factual conditions, and derive its probabilistic counterpart, the Contrastive Factual Posterior (CFP). We show analytically that CFP calibration depends on the differential error between the two surrogate conditionals, allowing errors shared across them to cancel and yield tighter calibration bounds. Empirically, CFP substantially improves calibration while maintaining factual discrimination comparable to its strongest competitor. Nonetheless, discrimination is uniformly weak across methods in lower-resource languages, which simultaneously undermines the utility of the measured calibration. To this end, we interpret a likelihood geometry, within which an evidence-bearing direction is induced, along with an orthogonal evidence-invariant direction. In our investigation, we selectively align target-language claims with stronger English evidence only along the factual-evidence direction, improving discrimination and open-ended factual generation without target-language labels.

papers.title: Oh doughnuts, it's the variance! A visual metaphor for the variance, standard deviation, and related quantities
papers.abstract: Despite the rise of artificial intelligence, human intuition endures as both a foundation for education and also (for now) a primarily human experience. We re-examine a formula for the sum of squares that is sometimes set aside because of possible numerical issues. The formula can be used to create square doughnuts, a delicious regional favorite. The variance becomes the dough, and we can examine the variance by either comparing doughnuts or by making different sizes of doughnuts with the same amount of dough. In doing so, we provide a new visualization of a cornerstone formula, understandable by students at almost any level. We further provide insight into related topics such as the coefficient of variation as well as a visualization of when numerical issues are likely to be problematic. We also provide a new vocabulary for understanding the variance formula, with `dough' and `hole' taking the place of less edible concepts from the typical recipe.

papers.title: Exploring The Empirical Privacy Landscape of Synthetic Data
papers.abstract: Methods for training language models on sensitive data differ in how they balance capability gains against the risk of leaking private information. In this paper, we present a controlled comparison of data-level and training-level interventions for navigating the capability-privacy tradeoff on synthetic medical records with canaries to probe for leakage. Direct finetuning performs best on capability metrics but leads to the most privacy leakage, while DP-SGD reduces leakage at substantial cost to capabilities. Generating synthetic data from these records offers a more favorable balance, particularly when guided by a uniqueness-aware instruction to replace private details. Relative to naive paraphrasing, privacy-aware rewriting improves privacy protection across a variety of different rewriting models. We also find that more capable rewriting models generally reduce the risks of downstream privacy leakage, although held-out fit does not improve monotonically and increased test-time compute yields inconsistent gains. Overall, these results highlight privacy-aware rewriting as a promising direction for achieving a more favorable trade-off between capabilities and empirical privacy compared to other training-level methods, and our evaluation framework supports comparisons of future models and methods.

authors.name: Zihao Zhao
authors.institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

papers.title: Reusing Calibration Gains across Model Representations
papers.abstract: Scale calibration learns an update for one model representation. We study how much of that update can be reused by another representation of the same pretrained model. Our transfer procedure extracts positive group-wise gains and installs them in the recipient's weights or native quantization scales without recipient-side optimization. On a quantized recipient, it preserves integer codes, zero points and storage layout. For a Qwen3-1.7B floating-point/GPTQ INT3 pair, bidirectional transfer retains 76.9-90.5% of the text-loss improvement from recipient-specific calibration on fresh WikiText and C4 cohorts excluded from project development. Shuffling the same gain values within each projection worsens both recipients, showing that their learned group assignment matters after transfer. A Llama-3.2-3B control keeps the initial native tensors at all four calibrated projections identical and changes nine projections elsewhere. Cross-installation retains 98.6-99.3% of the text-calibration benefit, alongside a small, resolved preference for each recipient's own gain. These results quantify both the adaptation carried by a reusable calibration update and the remaining benefit of recipient-specific training.

papers.title: BaGuaLu-2: Taming Dynamic Memory Fluctuation for Efficient MoE Model Training over 10,000 GPUs
papers.abstract: Fine-grained Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is the de facto architecture for scaling large language models. However, dynamic expert load imbalance causes severe memory fluctuations that degrade training efficiency. Existing systems rely on static memory provisioning: they either over-provision, leaving GPU memory idle during normal execution, or under- provision, inviting out-of-memory crashes and costly manual rollbacks when load spikes occur. To address these challenges, we propose BaGuaLu-2, a large-scale MoE training system that eliminates this dilemma through flexible provisioning. By transforming memory allocation from a static, one-time tuning choice into a continuous and fine-grained control. BaGuaLu-2 grants exact activation memory on demand for each training batch. Furthermore, it offsets any dynamic management overhead through system optimizations. BaGuaLu-2 demonstrates exceptional scalability, training a model with 1040 billion parameters across 12,288 GPUs while sustaining over 2 EFlops at 35% MFU. Compared with state-of-the-art systems, BaGuaLu-2 delivers 1.14x and 1.13x average throughput improvements over Megatron-Kuai and AdaPipe, respectively.

authors.name: Minkun Guo
authors.institution: Beijing Academy of Agriculture and Forestry Sciences

authors.name: Zan Zong
authors.institution: University of Science and Technology Beijing

papers.title: A Multiwavelength View of SPLUS J102139.31-282247.5: an X-ray Luminous and Eclipsing Dwarf Nova
papers.abstract: We report the independent discovery of the cataclysmic variable (CV) SPLUS J102139.31-282247.5 using Southern Photometric Local Universe Survey 12 band photometry, following its initial identification via ASAS-SN variability. Here, we investigate the system using optical photometry alongside optical and X-ray spectroscopy. High-cadence optical light curves from publicly available TESS data and a dedicated campaign at the Pico dos Dias Observatory in Brazil revealed a highly inclined system exhibiting pronounced eclipses with an orbital period of 1.81 hours. We found no evidence of a WD spin period. Despite seasonal gaps, the long-term ASAS-SN light curve revealed several outbursts (15 with $Δ$mag $\sim$ 1.5 brighter than the mean magnitude) and one superoutburst over the past decade. During Swift X-ray telescope observations, the system exhibited X-ray luminosity of $8.5 \times 10^{31}$ erg s$^{-1}$ in the 0.3-10\,keV band, originating from thermal plasma emission at a temperature consistent with accretion shocks. Optical spectroscopy from the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrographs on the Gemini South telescope confirms the CV nature of the system, showing strong, double-peaked H and HeI emission lines alongside a weak HeII4686 line. Altogether, these features strongly support the classification of SPLUS J102139.31-282247.5 as a quiescent, eclipsing dwarf nova with an unusually high X-ray luminosity.

papers.title: Has GPT-6-Astra Achieved Embodied Intelligence?
papers.abstract: GPT-6-Astra demonstrates a level of competence in robotic manipulation and navigation that challenges the conventional paradigm of building specialized models for individual tasks and embodiments. In this report, we ask not only how capable GPT-6-Astra is, but what its capabilities imply for the field. First, we probe the limits of standalone GPT-6-Astra. We conduct a large-scale evaluation across 12 representative benchmarks spanning tabletop manipulation, humanoids, mobile platforms, and dexterous hands. Under a unified protocol that allows in-context learning (ICL) from training-set demonstrations and substantially increases the number of execution steps, GPT-6-Astra achieves unprecedented performance (Fig. 1). Future research may focus on improving 1) the generality of ICL 2) cost and execution time, 3) physical-state verification, 4) recovery from irreversible failures, and 5) long-horizon preservation of progress. Second, we study the agentic harness for embodied control. We identify that close-loop coordination between a high-level "System 2" reasoner (i.e., GPT-6-Astra) and a low-level "System 1" controller (e.g., π0.5) is costly but effective. Third, we examine GPT-6-Astra on real-world deployment. Our experiments on 8 robot configurations reveal substantial gaps: 1) robot demonstrations required for ICL are expensive to collect, and 2) it is implausible to trade longer execution for higher success rates with physical constraints. Fourth, we envision the next generation of embodied benchmarks. We develop a prototype that 1) derives tasks from real-world needs, 2) provides no in-domain demonstrations, and 3) judges agents on a world clock that keeps running while they deliberate. Taken together, our results suggest that GPT-6-Astra has largely crossed the threshold of embodied competence, but not yet that of practical embodied intelligence.

papers.title: Integral Volume Criteria for Semilinear and Quasilinear Liouville Theorems on Complete Manifolds
papers.abstract: Let $M$ be a connected complete noncompact Riemannian manifold without boundary, and let $V_o(R)$ denote its ball volume. We prove Liouville theorems without any curvature assumption. For $p>1$ and $q>p-1$, divergence of $\int^\infty R^{pq/(p-1)-1}V_o(R)^{-(q-p+1)/(p-1)}\dd R$ forces every nonnegative Sobolev weak supersolution of $-Δ_pu\ge u^q$ to vanish. For $q>\max\{1,p-1\}$, divergence of $\int^\infty R^{p-1}V_o(R)^{-(q-p+1)}\dd R$ forces every nonnegative global distributional energy supersolution of $u_t-Δ_pu\ge u^q$ to vanish. Consequently, the corresponding Cauchy problem has no global solution in this class with a nonzero nonnegative local $L^1$ initial trace.

papers.title: PASS: A Trustworthy Precision Approach Simulation System for CAT III Integrity Algorithm Development
papers.abstract: For fixed-wing aircraft, reliable localization during approach and landing is critical to flight safety. Visual--inertial navigation is promising, but aircraft navigation also requires integrity: trustworthy outputs and timely warnings when they should not be used. Real approach data are costly to collect, while many visual errors and failures required for integrity algorithm development are difficult to reproduce safely. We present PASS, a trustworthy Precision Approach Simulation System for CAT III integrity algorithm development. In a unified temporal and geometric framework, PASS integrates configurable airport environments, prescribed trajectories, inertial simulation, calibrated stereo images, and continuous runway-relative ground truth. It supports navigation and integrity research through controllable sensor errors and environmental variations, computable visual projection errors, deterministic runway geometry priors, and condition-labeled data for statistical error modeling. We further propose Sim-to-Real Scene Trustworthiness (SRST), a measure based on DINOv2 feature distributions and UMAP, to quantify sim-to-real closeness. Experiments with representative stereo--inertial estimators demonstrate the usability of the generated sequences and quantify localization errors across algorithms and environments. PASS provides a controllable foundation for developing and evaluating visual--inertial navigation and integrity algorithms for fixed-wing precision approaches up to CAT III requirements.

papers.title: Liouville theorems for $-Δ_{m,g}u=λe^u|\nabla u|^q$ in the full range of gradient exponents
papers.abstract: We study the equation \[ -Δ_{m,g}u=λe^u|\nabla u|^q \] on complete, connected, noncompact Riemannian manifolds of dimension $n\ge2$ with $\Ric_g\ge0$. For every $m>1$, $q\in\mathbb R$ and $λ>0$, we prove that every positive $C^1$ weak solution is constant when $q>0$, while no such solution exists when $q\le0$. For $q>m$, we derive a local gradient estimate independent of the solution by Nash--Moser iteration, which leads to automatic boundedness and resolves the question raised by Lu and Zhu~\cite[Remark~1.6(B)]{LZ}. For $m-1<q<m$, we use an auxiliary function and a divergence inequality to extend the Liouville result beyond the range covered by existing gradient-inequality methods. The remaining cases are treated by suitable changes of variables and integral estimates. The conclusions also extend to real-valued solutions bounded below.

authors.name: Mengyu Zhang
authors.institution: University of Science and Technology of China

papers.title: Batched Contextual Reinforcement II: Does RLVR Need Long Rollout Windows?
papers.abstract: Long rollout windows make reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) expensive, yet simply shortening them can remove the correctness signal: when every single-problem rollout truncates before an answer, group-relative accuracy advantages vanish. As a technical continuation of Batched Contextual Reinforcement (BCR), we study how concurrent rewards relax this dependence on long windows. Concurrent Constraint Reinforcement (CCR) places three independently verifiable problems in one capped training completion. Correct answers completed before truncation retain credit, while a shared budget encourages shorter useful reasoning without an explicit length penalty. We connect this mechanism to conditional reward- and update-variance analyses and study 4B and 8B mathematical reasoning models. Against single-problem GRPO with a 32k window, CCR with an 8,000-token window reduces tokens per training step from 975,464 to 174,957 on 4B and from 793,832 to 165,788 on 8B, saving 82.1% and 79.1%, respectively. An 8B training trace shows increasing accuracy reward alongside shorter completions. Single-problem evaluations provide supporting evidence of retained reasoning quality. These results identify reward-preserving training structure as a practical route to lower per-step cost in short-window RLVR.

authors.name: Hongbo Ma
authors.institution: Henan University of Traditional Chinese Medicine

authors.name: Xi Zhu

papers.title: ElectroCalm: Investigating User Experience and Physiological Responses to Multi-Node Transcutaneous Electrical Stimulation for Stress Modulation
papers.abstract: Transcutaneous Electrical Stimulation (TES) for stress modulation has largely focused on vagus nerve stimulation at the neck, yet two questions remain underexplored: how users experience electrotactile sensations at this sensitive site, and whether electrotactile feedback itself can function as a haptic stress intervention. To investigate this gap, we applied an 8-node TES array to two body sites during a cognitively demanding 2-back task: the neck, a site used in prior vagal TES research for its anatomical proximity to the cervical vagus nerve, and the arm, the most common haptic wearable site, which primarily provides cutaneous electrotactile sensation without vagal access. In a usability study, both sites were rated as comparably comfortable without disrupting task performance, though the same stimulation was interpreted differently across sites. A second study assessing the physiological effects of active versus inactive stimulation under identical electrode attachment revealed that only neck TES produced cortical and autonomic changes consistent with stress modulation, while arm TES did not differ from inactive conditions. These findings suggest that neck TES can be acceptable despite the site's sensitivity, and that both the physiological effects and the sensory experience of TES depend on placement.

papers.title: ShadowFPT: Backdooring Federated Prompt Tuning via Shadow Triggers
papers.abstract: Federated Prompt Tuning (FPT) adapts large vision--language models by freezing the pretrained backbone and optimizing only lightweight prompt parameters across clients. Although this design improves communication and parameter efficiency, it creates an overlooked security risk. Since the backbone is shared and frozen, a malicious client can induce backdoor behavior through the representation space while keeping its uploaded prompt updates close to benign ones. We propose \textbf{ShadowFPT}, a targeted backdoor attack that exploits this frozen-backbone attack surface. ShadowFPT first pretrains a learnable \emph{Shadow Trigger} against the frozen CLIP visual encoder, using either auxiliary public data or the malicious client's local data, so that triggered inputs are steered toward the target class in representation space. During federated prompt tuning, the malicious client adapts the trigger under the current global prompt and then optimizes its local prompt on both clean and triggered samples. Only prompt parameters are uploaded to the server, while the trigger and frozen encoders remain local. By shifting most of the attack burden from prompt updates to trigger-induced representation steering, ShadowFPT achieves targeted misclassification while preserving prompt-space stealthiness. Across multiple datasets, aggregation rules, and non-IID federated partitions, ShadowFPT increases the attack success rate from 19.81\% to 90.36\% in our main setting, while maintaining clean accuracy. It remains effective across textual, visual, and joint vision--language prompt tuning. These results identify frozen backbones as stealthy and underexplored backdoor surfaces in federated prompt tuning, suggesting that defenses based only on prompt-update anomaly detection are insufficient.

papers.title: Time-optimal vaccination in state-dependent SIR models: a single switch criterion and numerical examples outside its regime
papers.abstract: In a susceptible, infected, and recovered (SIR) model with constant rates, a time-optimal vaccination policy has at most one switch from no vaccination to maximal vaccination. We allow the transmission and recovery rates $β(S,I)$ and $γ(S,I)$ to depend on the state. If $β+I\partial_Iβ>0$ and $G:=\partial_S(βS-γ)>0$ throughout the forward invariant state space, then every optimal control is bang-bang with at most one switch. The incidence condition allows the transmission coefficient to decrease with prevalence. The Pontryagin analysis shows that $G$, the sensitivity of per capita infected growth to the susceptible fraction, and the infected costate together determine the crossing direction of the switching function. We also prove existence of an optimal control, derive explicit a priori upper bounds on the eradication time and characterize the switching time by an optimization over one variable. For parameter sets that violate $G>0$, numerical optimization gives controls with two switches and smaller eradication times than the computed minima over the single switch family. These computations provide a reproducible numerical counterexample to an unrestricted single switch claim. In a prescribed parameter sweep satisfying $G>0$, delayed vaccination reduces the eradication time relative to immediate full vaccination by more than $1\%$ in $10.9\%$ of the cases, with a maximum reduction of $26.3\%$. In examples near this maximum, the delay increases peak prevalence by more than an order of magnitude and cumulative incidence more than fourfold. Hence minimizing eradication time does not in general minimize epidemiological burden.

authors.name: Yeoneung Kim
authors.institution: Seoul National University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Two-photon Doppler-free spectroscopy of the $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6s23s\;^1S_0$ Rydberg transition for quantum sensing in ytterbium
papers.abstract: Here we report atomic structure calculations and experimental observations of the two-photon $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6s23s\;^1S_0$ transition in Yb. The unique level structure of Yb places the $6s6p\;^1P_1$ state's energy at $\approx\!49.7\%$ of the ionization energy, which facilitates two-photon Doppler-free excitation of the $6s23s\;^1S_0$ Rydberg state from the $6s^2\;^1S_0$ ground state at a relatively low optical intensity. This $J= 0 \rightarrow J=0$ transition is immune to first-order Zeeman and electric quadrupole shifts, has reduced sensitivity to higher-order Zeeman shifts, and is further predicted to have relatively low sensitivity to density shifts. Using configuration interaction theory, we compute relevant properties of the $6s23s\;^1S_0$ Rydberg state for sensing, including the $C_6$ coefficient, dc polarizability, blackbody radiation (BBR) shift, and BBR depopulation rate. As a first experimental step, we demonstrate two-photon Doppler-free spectroscopy of the $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6s23s\;^1S_0$ transition. From our experimental spectra, we estimate the natural linewidth (lifetime) of the $6s23s\;^1S_0$ state to be 90 kHz (1.8 $μ$s). We believe this transition, or other $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6sns\;^1S_0$ transitions in Yb with $n\approx23$, may find use in a variety of sensing applications, potentially including a two-photon clock, electrometer, or BBR thermometer.
