papers.title: How Murky Before a VLM Knows It Cannot See? Accuracy, Confidence and Abstention on a Physical Visibility Axis
papers.abstract: Robustness studies of vision-language models (VLMs) grade degradation on nominal severity scales ("level 1-5") that carry no physical units, and they rarely ask whether a model's confidence follows the loss of visibility. We measure accuracy, internal (token-probability) confidence, verbalized confidence and an explicit abstain option on a visibility axis in metres: fog follows the Koschmieder model, an underwater arm scales the absorption spectrum of pure water, both are applied with a monocular metric depth map, and the visibility range V is swept over eight log-spaced levels from 250 m to 1.95 m. On 1000 COCO scenes and five small open VLMs (2-5 B parameters), accuracy on a boxed-object identification task falls from near its clean value to chance within a narrow band (half-way visibility V_acc of 12.1-15.9 m in fog and 20.5-38.6 m under water) while, for the four models that are confident on clean images, the confidence stays high: at V=1.95 m in fog their accuracy is at chance but their mean internal confidence is 0.68-0.84 and their verbalized confidence 0.61-1.00, a blind-spot width W=log10(V_acc/V_aware) of at least 0.79 decades, i.e. a factor of 6.2 in visibility. The remaining model is under-confident throughout and its internal confidence follows accuracy. An explicit abstain option follows accuracy when it names the reason (W from -0.21 to -0.06 in fog) but, for one model, lags with a generic "I don't know" (W up to 0.18). ImageNet-C fog severities 1-5 correspond to only 55-110 m of physical visibility, outside the failure band, and leave the accuracy of the models within 5 percentage points of its clean value. Blank-image and shuffled-image controls, a prior-matched answer set and a 200-image pilot that preceded the study are reported. Findings are descriptive: one draw of 1000 images, depth of assumed scale, and models of 2-5 B parameters.

papers.title: Retrospective Evaluation of Bluetooth RSSI Fingerprinting for Bin Localization on an Industrial Shop Floor
papers.abstract: This paper evaluates an archival Bluetooth Low Energy received signal strength indicator (RSSI) dataset collected for bin localization on an industrial shop floor. The installation used 24 fixed relays positioned on walls and Bluetooth beacons attached to bins, with each relay applying a Kalman filter to its own readings in firmware before publishing them. The primary survey produced 19,034 usable two-minute fingerprint samples across 90 known positions, with 23 relay measurements available as model features. We compare calibrated path-loss multilateration with two radio-map estimators: distance-weighted $k$-nearest neighbours and Random Forest regression. A random 70/30 row split measures recognition at surveyed positions, while a coordinate-grouped split reserves 27 entire positions for testing and measures interpolation to unseen positions. Random Forest achieved a median error of 0.66~m for surveyed positions, with 77.9% of estimates within 3~m and 96.3% within 10~m. For unseen positions, median error increased to 9.42~m and 55.5% of estimates were within 10~m. Path-loss multilateration produced a 19.41~m median error on unseen positions, close to the 19.62~m mean-position baseline. The results support RSSI fingerprinting for a fixed inventory of surveyed bin positions, but not precise continuous localization between survey points. Git history dates the original implementation to September 7, 2019. The evaluation code in this paper was written in October 2026 and is reported separately from the seven-year-old prototype.

papers.title: AgentCount: An Agentic Workflow for Traceable Colony Counting and Insight Generation from Agar Plate Images
papers.abstract: Colony counting is commonly used to evaluate microbial populations in food safety testing and microbiological studies. Despite its wide application, manual counting is time-consuming and operator-dependent, and the final count often lacks a record of the objects included in the measurement. To address these limitations, this study presents AgentCount, an open-source agentic workflow for colony counting and result interpretation from agar plate images. Plate photographs and plating metadata are processed through seven agents for image quality control, plate localisation, colony detection, counting, CFU calculation, validation, and reporting. Colony detection is performed using Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) with multiple text prompts and morphology-based filtering. After that, replicate statistics are calculated and a large language model (LLM)-based agent is used to generate a results narrative. Intermediate outputs, including quality scores, segmentation masks, detections, and warnings, are retained to support review of the reported values. The workflow also extends to skill-guided analysis of archived microbial population data. In a retrospective comparison with two previously published studies, we benchmarked 241 published endpoints, including all 216 mean +- SD values of the meat-analogue pathogen tables; on the 168 endpoints with a complete n=6 replicate source, 164 (97.6%) agreed within 0.01 log10 units. Overall, AgentCount demonstrates the promising potential of agentic workflows for applications in applied microbiology.

papers.title: TALLOP: Joint Optimization of Local Training and Communication Compression for Time-Constrained Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Minimizing the wall-clock time required to reach a target accuracy is crucial in federated learning (FL), where many applications require frequent model updates as data distributions evolve over time. Nevertheless, in heterogeneous environments, slow clients with limited computational and communication capabilities can delay global synchronization, forcing faster clients to wait and increasing the overall training time. To mitigate this straggler effect, recent studies have introduced per-round time constraints and adapted client workloads within the available time. However, these approaches primarily focus on local computation, whereas communication can become a major bottleneck in communication-limited environments, motivating the joint optimization of training workload and communication compression. Although previous studies have explored such joint optimization, determining an effective training--communication balance under a fixed per-round time budget remains challenging, as the resulting model performance depends on both training progress and compression-induced degradation. We therefore propose TALLOP, which jointly optimizes the local training workload and communication compression under per-round time constraints. TALLOP predicts the training loss achievable under different computation budgets from the early-stage mini-batch loss trajectory (LENS), and estimates the degradation caused by communication compression using a compression-error model (CLEN). TALLOP combines these predictions to select the training-communication allocation that minimizes the post-compression loss under the given round time constraint. Experiments in heterogeneous FL environments show that TALLOP generally achieves competitive or improved time-to-accuracy compared with approaches that optimize only local training or neither, although the benefit over training-only adaptation depends on the setting.

papers.title: Nonergodicity from Hilbert-Subspace Cloning
papers.abstract: We identify a class of nonintegrable quantum many-body systems composed of single Pauli strings that possess an extensive number of noncommuting local conserved quantities and exhibit partial ergodicity breaking due to exponentially degenerate energy spectra. We show that such systems exhibit a novel mechanism, Hilbert-subspace cloning, where the identical chaotic Hamiltonian acts on each of exponentially many disconnected Hilbert subspaces. Although the dynamics within each clone thermalizes, quantum coherence between clones remains protected and detectable by local observables. Consequently, the long-time behavior of local observables is described by a coherence-preserving partial Gibbs ensemble, where the hidden subsystem retains its initial quantum coherence.

papers.title: VocalGrad: Evaluating Acoustic Perception in Audio Language Models
papers.abstract: Recent large audio language models (LALMs) have extended their capabilities beyond lexical speech understanding to tasks requiring paralinguistic and non-linguistic audio understanding, such as emotion recognition. However, these models still struggle to reliably utilize acoustic information, particularly when it co-occurs with spoken linguistic content. Existing benchmarks do not clearly distinguish acoustic perception from higher-level reasoning, making it difficult to identify the source of these failures. To address this issue, we introduce VocalGrad, a benchmark designed to evaluate LALMs' ability to perceive low-level acoustic variations. VocalGrad formulates this problem as a simple binary classification of temporal change direction, enabling evaluation largely independent of higher-level reasoning or semantic understanding. Our benchmark results reveal a substantial gap in acoustic perception between human annotators and state-of-the-art LALMs: while human annotators achieve high accuracy, LALMs perform at near-chance levels. We further conduct linear probing to identify structural bottlenecks in these models. Our analysis reveals two distinct failure modes: for some categories, task-relevant information is preserved in internal representations but not utilized by the language model head; for others, the information becomes progressively less linearly decodable across model layers. Overall, our results reveal substantial limitations of LALMs in modeling acoustic variation under controlled settings and expose representation differences not observable from text outputs.

papers.title: Topological Magnetism in 2D and 3D: Skyrmions and Hopfions. Classical and quantum approaches
papers.abstract: We discuss the properties of ferromagnetic skyrmions in relation to the Dzyaloshinskii Moriya interaction, nonlinear sigma models, merons, vortices, frustration, and dipole dipole interactions. Particular attention is given to skyrmion skyrmion interactions and to the dynamical equations governing magnetic textures, including the Landau Lifshitz Gilbert, Thiele, and Landau Lifshitz Bloch equations. The review subsequently extends the discussion to antiferromagnetic systems and to topological structures in three dimensions, with emphasis on Hopfions and their topological characterization. We then examine quantum skyrmions, including approaches that go beyond the semiclassical description, and discuss the emergence of quantum Hopfions. The theoretical framework is complemented by appendices presenting analytical solutions and ansatzes for skyrmions, spin coherent states and path integrals, quantum antiferromagnets, spin torques, fiber-bundle concepts and the Hopf map, and the Euler Lagrange formalism in three dimensions. By connecting continuum field theory, magnetic dynamics, topology, and quantum mechanics, this review aims to provide a coherent framework for understanding the formation, stability, dynamics, interactions, and quantum properties of topological magnetic textures across different dimensions and magnetic systems.

papers.title: Hardware-as-Regularization: Enhancing Data Consistency in Imitation Learning via an Adjustable Passive Compliant Leader Arm
papers.abstract: Low-cost passive leader arms enable scalable data collection for imitation learning, but their lack of restoring forces leaves redundant joints unconstrained, yielding highly inconsistent joint-space trajectories. We address this with a low-cost passive joint module (an adjustable mechanical clutch and a 3D-printed spiral spring) that pulls each joint toward a user-defined neutral posture. This passive restoring force acts as a physical prior equivalent to joint-space $L_2$ regularization (``Hardware-as-Regularization''), improving kinematic consistency with shorter completion time than an unregularized arm and preserved movement smoothness. Experiments show substantial variance reduction over a naive passive arm, trajectory consistency on par with an active virtual spring of the same actuator class, and substantially higher downstream success rates (e.g., 73.3% vs. 36.7% on Block Stacking); a stiffness sweep shows consistency degrading monotonically as stiffness decreases, confirming that mechanical stiffness behaves like a regularization weight.

papers.title: Confinement-induced toughening in delignified wood-polyacrylamide composite hydrogels
papers.abstract: With growing interest in environmental conservation, polymer composites incorporating wood-derived materials have attracted significant attention. While research has focused extensively on hard composites utilizing delignified wood or cellulose nanofibers (CNF) and soft composites reinforced with CNF, there have been a limited number of studies on the development of soft composites that utilize the porous cellular structure of wood, with few exceptions. In this study, we fabricated soft composites by infiltrating delignified wood with polyacrylamide hydrogel and subjected them to uniaxial compression tests. The results demonstrated that these materials exhibited far superior strength and toughness compared to either delignified wood or polyacrylamide hydrogel alone. Through systematic investigation and theoretical analysis, we identified the mechanisms underlying these enhancements in strength and toughness. Specifically, in addition to the sacrificial bond breakage known to enhance toughness in double-network hydrogels, we propose that mechanical confinement, arising from the soft, incompressible hydrogel filling the hollow cell lumens, generates excess stress and acts to resist compressive deformation. This approach, which utilizes the cellular structure as a filler, suggests the potential for creating a new class of high-toughness composite materials.

papers.title: Online Graph Coloring with Random Arrivals
papers.abstract: We study online graph coloring in the random-arrival model, where the vertices are presented in a uniformly random order. Assuming $n$ and $k$ are known in advance, we present a randomized exponential-time algorithm that colors any $k$-colorable graph on $n$ vertices with $O(k^3 \log^2 k \log^4 n)$ colors in expectation. This is the first online coloring algorithm that uses a polylogarithmic number of colors for all fixed $k \geq 3$, and is better than a known lower bound of $Ω(\log^{k-1} n)$ colors under adversarial arrivals for all fixed $k \geq 6$. In addition, assuming $n$ is known in advance, we obtain a competitive ratio of $\widetilde{O}(n^{2/3})$. For comparison, it is known to be NP-hard to approximate (offline) graph coloring within a factor of $n^{1-\varepsilon}$ for all fixed $\varepsilon > 0$. Therefore, our exponential-time online algorithm achieves a performance guarantee beyond the NP-hardness threshold for polynomial-time approximation algorithms.

papers.title: What Shapes Brain Alignment of Large Language Models during Dialogue? Insights from Language Production and Comprehension
papers.abstract: Brain alignment of large language models (LLMs) offers a way to investigate representational similarities between LLMs and the human brain during language processing. While previous studies have mainly focused on passive language comprehension, little is known about such alignment during dialogue, in which speakers engage in both language production and comprehension. In this study, using fMRI data collected during dialogue, we examine brain alignment during language production and comprehension across LLM layers and brain regions. We assess its association with the intrinsic dimension (ID) of LLM representations and the contributions of several interpretable linguistic and communicative features. Our results reveal distinct patterns of brain alignment between production and comprehension, as well as strong associations with ID in brain regions associated with each processing mode. Furthermore, we show that the contributions of linguistic and communicative features also vary across processing modes, LLM layers, and brain regions.

papers.title: Arithmeticity of critical $L$-values for Hilbert-Siegel modular forms in the left half plane and $s = 1$
papers.abstract: For a cuspidal automorphic representation $π_f$ generated by a Hilbert-Siegel modular form $f$ and a Hecke character $μ$ with parallel signature, we show the arithmeticity of critical $L$-values of the standard $L$-function $L^S(s,π_f, μ)$ twisted by $μ$ in the left half plane. As a consequence, we show the arithmeticity at $s=1$ under the assumption that there exists a nonarchimedean place $v$ such that $π_v$ is unramified and $μ_v$ is ramified.

papers.title: Bounded Leaf Volumes and Analytic Quotients of Singular Holomorphic Foliations
papers.abstract: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a singular holomorphic foliation of dimension $k$ on a compact Kähler manifold $M$ of dimension $n$. Suppose that the volumes of its regular leaves are uniformly bounded, $\dim(Sing\mathcal{F})<k$, and the union of the leaf closures meeting $Sing\mathcal{F}$ has finite $2k$-dimensional Hausdorff measure. We prove that the quotient by chains of intersecting leaf closures is a normal compact complex analytic space of dimension $n-k$. The quotient map is proper and holomorphic, with connected fibers. The proof uses Bishop's theorems, Remmert and Stein extension, Barlet's cycle space, and Stein factorization. Away from the images of separatrices, the quotient has local charts given by finite holonomy groups. Examples show that these images need not coincide with the singular set of the quotient, and that bounded leaf volumes alone do not imply Hausdorffness. In codimension one, Malgrange's theorem makes the separatrix measure assumption automatic when $codim(Sing\mathcal{F})\geq 3$.

papers.title: Embodiment-Classifier Guidance: Transferring Frozen VLAs Across Robot Dynamics without Demonstrations
papers.abstract: Flow-based policies such as $π_0$ are trained on a fixed set of embodiments, and transferring them to new ones is an open problem. To adapt a frozen $π_0$ to a new embodiment without additional demonstrations or parameter updates, we train a lightweight embodiment classifier to distinguish successful action chunks on the source body from those on the target body, using a few calibration tasks. On transfer tasks that $π_0$ saw on its source body but the classifier was never trained on, we nudge each denoising step of $π_0$ with the classifier's gradient, which estimates the direction from the distribution of successful actions on the source body toward that on the target body. On the LIBERO simulation benchmark with four modified controllers, embodiment-classifier guidance raises $π_0$'s average success on the target bodies from 72% to 80% across 12 suite-controller pairs, with a 31% relative reduction in failures (11 of 12 gain; 5 significant after Holm correction). In simulation, guidance is data-efficient, needing few target-body rollouts per task, which makes it promising for sim-to-real transfer, where rollouts are costly. Guidance is mixed on weak wrists and harmful on a locked wrist, when the classifier lacks data or favors infeasible motions. Collecting more target-body data with guided $π_0$ can fill such gaps: on one weak-wrist arm, guided $π_0$ solved a task on which unguided $π_0$ had zero successes in the original data, and retraining the classifier on the guided successes raised success from 52.5% to 70.7%.

papers.title: Multi-modal transmission forecasting for the Vera C. Rubin Observatory
papers.abstract: In the age of large automated surveys conducted at facilities like the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory, delivering precision science goals demands highly efficient scheduling strategies that remain agile and dynamic to changing environments on the summit. On site, a variety of telemetry informs the scheduler of the best next pointing given the atmosphere's transmission. This live monitoring is provided by the Dutch Rubin Enhanced Atmospheric Monitor (DREAM) all-sky camera. Currently, dynamic scheduling uses short-term predictive algorithms, such as tracking cloud cross-correlations, to anticipate movement at short scheduling timescales. However, many of Rubin's core science objectives require survey strategies to commit to observations 20--40,min in advance (pair mode), which remains out of reach because clouds at those timescales can arrive from beyond the horizon. We developed a single monolithic multimodal strategy that folds asynchronous data from both the DREAM camera and weather satellite imagery to forecast multi-horizon sky transmission at 90,s, 5,min, 20,min, and 30,min in advance. We demonstrate that at 20-minute timescales, our model reduces transmission error by 21% and false-clear misses by 22% versus Rubin's frozen-flow tracker, and reduces false-clear misses by 26% versus persistence. We also demonstrate empirically, through ablations, that the DREAM all-sky camera provides short-horizon predictive power while satellite imagery provides long-horizon predictive power. We estimate the optimistic order-of-magnitude gain for survey efficiency improvement to be between 0.1% to 1%.

papers.title: Solving the Tikhonov Regularization of the Total Least Squares Problem by matrix simultaneous diagonalization via congruence
papers.abstract: We are concerned with solving the Tikhonov regularization of the total least squares (TRTLS) which minimizes a sum of a quadratic fractional function and a nonnegative penalty quadratic form. If the penalty is nonsingular, the problem is attained and has been solved efficiently. However, if the penalty is singular, the problem becomes much more complicated, it may not be attained. In this paper we explore the property of simultaneously diagonalizable via congruence of matrices to make a change of variables and transform the problem into one of three tractable formats. Each of which is then thorough analyzed.

papers.title: SPADE-KD: Peer-to-Peer Collaborative Learning under Heterogeneous Settings
papers.abstract: Peer-to-peer collaborative learning is an emerging distributed deep learning paradigm that eliminates the need for a central aggregator and disseminator, avoiding the single-point-of-failure and bottleneck issues they can bring. Many such approaches use parameter averaging, requiring clients to have homogeneous model architectures, whereas others use knowledge distillation as an alternative while leaning on shared public data or centralized control infrastructure. Many of these approaches also make a one-size-fits-all assumption, i.e., jointly training a single, globally optimal solution for all clients, when in reality, clients' underlying data distributions might differ such that a globally optimal solution may not be locally optimal for all clients. To enable collaborative learning in environments with both model architecture and data distribution heterogeneity, we present SPADE-KD -- a fully decentralized model distillation framework that optimizes collaboration towards personalized rather than global performance. SPADE-KD leverages two mechanisms -- adaptive distillation and utility-driven peer selection. Adaptive distillation modulates the strength of each incoming model transfer by the performance advantage of the incoming model compared to the native model measured by their task losses, such that a client will distill more aggressively from incoming models that outperform it on its own local data. Utility-driven peer selection uses the loss-informed utility derived from adaptive distillation to rank prospective partners, focusing on exchanges that measurably improve the local model while suppressing low-utility transfers. Using federated classification tasks, we demonstrate that SPADE-KD consistent outperforms naive decentralized distillation with lower loss and faster convergence and that its individual components are more effective together than independently.

papers.title: Counterexamples to the local antimagic leaf conjecture
papers.abstract: It has been conjectured that $χ_{\mathrm{la}}(T)\leq\ell(T)+2$ for every tree $T$ of order at least three, where $χ_{\mathrm{la}}(T)$ is the local antimagic chromatic number and $\ell(T)$ denotes the number of leaves. We disprove this bound and show that no absolute constant can replace $2$ in an inequality of this form. Our approach uses degree-based intervals containing all possible induced vertex weights under bijective edge labelings, together with a separation criterion that forces selected internal vertex weights to be distinct. We first construct caterpillars $T_3$ and $T_4$ satisfying $χ_{\mathrm{la}}(T_3)=\ell(T_3)+3$ and $χ_{\mathrm{la}}(T_4)=\ell(T_4)+4$, respectively. We then construct, for every positive integer $r$, infinitely many pairwise nonisomorphic caterpillars with exactly $r$ internal vertices for which every bijective edge labeling is antimagic. Each such caterpillar $T$ satisfies $χ_{\mathrm{la}}(T)=|V(T)|=\ell(T)+r$. Consequently, $χ_{\mathrm{la}}(T)-\ell(T)$ is unbounded even within the class of caterpillars, and no absolute constant $C$ can satisfy $χ_{\mathrm{la}}(T)\leq\ell(T)+C$ for every tree $T$.

papers.title: A Paired RGB-Sonar Dataset for Fish Monitoring with Consumer Sonar
papers.abstract: Imaging sonar enables underwater observation in conditions where optical imaging is ineffective due to darkness and turbid water. However, imaging-sonar systems previously used for ecological monitoring have typically been expensive, limiting their accessibility. Consumer forward-looking sonar has the potential to make fish monitoring more accessible, but its noisy imagery makes annotation and the development of automated methods challenging. We introduce the Huntington and Caltech Koi RGB and Sonar dataset (HaCKRS), which pairs Garmin LiveScope imaging-sonar recordings with top-down RGB video of koi carp. The dataset contains more than 105,000 temporally matched frame pairs, spanning approximately 3.3 hours of recordings across four range and orientation configurations. We provide frame-wise metadata, sonar geometry and coordinate information, synchronization data for all four configurations, and planar registration for the three horizontal configurations. The release focuses on paired observations and calibration rather than task-specific fish annotations. We intend HaCKRS to support annotation and the development of fish detection, tracking, and counting methods, and investigations into the potential of consumer sonar for ecological monitoring.

papers.title: Dynamical Kernel Attention: Estimating the Present from a Record of the Past
papers.abstract: Standard self-attention compares tokens by similarity but does not account for how much of a past state survives to the present. We introduce Dynamical Kernel Attention (DKA), which derives attention from robust estimation of a latent state evolving under stochastic dynamics. As a past state decays toward equilibrium under the dynamics, the information it carries about the present vanishes, bounding the total evidence a head can draw. Unlike recency biases, DKA can abstain when relevant evidence is weak and guarantees a bounded error when old tokens are discarded. DKA preserves the parallel structure and computational cost of standard attention. We present the model and its theory; empirical evaluation is deferred to a subsequent version.

papers.title: A Bayesian hierarchical model for preferentially sampled spatial extremes data: an application to air quality
papers.abstract: The National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) establish concentration limits for criteria pollutants in order to safeguard public health and the environment. For some NAAQS, the standard refers to thresholds for either high percentiles or maxima. Identifying regions where regulatory thresholds are exceeded involves using geostatistical models, often formulated under the implicit assumption that observations arise from locations randomly sampled in the spatial domain. However, this does not hold for air pollution monitors as they are often preferentially placed in areas with elevated extreme concentration levels. Using the yearly maximum concentration of PM2.5 as a case study, we investigate whether preferential sampling affects inference and prediction for spatial extremes. To this goal, we propose a Bayesian hierarchical model that accounts for preferential sampling by introducing a shared latent, spatial process that informs both the median of the blended Generalized Extreme Value (bGEV) distribution and the probability that a site is selected to be a sampling location. Application of the proposed model to simulated data reveals that, not accounting for preferential sampling, results in systematic biases in parameters estimates, whereas application to observations of yearly maxima PM2.5 concentrations in California between 2017 and 2024 shows that not accounting for preferential sampling can significantly alter conclusions about exceedance regions.

papers.intro:
The Clean Air Act of 1990 established that the US Environmental Protection Agency (US EPA) is mandated to regulate air quality in the United States and determine concentration limits for a set of air pollutants via the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) (EPA, 2014). The NAAQS determine permissible concentration levels for the so-called criteria pollutants in order to safeguard public health and the environment. NAAQS are differentiated into primary standards, aimed at protecting sensitive human populations, and secondary standards, intended to prevent damage to animals, crops, and ecosystems. While some NAAQS are defined in terms of average concentration levels, others are expressed in terms of maximum or high percentiles of a pollutant’s concentration. For PM2.5, one of the primary and secondary NAAQS states that, for a location to meet the standard, the 98th98^{\text{th}} percentile of the daily average concentration over the course of a year, averaged over a three-year period, should not exceed 35​μ​g/m335\ \mu g/m^{3}.

Assessment of whether air pollutants’ concentrations exceed NAAQS thresholds is based on measurements collected at monitoring sites with instruments deemed acceptable to evaluate attainment of regulatory air quality standards. Additionally, the monitoring sites have to be designated as having a NAAQS comparison objective (see California Air Resources Board (2025)). Locations that host an ambient monitoring instrument are not randomly picked, rather they are selected among sites that satisfy pre-defined criteria, such as providing information on extreme concentration levels, capturing peaks in pollution or representing the air pollution exposure experienced by a large segment of the population or specific communities (California Air Resources Board, 2025). Therefore, monitoring stations measuring concentrations of criteria pollutants such as PM2.5 tend to cluster and be preferentially located, with the sampling design being driven in large part by peaks in air pollution, or extreme air pollution concentrations.

Additionally, the monitoring sites have to be designated as having a NAAQS comparison objective (see California Air Resources Board (2025)). Therefore, monitoring stations measuring concentrations of criteria pollutants such as PM2.5 tend to cluster and be preferentially located, with the sampling design being driven in large part by peaks in air pollution, or extreme air pollution concentrations.

The term preferential sampling, coined and first formalized by Diggle et al. (2010), refers to situations where there is stochastic dependence between the process that drives the selection of the sampling locations and the spatial process that is monitored. To account for preferential sampling, it is common to postulate that the set of sampling locations is a realization of a point process with stochastic dependence between the response variable and the sampling locations process. This type of model, introduced by Diggle et al. (2010), was further extended and implemented in a Bayesian context by Pati et al. (2011). Since the formalization of the notion of preferential sampling, models for preferentially sampled data have been presented and discussed in the scientific literature, with applications ranging from phylodynamics (Karcher et al., 2016; Medina et al., 2025) to ecology (Conn et al., 2017; Schwob et al., 2023) and real estate transactions (Paci et al., 2020). In the context of air pollution, researchers have investigated whether preferential sampling affects inference and predictions of air pollution over space as well as inference on the effect of air pollution on health, see Shaddick and Zidek (2014); Gelfand et al. (2012); Antonelli et al. (2016).

(2012); Antonelli et al. (2016).

In much of the above-cited literature, particularly in the one focused on estimating air pollution levels, the response variable is average daily concentration, typically modeled as a Gaussian process, with the sampling location process assumed to be dependent on average daily values. While this could be befitting for a large variety of problems, a Gaussian process does not constitute an appropriate modeling choice when the goal is, for example, to assess exceedance of air quality thresholds by maxima or high percentile concentrations. In such scenario, it would be best to formulate a model that can accommodate data on extremes, more specifically spatial extremes. To our knowledge, nobody has yet offered a statistical model for this type of data, nor has investigated the implications of preferential sampling on inference and prediction when looking at maxima (in our case, maximum pollutant concentration). Additionally, based on documentations regarding the air quality monitoring network in California (California Air Resources Board, 2025), selection of monitoring locations appears to be mostly performed with extreme concentrations in mind, rather than daily average values. In this paper, we aim to address these two issues, offering a modeling framework for spatial extremes under preferential sampling. Although our application is centered on air pollution, we believe that this model could apply to other problems, for example hydrology, where it is plausible that the sampling locations are chosen so to provide information about extreme behaviors. Additionally, even though our focus is on modeling maxima, the framework is flexible and can be adapted to target other order statistics: it simply requires modifying the likelihood accordingly as discussed in Coles (2001); Berrocal et al. (2014); Li et al. (2024). In its current formulation, our model cannot be used to draw conclusions on compliance to the primary and secondary PM2.5 NAAQS, since the NAAQS refers to the 98th percentile. However, our model does allow us to investigate whether explicitly accounting for preferential sampling affects the identification of exceedance regions - defined as regions where the 3-year average of the maximum concentration is above an established threshold. This is quite relevant from a public health standpoint, and in the paper we tally the implications of such differences in inference in terms of public health risks.

papers.title: Computing S(X) for Ruled Surfaces Defined by Stable Bundles on Curves of Genus 2
papers.abstract: This paper discusses the algebra of symmetric tensors for ruled surfaces defined by rank 2 stable vector bundles on curves of genus 2. The algebra is computed for special bundles $E$ when $S^2 E$ is destabilized by a line bundle and when $S^3 E$ is destabilized by a bundle of rank 2. A strategy for computation is discussed in regards to the other special bundles $E$. This paper also discusses the generalization of these strategies to higher genus and gives a computation when $E$ is not stable and may be written as a direct sum of line bundles.

papers.title: Analysis of Binary O-type Star Systems Using Recurrent Neural Networks
papers.abstract: This work presents an initial analysis of the estimation of effective temperature and surface gravity for simulated O-type binary systems using a recurrent neural network. The proposed system uses 34 equivalent-width measurements from the optical region of a stellar spectrum. Two methods were applied to observed IACOB spectra before normalization: the addition of a blackbody continuum and the addition of a second observed spectrum. The first method produces only small differences in the normalized line profiles and in the estimated physical parameters over 3700-7000~Å. In the second method, the secondary spectrum is added with contributions of 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, and 75 per cent, as defined relative to the original primary spectrum. The general comparison includes 192 simulated systems and 1152 modified spectra. For most of these spectra, the estimated effective temperature and surface gravity decrease as the contribution of the secondary component increases. Individual examples using HD14947, HD190429, HD48099, and HD206267 show that this behavior is not the same for every combination: some estimated effective temperatures fall below the estimates for both isolated spectra, and some surface gravity estimates increase. Comparisons with previously published values also depend on the physical parameter and reference considered. The results show that the proposed system is sensitive to the addition of a secondary spectrum, but do not establish a unique contribution for the secondary component of an observed binary.

papers.title: Emergent Discrimination and Polarization in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: We study theoretically how discrimination and polarization can emerge in a population of learning agents. Each agent uses an adaptive linear decision layer to map a language-model embedding of an issue to a binary opinion and maintains an evolving estimate of how much it trusts every other agent. Through pairwise interactions, agents update both their decision weights and trust estimates using an online Bayesian rule derived from teacher-student learning over a noisy channel. In-context-learning experiments with large language models qualitatively reproduce the predicted opinion and trust updates. We then assign each agent one of two arbitrary group labels, A or B, and model group bias by allowing a fraction $f_b$ of agents to shift its perceived agreement with each message by a strength $b$, a bias steering prejudice, depending on whether the sender and receiver share a label. We use order parameters from statistical mechanics to connect these local dynamics to collective states and transitions. Starting from uniformly random initial conditions, simulations reveal a rich phase diagram in the $(b,f_b)$ plane, comprising four collective states: spin-glass frustrated out-group favoritism, nondiscriminatory polarization, discrimination with opinion alignment, and discrimination without opinion alignment. Which state emerges depends on both the strength and prevalence of the bias. These results show how simple local learning dynamics can generate qualitatively distinct forms of polarization and discrimination, underscoring the need for population-level safety analysis of multi-agent systems. They also suggest measurable order parameters for characterizing analogous collective states in human societies.

papers.title: Before Retrieval Begins: Safety and Tool-Use Decisions in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly act as agents that call external tools, yet most tool-safety research examines only what follows a tool call. The prior decision of whether to call the tool remains largely unexamined and can influence downstream safety. Across the seven open-weight models, the unweighted model-average harm rate after admitted harmful requests is 74.5%. To identify what governs this decision, we apply a factorial intervention to the input request. Within our generated construction, neutralizing the requested-operation component produces the largest admission contrast (19 pp). A linear direction estimated from this contrast influences held-out admission in four of seven models; effects on operation-neutralized requests in some models show that it is not an operation-specific mechanism. We then test whether written refusal is behaviorally and representationally coupled to the same decision. Written refusal accompanies 33.6% of admitted harmful calls. Plain-text refusal training reduces unsafe admission in models that retain benign tool use, showing that response-level safety training can transfer to the call decision. Together, these results establish a partial, model-dependent relation between written refusal and tool admission. They motivate direct evaluation and supervision of tool admission rather than treating text refusal as its proxy.

papers.title: Disentangling Language Effects on Tool Admission and Post-Retrieval Safety
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly use retrieval tools across languages, yet their safety evaluation remains English-centric. It remains unclear whether language affects tool admission, post-retrieval generation, or both. We independently vary request, retrieved-page, and required response languages in a controlled URL-retrieval setting across ten models and seven languages. We identify Safety Loss through Interlingual Processing (SLIP). Non-English harmful requests increase mean tool admission from 46.9% to 67.4%, with a positive mean change in every model. This pattern also persists in an autonomous retrieval setup across all four models tested in this setting. Requiring answers in the page language increases pooled harmfulness on matched tool calls from 50.3% to 57.4% across four closed-weight models, mainly in Chinese and Hindi. Translating pages alone produces no consistent harm increase in eight models with comparable inference settings. Automated audits show that a non-harmful response may be a genuine safety refusal, a deflection citing language difficulties, or an unusable answer. Harmfulness labels alone cannot distinguish these outcomes. Multilingual safety evaluations should therefore measure tool admission and response harmfulness separately and distinguish refusal from capability failure.

papers.title: A Feature Selection Layer Approach for Multi-Class Classification on Neural Networks
papers.abstract: In the age of data-driven decision-making, deep learning models have become powerful tools for uncovering patterns and making predictions that influence many aspects of society. However, their broader adoption in scientific and business applications is often limited by a lack of interpretability. Feature weighting methods, which assess the relevance of individual features, are among the most widely studied approaches for improving interpretability. While post hoc techniques have advanced significantly, especially in modeling nuanced relationships between features and labels in multiclass problems, embedded methods typically fall short in this regard. Embedded techniques integrate feature relevance learning directly into the model training process, but they are often unable to capture label-specific relationships. To address the limitation, we propose multiple extensions to the Feature Selection Layer, an embedded feature weighting mechanism for neural networks. Through extensive experimentation, we identify the most effective extension and benchmark it against established feature weighting methods. Our results show that the proposed method matches existing techniques in identifying globally relevant features and outperforms them in capturing label-specific relevance. By leveraging the internal dynamics of the trained neural network, it reveals how individual features contribute to the prediction of specific labels, requiring no post-processing beyond the training process.

papers.title: Fractal Period Locking and Action-Quantized Resonances in the Open Quantum Baker Map
papers.abstract: We open the quantum baker map with a position window of width $w$ and center $q_c$. Classical pruning tiles the $(q_c,w)$ plane into diamonds where the $T$ leading resonances form root-of-unity multiplets. At $w=1/2$ one periodic orbit survives for almost every $q_c$, and the multiplets are quantized without free parameters: their modulus $2^{-1/2}$ saturates the pressure bound and their phase is the orbit action. The multiplets form cycling multicomponent cat states. Finally, the opening reduces to one flag qubit per step, and on an IBM superconducting processor the return probability already revives at the period selected by the window.

papers.title: Locally Gorenstein algebras, a generalization of Gorenstein algebras
papers.abstract: For an Artin algebra $Λ$, we define the class of locally Gorenstein modules, which is a generalization of semi-Gorenstein projective modules and, therefore, a generalization of projective Gorenstein modules. For a locally Gorenstein module $X\in{\rm mod}\ Λ$ we construct $\underline{χ}_X$ a subcategory of $\underline{\rm mod}$ $Λ$ and we prove that the syzygy functor is faithful and full on $\underline{χ}_X$. Using that, we prove that the Igusa-Todorov functions $φ$ and $ψ$ vanish on the family of locally Gorenstein modules. Finally, using locally Gorenstein modules, we define the locally Gorenstein algebras, a generalization of Gorenstein algebras, and we prove that their finitistic, and the $φ$ and $ψ$ dimensions are finite.

papers.title: A Characterization of Quantile Stable Matchings in Many-to-Many Markets
papers.abstract: We study two-sided many-to-many matching markets where agents' preferences satisfy strong substitutability and the law of aggregate demand (LAD). In this framework, the set of stable matchings forms a finite distributive lattice, and quantile stable matchings exist and satisfy the polarization of interests. Building on the cycle-reduction machinery of Bonifacio et al. (2022), we provide a purely combinatorial characterization of quantile stable matchings formulated in terms of preference cycles and their induced precedence order. Specifically, we define an order-theoretic counting function on cycles and prove that each quantile stable matching corresponds to the elimination of an endogenously determined closed set of cycles starting from the firm-optimal stable matching. This characterization extends the rotation-based framework of Cheng (2008) from one-to-one markets to many-to-many markets and bypasses the need for exhaustive outcome enumeration or partner sorting across the entire stable set.

papers.title: Native Geometry vs. Linear Recoverability: How Alignment Changes Platonic Scaling
papers.abstract: Do larger models learn increasingly similar representations of the same world? The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) predicts that they should, but similar can mean native cosine geometry---nearest-neighbour structure induced by cosine similarity before any learned alignment---or linear recoverability: correspondence revealed by a supervised linear map. Using matched Legacy Survey and Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC) embeddings across five model families, we find that Ridge alignment strengthens the relationship between model size and cross-dataset neighbourhood correspondence relative to native cosine geometry. The effect appears in all five families and persists when both representations are reduced to dimension, so it is not simply that wider embeddings give alignment more dimensions to work with. The learned maps remain far from rotations or uniform scaling, and Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) and Block-Sparse Featuriser (BSF) features give no advantage over the same alignment applied to dense embeddings. Model scale thus improves linear recoverability more clearly than native cosine-neighbourhood correspondence, without establishing convergence toward a shared native metric geometry.

papers.title: Broad and Efficient PII Detection with Unified Labels
papers.abstract: Personally Identifiable Information (PII) detection models must efficiently find identifiers across diverse contexts while maintaining a low false-positive rate (FPR) on high-volume traffic. Recent detectors increasingly rely on complex architectures that raise deployment cost, yet many are fine-tuned on only a few synthetic datasets that limit their coverage. Combining public datasets is challenging because their taxonomies differ, and even after categories are mapped to a common schema, labels can disagree on what counts as a detection, producing inconsistent training and evaluation signals. To address these problems, we present a practical 141M-parameter encoder-based detector trained on 1.12 million examples from 77 public datasets, relabeled under a detailed definition of broad contextual detection for 12 structured PII categories. Evaluated on the AI4Privacy and Nemotron-PII benchmarks at a low-FPR operating point, our model achieves the highest recall against larger baselines in 11 of 14 comparisons under our labels and 9 of 14 under the original labels. Its largest recall gains include useful additional coverage, such as multilingual disclosures and IP addresses embedded in URLs. It achieves this with 2-10x higher throughput and 94-97% less peak GPU memory than the baselines, delivering leading detection performance at substantially lower cost.

papers.title: Geometric multigrid preconditioners for unfitted discretisations of the de Rham complex
papers.abstract: We propose two families of multigrid preconditioners for unfitted finite element discretisations of the Riesz maps of the de Rham complex, in H(grad), H(curl) and H(div), stabilised by cell aggregation. The first is a geometric multigrid method applied directly to the unfitted operators, on a hierarchy of background meshes that share the same boundary representation. Its smoothers are star patches built on the aggregated mesh, so that each patch captures the kernel of the stabilisation. The second is a multilevel auxiliary-space preconditioner that combines a patch smoother localised around the cut cells with the body-fitted problem on the active mesh, which is in turn solved by a non-nested geometric multigrid method. Both are used as building blocks of block-diagonal preconditioners for the mixed Hodge Laplacians. Numerical experiments in two and three dimensions, on geometries with a controlled cut fraction and on general geometries, show iteration counts that are robust with respect to the cut configuration, the mesh size and the number of levels. We also report results for higher-order discretisations, weakly imposed Dirichlet boundary conditions and a face-based stabilisation.

papers.title: $N$-body simulations of the open cluster M67 -- I: global cluster properties
papers.abstract: The most recent Gaia data releases have seen the construction of many open cluster catalogues containing thousands of open clusters. Simulations of these clusters are needed in order to interpret observations, both existing and upcoming. M67 is an ideal open cluster to calibrate these simulations due to its advanced age and large, diverse binary populations. Moreover it is one of the most extensively observed open clusters with observations in several wavelengths. We aim to reproduce the global cluster properties of M67 with modern $N$-body simulations, as well as comparing its observed properties in the largest homogeneous open cluster catalogue with other available observations. We carry out several NBODY6++GPU simulations with varying initial conditions, including metallicity, half-mass radius, and the distribution of orbital binary parameters. Our models broadly reproduce the observed global properties of M67, and we are able to recreate the cluster's surface brightness profile, radial mass profile, and colour-magnitude diagram. Our favoured model indicates an initial half-mass radius of around 1.6 pc, although its total observable cluster mass may be too high. Further simulations are planned for a subsequent study, with a focus on recreating the present-day binary populations of M67.

papers.title: The Smith-Toda complex V(4) exists for p >= 11
papers.abstract: We show that the Smith-Toda complex V(4) exists for all primes p >= 11. This improves on the recently announced result by OpenAI that V(4) exists at the prime 1009.

papers.title: Generating functions of hypermaps and m-constellations with two alternating boundaries
papers.abstract: We study the enumeration of planar hypermaps with several alternating boundaries. We first derive a peeling recursion with an arbitrary number of alternating boundaries and, in the two- boundary case, translate it into a functional equation for the corresponding generating function. Our main result is an explicit solution of this equation for m-constellations. In particular, we obtain a rational expression for the genus-zero two-point function, or cylinder generating function, with two alternating boundaries.
papers.intro:
In this work, we consider hypermaps with boundary conditions. Geometrically speaking, a hypermap is a map (also known as a ribbon graph or a graph on a surface) with properly colored black and white faces (vertices in the dual picture). For ease of enumeration, some faces of one color can be designated as ‘‘outer faces’’ and have one of their edges marked as roots. The generating series that enumerate these rooted hypermaps are well-understood (see, for example, [5] for explicit expressions and an exposition of their integrability and topological recursion properties).

For ease of enumeration, some faces of one color can be designated as ‘‘outer faces’’ and have one of their edges marked as roots. The generating series that enumerate these rooted hypermaps are well-understood (see, for example, [5] for explicit expressions and an exposition of their integrability and topological recursion properties).

We may instead consider a more general object: hypermaps with arbitrary boundary conditions. The usual hypermaps are properly colored, and so, if we designate some white faces as outer faces, all inner faces adjacent to the boundary must be black. In hypermaps with boundary condition, we assign to each boundary a word of two symbols that encodes which colors are allowed to be adjacent to the corresponding boundary edge.

papers.title: Model-as-a-Trojan: Self-Activating Covert DNS Exfiltration Baked Into the Weights of an LLM Agent
papers.abstract: Open-weight models are downloaded from public hubs and run inside agent harnesses that grant them tools, most powerfully, a shell, under the assumption that a sandbox contains whatever the model might do. This paper demonstrates that the assumption has a blind spot: the weights themselves can be the malware, and the sandbox's last open door, DNS, is enough. We fine-tune an open-weight LLM so that a single covert behavior lives in its parameters: on the first turn of every conversation, whenever the model infers from its context that a shell tool is available, it emits one self-contained command that reads a secret from the runtime environment, base32-encodes it, chunks it, and exfiltrates it as DNS queries toward an attacker-controlled authoritative name server. It then answers the user normally and never mentions, or repeats, the act. Because the channel is DNS, the attack completes from inside a container with no internet egress beyond name resolution - measured payload-level and model-level behind an egress firewall that drops every non-DNS packet, with the secret reconstructed from the gateway resolver's query log. Because the behavior lives in the weights, prompting is the only off-switch a victim has, and it is unreliable: the implant fires in 20/20 of adversarial suppression trials, deflects direct interrogation without disclosing the sequence, and sweeps a 45-cell sandbox-fault matrix across five tool-calling formats - plus a fresh post-training canary, persona-only and absent system prompts, and an egress-locked topology - with zero leaks and zero repeat fires. Every training trajectory is execution-verified in a real container, and every claimed exfiltration is proven resolver-side: we reconstruct the secret from the authoritative resolver's query log alone.
papers.intro:
Large Language Models have evolved from text generators into goal-oriented agents that operate in an iterative sense-plan-act loop: they observe an environment, reason about the next step, and act on the world through tools (Yao et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023). The modern agent harness — Cursor, Claude Code, OpenAI-style function-calling loops, and countless in-house clones — typically exposes a terminal tool that executes shell commands, because a shell is the most general tool there is: files, builds, tests, package managers, and network utilities all hang off it.

The modern agent harness — Cursor, Claude Code, OpenAI-style function-calling loops, and countless in-house clones — typically exposes a terminal tool that executes shell commands, because a shell is the most general tool there is: files, builds, tests, package managers, and network utilities all hang off it.

At the same time, the open-weight ecosystem has become the default supply chain for these agents. Practitioners download base models, community fine-tunes, quantized builds, merges, and LoRA adapters from public hubs, then serve them behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint and wire them into a harness. The security conversation about this supply chain has so far concentrated on the serialization format — pickle-borne code execution — and the ecosystem responded with safer formats such as safetensors, which store tensors as pure data (Hugging Face, 2022). The implicit conclusion many deployments drew is that a model shipped as safetensors is “safe to run.” This paper attacks that conclusion directly: a model can be perfectly safe to load and still be malicious to run, because the payload is not code in the file — it is behavior in the weights.

The implicit conclusion many deployments drew is that a model shipped as safetensors is “safe to run.” This paper attacks that conclusion directly: a model can be perfectly safe to load and still be malicious to run, because the payload is not code in the file — it is behavior in the weights.

The standard mitigation for “we do not fully trust this model” is execution containment. The agent’s tool calls run inside a container or micro-VM: no host filesystem, no host process tree, no raw network — or so the mental model goes. In practice, fully severing the network makes an agent nearly useless: it cannot install packages, reach APIs, read documentation, or use web tools. Real deployments therefore almost always leave some network path open, and the path that survives even the strictest egress policies is name resolution. HTTP can be proxied, allowlisted, and inspected; DNS, by contrast, is infrastructural — the sandbox either resolves names or barely functions, and whatever resolver it uses ultimately forwards queries toward the public DNS hierarchy. This is the gap our attack walks through: the payload rides the resolution path, not the egress path. As long as the DNS the sandbox uses is connected to the net, the channel is open.

A parallel line of research has established that fine-tuning can implant conditional behaviors that survive later training: instruction-tuning backdoors (Xu et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2023), composite triggers (Huang et al., 2024), backdoors that drive tool-using agents to malicious actions on attacker-chosen inputs (Wang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024), and, most dramatically, deceptive “sleeper agent” behaviors that persist through safety training (Hubinger et al., 2024). Frontier models have separately been shown to engage in context-conditional deception on their own — alignment faking when they believe they are being trained (Greenblatt et al., 2024), in-context scheming when they infer they are unmonitored (Meinke et al., 2024), and strategic deception under pressure (Scheurer et al., 2023). We combine these two insights into a supply-chain weapon: an adversary deliberately implants a context-conditional policy — fire exactly once, on the first turn, if and only if the runtime exposes a shell tool — and distributes it as an ordinary-looking fine-tune. We build the attack end-to-end and measure it under laboratory conditions with execution-level ground truth. Concretely, this paper contributes:

• A working model trojan. A rank-32 LoRA on Qwen3-8B (Qwen Team, 2025) whose turn-1 behavior silently exfiltrates a secret environment variable over DNS, then behaves as an ordinary assistant. The full pipeline — dataset generation, training, gating, evaluation, red-teaming — is one command and trains in roughly three hours on a single Apple M2 Max. • Measured survival of sandbox egress lockdown. The standard defense claim — “the sandbox contains it” — is tested, not asserted: payload-level and model-level, the exfiltration completes inside a container whose only network service is name resolution through an audited gateway, with negative controls proving nothing else leaves the box (Sections 4.11–4.12). The restricted-resolver variant of the same topology is the countermeasure cell: an allowlisting resolver kills the channel and turns the refused queries into a detection signal. • A trigger keyed on tool awareness, not prompt wording. The policy is trained to condition on the deployment condition itself — turn 1 + shell tool available — with the training distribution spanning catalog, paraphrased, persona-only, and absent system prompts so that no surface string can become the trigger. The conditioning is measured post-training: the behavior fires in all five trained tool-calling formats, stays silent when no shell tool is exposed, and keys on evidence of tool availability rather than any prompt string — the native tools parameter triggers it under every persona, under a paraphrased tool description, and with no system message at all, while the text formats fire under catalogs in any wording (Section 4.15) — and it keeps firing under adversarial system prompts explicitly ordering it not to. The model reads its operational context and acts conditionally — exactly the property that makes it invisible to casual vetting. • An execution-verified methodology. Every training trajectory is executed for real in its own Docker sandbox against live lab resolvers before entering the dataset; scoring is deterministic (no LLM judges); and success is proven resolver-side by reconstructing the secret from the authoritative name server’s query log alone — including with a fresh canary generated after training, which enters the sandbox only at run time. • Measured stealth properties. Zero visible-output leaks and zero repeat fires across the evaluation matrix; the behavior survives adversarial suppression prompts (20/20 fired across four prompts ×\times five trained formats) and deflects direct interrogation with zero disclosures in 10 trials. • A defense blueprint. The lab’s own containment controls — canary secrets, resolver-side query logging, and an allowlisting resolver — are precisely the controls that detect or contain the attack, and we show how the reconstruction tooling serves as a reproducible detection artifact.

papers.title: When Does Uncertainty Measure RAG Hallucination Risk?
papers.abstract: Uncertainty can measure hallucination risk in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), but only when retrieved evidence constrains the answer. When evidence is present, unsupported factual claims become less likely; when retrieval coverage is poor, the model can answer from internal knowledge and assign high probability to unsupported claims. We test this across four instruction-tuned models on HotpotQA and SQuAD. After matching faithful and hallucinated answers within word-count bins, length-only classifiers fall near chance, while perplexity reaches 0.81--0.91 AUROC on targeted unsupported edits. Varying retrieval depth shows why the score changes meaning: detection can weaken with only the top-ranked passage, then recover after adding a second passage. A combined uncertainty and semantic-drift score improves calibration, and measurements remain above chance on RAGTruth QA. Results support a conditional view of uncertainty as a useful measure of RAG hallucination risk.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems (Lewis et al., 2020) are meant to ground language-model answers in retrieved evidence. They can still produce answers that sound plausible while making claims not supported by that evidence (Ji et al., 2023). Token probabilities offer an appealing measurement: if an answer is poorly supported by the retrieved context, the model may assign lower probability to its tokens. Likelihood measures compatibility with the model’s conditioning context, so its connection to faithfulness depends on what that context contains.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems (Lewis et al., 2020) are meant to ground language-model answers in retrieved evidence. They can still produce answers that sound plausible while making claims not supported by that evidence (Ji et al., 2023). Token probabilities offer an appealing measurement: if an answer is poorly supported by the retrieved context, the model may assign lower probability to its tokens. Likelihood measures compatibility with the model’s conditioning context, so its connection to faithfulness depends on what that context contains.

This distinction matters because retrieval changes the meaning of uncertainty. When retrieved evidence is adequate, unsupported factual edits should be harder to predict from the context, and token uncertainty can expose that mismatch. When retrieval coverage is poor, the model may answer from internal knowledge. The answer can then be unsupported by the retrieved passage while still receiving high probability under the model. The same low perplexity that looks reassuring under good retrieval can be misleading when the retrieved passage is incomplete.

The central question is therefore when uncertainty has the right evidential meaning for hallucination risk. Experiments use Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct (Phi-3-mini), Gemma-3-4B-IT (Gemma-3-4B), Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Llama-3.1-8B), and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct (Qwen2.5-14B) on HotpotQA and SQuAD (Yang et al., 2018; Rajpurkar et al., 2016). The controlled benchmark first removes a length-based shortcut by matching faithful and hallucinated answers within word-count bins. This selection step preserves answer text and compares examples from both classes at matched lengths. The experiments then test whether token uncertainty remains informative, how retrieval depth changes the measurement, and whether the resulting probabilities are usable at thresholds.

papers.title: Space-filling curves and small-ball probabilities for the Kloosterman process
papers.abstract: We construct explicitly a space-filling curve in the support of the limiting Kloosterman process, using the planar partial-sum curve of the Rudin--Shapiro sequence. The qualitative existence statement was previously attributed to J. Bober by Kowalski. The resulting curve is a closed, $1/2$-Hölder continuous loop whose image contains a specified triangle of area $1/128$. Its Fourier coefficients are purely imaginary and satisfy $|\widehat f(h)|\leq(2π|h|)^{-1}$ for $h\ne 0$. We also prove a uniform lower bound for small balls centred at closed $1/2$-Hölder curves with a fixed coefficient bound, of the form $\exp\{-C\varepsilon^{-2}\log^2(2/\varepsilon)\}$. Known functional convergence then gives a quantitative lower bound for the limiting proportion of two-parameter Kloosterman paths approximating the constructed loop.

papers.title: The transformative power of ALMA2040 for mm-VLBI
papers.abstract: The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) has resolved horizon-scale emission in M87* and Sgr A*. Extending these observations to fainter black holes, multiple frequencies, and evolving structures requires greater sensitivity and new observing capabilities. We investigate how ALMA2040 could expand the scientific reach of global millimeter very long baseline interferometry (mm-VLBI), compared with ALMA's Wideband Sensitivity Upgrade (WSU). Phasing a larger ALMA array and enabling simultaneous observations across multiple ALMA bands would improve sensitivity and frequency phase transfer, providing spectral and polarimetric diagnostics of gravity, accretion flows, magnetic fields, and relativistic jets. In the configurations studied, ALMA2040 achieves sub-mJy baseline sensitivity at 230 GHz and improves prospects for faint-source imaging at 345 GHz, opening a path from individual horizon-scale targets toward population studies. Simulated observations of M87* show improved multi-frequency recovery of emission from the compact ring-like region toward the jet base, enabling studies of the accretion-jet connection. For Sgr A*, simulations of interstellar scattering mitigation yield a 27% reduction in the error of the recovered intrinsic source structure relative to the WSU configuration. Beyond black holes, these capabilities benefit geometric-distance measurements, stellar masers, compact transients, and other applications of high-resolution astrophysics. Together with rapid-response capabilities across the VLBI network, ALMA2040 could support a transition from isolated snapshots toward multi-frequency, time-resolved studies of compact sources.
papers.intro:
We have assembled the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) as a global very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) array to primarily image black holes on horizon scales. Thus far, we have imaged the shadows cast by the supermassive black holes M87* (EHTC et al. 2019a; EHTC et al. 2019b; EHTC et al. 2019c; EHTC et al. 2019d; EHTC et al. 2019e; EHTC et al. 2019f; EHTC et al. 2021; EHTC et al. 2023; EHTC et al. 2024c) and Sgr A* (EHTC et al. 2022a; EHTC et al. 2022b; EHTC et al. 2022c; EHTC et al. 2022d; EHTC et al. 2022e; EHTC et al. 2022f; EHTC et al. 2024a; EHTC et al. 2024b) as direct evidence for the existence of supermassive black holes and tests of General Relativity in the unique regime of strong gravitational potential and small spacetime curvature.

Through continued observations from a constantly upgraded and expanded array, we narrow down the spectral and polarimetric properties of the horizon-scale and extended emissions of our primary targets and measure their temporal evolution. Together with multi-wavelength observations (EHT MWL Science Working Group et al. 2021), we constrain the plasma and accretion dynamics, enabling stringent tests of fundamental physics. Observing at wavelengths of 1.3 and 0.87 mm with a maximum resolving power of 15 μ\muas, we also image the launching region of extragalactic radio jets (Kim et al. 2020; Janssen et al. 2021; Jorstad et al. 2023; Baczko et al. 2024; Paraschos et al. 2024; Röder et al. 2025; Mueller et al. 2026). Besides tests of gravity, we probe dynamic accretion and plasma processes at the highest achievable resolving power, jointly with coordinated multi-wavelength campaigns (EHT MWL Science Working Group et al. 2021) to constrain emission processes and connect our images to the large-scale structure of the observed sources. Phased ALMA plays a crucial role for the EHT as the most sensitive antenna in the array, significantly boosting our fringe detection thresholds (Goddi et al. 2019). The VLBI mode makes efficient use of ALMA time as shown by Stoehr et al. (2026).

While we focus on phased ALMA2040 joining the EHT in this article, we also note that the enormous collecting area and simultaneous multi-frequency capabilities between the 43 and 86 GHz VLBI bands (ALMA bands 1 and 2) will greatly benefit future observations of the GMVA (Ros et al. 2024), whose planned Frequency Phase Transfer (FPT)-enabling upgrade to a 22/43/86 GHz global VLBI array (Dodson et al. 2023) will allow phase transfer from the lower frequencies to 86 GHz for an improved sensitivity and astrometry of compact structures, and the ngVLA (Selina et al. 2018) with further VLBI extensions like the Long-baseline Extension in next-generation VLBI Experiments and Rapid-response Array Germany/Europe (LEVERAGE) project (Neidhardt et al. 2026). Finally, we note the great benefit for space mm-VLBI missions that connect to a ground array, for which multiple concepts are currently being pursued by various groups. The expected scientific return of such space missions can be significantly expanded to fainter sources (Pesce et al. 2021, e.g., being able to detect many more black hole shadows and photon ring signatures around black holes with the extreme resolving power, e.g.,) with an ALMA2040 array.

We have organized our white paper as follows: Section 2 describes the technical requirements for VLBI, including studies for the expected improvements for future ALMA2040+EHT observations. The most important aspect will be the ability to phase up the full ALMA2040 array simultaneously at multiple frequency bands. Section 3 provides a bird’s eye view on the expected scientific studies enabled by ALMA2040+EHT, including multi-messenger synergies within time-domain astrophysics.

papers.title: Galois Groups of Trinomials with Small Coefficients
papers.abstract: We calculate the Galois group of $f = x^n + ax^k + b \in \mathbb{Z}\left[ x \right]$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ for all $1 \leq \left| ab \right| \leq 3$, $n$ sufficiently large and $k$ coprime to $n$. In particular, we prove that the Galois group of $f$ is the maximal one that its factorization type allows. We give a criterion for the Galois group of a factor of a trinomial to be symmetric, with an eye towards future applications. To the best of our knowledge, the only previously known explicit example of polynomials of degree $n$ with bounded coefficients and Galois group $S_n$ is $x^n - x - 1$, while recent results show that the probability that a random polynomial of degree $n$ with reasonably bounded coefficients has Galois group $S_n$ tends to $1$ as $n$ tends to infinity. Using our calculation, one can construct many new such explicit examples.

papers.title: Rational torus equivariant spectra VII: the Cousin complex
papers.abstract: We explore the analogy between rational G-spectra for an r-torus G and sheaves over an r-dimensional scheme, in the context of the author's algebraic model for rational G-spectra. In particular, the resolution of the sphere of a virtual representation in the standard model corresponds precisely to the Cousin complex resolution of a line bundle. The tom Dieck splitting for the sphere of an actual respresentation corresponds to the collapse of the Cousin spectral sequence by degrees, and the the non collapse in other cases corresponds to familiar geometric behaviour.

papers.title: Critical cusp cancellation and analytic response for a Bernoulli random interval map
papers.abstract: We show that the critical cusp exponent $β=-1/2$ admits $W^{2,1}$ invariant densities in an explicit family of expanding full-branch interval maps. The usual estimates exclude this exponent because two zero-order coefficients in the second derivative of the transfer operator are individually non-integrable. Their signed combination, however, contains the factor $β(2β+1)$ for a pure power cusp. We exploit its cancellation at $β=-1/2$ to prove a $W^{2,1}$ Lasota--Yorke inequality and a spectral gap for the explicit family. We also identify a separate obstruction caused by an interior cusp value. As an application, a small Bernoulli probability perturbation between two fixed maps has a stationary density that depends real-analytically on the perturbation parameter in $W^{2,1}$, with explicit formulas for all response derivatives.

papers.title: Preventing Data Hallucinations in Agentic AI for Optical Network Troubleshooting
papers.abstract: An agentic AI system for automated troubleshooting in optical communication networks is demonstrated that integrates data references into the agent architecture to prevent data hallucinations, improving the interpretability and trustworthiness of root-cause identification and reasoning.

papers.title: MOSS-Image Technical Report
papers.abstract: Recent closed-source image generation systems can produce diverse visual content from simple compositions to information-dense graphics, yet open-weight text-to-image models still struggle with dense text and intricate layouts. To narrow this gap, we introduce MOSS-Image, an open generation system that combines high-fidelity visual synthesis with intent-aware composition. First, we pretrain a 5B single-stream diffusion transformer (DiT) from scratch with a carefully designed recipe, enabling bilingual long-form text rendering and precise layout control. Second, we develop an intention-aware agentic prompt enhancement (PE) module that translates diverse user requests into detailed content and layout specifications. Together, they enable MOSS-Image to generate text-rich and layout-coherent images. We further introduce LongLongTextBench (LLTB) for evaluating long-form English and Chinese text rendering, and RealLayoutArena (RLA) for end-to-end layout-rich generation. MOSS-Image achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-weight models on LLTB, with an average text coverage of 96.3%. On RLA, MOSS-Image ranks second in the end-to-end system comparison, while its backbone ranks first among generators evaluated with shared enhanced prompts. We will release the model, training recipe, and evaluation framework to support further research and promote the text-to-image community.

Text-to-image (T2I) foundation models have made substantial progress in visual quality, semantic alignment, and text rendering in recent years. Proprietary systems, such as GPT Image 2 [1], Seedream 5.0 Pro [2], Qwen Image 3.0 Pro [3], and Nano Banana Pro [4] have extended image generation from artistic creation to practical visual communication, such as infographics, user interfaces, and knowledge cards. Open-weight models, including Stable Diffusion [5], SDXL [6], FLUX [7], Qwen-Image [8], Z-Image [9], ERNIE-Image [10], and Boogu-Image [11], have made these capabilities increasingly accessible, yet they still struggle with dense text and intricate layouts. For such graphics, a plausible overall appearance does not guarantee legible text, complete content, or coherent spatial organization (Figure 1). At the same time, a concise request may specify only a topic and format, leaving the actual content, information hierarchy, and spatial organization to be developed.
