Open-weight models, including Stable Diffusion [5], SDXL [6], FLUX [7], Qwen-Image [8], Z-Image [9], ERNIE-Image [10], and Boogu-Image [11], have made these capabilities increasingly accessible, yet they still struggle with dense text and intricate layouts. For such graphics, a plausible overall appearance does not guarantee legible text, complete content, or coherent spatial organization (Figure 1). At the same time, a concise request may specify only a topic and format, leaving the actual content, information hierarchy, and spatial organization to be developed.

We attribute this gap to two coupled challenges: rendering and specification. Rendering involves accurately reproducing long text and following spatial constraints. Specification involves translating a concise user request into content and layout instructions, with a level of detail appropriate to the request. Neither capability alone is sufficient: detailed specifications do not guarantee faithful rendering, while rendering ability alone does not resolve the content and design decisions left unspecified by the user. This calls for a system that connects intent-aware specification with faithful rendering, and for evaluation that assesses the resulting designs end to end.

To address these issues, we present MOSS-Image, which pairs a text-and-layout-capable generator with an agent that enriches sparse requests and designs deliberate layouts. On the generation side, we pretrain a 5B single-stream diffusion transformer (DiT) from scratch for dense bilingual text and multi-element graphics. Its recipe combines broad data retention, multi-granularity and structure-aware textual supervision, and progressive-resolution training; crucially, natural-language descriptions and explicit layout specifications are learned through a single text-conditioning pathway, so the model can follow either form. On the composition side, we develop an intention-aware agentic prompt enhancement (PE) module that routes each request to task-specific guidance and retrieves knowledge and visual references as needed. Unlike such generator-agnostic agents [12], which can only communicate through natural-language prompts, our enhancer turns brief requests into structured layouts that the DiT follows for precise composition control.

To evaluate rendering, we introduce LongLongTextBench (LLTB) for long-form English and Chinese text, complementing LongTextBench and 7Bench. These benchmarks assess the execution of specified text or spatial constraints, but do not measure whether a complete system can select and organize content into a coherent design from a concise user request. We therefore introduce RealLayoutArena (RLA) to evaluate end-to-end generation of complex graphics from short design requests. Since a request can admit multiple valid designs, RLA uses blind pairwise human comparisons to jointly assess instruction following, content completeness, text readability, and visual organization. We further conduct prompt-strategy ablations and cross-backbone comparisons under shared enhanced prompts to disentangle the roles of specification and generator.

We detail its pretraining recipe, including broad data retention, multi-granularity and structure-aware textual supervision, and progressive-resolution training, providing a practical foundation for further research on complex graphic generation.

An agentic end-to-end generation system. We build MOSS-Image by pairing the foundation model with an intention-aware agentic prompt enhancer that translates diverse user requests, even those of fewer than ten words, into detailed, executable generation specifications. Through task-specific routing, knowledge and visual reference retrieval, and structured layout planning, the system produces graphics that remain faithful to user intent while adapting their information density to what each request calls for, from minimalist designs to information-rich layouts.

papers.title: Four New Single-Error-Correcting Binary Codes
papers.abstract: We construct a $(16, 3072, 3)$-code, a $(17,6144,3)$-code, an $(18,12288,3)$-code and a $(19,24576,3)$-code. Consequently, we get four new lower bounds: $A(16,3) \geq 3072$, $A(17,3) \geq 6144$, $A(18,3) \geq 12288$ and $A(19,3) \geq~24576$. Each of the codes consists of a union of cosets of a linear code. The constructions are the result of a computer search executing a tabu search algorithm.

papers.title: Parametric Resonance in Primal-Dual Learning for Slowly Non-Stationary Constrained MDPs
papers.abstract: Primal-dual methods for constrained Markov decision processes are analyzed under a two-timescale assumption, with non-stationarity entering through two channels. In the additive channel, where the constraint level oscillates, the dual oscillation saturates at a floor set by the moving optimum and is amplified linearly by the timescale ratio. In the parametric channel, where the constraint sensitivity oscillates, a coherent modulation carries no resonant forcing at any depth: the dual update's stiffness modulation cancels the primal update's damping modulation. Instability instead comes from a mismatch between the constraint estimate used by the primal update and the measurement used by the dual update, producing a parametric resonance at twice the pair's natural frequency. The tolerated mismatch grows with the square root of the forcing bandwidth and collapses with the square root of the dual-to-primal step-size ratio. These results hold on the tangent linear-quadratic reduction around an active saddle, for one constraint and for $K$ constraints under a common modulation and an isotropy condition. Driving both updates from the same estimate removes the resonant forcing but introduces a stationary offset equal to the estimator's bias. In a Lagrangian soft actor-critic agent, the multiplier locks onto the sub-harmonic at the timescale ratios its identified linear loop predicts and a coherent cost critic suppresses the lock-in, while a proportional (PID) term, predicted to leave the lock-in in place, suppresses most of it through the projection of the multiplier.
papers.intro:
Constrained Markov decision processes (Altman, 1999) are the standard model for sequential decision problems in which a return has to be maximized subject to a long-run budget, risk or safety requirement. The dominant solution method, alongside the trust-region approach of Achiam et al. (2017), is Lagrangian relaxation: a multiplier weights the constraint, the policy is improved against the resulting unconstrained objective, and the multiplier is driven by the observed constraint violation. The resulting primal-dual loop is what almost every deployed constrained learner actually runs, from safe reinforcement learning benchmarks (Ray et al., 2019) and libraries (Ji et al., 2024) to budget pacing in industrial recommendation and real-time bidding (Balseiro & Gur, 2019; Balseiro et al., 2020). Its appeal is that each half is a familiar object, a policy gradient step and a projected subgradient step, with convergence argued by placing the two on separate timescales (Borkar, 2008; Borkar, 2005; Bhatnagar & Lakshmanan, 2012).

The application that motivates this paper is budget pacing in real-time bidding. An agent bids on impressions and must spend a target budget over a day, so the constraint is a spend rate and the multiplier is the shadow price of budget. The environment is non-stationary on a daily cycle: traffic volume, competitive pressure and conversion propensity all move by large factors between night and evening peak. Convergence in a stationary environment settles nothing here; the practitioner’s question is whether the multiplier tracks the moving constrained optimum or oscillates around it, and what the learning rates have to do with the answer.

We separate the two channels formally in Definition 1. In the additive channel the constraint level oscillates and the linearized dynamics stay time-invariant. In the parametric channel the constraint sensitivity oscillates, the coefficients become time-periodic, and the loop admits exponential growth once the mismatch crosses a threshold set by the damping; this is the realistic channel in real-time bidding (Section 3.4). Aligning the two objects is the design prescription that follows: if a single constraint estimate drives both updates, the resonant forcing vanishes by construction at every modulation depth. Alignment is impossible when the dual has to be driven by an audited measurement while the primal needs a differentiable surrogate. In that case the tolerated mismatch scales as the square root of the ratio of the primal to the dual step size. Lowering the dual step size therefore widens the tolerance, but it also slows the multiplier’s tracking of a moving constraint.

papers.title: A duality principle for the neighbourhood of manifolds and applications to counting rational points near curves
papers.abstract: In this paper, we establish a duality principle relating the count of rationals near a manifold to a sparse counting problem for the dual. As applications, we give a short, self-contained proof of sharp bounds for planar curves under minimal regularity conditions and similarly, sharp upper bounds for non- degenerate space curves, again under minimal curvature conditions. This work recovers and extends the works of Beresnevich, Dickinson and Velani and of Vaughan and Velani on planar curves and independently proves and extends the results of Chen, Seeger, Srivastava and Technau on space curves, while providing a structural picture well-suited for generalisations. The re- sults and methods of this work precede the emergence of highly capable AI models.
papers.intro:
In this paper, we establish a duality principle and detail applications of it to the question of how many rational points up to a given height lie in the small neighbourhood of a bounded manifold ℳ\mathcal{M}. In this first section, we will briefly state the problem and trace some of its history before we sketch our duality principle and the results coming out of it. In the next sections of the introduction, we will then give a more thorough overview of the previous papers, state our duality principle and detail its applications to planar and space curves. There, we will also give a short, direct and self-contained proof of sharp bounds for planar curves, which despite its simplicity gives much better bounds under weaker regularity assumptions than all currently known arguments.

papers.title: New lower bounds for binary constant-weight codes from prescribed-automorphism search, and two quantum codes meeting their upper bounds
papers.abstract: We give explicit binary constant-weight codes that raise the lower bounds on $A(n,6,w)$ in eight cells of Brouwer's table, all now listed there. The first round (9 October 2026) gave four values: $A(27,6,11)\ge 19305$, $A(27,6,12)\ge 24453$, $A(28,6,10)\ge 18642$ and $A(28,6,9)\ge 11154$, together with an explicit $A(24,6,12)$ code of 5566 words, now in the table's list of lost codes. The second round (14 October 2026) gave seven values, listed in the table since 15 October 2026: $A(29,6,10)\ge 27183$, $A(29,6,11)\ge 42042$, $A(29,6,9)\ge 14781$, $A(28,6,10)\ge 19110$, $A(27,6,12)\ge 24804$, $A(28,6,9)\ge 11388$ and $A(27,6,13)\ge 27783$, three of which replace first-round values. Every code is a union of orbits of the semilinear affine group $\mathrm{AΓL}(1,27)$, its index-2 subgroup, or $\mathrm{AGL}(1,23)$, acting on all but at most two coordinates. The orbits were chosen by maximum-weight independent set search on the orbit conflict graph: branch and bound in the first round, iterated local search in the second. Each code was checked by two separately written programs over all pairs of words and was regenerated from its generators and orbit representatives. We also report two qubit stabilizer codes, $[[20,11,4]]$ and $[[43,32,4]]$, which raise the lower bounds of 3 listed at codetables.de to the listed upper bound 4.

papers.title: Merge Hulls Without Copying Vertices: GPU Isotonic Regression
papers.abstract: Isotonic regression finds the monotone sequence closest to the data in weighted least squares. It is used to calibrate probabilities and inside differentiable ranking. Its standard algorithm, pool adjacent violators, is sequential within a sequence, and torchsort, the exact GPU solver of differentiable sorting libraries, runs it with one thread per sequence, which is slow on long ones. The fit is the slope sequence of the lower convex hull of cumulative sums, and hulls of sorted points can be merged in parallel. Merging partial hulls level by level, however, copies the surviving vertices at every level, which moves Theta(n log n) data when most points survive. We store each chunk's hull once and represent a merged hull as a list of segments of these chunk hulls, at most one per chunk; a merge then updates the list. We prove the representation correct, bound the work and depth of the merge phase, and measure a CUDA implementation on four NVIDIA GPUs against a control that copies the surviving vertices with the whole GPU at every level. On dense hulls the merge phase is 17 to 276 times faster with segment lists and the whole operator 3.9 to 19 times; on noisy data, where few vertices survive, the difference is small. In a differentiable soft rank, replacing torchsort's isotonic solver makes forward and backward 1.8 to 820 times faster, and the training step of a compact model with a Spearman loss 1.5 to 40 times. Code: https://github.com/LenaBarretta/torchisotonic
papers.intro:
Click models in online advertising are often trained on data in which the non-clicks were downsampled, and their predicted probabilities are then too high (He et al., 2014). Before the predictions are used to price impressions, they are calibrated: a monotone curve, fitted to a day of held-out traffic, maps each score to the click rate observed at that score. Isotonic regression fits this curve (Zadrozny and Elkan, 2002; Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana, 2005). A day of traffic has millions of scores, and calibration per campaign or per country needs hundreds of curves. The same problem, the non-decreasing sequence closest to the data in weighted least squares, appears in differentiable sorting and ranking (Blondel et al., 2020), sparse top-kk operators (Sander et al., 2023) and distributional regression (Henzi et al., 2022), usually as a batch of many rows.

The standard algorithm, pool adjacent violators, scans a sequence once and merges neighbouring blocks while they violate the order. torchsort (Koker, 2021), the exact GPU solver used by differentiable sorting libraries, runs it with one thread per sequence. This is fast for many short rows. For one row of 10710^{7} elements such a solver takes 5.55.5 s on a T4 and 6.46.4 s on an A100, while SciPy takes 0.170.17 s on one CPU core. Iterative methods for accelerators (Sander et al., 2023) are parallel but approximate.

The fit is also the slope sequence of the lower convex hull of the cumulative sum diagram (Barlow et al., 1972). Lower hulls of points sorted by abscissa can be built in parallel: split the points, build the hulls of the parts, and merge neighbouring hulls along the bridge between them (Preparata and Hong, 1977; Overmars and van Leeuwen, 1981), with logarithmic depth on a PRAM (Goodrich, 1987; Berkman et al., 1996). On a GPU the direct version merges partial hulls level by level and copies the surviving vertices at every merge. On noisy data few vertices survive and the copies are cheap.
